w-adys-aw-ii-jagie-o: Little is known of Jogaila's early life, and even his year of birth is uncertain: historians once assumed about 1352, but some recent research suggests about 1362. He was the son of Algirdas, Grand Duke of Lithuania, and Algirdas's second wife, Uliana of Tver, and spent most of his early years in Vilnius. His father designated him heir in place of his older half-brother Fiodor, and he ascended the Lithuanian throne after Algirdas died in 1377. In his early reign his mother acted as regent, and his uncle Kęstutis, Duke of Trakai, continued to rule the north-western region.

Jogaila was raised a Lithuanian polytheist. His mother urged a marriage with Sofia, daughter of Prince Dmitri of Moscow, which would have required conversion to Orthodoxy, but that would not have stopped the crusades of the Teutonic Knights. He chose instead a Polish proposal to become a Catholic and marry the eleven-year-old Queen Jadwiga. On 14 August 1385 at Kreva Castle he confirmed his promises in the Union of Krewo, including the adoption of Christianity. He was baptised in Kraków as Ladislaus in 1386, married Jadwiga on 18 February 1386 and was crowned king, and in 1387 he converted Lithuania to Catholicism.

He ruled as co-monarch with Jadwiga, who attended to cultural and charitable activity, until her death in 1399, after which he was sole ruler. In 1402 he married Anna of Cilli, a granddaughter of Casimir III, a match that restored legitimacy to his reign. The Union of Vilnius and Radom of 1401 made his cousin Vytautas the Grand Duke under his overlordship, forging a permanent defensive alliance between the two states. His brother Švitrigaila stirred up revolts in Lithuania and won the backing of the Teutonic Knights. The allied victory over the Order at Grunwald in 1410, followed by the Peace of Thorn, secured the borders of Poland and Lithuania.

He also granted Vilnius a city charter modelled on Magdeburg Law, and in 1387 and 1413 Catholic boyars of Lithuania received privileges denied to the Orthodox. His policy of unifying the two legal systems was partial at first, but by the Union of Lublin in 1569 there was little difference between them.

Jogaila died on 1 June 1434. He was the last pagan ruler of medieval Lithuania and founded the Jagiellonian dynasty, which ruled both states until 1572. His reign extended Polish frontiers and is often considered the beginning of Poland's Golden Age. His sons Władysław III and Casimir Andrew both ruled Poland. He kept close ties with Ruthenian culture, bringing Ruthenian masters to Poland to paint frescoes, among them the king's bedroom at Wawel Castle in 1393-1394. He appears on the obverse of the 100 złoty banknote.
w-adys-aw-iv-vasa: Władysław was born on 9 June 1595 at the royal summer residence of Łobzów, near Kraków, the eldest son of Sigismund III Vasa and his first wife, Anna of Austria. His father had inherited the Swedish throne in 1592 but was deposed in 1599 by his uncle, later Charles IX, which began a long feud in which the Commonwealth's Vasa kings claimed the Swedish crown.

His mother died in 1598, and he was raised by Urszula Meierin, a former lady of her court. He studied for several years at the Kraków Academy and for two years in Rome, and spoke and wrote German, Italian and Latin.

In the Time of Troubles the Seven Boyars elected the young Władysław tsar after the overthrow of Vasily Shuysky. His father, who aimed to convert Russia to Roman Catholicism, refused the boyars' request to send him to Moscow and have him adopt Orthodoxy, and he never reigned. He mounted his own campaign in 1616, but could not take Moscow, and he kept the title of grand duke of Moscow without power until 1634.

In 1621 he was a commander at Chocim in the war with the Ottomans, where he urged the other commanders to stay and fight. In 1624 and 1625 he travelled in western Europe under the name Snopkowski, met Rubens in Antwerp and was impressed by opera in Florence.

The election sejm of 1632 chose Władysław without serious rivals, and he was crowned in Wawel Cathedral on 6 February 1633. In the Smolensk War of 1632 to 1634 he broke the Russian siege of Smolensk in September 1633 and surrounded the army of Mikhail Shein, which surrendered on 1 March 1634. He modernised the army with Western infantry and artillery and tried to found a navy, which led to the port village of Władysławowo, but the ships were gone by the 1640s.

A Catholic, he was tolerant: the Senate had 6 Protestant members when he took power and 11 when he died. The szlachta thwarted his efforts to strengthen the monarchy, and he died on 20 May 1648 without a legitimate son. His half-brother John II Casimir Vasa succeeded him, and his reign was later remembered as a golden era of stability before the Khmelnytsky Uprising and the Deluge.
w-arthur-lewis: William Arthur Lewis was born in Castries, Saint Lucia, then part of the British Windward Islands federal colony, the fourth of five sons of George Ferdinand and Ida Lewis, who had migrated from Antigua. His father died when Arthur was seven, and Ida raised the children alone. A gifted student, he finished school at 14 and worked as a clerk until he could sit the examination for a government scholarship.

He had hoped to be an engineer, but, as he later said, neither the government nor the white firms would employ a black engineer, so he turned to business administration. At 18 he won the scholarship to the London School of Economics, where he studied under John Hicks, Arnold Plant, Lionel Robbins and Friedrich Hayek.

Lewis graduated in 1937 with first-class honours and took a PhD in industrial economics under Arnold Plant. He became the first black faculty member at the school and worked there until 1948. In 1947 he became a lecturer at the Victoria University of Manchester, and in 1948 a full professor, teaching there until 1957. He advised the governments of Nigeria, Ghana, Trinidad and Tobago, Jamaica and Barbados. When Ghana became independent in 1957 he was appointed its first economic advisor and helped draw up its first Five-Year Development Plan, for 1959 to 1963.

In 1959 he became Vice Chancellor of the University of the West Indies. He was knighted in 1963 and that year joined Princeton University, where he held a full professorship and later the James Madison chair until he retired in 1983. He also served as Chancellor of the University of Guyana from 1966 to 1973 and was the first president of the Caribbean Development Bank, from 1970 to 1973. In 1979 he shared the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences with Theodore Schultz for pioneering research on economic development.

Lewis's Labour in the West Indies (1939) was an account of the Caribbean labour movement of the 1930s. His article of 1954, Economic Development with Unlimited Supplies of Labour, introduced the dual sector model. A capitalist sector grows by drawing labour from a subsistence sector, where workers can be paid above their marginal product.

Because labour is in unlimited supply, the capitalist sector can expand without raising wages, profits are reinvested, and the process becomes self-sustaining. The point at which the surplus labour is absorbed is called the Lewisian turning point. He also wrote The Theory of Economic Growth (1955) and Politics in West Africa (1965), which argues for power-sharing through proportional representation, federalism and coalition governments. He died in Bridgetown, Barbados, in 1991.
w-b-yeats: William Butler Yeats was born in Sandymount, County Dublin, on 13 June 1865, a Protestant of Anglo-Irish descent. His father, John, studied law and became a portrait painter. His mother, Susan Mary Pollexfen, came from a wealthy merchant family in Sligo, and the family soon moved to Merville in Sligo, which he came to think of as his spiritual home. He was educated in Dublin and London, and began writing at seventeen, drawing heavily on Shelley, Spenser and pre-Raphaelite verse before turning to Irish mythology, folklore and Blake.

His first collection, The Wanderings of Oisin and Other Poems, appeared in 1889. He had a lifelong interest in mysticism, spiritualism and the occult. In 1889 he met Maud Gonne, an ardent Irish nationalist, and his unrequited love for her had a lasting effect on his poetry. She refused his proposals in 1891, 1899, 1900 and 1901 and in 1903 married Major John MacBride. In 1899 Yeats, Lady Gregory, Edward Martyn and George Moore founded the Irish Literary Theatre, and with Lady Gregory and John Millington Synge he founded the Abbey Theatre, serving as its chief in its early years. His plays include Cathleen ni Houlihan (1902).

From 1900 his poetry became more rooted in the physical world, realistic and political. Collections of this phase include The Wild Swans at Coole (1919) and The Tower (1928). In 1922 he was appointed to the first Senate of the Irish Free State, and he served a second term from 1925. In December 1923 he received the Nobel Prize in Literature for poetry that gives expression to the spirit of a whole nation, and the money allowed him to repay his own debts and his father's. In the 1930s he composed marching songs for the Blueshirts, never used, and later distanced himself from the movement.

Yeats died of heart failure at Roquebrune-Cap-Martin, France, on 28 January 1939, aged 73. He had wished to be buried quickly in France and moved to Sligo a year later. In September 1948 his body was taken to the churchyard of St Columba's Church at Drumcliff, County Sligo, aboard the Irish Naval Service corvette LÉ Macha. His epitaph comes from the last lines of Under Ben Bulben.
w-e-b-du-bois: Du Bois was born on 23 February 1868 in Great Barrington, Massachusetts, to Alfred and Mary Silvina Burghardt Du Bois. His mother's family belonged to the very small free black population of the town and had long owned land there. With money donated by neighbours Du Bois attended Fisk University in Nashville from 1885 to 1888. His residence in the South gave him his first experience of Jim Crow laws, the suppression of black voting and lynching. He then completed graduate work at Harvard.

In 1896 he took a one-year research post at the University of Pennsylvania, and his fieldwork in Philadelphia's African-American neighbourhoods led to The Philadelphia Negro (1899), the first case study of a black community in the United States. In July 1897 he became professor of history and economics at Atlanta University. At the First Pan-African Conference in London in July 1900 he delivered a speech, To the Nations of the World, asking European leaders to allow their colonies self-government and to recognise the rights of African Americans.

His collection of 14 essays, The Souls of Black Folk (1903), made him a spokesman of his race, second only to Booker T. Washington. He opposed Washington's Atlanta Compromise, which asked Southern blacks to accept segregation and disenfranchisement, and held that African Americans should fight for equal rights, to be won by an educated elite he called the talented tenth. In 1905 he and others met near Niagara Falls and wrote the principles of what became the Niagara Movement.

Du Bois attended a conference in New York in 1909 and a second in 1910, which created the NAACP; at his suggestion the word colored was used, to include dark-skinned people everywhere. In 1910 he became its Director of Publicity and Research, left Atlanta University and moved to New York to edit The Crisis, whose circulation reached 100,000 in 1920. After the First World War he attended the Pan-African Congresses, embraced socialism and held capitalism a primary cause of racism.

After the Second World War he took part in peace activism and was targeted by the Federal Bureau of Investigation. He spent the last years of his life in Ghana and died in Accra on 27 August 1963. His Black Reconstruction in America (1935) challenged the prevailing view that Black Americans were responsible for the failures of Reconstruction, and his autobiography Dusk of Dawn (1940) is regarded in part as one of the first scientific treatises in American sociology.
wabash-river: The Wabash drains most of Indiana and a significant part of Illinois. It rises about four miles south of Fort Recovery, Ohio, from farmland drainage, flows north and then sharply west into Indiana, crosses northern Indiana to the south-west and turns south near the Illinois border, where its southern part forms the boundary between the two states. It is the largest northern tributary of the Ohio River and the third largest overall, after the Cumberland and Tennessee. Its major tributaries are the Tippecanoe, White, Embarras and Little Wabash rivers. The name is the English form of the French Ouabache, which adopted the Miami-Illinois word waapaahšiiki, meaning water over white stones, since the river bottom in Huntington County is white limestone.

As the Laurentide Ice Sheet retreated 14,000 to 15,000 years ago, meltwater formed proglacial Lake Maumee. Around 11,000 years ago it broke through the Fort Wayne Moraine and drained catastrophically, scouring a valley one to two miles wide, the Wabash-Erie Channel. For part of its course the Wabash follows the path of the pre-glacial Teays River.

French explorers first mapped the river to the Mississippi in the latter half of the 17th century. Until the mid-18th century the Ohio was considered a tributary of the Wabash, and French traders used it as a vital route between Canada and the Gulf of Mexico. In the 18th century the Miami people controlled at Kekionga the profitable 8-mile portage between the Maumee and the Wabash.

The United States fought five colonial and frontier-era battles on or near the river: Vincennes in 1779, St. Clair's Defeat in 1791, the Attack on Fort Recovery in 1794, Tippecanoe in 1811 and the Siege of Fort Harrison in 1812. In the mid-19th century the Wabash and Erie Canal, one of the longest in the world, was built along much of the river, but railroads surpassed it and most of the canal no longer exists. The river below Terre Haute was navigable by large ships during much of the 19th century, with steamships calling regularly. By the late 19th century erosion from farming and runoff had made it impassable to them, and dredging was not undertaken because railroads were preferred.

The river is about 503 miles long, or 810 kilometres, and flows freely for 411 miles from the dam near Huntington, Indiana, to the Ohio. It is the state river of Indiana and the subject of the state song, On the Banks of the Wabash, Far Away, by Paul Dresser. Counties, townships, colleges and a canal bear its name, as did four US Navy warships. A 329-acre remnant of the old-growth forests that bordered it survives at Beall Woods State Park, near Mount Carmel, Illinois.
wadenswil: Wädenswil lies on the Zürichsee lakeshore in the district of Horgen in the canton of Zürich, Switzerland, and is locally often called Wättischwiil, Wädischwiil or Wädi. On 1 January 2019 the former municipalities of Hütten and Schönenberg were merged into it. Before that merger it covered 17.4 square kilometres, of which 59.3 per cent was used for agriculture, 9.6 per cent was forest and 29.8 per cent was settled. Most of its people speak German, with Italian and Serbo-Croatian the next most common languages in the census of 2000.

Since the early 1500s Wädenswil and nearby Richterswil have been home to groups of Anabaptists, many of whom emigrated to Pennsylvania in the 1700s. Many of the surnames common in the area are still found plentifully in the southeastern part of that state.

The Wädenswil brewery was a brewery from 1833 until 1990. Its building was partly demolished in 2003, but brewing in the town has continued since 1992 with the Wadi-Brau-Huus AG. The Schloss Au on the Au Peninsula, with its auxiliary buildings and park, is listed in the Swiss inventory of cultural property as an object of regional importance.

Wädenswil–Vorder Au is one of the 56 Swiss sites that make up the UNESCO World Heritage Site Prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps, and the settlement is listed in the Swiss inventory of cultural property as a Class A object of national significance. The town lies on the A3 motorway and on the lakeside railway line to Zürich, and ships serve it across the lake. It is the seat of the ZHAW Wädenswil, a centre for life sciences and facility management.

Natives of the town include the landscape artist Johann Gottfried Steffan, the politician Walter Hauser, a member of the Swiss Federal Council from 1888 to 1902, the architect Hans Auer, who designed the Federal Palace of Switzerland, the politician Robert Haab, a member of the Federal Council from 1917 to 1929, and the prehistorian Otto Hauser.
wadjet: Wadjet, whose name means Green One, was originally the local goddess of the city of Dep or Buto in Lower Egypt, an important site in prehistoric Egypt. Her worship began in the Predynastic period and developed from that of a local goddess to a patron goddess. From about the 4th dynasty she was claimed as the patron and protector of the whole of Lower Egypt. A temple in Per-Wadjet gave the city its name, and its oracle may have been the source of the oracular tradition that spread to Greece. She also had a large temple at Imet, now Tell Nebesha, where she was worshipped as Lady of Imet.

Wadjet was usually shown as an Egyptian cobra, later also as a woman with a snake's head or a woman wearing the uraeus. The image of Wadjet with the sun disk is called the uraeus, the emblem on the crown of the rulers. She was also shown as a winged cobra, as a vulture like her sister Nekhbet, or as a lion-headed goddess, though some historians doubt that the seated lion-headed bronzes depict her rather than Sekhmet. One of her earliest depictions, from before 3100 BCE, is a cobra entwined around a papyrus stem.
She was closely associated with the Eye of Ra and the Eye of Horus, and the green and blue Wadjet eye amulets of daily life were a token of fertility and protection.

Wadjet was the protector of kings and of women in childbirth. After unification she and her sister Nekhbet, goddess of Upper Egypt, jointly protected all Egypt; the two were called the Two Ladies, and scenes of the sisters as two cobras appear in the tomb of Sety I. In myth she was Ra's daughter and his seeing eye, and she was also the nurse of the infant Horus, who was hidden with his mother Isis in the swamps of the Nile Delta from his uncle Set.

Wadjet and Nekhbet appear in the Pyramid Texts as nurses who sustain the king's divinity, and a pendant from the tomb of Tutankhamun shows Wadjet suckling the adult king. She also appears in the tomb of Nefertari, wearing the double crown.
waffen-ss: The Waffen-SS, meaning Armed SS, was the combat branch of the Nazi Party's paramilitary Schutzstaffel. Its origins lie in the selection on 17 March 1933 of 120 SS men by Sepp Dietrich to form the Sonderkommando Berlin. By November 1933 it had 800 men and swore allegiance to Adolf Hitler alone, and it became the Leibstandarte SS Adolf Hitler on 13 April 1934. At the outbreak of the war Heinrich Himmler's military formations included this regiment, the Verfügungstruppe under Paul Hausser, and the Death's Head units of Theodor Eicke, made up of concentration camp guards.

In August 1939 Hitler placed the Leibstandarte and the Verfügungstruppe under the operational control of the Army High Command, while Himmler kept the Death's Head regiments for what were called special tasks of a police nature behind the advancing armies. By spring 1941 the force equalled six or seven divisions. In keeping with Nazi racial policy, membership was at first open only to people of Germanic origin, but after the invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941 propaganda called the war a European crusade against Bolshevism, and units of foreign volunteers and conscripts were raised. Ethnic Poles, regarded as subhumans, were barred.

From 1942 growing numbers of foreigners, many not volunteers, entered the ranks. The 7th SS Division Prinz Eugen was drafted from ethnic Germans under threat of punishment and used in anti-partisan operations in the Balkans. In 1943 came the 13th Waffen Mountain Division Handschar, a Bosnian Muslim unit and the first non-Germanic division, and the 14th Galician division. The 15th Latvian, 19th Latvian and 20th Estonian divisions followed, the last formed by general conscription in February 1944. Late-formed divisions were often small battle groups in name only. The Waffen-SS was disbanded in May 1945.

The Waffen-SS took part in numerous atrocities. As an integral part of the SS it was declared a criminal organisation by the International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg in 1946, because of its involvement in the Holocaust, the Porajmos and war crimes, including executions of prisoners of war and mass killings of civilians, often during anti-partisan operations. Members, except conscripts, who made up about a third of the membership, were denied many of the rights given to military veterans.
wahhabism: Wahhabism takes its name from the Hanbali scholar Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab (1703 to 1792), who was inspired by the earlier Hanbali scholars Ibn Taymiyya and Ibn al-Qayyim. The name is primarily an exonym. It was probably first used by his brother Sulayman ibn Abd al-Wahhab, a staunch opponent of his views until 1776, and the movement's political opponents widely used it. Ibn Abd al-Wahhab and his early followers called themselves Muwahhidun, the monotheists, from tawhid, the oneness of God. Present-day followers reject the term and often call themselves Salafi.

The movement began as a revivalist effort in central Arabia in the early eighteenth century. Ibn Abd al-Wahhab called on his disciples to denounce practices associated with Sufi orders as idolatrous impurities and innovations, and to turn to the Quran and hadith. Historians have called the movement puritanical, while its adherents describe it as a reform movement to restore pure monotheistic worship. It also represented the first major Arab-led revolt against the foreign empires that had dominated the Islamic world since the Mongol invasions and the fall of the Abbasid Caliphate.

In theology Wahhabism is closely aligned with the Athari school, which relies on the literal meaning of the Quran and hadith and opposes the rational argument favoured by Ash'arite and Maturidite theologies. Its central emphasis is tawhid al-ibada, the doctrine that worship belongs to God alone. The intercession of prophets and saints, widespread among other Muslims, is therefore considered a violation of tawhid. The dispute with other Muslims is not over tawhid itself but over what counts as tawhid.

In law, Ibn Abd al-Wahhab emphasised the Quran and the Sunna, accepted consensus only where it confirmed them, and rejected deference to past juristic opinion, taqlid, in favour of independent reasoning, ijtihad. This set the movement against the Ottoman Sufi ulema, who upheld taqlid. He defined armed jihad as an endeavour that needs a religious justification and can be declared only by an imam, and the soldiers of the Emirate of Diriyah were forbidden to attack women, children and non-combatants.

Ibn Abd al-Wahhab's teachings were the official creed of the three Saudi states for more than two centuries. Wahhabism was also one of several Islamic revivalist currents of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, which included Uthman dan Fodio's movement in Nigeria, the Padri movement in Indonesia and the Mahdist movement in Sudan. From the nineteenth century Arab Salafiyya reformers corresponded with Wahhabis and defended them against Sufi attacks.

Scholars distinguish Wahhabism from Salafism in different ways. Some call Wahhabism a conservative creed centred on Saudi Arabia and Salafism a broader movement that arose independently in many places, while others see Wahhabism as the Salafism native to Arabia. Critics, including other Sunnis, have compared its doctrines to those of the Kharijites.
waikato: The Waikato stretches from the Coromandel Peninsula in the north to the north-eastern slopes of Mount Ruapehu in the south and from the west coast to the east coast of the North Island. Broadly it follows the catchment of the Waikato River, whose name the region takes; waikato is a Māori word traditionally translated as flowing water.

The west coast is rough hill country with three large natural harbours, Raglan, Aotea and Kāwhia. Inland lies the broad alluvial plain of the river, now largely pastoral land created by European settlers who drained the natural swamps, and to the east rise the forested Kaimai and Mamaku Ranges. The river flows out of Lake Taupō and is used for hydroelectricity.

Before Europeans arrived, the Waikato held the third most densely populated part of New Zealand, after Northland and Auckland and the Bay of Plenty. It was inhabited by iwi of the Tainui confederation, and between about 1750 and 1842 it was subject to many invasions and migrations by other Māori groups. In 1840 forty-four Waikato chiefs travelled to the Manukau Harbour to sign the Treaty of Waitangi. From 1840 to 1860 Anglican missionaries helped Waikato Māori build a trade in crops such as peaches, maize and wheat, with eight flour mills supplying the Auckland market until the boom ended in 1856 to 1857.

In the late 1850s Māori grew dissatisfied with the price the government paid for land: an average of 6d an acre, sold to settlers for 10 shillings. Some Waikato hapū formed a separate kingdom, the King Movement or Kīngitanga, and Waikato Māori had helped Taranaki Māori in the First Taranaki War. In 1863 and 1864 the colonial government, with troops from Britain and Māori loyal to the Crown, invaded the Waikato. Fighting at Rangiriri, Ngāruawāhia, Rangiaowhia and Ōrākau among other places ended in defeat for the Kīngitanga, whose forces withdrew south of the Puniu River to the area still known as the King Country.

The Waikato is governed by the Waikato Regional Council, established in 1989, and covers about 23,900 square kilometres. Its largest city is Hamilton, home to the University of Waikato, and its population was 498,771 at the 2023 census. The economy rests largely on dairy farming, which has been the main agricultural activity since the late 19th century. The headquarters of the Māori King Movement are at Tūrangawaewae Marae at Ngāruawāhia.
waikiki: The Hawaiian name Waikīkī means spouting fresh water, likely a reference to the springs and streams that fed the wetlands which once separated it from the interior of the island. The neighbourhood now extends from the Ala Wai Canal, a channel dug to drain those wetlands, on the west and north, to Diamond Head (Lēʻahi, tuna brow) on the east. The beach is noted for its views of the Diamond Head tuff cone, its usually warm and cloud-free climate and its surf break. Before 1950 it was continuous and known simply as Waikīkī Beach; seawalls and other developments have since divided the coast into eight beaches.

After the founding of the Kingdom of Hawaii, Waikīkī was its first capital, from 1795 to 1796. In the 1800s it was a retreat for Hawaiian royalty, who surfed there on early forms of longboards. A few small hotels opened in the 1880s. In 1893 the Greek-American George Lycurgus leased a guest house and renamed it Sans Souci, creating one of the first beach resorts; Robert Louis Stevenson stayed there that year, and the place became popular with tourists from the mainland.

In the early 1900s developers dug the Ala Wai Canal, then called the Waikīkī Drainage Canal, to get rid of the wetlands, which were claimed to harbour disease-carrying mosquitoes. A Hawaiian dredging company run by Walter F. Dillingham carried out the project between 1921 and 1928. The surfer Duke Kahanamoku, who competed in the Olympics, made the beach a surfing centre. The first high-rise hotels were built in 1955, including the Waikiki Biltmore and the Sheraton Princess Kaiulani Hotel, and large resort hotels filled the area, alongside early 20th-century hotels such as the Moana Surfrider and the Royal Hawaiian.

The beach is almost entirely man-made. Hotels and homes built too close to the natural shoreline, and seawalls and groins that blocked the movement of sand, caused erosion from the late 1800s; by 1950 more than 80 structures occupied the shoreline. Sand was imported from California in the 1920s and 1930s and again until the 1970s, and restoration projects have been carried out since, including a partial one completed in 2012.

Waikīkī includes Kapiʻolani Park, Fort DeRussy and Kūhiō Beach Park. Its main thoroughfare is Kalākaua Avenue, named after King Kalākaua, and Kūhiō Avenue is named after Prince Kūhiō. A bronze statue of Duke Kahanamoku, installed in 1990, stands at the beach.
wailuku: Wailuku lies at the mouth of the ʻĪao Valley, 249 feet (76 m) above sea level at the base of West Maui Volcano, on the northern edge of the isthmus between East Maui (Haleakalā) and West Maui. It is just west of Kahului. The name means destroying water. Wailuku is also known as Pūʻalikomohana or Nā Wai ʻEhā, the four waters, which are the land divisions of Waikapū, Wailuku, Waiʻehu and Waiheʻe. It is one of the three moku, or districts, of west Maui, with Lāhaina and Kāʻanapali.

The area was a centre of power and population in prehistoric Hawaii and the home of some of Maui's rulers. Tradition names Wakalana as a leading Wailuku chief, and holds that Kapawa, king of Hawaiʻi before Pili, was buried here. In the late 15th century Maui's ruler Kakaʻe designated the ʻĪao Valley as a burial ground for aliʻi, whose remains were buried in secret places. In 1790 Kamehameha the Great defeated Kalanikūpule and the Maui army there at the Battle of Kepaniwai, during his campaign to unify the islands. The fighting was said to be so bloody that bodies blocked ʻĪao Stream, giving the site its name, the damming of the waters.

New England missionaries arrived in the mid-1800s and brought their religion, skills, implements and agricultural methods. By the 1860s the Wailuku Sugar Company, owned by C. Brewer & Co., and other plantations were growing and milling sugarcane, with irrigation ditches carrying water from the mountains. The industry flourished to the detriment of the native people. Thousands of workers came from China, Japan, Okinawa, Korea, the Philippines, Europe and America, and many settled in Wailuku. In 1905 it became the county seat of Maui, a centre of government and business, and growth continued until the late 1960s, when the sugar industry reduced its operations.

Historic sites include Kaʻahumanu Church, dating to 1876 and named after Queen Kaʻahumanu, wife of Kamehameha I, the Wailuku Civic Center Historic District, and the Bailey House, a 19th-century former seminary and home that now holds a history museum and the Maui Historical Society. Two ancient temples near the town, the Halekiʻi Heiau and the Pihanakalani Heiau, date back hundreds of years and were used for religious purposes by native Hawaiians. In the 1990s the former C. Brewer land was developed as the Kehalani neighbourhood. The population was 17,697 at the 2020 census.
wakayama-prefecture: Wakayama Prefecture lies in the Kansai region of Honshu and has an area of 4,724 square kilometres. It borders Osaka Prefecture to the north and Mie Prefecture and Nara Prefecture to the north-east. It occupies the south-western coast of the Kii Peninsula on the Kii Channel, which connects the Pacific Ocean with the Seto Inland Sea, across from Tokushima Prefecture on Shikoku. Present-day Wakayama is mostly the western part of the old province of Kii. The city of Wakayama is its capital and largest city, with Tanabe, Hashimoto and Kinokawa among the other major cities.

On 17 and 18 July 1953 torrential rain was followed by the collapse of levees, river flooding and landslides over a wide area of the prefecture. Many bridges and houses were destroyed. The Government of Japan officially confirmed that 1,015 people died, 5,709 were injured and 7,115 houses were lost.

Mount Kōya, in the Ito District, is the headquarters of the Shingon sect of Japanese Buddhism. It has one of the first Japanese style Buddhist temples in Japan and remains a pilgrimage site, its ancient temples standing among tall cedars. The Sacred sites and pilgrimage routes in the Kii Mountain Range, which extend for miles through the prefecture, are recognised as Japan's 11th UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Kumano Shrines stand on its southern tip.

The prefecture has been growing oranges for centuries: in the Arida District they have been produced for more than 400 years. It is also known for ume, the Chinese flowering plum, and has hot springs such as Nanki-Shirahama Onsen, Kawayu Onsen and Yunomine Onsen.
walata: Oualata, also written Walata, is a small oasis town at the eastern end of the Aoukar basin in south-eastern Mauritania. The chronicles of the 17th century call it Biru. The whole commune covers 93,092 square kilometres, mostly desert, and the main town lies in its south. The area is believed to have been settled first by an agro-pastoral people akin to the Mandé Soninke, who lived along the rocky promontories of the Tichitt-Oualata and Tagant cliffs facing the basin and built some of the oldest stone settlements on the African continent.

The town formed part of the Ghana Empire and grew wealthy through trade. At the beginning of the thirteenth century it replaced Aoudaghost as the principal southern terminus of the trans-Saharan trade and became an important commercial and religious centre; by the fourteenth century it belonged to the Mali Empire. A route from Sijilmasa through the salt mines of Taghaza ended there. Raymond Mauny estimated that in the Middle Ages the town held between 2,000 and 3,000 people.

Ibn Battuta found its people Muslim and mainly Massufa, a section of the Sanhaja, and was surprised by the respect and independence that women enjoyed. He stayed about fifty days and noted the heat, a few small date palms shading watermelons, underground water and plenty of mutton.

From the second half of the 14th century Timbuktu gradually replaced Oualata as the terminus of the route, and the town declined. In 1433 the Mali Empire lost control of it, and in 1480 it was besieged for a month and sacked by the Mossi; the inhabitants regrouped, pursued the invaders and rescued many of the captives.

Leo Africanus, visiting in 1509-1510, described a small kingdom of three large villages and some huts among the palm groves, with a large Songhai-speaking population, and tributary to the king of Timbuktu. In the early 17th century Hassaniya Arabs arrived, and their influence produced the present name. For a century and a half the Lemhajib, three Soninke families, dominated local politics before being absorbed into the Berber and Arab milieu.

The old town covers about 600 by 300 metres, some of it in ruins. Its sandstone buildings are coated with banco, and some are decorated with geometric designs; the town is known for its highly decorative vernacular architecture. The mosque now lies on the eastern edge, and a museum holds manuscripts. Oualata was made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996, together with Ouadane, Chinguetti and Tichitt.
walcheren: Walcheren is a region and former island in Zeeland at the mouth of the Scheldt estuary, between the Eastern Scheldt in the north and the Western Scheldt in the south, roughly rhombus-shaped. Its two sides facing the North Sea are dunes and the rest of its coast is dykes. Middelburg, the provincial capital, lies at its centre, Vlissingen is the main harbour 9 kilometres to the south, and Veere is the third municipality in the north.

The island was joined to its neighbours by later works: the Sloedam, built in 1871 for a railway, and polders made after the Second World War connected it to Zuid-Beveland, and the Veerse Gatdam, completed in 1961, linked it to Noord-Beveland. The name is first attested in Latin spellings such as villam Walichrum about 790, and probably combines a word for moist with one for a sandy ridge.

In Roman times the island was a point of departure for ships going to Britain and had a temple of the goddess Nehalennia, popular with those crossing the North Sea. In the ninth century it was the seat of the Danish Viking Harald, who conquered part of what became the Netherlands with his brother Rorik. In 1588 Dutch rebels and English fighters held Walcheren, which blocked access to Antwerp and denied the Spanish Armada a deep-water port for supplies and shelter. Under the Secret Treaty of Dover of 1670 England was to receive Walcheren, but the plan failed when Dutch resistance repulsed the French and English attack.

On 30 July 1809 a British expeditionary force landed to attack the French fleet at Flushing and to assist the Austrians against Napoleon. British troops captured Flushing, but the Austrians had been defeated at Wagram in early July and the French fleet had moved to Antwerp. The force lost over 4,000 men to Walcheren Fever, thought to be a combination of malaria and typhus, against 106 killed by enemy action, and withdrew in December.

Walcheren was fought over in 1940 and again in 1944, in the final stage of the Battle of the Scheldt, because it commanded the route to Antwerp. On 3 October 1944 the RAF bombed the sea wall at Westkapelle, flooding the island. Canadian troops fought along the narrow Walcheren Causeway from 31 October, and British Commandos landed at Westkapelle on 1 November in Operation Infatuate to silence the German coastal batteries. All German resistance on the island had ceased by 8 November 1944.
wales: Wales is a generally mountainous country on the western side of central southern Great Britain, about 270 kilometres from north to south. It is bordered by England to the east and by sea in all other directions, with about 2,700 kilometres of coastline. The highest mountains are in Snowdonia, where Snowdon (Yr Wyddfa) rises to 1,085 metres. The English words Wales and Welsh derive from an Old English word, Wealh, which the Anglo-Saxons used for the Britons; the Welsh name for themselves, Cymry, descends from a Brythonic word meaning 'fellow-countrymen'.

The territory was permanently settled from the end of the last ice age. In the Bronze Age the Great Orme in North Wales became Britain's premier producer of copper. After the Roman withdrawal, Britain fractured into kingdoms, and Anglo-Saxon settlers gradually displaced the culture and language of the Britons, leaving one group isolated in the western peninsula, whom their English neighbours called Welsh. Medieval Wales stayed divided into kingdoms that fought each other as much as the English.

In the 10th century Hywel ap Cadell, later Hywel Dda, gained control of Gwynedd and Powys in 942 and so of nearly all of Wales, and codified Welsh law. Wales was briefly united under Gruffudd ap Llywelyn in 1055. Owain Glyndŵr led the Welsh Revolt in the early 15th century and briefly re-established an independent state with its own parliament. In the 19th century mining and metallurgy transformed Wales into an industrial society, and the population rose from 587,000 in 1801 to 2,421,000 by 1911.

Both Welsh and English are official languages, and Welsh is dominant in parts of the north and west. Wales has four UNESCO World Heritage Sites: the Castles and Town Walls of King Edward I in Gwynedd, the Pontcysyllte Aqueduct and Canal, the Blaenavon Industrial Landscape and the Slate Landscape of Northwest Wales. Medieval Welsh manuscripts such as the Red Book of Hergest preserve the Mabinogion and the earliest forms of the Arthurian legend.
wallia: Wallia was elected king of the Visigoths in 415, after the assassinations of Athaulf and Sigeric. Athaulf, who had married Galla Placidia in 414, was murdered by followers who believed him a puppet of Roman interests. Sigeric ignored Visigothic rights of procedure for military leadership and seemed likewise to acquiesce to the Romans, and he died seven days after taking power. Wallia was chosen because the Visigoths were convinced he would end any peace negotiations with Rome. At the time the main antagonist of the Goths was Constantius, the magister militum of Emperor Honorius.

Like his predecessor Alaric, Wallia tried to take his forces to northern Africa but foundered in the Sea of Gibraltar, a failure that led him to sue for peace. He accepted a treaty offered by Honorius. The writer Orosius reported that the terms agreed in 416 and 418 were very favourable to the Romans and included the return of Honorius's sister Galla Placidia. The historian Michael Kulikowski described her recovery by Constantius as a route into the imperial family.

As Roman federates, Wallia's Goths marched against the Alans and Vandals in Baetica and Lusitania, at the behest of Constantius. Between 417 and 418 they inflicted considerable defeats on both and killed the Alan ruler Addax. Hydatius recorded that Wallia, in the name of Rome, inflicted a vast slaughter on the barbarians in Spain. Constantius then recalled the Goths, perhaps, as the historian Randers-Pehrson suggests, out of fear at their success, and settled them in southern Gaul, in the Garonne valley from Toulouse to Bordeaux and along the Atlantic coast from Les Landes to the Loire.

Wallia died before he was able to leave Spain, and Theodoric I succeeded him. His daughter was the mother of Ricimer and the mother-in-law of Gundowech, King of the Burgundians. He is sometimes assumed to have been the historical model for Walter of Aquitaine, a figure of legend.
wallis-island: Wallis, called ʻUvea in Wallisian, is a Polynesian island and atoll in the Pacific Ocean belonging to the French overseas collectivity of Wallis and Futuna. It lies north of Tonga, northeast of Fiji and west of Samoa, and is of volcanic origin, with fertile soil that allows subsistence farming. Its highest point is Mount Lulu Fakahega, 131 metres. Several crater lakes, among them Lalolalo, are almost perfect circles with straight vertical walls.

Together with some fifteen smaller islands on a large barrier reef, Wallis forms the Wallis archipelago, 240 kilometres northeast of Futuna and Alofi. The climate is hot and humid, with an average temperature around 26 °C and a rainy season from November to April, which is also the season of tropical cyclones. The island is divided into three districts: Hihifo in the north, Hahake and Muʻa in the south.

Archaeological excavations have identified sites on Wallis dating from about 1400. The island was part of the Tongan maritime empire, but the influence of the Tuʻi Tonga declined until ʻUvea became important in itself. Several high-ranking Tongan titles, such as Halaevalu, trace their descent from ʻUvea, and the large canoe Lomipeau, according to legend, was built there as a gift to the Tuʻi Tonga. The fortress of Talietumu, near Lotoalahi in Muʻa, was the last holdout of the Tongans until they were defeated.

The island was named after Captain Samuel Wallis, who saw it on 16 August 1767 from HMS Dolphin, after he had found Tahiti. In 1835 armed missionaries from Tonga attacked, trying to convert the island to Protestantism by force. In October 1837 Jean-Baptiste Pompallier visited and left a priest and a brother, and four years later Wallis was reported to be a Catholic community. On 5 April 1842 its authorities requested French protection, and a protectorate treaty was signed in April 1887.

In 1942 the island's administration, pro-Vichy until then, was deposed on 26 May by a Free French corvette from New Caledonia, and US Marine Corps units landed on 29 May. After a referendum in 1959, Wallis became a French overseas territory in 1961. The population was 8,333 in 2018, about 72 per cent of the territory, and most people speak ʻUvean as their mother tongue. Almost all are Roman Catholic, and the chief church is the Cathedral of Mata Utu, the capital.
wallonia: Wallonia is one of the three regions of Belgium, with Flanders and Brussels. It is landlocked, covers 16,901 square kilometres, 55 per cent of the country's area, and holds about 31 per cent of its people. Most of its major cities and two thirds of its population lie in the east to west valley of the Sambre and Meuse, the former industrial backbone of Belgium. To the north of the valley lies the fertile Central Belgian Plateau, and the south and south-east form the forested highlands of the Ardennes. Its largest city is Charleroi and its capital is Namur.

Julius Caesar conquered Gaul in 57 BCE, and the Low Countries became part of the province of Gallia Belgica. Its people were Celtic with a Germanic influence that was stronger in the north. They became Gallo-Romans, whom their Germanic neighbours called Walha, and they gave up their Celtic dialects for Vulgar Latin. The Sambre and Meuse valley was already an important industrial area in the Roman Empire.

In the Middle Ages the region was a centre of brass and bronze working, with Huy, Dinant and Chimay as important towns, and Mosan art, a regional Romanesque style, flourished in the Meuse valley in the 11th to 13th centuries. In the 12th and 13th centuries the iron masters of Liège developed a way of refining iron ore with a blast furnace, called the Walloon Method.

Wallonia was the first fully industrialised area in continental Europe, in the 19th century, and was second only to the United Kingdom in industrialisation. The coal and iron valley from Liège to Charleroi became known as the sillon industriel. Strikes and general strikes took place there, among them the Walloon jacquerie of 1886 and the general strikes of 1893, 1902 and 1913, the last for universal suffrage. After the Second World War a general strike of 1950 was directed against Leopold III and the winter general strike of 1960 to 1961 demanded autonomy for Wallonia.

Belgium is a federal state, and the Walloon Region is governed by the Parliament of Wallonia and the Government of Wallonia. The first regional council sat on 15 October 1980, and a directly elected parliament was created in June 1995. French is the official language, and German also in the eastern cantons annexed from the German Empire at the end of the First World War. Traditional regional Romance languages such as Walloon and Picard are in decline. In 1995 Walloon Brabant became the youngest of its five provinces.
walloon-brabant: Walloon Brabant lies in Belgium's French-speaking region of Wallonia and borders Flemish Brabant to the north and the provinces of Liège, Namur and Hainaut. It covers 1,097 square kilometres and has about 414,000 inhabitants. Its capital is Wavre, although the municipality of Braine-l'Alleud is slightly more populous. Its only administrative district, the arrondissement of Nivelles, has 27 municipalities. The word Walloon descends from an old West Germanic word meaning foreigner or speaker of Celtic or Latin, and Brabant comes from Old Dutch words meaning fallow district.

The names Walloon and Brabant are much older than the political entity. In 1628 Louis de Haynin described Belgium as divided into two roughly equal regions, Walloon and Flemish, according to whether people spoke French or a Low German that foreigners called Flemish. He contrasted Lothier, or Walloon Brabant, with the larger German or Flemish part of Brabant, which then stretched into what is now the Netherlands.

The Battle of Waterloo took place in this province in June 1815. The province itself was created in 1995 when the former province of Brabant was split into three parts: Walloon Brabant, Flemish Brabant and the Brussels Capital Region, which belongs to no province. The split accommodated the federalisation of Belgium into the three regions of Flanders, Wallonia and Brussels.

Nivelles is the most important town and has the Collegiate Church of Saint Gertrude with its westwork. The towns include Waterloo, Wavre and Ottignies-Louvain-la-Neuve, where the University of Louvain (UCLouvain) is located, alongside a science park of 231 hectares with life sciences, fine chemistry, information technology and engineering. Industrial steel production at Clabecq continues, and the Ronquières inclined plane on the Brussels-Charleroi Canal links canal traffic between Charleroi and Brussels. Many residents work in neighbouring Brussels. The Piétrain breed of pig takes its name from a village in Jodoigne. The castle of Corroy-le-Château is among the best-preserved castles of its period in northern Europe.
walloons: The term Walloon derives from the Proto-Germanic *walha, used for Celtic and Latin speakers. Its oldest written trace is in Jean de Haynin's memoirs of 1465, where it refers to the Roman populations of the Burgundian Netherlands. From the 16th century to the Belgian revolution the terms provinces wallonnes and pays wallon named a territory, and at Belgian independence the word came to mean Belgians who spoke a Romance language such as French, Walloon or Picard. The area now called Wallonia was settled by Celtic tribes and later by Roman and Frankish settlers, and from the early Middle Ages to the early modern period it was divided among many city-states and external powers.

Walloons are historically credited with pioneering the Industrial Revolution on the Continent in the early 19th century, and the Walloon region, a major coal and steel area, became the economic centre of Belgium. Between the 1930s and the 1970s the decline of steel and coal shifted the balance towards Flanders.

The Walloon Movement began at the end of the 19th century to assert the identity of Walloons as French speakers, and the concept of Wallonia as their heartland was invented in 1886. The Walloon language, widespread until the Second World War, has been dying out, in part because the public schools prohibited it in favour of French. The heartland of Walloon culture is the Meuse and Sambre valleys, with Charleroi, Dinant, Namur, Huy, Verviers and Liège.

Walloons are primarily Roman Catholic, with a historical Protestant minority dating from the Reformation. Walloon migrants settled widely. From the 11th century the Meuse towns of Dinant, Huy and Liège traded with Germany, where Wallengassen, Walloons' quarters, were founded; in Cologne they were the most important foreign community. Walloons settled in Wrocław in Poland probably from the 12th century, and numerous Walloons took part in the German colonisation of Transylvania in the 13th century.

From the 1620s Walloon miners and ironworkers, led by the entrepreneur Louis de Geer, came to Sweden, and later to Finland. Between 5,000 and 7,500 emigrants described as Brabantines and Hesbignons went to Wisconsin from 1852 to 1856.
walls-of-constantinople: Byzantium, according to tradition, was founded by Greek colonists from Megara led by Byzas around 658 BCE, and it was enclosed by a small wall of twenty-seven towers. The researcher Raymond Janin thinks the wall known from late sources reflects the city as rebuilt by the Spartan general Pausanias after 479 BCE. Tombstones were used to repair it in 340 BCE against an attack by Philip II of Macedon.

Constantine the Great rebuilt the city from 324 to 336 and inaugurated it on 11 May 330 as New Rome. His wall, a single line reinforced with towers, ran about 2.8 kilometres west of the earlier Severan wall. It was begun in 324 and completed under his son Constantius II (r. 337-361). By the early 5th century the city had already spread beyond it.

The Theodosian walls lie about 2 kilometres west of the Constantinian wall and take their name from Emperor Theodosius II (r. 402-450). The work was done in two phases, the first under Anthemius, praetorian prefect of the East, and a law in the Codex Theodosianus shows it finished in 413. An inscription found in 1993 records nine years of work, which suggests that building began around 404 or 405.

Earthquakes on 25 September 437 and 6 November 447 damaged the walls, the second destroying 57 towers. With Attila the Hun in the Balkans, Theodosius II had them restored in 60 days, using the chariot-racing factions as labour. Most scholars date the outer wall and the wide moat to this repair, though the outer wall may have been part of the original plan.

The Blachernae walls join the Theodosian line to the sea wall at the Golden Horn. They are 12 to 15 metres high and thicker than the Theodosian walls. The Golden Horn wall ran 5,600 metres, and the Propontis wall almost 8,460 metres, with thirteen gates and 188 towers.

The garrison was small: the imperial guards and the city watch under the urban prefect. Threats were met by the field armies in the provinces, and in emergencies such as the earthquake of 447 the guilds and hippodrome factions were conscripted. The walls saved the city during sieges by the Avar-Sassanian coalition, Arabs, Rus' and Bulgars, among others.

Further defences stood beyond the city, including the 56-kilometre Anastasian Wall, built in the mid-5th century about 65 kilometres to the west and abandoned in the 7th. Before the last Ottoman assault, Sultan Mehmed II built Rumelihisarı on the Bosphorus in just over four months in 1452. Restoration began in the 1980s with UNESCO support, but it was criticised, and the World Monuments Fund placed the walls on its 2008 Watch List.
walter-bagehot: Walter Bagehot was born in Langport, Somerset, on 3 February 1826. His father, Thomas Watson Bagehot, was managing director and vice-chairman of Stuckey's Bank. He studied mathematics at University College London and in 1848 earned a master's degree in moral philosophy. Called to the Bar by Lincoln's Inn, he preferred to join his father in 1852 in the family's shipping and banking business. In 1858 he married Elizabeth Wilson, whose father, James Wilson, was the founder and owner of The Economist; the couple had no children.

In 1855 Bagehot founded the National Review with his friend Richard Holt Hutton, and in 1861 he became editor-in-chief of The Economist. During his 16 years as editor he expanded its reporting of politics and increased its influence among policy-makers. He was widely accepted by the British establishment and was elected to the Athenaeum in 1875.

The English Constitution (1867) explores the constitution of the United Kingdom, in particular its Parliament and monarchy. It appeared as Parliament enacted the Reform Act 1867, so Bagehot wrote an extended introduction for the second edition of 1872. In Lombard Street: A Description of the Money Market (1873) he sought to explain the world of finance and banking; Bagehot's dictum holds that in a crisis central banks should lend freely to solvent institutions, but only against sound collateral and at interest rates high enough to deter borrowers not genuinely in need.

In Physics and Politics (1872) he examined how civilisations sustain themselves, arguing that in their earliest phase they are sustained by conformism and military success, and that once secure they can mature into systems allowing greater diversity and freedom. His view rested on a distinction between the accomplished man and the rude man, which he thought the result of inheritance through the generations, and he used the same reasoning to develop a form of pseudoscientific racism. He cited John Lubbock and Edward Tylor, though neither accepted innate hereditary differences, and Tylor rejected his emphasis on physical heredity.

Bagehot never fully recovered from a bout of pneumonia in 1867 and died on 24 March 1877 from complications of what was said to be a cold. Collections of his literary, political and economic essays were published after his death, on subjects from Shakespeare and Disraeli to the price of silver. His collected works were issued in 15 volumes by The Economist between 1965 and 1986. The minor planet 2901 Bagehot is named in his honour.
walter-burley-griffin: Walter Burley Griffin was born on 24 November 1876 in Maywood, Illinois, a suburb of Chicago, the eldest of four children. He completed a degree in architecture at the University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign in 1899, also taking courses in horticulture and forestry. In Chicago he worked for progressive architects in the Prairie School style, then from 1901 for Frank Lloyd Wright, overseeing the construction of several of Wright's houses. The two quarrelled after Wright's trip to Japan in 1905, and Griffin set up his own practice in 1906. On 29 June 1911 he married Marion Lucy Mahony, an architect who had worked in Wright's office.

In April 1911 the Australian Commonwealth Government held an international competition for its new federal capital. On 23 May 1912 Griffin's design, with renderings by his wife, was chosen from 137 entries. He went to Australia in 1913 and became Federal Capital Director of Design and Construction. The First World War forced cuts to his plans, funds were short, and he struggled with political and bureaucratic opposition. A Royal Commission in 1917 found that officials had supplied him with false data. He resigned in December 1920, and the only permanent structure of his design built in Canberra was the grave of General Bridges.

The Griffins also designed the New South Wales towns of Leeton and Griffith, Newman College at the University of Melbourne and the Capitol Theatre in Melbourne, which opened in 1924. From 1919 they developed the Sydney suburb of Castlecrag, with small flat-roofed houses set in native bushland. Griffin also devised a modular concrete system called Knitlock. In the 1930s he designed incinerators, twelve between 1930 and 1938.

Through contacts in the anthroposophy movement Griffin won a commission in 1935 to design the library of the University of Lucknow in India, and he then received more than 40 further commissions there. He died of peritonitis in early 1937, five days after gall bladder surgery, and was buried in Lucknow. Marion Mahony Griffin completed the Pioneer Building he had been working on.

Griffin was largely under-appreciated in Australia during his lifetime. In 1964, when Canberra's central lake was filled as he had intended, Prime Minister Robert Menzies named it Lake Burley Griffin. In 1988 the Royal Australian Institute of Architects named its national Civic Design Award after him.
walter-gropius: Walter Adolph Georg Gropius was born in Berlin on 18 May 1883, the third child of Walter Adolph Gropius and Manon Auguste Pauline Scharnweber. His great-uncle Martin Gropius designed the Kunstgewerbemuseum in Berlin as a follower of Karl Friedrich Schinkel. After studying architecture in Munich and Berlin for four semesters, he joined the office of Peter Behrens in 1908, where his colleagues included Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and Le Corbusier.

In 1910 he set up a practice in Berlin with Adolf Meyer. The glass curtain walls of their Faguswerk shoe-last factory at Alfeld-an-der-Leine became a founding monument of European modernism. In 1914 he was drafted and served on the Western front, was wounded, and received the Iron Cross twice.

In 1919 Gropius became master of the Grand-Ducal Saxon School of Arts and Crafts in Weimar, on the recommendation of Henry van de Velde, and transformed it into the Bauhaus. The faculty included Paul Klee, Johannes Itten, Josef Albers, László Moholy-Nagy and Wassily Kandinsky. The school aimed to extend beauty and quality to every home through well-designed industrial objects.

Its first major commission, the Sommerfeld House of 1921, was designed with Meyer. Facing political and financial difficulties, Gropius and the Bauhaus moved to Dessau in 1925, where he designed the school building, the Master Houses and the Törten housing estate. He left the Bauhaus in 1928, and Hannes Meyer took over.

In 1934 Gropius left Nazi Germany with the help of Maxwell Fry, on the pretext of a visit to Italy, and lived in London with the Isokon group. He moved to the United States in February 1937 and taught at the Harvard Graduate School of Design, where he chaired the Department of Architecture from 1938 until 1952. With Marcel Breuer he designed projects such as the Aluminum City Terrace housing in Pennsylvania, and in 1938 he built his own house in Lincoln, Massachusetts. In 1945 he became senior partner of The Architects Collaborative, and in 1959 he won the AIA Gold Medal.

Gropius died in Boston on 5 July 1969, aged 86, after an operation in June. His widow, Ise Gropius, gave the Gropius House in Lincoln to Historic New England in 1980, and it is now a house museum. In 1996 the Bauhaus Building and the Master Houses in Dessau were added to the list of UNESCO World Heritage Sites. The Berlin district of Gropiusstadt is named after him. The Gropius-Bau in Berlin, by contrast, is named for his great-uncle Martin.
walter-raleigh: Raleigh was born into a landed gentry family of Protestant faith at Hayes Barton, in East Devon, the youngest of five sons of Walter Raleigh of Fardel Manor. His mother, Katherine Champernowne, was the third wife of his father. His half-brothers included Humphrey Gilbert and Adrian Gilbert, and through the Champernowne connection the Raleigh and Gilbert brothers all became prominent under Elizabeth I and James I. Little is known of his early life, though in his late teens he spent some time in France taking part in the religious civil wars.

From 1579 to late 1580 Raleigh took part in suppressing the Desmond Rebellions in Ireland and was present at the siege of Smerwick. In 1585 he received 40,000 acres in the Munster Plantation, including Youghal, where he was mayor in 1588 and 1589. A royal charter of 25 March 1584 authorised him to explore and colonise lands not held by any Christian prince, and the region reached by the first expedition was named Virginia for Elizabeth. He was knighted in 1585. In 1591 he secretly married Elizabeth Throckmorton, one of the queen's ladies-in-waiting, and the couple were imprisoned in the Tower of London in 1592.

Raleigh heard of a city of gold in South America and explored what is now Guyana and eastern Venezuela in search of Lake Parime and Manoa. His Discovery of Guiana, published in 1596, made exaggerated claims and contributed to the El Dorado legend. He took part in the capture of Cádiz in 1596 and in the Islands Voyage of 1597, and from 1600 to 1603 as governor of Jersey he modernised its defences, including the building of Elizabeth Castle.

Arrested on 19 July 1603 for involvement in the Main Plot against James I, Raleigh defended himself at his trial at Winchester. The chief evidence was the sworn confession of Henry Brooke, 11th Baron Cobham, whom the tribunal refused to call as a witness. He was convicted, but the king spared his life. Pardoned in 1617, he led a second expedition to Venezuela, during which men under Lawrence Kemys attacked the Spanish outpost of Santo Tomé de Guayana, and his son Walter was killed. On his return the Spanish ambassador demanded that the sentence be reinstated, and Raleigh was beheaded at the Old Palace Yard on 29 October 1618. His poetry, in the plain style, includes The Nymph's Reply to the Shepherd.
walther-von-der-vogelweide: Little is known of Walther's life. His name appears in no contemporary record except one entry in the travel accounts of Bishop Wolfger von Erla of Passau, which notes five shillings paid to Walther the singer for a fur coat. He was a knight, but probably not a wealthy or landed one, and the surname von der Vogelweide, meaning bird-pasture, seems to point to a general geographic feature rather than a specific estate. His birthplace is unknown. Some scholars have argued for the Waldviertel in Lower Austria and others for the Wipptal in South Tyrol. He learned his craft at the court of Vienna under Duke Frederick I of the house of Babenberg, from the master Reinmar von Hagenau.

Duke Frederick's death in 1198 ended the period in which Walther produced most of his love lyrics, and he became a wanderer from court to court, singing for his lodging and bread. He left the court of Duke Bernhard of Carinthia and spent three years with Dietrich I of Meissen, complaining that he received neither money nor praise. Around 1214 he received a diamond from Diether III von Katzenelnbogen.

His political poems began in 1198 with an appeal to Germany against the ambitions of the princes. He attended the coronation of Philip at Mainz that year and supported him, backed Otto of Brunswick after Philip's murder in 1208, and turned to Frederick II after the Battle of Bouvines in 1214. Frederick gave him a small fief in Franconia. He opposed the extreme claims of the popes, though his religious poems show his sincere Catholicism.

Walther seems to have settled on his fief near Würzburg about 1224, and he died about 1230. He was buried at Würzburg, and a new monument, the Lusamgärtchen, was erected over the spot in 1843. His work survives in over 30 manuscripts, far more than that of his contemporaries. The Codex Manesse holds the largest collection, 440 strophes, and only a handful of his melodies survive, among them that of the Palästinalied. In the first decade of the 13th century Gottfried von Strassburg named him the leader of the Minnesänger after Reinmar's death. He is one of the competitors in the tale of the Wartburg song contest, which appears in Richard Wagner's Tannhäuser.
waltzing-matilda: The tune goes back to Scotland. Robert Tannahill wrote a poem, Thou Bonnie Wood of Craigielea, before 1806, and his friend James Barr set it to music, published in 1818. Thomas Bulch, an English expatriate in Australia, wrote a quick march for brass band called Craigielee, most likely in 1891. Christina Macpherson, who played the tune that Paterson set his words to, based it on her memory of that march. She played by ear and had little ability to write down note lengths, so her drafts contain mistakes, though the melody she recalled can be inferred with fair accuracy.

The words arose amid a bitter labour dispute. In 1894 striking shearers burned shearing sheds in central Queensland, and on 2 September the shed at Dagworth was set alight. The same day Samuel Hoffmeister, a leader of the strikers known as Frenchy, was found dead at a camp by a billabong near Kynuna. The inquest found suicide. Some historians, among them Ross Fitzgerald, see the strike and Hoffmeister's death behind the song, while others stress Paterson's relationship with Sarah Riley.

The song tells of a swagman, an itinerant worker, who boils his billy at a bush camp near a billabong and catches a stray jumbuck, or sheep. When the squatter who owns it and three troopers come to arrest him for theft, he cries that they will never catch him alive and drowns himself in the billabong, and his ghost haunts the place. The title is slang for travelling on foot with a swag, or bundle, slung on the back; Matilda is a romantic term for the swag. Coolibah is a kind of eucalyptus that grows near billabongs.

There are no official lyrics. Harry Nathan published the first setting on 20 December 1902, changing the melody and some words. On 12 January 1903 Paterson sold the rights, with some other pieces, to Angus & Robertson for five pounds. The tea trader James Inglis bought them for five guineas and asked Marie Cowan to turn the song into a jingle for Billy Tea. Her version, published in 1903, remains the best known.

The song was first recorded in 1926 by John Collinson and Russell Callow, and by 1995 at least 500 artists had recorded it. It has never been the official anthem of Australia, but from 1976 to 1984 it was one of three national songs that could replace God Save the Queen. In the plebiscite of 1977 it took 28 percent of the vote, against 43 for Advance Australia Fair. It is the quick march of the 1st Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment, and the official song of the US 1st Marine Division. Waltzing Matilda Day has been marked on 6 April since 2012, and the Waltzing Matilda Centre stands in Winton.
walvis-bay: Walvis Bay lies just north of the Tropic of Capricorn in the delta of the Kuiseb River. The bay is protected by the Pelican Point sand spit and is the only natural deep-water harbour on the country's coast. Its waters are rich in plankton and marine life and draw large numbers of southern right whales, which attracted whalers and fishing vessels. The Dutch called it Walvisch Baye and the English Whale Bay, and the Herero people called it Ezorongondo. The climate is a rare mild form of cold desert, with about 13 millimetres of rain a year and high humidity.

The Portuguese navigator Diogo Cão reached Cape Cross, north of the bay, in 1485, and Bartolomeu Dias anchored his flagship São Cristóvão in the bay on 8 December 1487, naming it O Golfo de Santa Maria da Conceição. The Portuguese made no formal claim. At the end of the 18th century the Dutch East India Company used it as a stopover between Cape Town and the Netherlands, but no year-round settlement was attempted and little commercial development took place until the late 19th century.

During the Scramble for Africa the British claimed the bay, and the Cape Colony completed its annexation in 1884, together with the Penguin Islands, after initial steps in 1878, while Germany annexed the surrounding land as German South West Africa. In 1910 the bay became part of the Union of South Africa as an exclave of the Cape. A boundary dispute with Germany was settled in 1911, with a confirmed area of 1,124 square kilometres. The Germans overran it early in the First World War, and South African forces ousted them in 1915.

South Africa held South West Africa under a League of Nations mandate, and in 1922 an Act placed Walvis Bay's administration under the mandated territory. In 1977 South Africa repealed it and returned control to the Cape Province, making the bay an exclave. The United Nations Security Council in Resolution 432 of 1978 called for its reintegration into Namibia. It stayed under South African sovereignty after Namibian independence in 1990. In 1992 the two countries set up a Joint Administrative Authority, and South Africa transferred sovereignty of Walvis Bay and the Penguin Islands to Namibia on 1 March 1994.

Walvis Bay is the second largest city in Namibia and its largest coastal city, with 102,704 people at the 2023 census. It lies at the end of the TransNamib Railway to Windhoek. Under South African administration it was developed as a segregated town, with Black residents in Kuisebmond, Coloured residents in Narraville and Whites in the centre. Fishing and the port form a major part of its economy, and tourists come for Dune 7, the salt works, birdlife and Bird Island.
wanderer-above-the-sea-of-fog: Caspar David Friedrich painted Wanderer above the Sea of Fog in 1818, though some sources indicate 1817. Its provenance in the 19th century is unclear. By 1939 it belonged to the gallery of Wilhelm August Luz in Berlin, and it was then apparently sold to the German lawyer Ernst Henke before returning to the Luz gallery. After passing between private collections it was acquired by the Hamburger Kunsthalle in 1970. In 1817 Friedrich had struck up a friendship with the scientist Carl Gustav Carus and the Norwegian painter Johan Christian Dahl, and in January 1818 he married Caroline Brommer.

A man in a dark green overcoat stands on a rocky precipice with his back to the viewer, gripping a walking stick in his right hand, his hair caught in the wind. Ridges and forested escarpments jut from the sea of fog in the middle ground, and faded mountains rise on the left and level into lowland plains on the right. The landscape is composed of elements of the Elbe Sandstone Mountains in Saxony and Bohemia, sketched in the field and rearranged by Friedrich in the studio. The Zirkelstein stands in the background on the right, and the rocks under the traveller are a group on the Kaiserkrone.

Friedrich used the Rückenfigur, a figure turned away from the viewer, considerably more often than other artists, and it is generally thought to invite viewers inside the painting. Helmut Börsch-Supan wrote that it is harder to imagine this landscape without a figure than in any other painting.

Some suggest the man is a self-portrait, pointing to his red hair, and the painting has been read as an emblem of self-reflection and as an evocation of the sublime. Friedrich wrote that the artist should paint not only what he has in front of him but also what he sees inside himself. He was an outspoken supporter of German liberal and nationalist feeling, and the art historian Norbert Wolf holds that the figure wears an Altdeutsch outfit, a political statement in that era; other scholars describe the clothing as a Jäger infantry uniform.

The painting and Friedrich's work were not at first regarded as masterpieces, though he was respected in German and Russian circles. His reputation improved in the 20th century, and the painting has since appeared on book covers and other objects. Robert Macfarlane calls it the archetypical image of the mountain-climbing visionary.
wang-anshi: Wang Anshi was born on 8 December 1021 in Linchuan, in present-day Jiangxi province, into a family of holders of the jinshi degree. He placed fourth in the palace examination and obtained his own jinshi degree in 1042. As a district magistrate at Yinxian he reorganised hydrological projects for irrigation and gave credits to the peasants. He observed a mourning period for his mother from 1063 to 1066 and in 1067 became governor of Jiangning. In 1058 he had sent Emperor Renzong a letter of ten thousand characters proposing administrative reforms, which went unanswered until Emperor Shenzong took the throne.

Shenzong faced declining taxes and a growing burden on commoners, since owners of large estates evaded their share. He sought Wang's advice in 1069 and made him vice counsellor, and a year later chancellor. Wang's New Policies aimed to cut government expenditure and strengthen the military in the north. They sought to relieve the peasantry and to check the monopolists of land and wealth, whom he called engrossers.

The measures included the equal tax law, a land survey meant to reveal hidden land, the green sprouts law, which lent money or seed to peasants, and the labour recruitment law, which replaced corvée labour with hired labour. The market exchange law set up bureaux to fix prices and buy surplus goods, and the baojia system organised households into security groups with police powers. A three college law reorganised the National University. Officials abused the loan scheme, and within months the government was charging 20 to 30 per cent annual interest.

The reforms divided the court into the Reformers and a Conservative faction led by Sima Guang, who argued that the elite families rather than the state should be the pillars of society. The poet Su Shi was jailed and exiled for criticising the reforms. After a famine in 1074 and the debts of farmers, Wang resigned in 1076. Shenzong died in 1085, Sima Guang returned, and the New Policies were abolished, though supporters regained power from 1093 and the policies largely continued under Emperor Huizong. Wang died on 21 May 1086.

Wang was also a major poet, writing in the shi form modelled on Du Fu, and was counted among the Eight Great Prose Masters of the Tang and Song. Chinese politicians and historians have looked back on his reforms as either principled and measured or misguided and disastrous.
wang-jingwei: Wang Zhaoming was born in Sanshui, Guangdong, of Zhejiang origin, and passed the county-level imperial examination for the xiucai degree in 1902. In 1903 he went to study at Hosei University in Japan on a Qing government scholarship. In 1905 he met the exiled revolutionary Sun Yat-sen and joined the Tongmenghui in Tokyo. He gained attention as a polemicist for its journal People's News, notably in debates with Liang Qichao, who advocated constitutional monarchy. His pen name Wang Jingwei, adopted in 1905, came from the mythical jingwei bird that tries to fill the ocean with twigs and pebbles.

In 1910 Wang and others in a Tongmenghui cell planted a bomb meant for the regent, Prince Chun. It was discovered, and he was arrested and sentenced to life imprisonment, but was released after the Wuchang Uprising. After Sun's death in 1925 he became the first president of the Nationalist government, then controlling only Guangdong, and adhered to Sun's policy of cooperation with the Soviet Union and the Chinese Communist Party. He became Chiang Kai-shek's principal rival in the Kuomintang.

In 1927 he led the left-wing government at Wuhan against Chiang's at Nanjing, but in the July 15 Incident he followed Chiang in purging the Communists. In 1930 he joined a coalition against Chiang that was defeated in the Central Plains War. After the Mukden Incident the two reached an accommodation, and Wang served as premier while Chiang commanded the army.

During the Second Sino-Japanese War Wang at first advocated resistance while negotiating, and from 1937 held secret talks with Konoe Fumimaro. In December 1938 he left the wartime capital Chongqing for Hanoi and called for a peace settlement with Japan, for which the Kuomintang expelled him. On 30 March 1940 he became head of the Reorganized National Government at Nanjing, which nominally governed Japanese-occupied China outside Manchuria. It copied the structure of the Republic of China's government and used its blue sky and white sun flag.

In March 1944 Wang went to Japan for treatment of a wound from an assassination attempt in 1935, and he died at the Nagoya Imperial University Hospital on 10 November 1944, less than a year before Japan's surrender. A testament attributed to him, published in the 1960s, claims to record his deathbed wishes; its authenticity remains disputed. Both the Kuomintang and the Chinese Communist Party denounced him as hanjian, a traitor to the Chinese people. He also wrote poetry, and his poems and a literary column on the South Society have been published.
wang-mang: Wang Mang, whose courtesy name was Jujun, was born in 45 BCE, a son of Wang Man, a younger brother of Empress Wang Zhengjun. His father died young, and unlike most of his brothers Wang Mang was not made a marquess. He became known for self-discipline and for promoting capable men, which began to reverse the general view of the Wang clan as arrogant and wasteful. He held the highest post in the government, commander of the armed forces, and after Emperor Cheng died in 7 BCE he remained powerful. He later retired, and in 5 BCE Emperor Ai sent him back to his march in Xindu.

Emperor Ai died in 1 BCE without an heir. Grand Empress Dowager Wang summoned Wang Mang back and placed him in charge of the armed forces and the government. The child Emperor Ping was enthroned and Wang Mang became his regent. He moved against his enemies, demoting and exiling the relatives of Emperor Ai and the Fu and Ding families. When Emperor Ping left no heir, Wang Mang passed over the 53 adult great-grandsons of Emperor Xuan and examined the 23 great-great-grandsons, all of them children, because he wanted a ruler he could control. He seized the throne in 9 CE and founded the Xin dynasty.

Wang Mang sought to restore the golden age of the early Zhou dynasty as described in the Book of Rites. He changed the structure of government and renamed places, including Chang'an. In 9 CE he declared all land the property of the empire under the wangtian system and abolished slavery, but landowners and officials resisted and he repealed the measures in 12 CE. The Yellow River flooded in 11 CE, and famine led to prophecies that he had lost the Mandate of Heaven.
