From about 17 CE rebellions arose, notably those of the Lülin and the Chimei, and relations with the Xiongnu broke down. Officials left counties without magistrates for years.

In spring 23 CE a Xin army of some 430,000 men failed to crush the new Han regime under the Gengshi Emperor. Rebel armies sacked Chang'an in October of that year, and Wang Mang was killed in the fighting at the palace. The Han dynasty was restored, and his rule marks the division between the Western and Eastern Han. Traditional Chinese historiography saw him as a tyrant and usurper, while some recent historians portray him as a visionary and selfless reformer.
wang-xizhi: Wang Xizhi was born around 303 in Linyi, in Langya Commandery, into the aristocratic Wang clan of Langya. His father, Wang Kuang, was governor of Huainan. After the Western Jin collapsed the family fled to southern China and helped establish the Eastern Jin in 317. He studied calligraphy under Wei Shuo, his father's cousin, and under his uncle Wang Yi, and after his parents died he lived in the household of his uncle Wang Dao. Around 323 he became engaged to Xi Xuan, daughter of the general Xi Jian. They had eight recorded children, among them Wang Xianzhi, who also became a skilled calligrapher; the two were later called the Two Wangs.

Between 324 and 354 Wang held various government posts, beginning as an assistant in the Palace Library. He served as a military aide to the general Yu Liang, became governor of Linchuan in 336, and was administrator of Kuaiji from 347, the year he received his highest title, General of the Right Army. He disliked war and never took part in fighting.

On 22 April 353 he hosted 41 friends, relatives and pupils at the Orchid Pavilion on Mount Kuaiji for the Double Third Festival. They played a winding stream party, composing poems as cups of rice wine floated towards them, and wrote 41 poems. Wang composed the Lantingji xu as a preface to the collection. In 355 he resigned, citing ill health, after a rival, Wang Shu, gained oversight of Kuaiji and investigated its finances. He moved to Jinting, devoted himself to Taoist practice, and died around 361.

Wang was skilled in regular, semi-cursive and cursive script, and is best known for his semi-cursive work, the style of the Lantingji xu. Apart from that preface and his letters, he mainly produced copies of existing texts. Emperor Taizong of Tang gathered over 2,000 of his works, had court scholars study his technique, and had tracing copies and ink rubbings made, which set Wang and his style as the standard of Chinese calligraphy. No original work by him is known to survive, only rubbings and a few tracing copies.

The authenticity of the Lantingji xu has been debated since the Song dynasty, and in 1965 Guo Moruo rejected Wang's authorship. The discovery of an Eastern Jin tomb inscribed in regular script in 1988 weakened one of his arguments. Wang was named the Sage of Calligraphy around the Tang dynasty, and his style was passed to Japan in the Nara and Heian periods.
wang-yangming: Wang Shouren was born in Yuyao, Zhejiang, on 26 October 1472, into a scholarly family with a tradition of bureaucratic service. His father, Wang Hua, placed first in the imperial examination of 1481 and rose to vice-minister of the Ministry of Rites, but was later demoted and expelled from government service for offending the eunuch Liu Jin. Wang earned the juren degree in 1492 and the jinshi degree in 1499. He served as an executive assistant in various departments until he was banished in 1506 for offending a eunuch, and his career then resumed when he became Governor of Jiangxi.

Wang was a successful general, known for the strict discipline he imposed on his troops. In 1517 and 1518 he was sent to suppress peasant revolts in Jiangxi, Fujian and Guangdong; concerned with the destruction of war, he petitioned the court to allow amnesty. In 1519 he faced the rebellion of Zhu Chenhao, the fourth Prince of Ning, whose base at Nanchang allowed him to sail down the Yangtze and capture Nanjing. Wang prepared for battle and deceived the prince into believing that armies were moving to surround him. The prince hesitated, giving time for Nanjing to be reinforced, and was defeated and captured.

As governor Wang also built schools and rehabilitated rebels. He was made an earl but was ostracized for opposing Zhu Xi. Thirty-eight years after his death he was given the titles Marquis and Completion of Culture, and in 1584 he was offered sacrifice in the Confucian Temple, the highest honour for a scholar.

Wang was the leading figure of the School of the Mind, founded by Lu Jiuyuan of the Southern Song, which unified knowledge with action; its rival, the School of Principle, treated gaining knowledge as a preparation for action. From the Cheng-Zhu Neo-Confucianism of his time he developed the idea of innate knowing: every person knows from birth the difference between good and evil, intuitively and not rationally. He held that knowledge and action are one, and that the mind alone is the source of all reason. To clear away selfish desires he practised sitting still, which resembles Chan meditation.

His school became one of the dominant Confucian schools of the mid and late Ming and of the Qing. In Japan, where it is called Ōyōmei-gaku, it influenced the samurai ethic; Nakae Tōju is regarded as its founder there, and Kumazawa Banzan, Saigō Takamori and Takasugi Shinsaku came from it.
wangen-im-allgau: Wangen im Allgäu lies in south-east Baden-Württemberg, north-east of Lake Constance, in the Westallgäu, on the north bank of the Obere Argen. The Untere Argen flows past the north-west of the city and unites with the Obere Argen to its south-west. The city is second in size in the Ravensburg district and a centre for the surrounding communities. Its name was officially given as Wangen in Allgäu in 1936.

The place was first mentioned in 815 as Wangun in a monastery document. In 1217 a royal document declared that Wangen should remain in royal hands, and in 1286 King Rudolph I granted it the status of a free imperial city. In the late Middle Ages its growth was helped by its position at the crossroads between Ravensburg, Lindau, Leutkirch and Isny and by the growing trade through the Alps. Scythes and canvas were its main manufactured exports, and they gave the city a large trade surplus, which it used to buy lands beyond its walls as a safeguard against economic swings.

During the German Mediatisation of 1802 Wangen lost its free status and was incorporated into the Kingdom of Bavaria; in 1810 it changed hands to the Kingdom of Württemberg. From 1938 to 1972 it was the seat of the Wangen rural district, and in 1973 the state government designated it a Große Kreisstadt, a large district town, because its population had passed 20,000.

Despite major fires in 1539, 1793 and 1858, the old town still joins architecture from the Early Middle Ages to the late Baroque. The Oberstadtkirche St. Martin, one of the oldest buildings, was already present in the 9th century and contains Romanesque and Gothic work. The Ravensburg Gate, the city's main landmark, was first mentioned in 1472 and probably took its present appearance in 1608, with Renaissance decoration; the Lindau Gate and the Pfaffenturm tower are of similar age. A local history museum, opened in 1974 in a former mill, shows the original mill mechanisms.
wanli-emperor: Zhu Yijun was born on 4 September 1563, during the reign of his grandfather, the Jiajing Emperor. His father, Zhu Zaiji, was the heir to the throne, and his mother, Lady Li, was one of his concubines. His father became the Longqing Emperor in 1567 and named him heir in 1568. When the Longqing Emperor died on 5 July 1572, Zhu Yijun succeeded two weeks later, on 19 July, at the age of nine, and adopted the era name Wanli, meaning "ten thousand years (of rule)".

For the first ten years Grand Secretary Zhang Juzheng effectively led the government, supported by the Emperor's mother and the eunuch Feng Bao. He centralized government, streamlined administration and strengthened the military, and the efficiency of administration improved markedly between 1572 and 1582. After Zhang died in 1582 the Emperor changed his administrative arrangements. From 1586 a dispute over the succession divided the bureaucracy: the Emperor favoured his third son, Zhu Changxun, the son of his consort Lady Zheng, while many officials upheld the claim of his eldest son, Zhu Changluo, who was named heir only in 1601.

In the 1590s the Ming put down a rebellion at Ningxia in 1592, drove the Japanese out of most of Korea by 1593 and thwarted a second Japanese invasion in 1597. In 1596 a shortage of silver after the costly rebuilding of palaces burnt in a fire led the Emperor to send eunuchs and officers to open mines, which local authorities opposed. In 1596 he also tried to set up a parallel administration of eunuchs, abandoned in 1606. The Donglin Academy, founded in 1604, became an intellectual centre critical of the court. In 1619 the Jurchens defeated Ming armies at the Battle of Sarhu and took part of Liaodong. After 1588 the Emperor no longer left Beijing.

The Emperor's health failed in 1620, and he died on 18 August. An edict the next day sent a million liang of silver to the frontier troops and ordered an end to mining and trade dues. His eldest son, Zhu Changluo, took the throne on 28 August as the Taichang Emperor. Traditional Chinese historiography portrays the Wanli Emperor as a main cause of the dynasty's decline, citing greed, misuse of eunuch power and seclusion. Confucian scholars' hostility came partly from his protection of military officers against complaints from civilian officials.
wannsee-conference: Discrimination against Jews was codified in Germany immediately after the Nazi seizure of power on 30 January 1933, and the Nuremberg Laws of September 1935 stripped Jews of citizenship. After the invasion of Poland in September 1939 the extermination of European Jews began, first through mobile death squads, the Einsatzgruppen, and it accelerated after the invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941.

On 31 July 1941 Hermann Göring gave Reinhard Heydrich written authorisation to prepare a plan for a total solution of the Jewish question in territories under German control. Heydrich sent invitations on 29 November 1941 for a meeting on 9 December, but it was postponed, and on 8 January 1942 he sent new invitations for 20 January.

The meeting took place at a villa at Am Großen Wannsee 56 to 58, bought by the Security Service in 1940 as a conference centre. Fifteen officials attended, mostly state secretaries and undersecretaries of the ministries together with SS officials; eight were lawyers. Heydrich spoke for nearly an hour. He reported that about 537,000 Jews had emigrated by 31 October 1941 and that there were about eleven million Jews in Europe.

Since emigration had been prohibited, Jews were to be evacuated to the east and allocated to labour, in the course of which a large portion would be eliminated by natural causes. Europe would be combed through from west to east, with Jews first sent to transit ghettos in the General Government. He also discussed who counted as a Jew and how people of mixed descent and Jews in mixed marriages would be treated.

Questions and comments followed for about thirty minutes. Wilhelm Stuckart and Otto Hofmann pointed to the legal difficulties over mixed marriages, and Josef Bühler, State Secretary of the General Government, hoped the killings would begin as soon as possible. Adolf Eichmann later said that after cognac was served the participants spoke bluntly of methods of killing and extermination. Eichmann wrote the minutes, the Wannsee Protocol, at Heydrich's instruction in office language rather than verbatim.

The conference lasted only about ninety minutes. Historians such as Peter Longerich and Laurence Rees hold that the decision to exterminate the Jews had already been made and that Heydrich met the officials to secure the cooperation of the ministries and to assert SS control over the deportees' fate. Copies of the minutes were destroyed at the end of the war.

Copy number 16 of 30 was found in 1947 by the US prosecutor Robert Kempner among files seized from the German Foreign Office, and it was used in the Nuremberg trials. On 20 January 1992, the fiftieth anniversary, the villa was opened as the Haus der Wannsee-Konferenz, a Holocaust memorial and museum.
waqf: There is no direct Quranic injunction about awqāf, but one is inferred from Surah Al Imran (3:92), which says that righteousness is not reached until a person gives some of what they cherish. The institution rests on hadiths. One tradition says that after the Hijrah the first waqf was a grove of 600 date palms whose proceeds fed the poor of Medina.

The two oldest known deeds, or waqfiyas, are from the 9th century and a third from the early 10th, all within the Abbasid Caliphate. In Egypt the earliest known waqf was a pond called Birkat Ḥabash with its orchards, founded in 919 to run a hydraulic complex and feed the poor. In India the 14th-century Insha-i-Mahru records that Muhammad of Ghor gave two villages to a congregational mosque in Multan.

A waqf is a contract, so the founder, the waqif, must be an adult of sound mind who can handle financial affairs. Being a Muslim is not required, and dhimmis may found one. The founder must name a specific beneficiary, may not reserve a right to sell or revoke, and must own the property outright. The founder appoints an administrator, a nāẓir or mutawallī, and sets the rules for successors.

A waqf is meant to last forever, but Islamic law admits conditions under which it ends: if its goods are destroyed or no longer used as the founder intended, or if a judge, the ḳāḍī, declares it void for an illegal act or purpose. It is also void if the founder converts to another religion.

Waqf revenue paid for mosques, madrasas, public kitchens, caravanserais and libraries. After waqf law and madrasa foundations were firmly established by the 10th century, the number of hospitals multiplied, and by the 11th century many Islamic cities had several. Waqfs paid doctors, surgeons and pharmacists, bought food, medicines and equipment, kept buildings in repair and supported medical schools. The institution was not popular everywhere: in West Africa very few examples are found, and they were limited to the area around Timbuktu and Djenné.
war-elephant: It is uncertain when elephant warfare began, but it is widely accepted that it began in ancient India. Elephants were widely used in warfare by the later Vedic period, by the 6th century BCE. From India the practice spread west to the Achaemenid Empire. At the Battle of Gaugamela in 331 BCE the Persians placed fifteen elephants at the centre of their line, and Alexander the Great, deeply impressed, took the first fifteen into his own army and added to their number. Kush also kept war elephants, perhaps in the Great Enclosure at Musawwarat al-Sufa, and supplied them to the Egyptians, the Ptolemies and the Syrians.

In battle elephants were usually placed in the centre of the line, to prevent a charge or to make one, and their size and appearance made them valued heavy cavalry. Rome brought back many elephants at the end of the Punic Wars and used them in Greece. At Cynoscephalae in 197 BCE their quick charge shattered the Macedonian left wing. The Gupta Empire formed local squads of one elephant, one chariot, three cavalrymen and five foot soldiers.

China used them sparingly: the Southern Han is the only state in Chinese history known to have kept a permanent corps, which Song crossbowmen defeated at Shao on 23 January 971. The Khmer Empire mounted double crossbows on elephants. Elephants were trained by mahouts using chains and a hook called an ankus.

Elephants could fail. In the Sack of Delhi, Timur's army, though three times the size of its opponents, almost lost for fear of the elephants, and is said to have won by tying flaming straw to its camels, which ran forward and frightened the elephants into crushing their own troops. With the arrival of gunpowder in the late 15th century the balance changed: elephants could withstand muskets, but a single cannon shot could knock one down. Nevertheless they remained in use in Southeast Asia until the end of the 19th century, and the Siamese army used them until 1893. The bishop in chess is called an elephant in many languages, including Sanskrit, Arabic and Russian.
war-in-afghanistan-2001-2021: The Taliban emerged from religious students who sought to end warlordism in Afghanistan through stricter adherence to Sharia. In 1996 they seized Kabul, with military support from Pakistan and financial support from Saudi Arabia, and founded the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan. They issued edicts forbidding women to work outside the home or attend school. The United Nations reported 15 massacres of civilians between 1996 and 2001, many targeting Shias and Hazaras. Under the Taliban, al-Qaeda trained fighters in Afghanistan, and an estimated 10,000 to 20,000 men passed through the camps before 11 September 2001.

On that day 19 al-Qaeda members hijacked four airliners and carried out coordinated attacks in the United States, in which 2,996 people died, including the hijackers. President George W. Bush demanded that the Taliban hand over Osama bin Laden and close the camps. The Taliban leader Mullah Omar refused, and the Taliban said bin Laden was protected by Pashtun laws of hospitality.

The United States officially invaded on 7 October 2001 with Operation Enduring Freedom, though CIA teams had entered the country weeks earlier to link up with the Northern Alliance in the Panjshir Valley. With American air support the Northern Alliance took several key cities within weeks, and by November the Taliban had lost most of the country. The coalition formed the International Security Assistance Force, and an Afghan Interim Administration was set up. By 2003 the Taliban had reorganised and begun an insurgency of guerrilla warfare, suicide attacks and reprisals against perceived collaborators.

Troop numbers grew, with a surge from late 2009 to September 2012. An American covert operation in Pakistan killed bin Laden in 2011. NATO formally ended ISAF combat operations in 2014 and handed security to the Afghan government, while a new NATO mission, Resolute Support, and the American Operation Freedom's Sentinel continued. The United States and the Taliban concluded a deal for the withdrawal of all American troops. In the summer of that withdrawal the Taliban launched an offensive and took Kabul on 15 August, the day President Ashraf Ghani fled the country.

The last American military aircraft left on 30 August. The war is estimated to have killed between 176,000 and 212,000 people, including 46,319 civilians, and a further 66,650 people died in the related war in north-west Pakistan. Although more than 5.7 million former refugees returned after 2001, 2.6 million Afghans were still refugees at the fall of Kabul and about 4 million were internally displaced. It was the longest war in American military history, surpassing the Vietnam War by seven months.
war-of-1812: The causes of the war have long been debated. The United States objected to the British orders in council of 1807, which restricted trade with Napoleonic France, and to the Royal Navy's impressment of seamen from American vessels, men whom Britain claimed as British subjects. Britain also supported Indigenous confederacies resisting American expansion in the Northwest Territory, and some Americans may have wished to annex part or all of Canada.

On 1 June 1812 President James Madison sent Congress a message setting out American grievances. The House voted 79 to 49 and the Senate 19 to 13 for war, divided on party lines, with no Federalist in favour. Madison signed the declaration on 18 June 1812, the first formal declaration of war by the United States, passed by the smallest margin of any in American history.

Neither side was ready. Britain was engaged against Napoleon, most of its army was in the Peninsular War, and it had officially 6,034 regular troops in Canada in July 1812. Its aims were defensive. American forces under William Hull crossed into Upper Canada on 12 July 1812 and reached Sandwich, but all the invasions of Canada failed. At sea the Royal Navy blockaded the American coast and raided the Chesapeake Bay, while American privateers inflicted limited damage on British commerce. About 4,000 African Americans escaped slavery aboard British ships.

After Napoleon's exile in April 1814 Britain reinforced North America, and in August 1814 it captured and burned Washington. American victories at Baltimore and Plattsburgh in September helped end major fighting in the north. In the south, American forces and their Indigenous allies defeated the Red Stick faction of the Muscogee, and Andrew Jackson's army repulsed a British attack on New Orleans in January 1815, after the Treaty of Ghent had been signed. The treaty was agreed in December 1814 and ratified by the Senate on 17 February 1815.

The treaty restored the pre-war territorial status quo and did not settle the maritime issues, though impressment largely ceased once the Napoleonic Wars ended. American losses were 2,260 killed in action and about 15,000 dead from all causes related to the war, while British losses were about 1,160 killed in action. At least 10,000 Indigenous people are estimated to have died.

The Indigenous allies of Britain lost their cause, since the proposed barrier state was rejected at Ghent, and the United States went on to negotiate over two hundred treaties for Indigenous land. In the United States the war was called a second war of independence and the Federalist Party collapsed. Britain remembers it little. Canadians later used its memory to help build a national identity after 1867.
war-of-devolution: The 1659 Treaty of the Pyrenees ended the Franco-Spanish War, and Louis XIV married Maria Theresa, eldest daughter of Philip IV of Spain. To prevent France from inheriting the Spanish Empire, she renounced her inheritance rights, and in return Louis was promised a dowry of 500,000 gold écus, which was never paid. After Cardinal Mazarin died in 1661, Louis began an expansionist policy, and Jean-Baptiste Colbert argued that control of the Spanish Netherlands was essential to French economic growth.

Philip's death in September 1665 left his four-year-old son Charles as king, with his widow Mariana of Austria as regent. French lawyers argued that the unpaid dowry made the renunciation invalid. The Spanish and imperial courts rejected the claim, since the law applied only in Brabant, Namur and Hainault and concerned private property, but it gave Louis a legal justification.

The French crossed the border on 24 May 1667 with Louis in attendance. Turenne, the supreme commander, took Charleroi, which the Spanish governor Castelo Rodrigo abandoned after destroying its fortifications, and by the end of July Tournai, Kortrijk and Oudenaarde had fallen. Turenne besieged Lille on 10 August, and its garrison surrendered on 28 August. Sickness proved a bigger problem for his troops than battle.

The Treaty of Breda of 31 July 1667 ended the Second Anglo-Dutch War and opened talks on a common front against France. England and the Dutch Republic signed the Triple Alliance on 23 January 1668, and Sweden joined on 5 May. In February 1668 the Prince de Condé invaded Franche-Comté, which had fewer than 2,000 defenders. Besançon surrendered on 7 February, Dole on 14 February and Gray on 19 February.

Turenne, Condé and Philippe of Orléans argued for continuing the war, while Lionne, Colbert and Le Tellier recommended peace, mainly on financial grounds. The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle was signed by Spain and France on 2 May 1668. France withdrew from Franche-Comté and from the Spanish Netherlands except for eleven towns, among them Lille, Douai, Tournai and Charleroi, and Vauban began work on the defence line known as the Ceinture de fer.

The invasion ended the long-standing Franco-Dutch alliance. Louis concluded that the best way to win Dutch agreement to his demands was to defeat the Republic first, and he began planning the Franco-Dutch War.
war-of-jenkins-ear: The Treaty of Utrecht of 1713 gave British merchants access to Spanish American markets through the Asiento de Negros, a monopoly to supply 5,000 slaves a year, and the Navío de Permiso, which allowed two ships a year to sell goods at Porto Bello and Veracruz. Both were held by the South Sea Company. Smuggling was too profitable to stop, and Spain tried either to manage the illegal trade or to use it as an instrument of policy.

The war is often portrayed as a trade dispute, but modern historians argue that Spanish concern over British colonial expansion in North America mattered equally. The Tory opposition, seeking to unseat Robert Walpole's Whig government, also campaigned for war. In April 1731 the Spanish guarda costa captain was alleged to have severed the ear of the British captain Robert Jenkins, and in 1738 opposition politicians used the incident to rouse support.

Admiral Edward Vernon captured Portobelo on 22 November 1739 with six ships of the line. Its fall was greeted with enthusiasm in Britain, and Rule Britannia was written in 1740 to mark it. Vernon then tried Cartagena de Indias, the Spanish gold-trading port in New Granada, three times. His largest attack, with an amphibious force from 13 March to 20 May 1741, failed against the fortifications and the strategy of the Spanish commander Blas de Lezo. Heavy British losses came mostly from disease, chiefly yellow fever, which took more lives than the fighting.

Commodore George Anson sailed for the Pacific in September 1740. Most of his men died of disease, but on 20 June 1743 he captured a Manila galleon carrying more than a million gold coins and returned to London having circled the globe. In North America, James Oglethorpe besieged St. Augustine in 1740 without success, and in 1742 he defeated a Spanish landing from 2,000 troops at Bloody Marsh. Privateers on both sides were active, and Spanish ones seized hundreds of British ships.

By mid-1742 the War of the Austrian Succession had broken out in Europe, and its scale drew attention away from the Americas. Vernon's return that year ended major offensive operations. France entered the war in 1744, and fear of a French invasion persuaded British policymakers against sending large forces overseas. Fighting formally ended with the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle of 1748, under which Britain largely failed to achieve its territorial and economic aims in the Americas.
war-of-the-austrian-succession: The Mutual Pact of Succession of 1703 provided that if the Habsburgs died out in the male line, their possessions would pass first to the daughters of Emperor Joseph I and then to those of his younger brother Charles. Since Salic law excluded women, the agreement needed the approval of the Habsburg territories and the Imperial Diet. Emperor Charles VI died on 20 October 1740.

Frederick II had become king of Prussia on 31 May 1740, aged 28, and wished to overcome the limits that his scattered territories set on Prussian power. The death gave him a chance to take resource-rich Silesia before Augustus of Saxony and Poland could act. Prussia's army of 80,000 was better trained than the Austrian one, and France had agreed to attack from the west.

Prussia occupied Silesia in December 1740. At Mollwitz on 10 April 1741 Frederick made mistakes and left the field, and his deputy von Schwerin won a narrow victory. A Franco-Bavarian force marched along the Danube and took Linz on 14 September 1741, and with a Saxon force of 20,000 advanced on Prague. On 12 February 1742 Charles Albert of Bavaria was crowned Emperor Charles VII, the first non-Habsburg emperor in 300 years, but Austrian troops captured Munich that day. Maria Theresa ended a secret truce with Frederick by publishing its terms, damaging his bond with his allies.

In 1743 the allied Pragmatic Army beat French troops at Dettingen, the last time a British monarch personally led troops in battle. After Charles VII died on 20 January 1745, his son Maximilian III Joseph signed the Treaty of Füssen on 22 April, agreeing to vote for Maria Theresa's husband Francis Stephen as emperor. In the Low Countries the French took Tournai after Fontenoy, then Ghent, Bruges and Antwerp, and won at Rocoux in October 1746. Elsewhere Britain and Spain fought at sea, in the war's North American theatre King George's War, and in India, where the French took Madras in September 1746.

By early 1748 France was close to bankruptcy, and a British naval blockade had collapsed its customs receipts and caused food shortages. Louis XV agreed to return the Austrian Netherlands, a decision that few of his countrymen understood and that gave rise to the phrase as stupid as the Peace. The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle, signed in October, confirmed Maria Theresa in her titles, but many signatories were unhappy. Britain's insistence that Austria cede Silesia undermined the Anglo-Austrian Alliance, since Austria felt it had gained little from large British subsidies. This led to the Diplomatic Revolution and, in 1756, the outbreak of the Seven Years' War.
war-of-the-fifth-coalition: Austria had been defeated in 1805 and spent three years reforming its army. Encouraged by events in Spain, where much of the French army was committed to the Peninsular War, it sought a new confrontation to avenge its defeats and regain lost territory. Its ally Russia had made peace with Napoleon at Tilsit, and at the Congress of Erfurt in 1808 agreed to support France if Austria attacked. Austria built the largest army in its history, conscripted from across the empire, but its quality was hampered by incomplete training and the army's multinational nature. The Austrians hoped Prussia would join them, but it stayed neutral.

On 10 April 1809 Austrian forces under Archduke Charles crossed the Inn into Bavaria, a French client state, without a formal declaration of war. The attack came about a week before Napoleon expected it, and the first French response under Louis-Alexandre Berthier was disorganised until Napoleon arrived on 17 April. After fighting around Regensburg and Landshut, Charles retreated eastwards but failed to reach Vienna before the French. A French crossing of the Danube was repulsed on 21–22 May at the Battle of Aspern-Essling. After more than six weeks of preparation the French crossed again, and on 5–6 July Napoleon won the Battle of Wagram, a close battle in which the Austrians withdrew in good order.

Elsewhere Archduke John defeated Eugène de Beauharnais at Caldiero on 30 April but was beaten at the Piave on 8 May and driven from Italy. The Austrians invaded the Duchy of Warsaw, and in July a British force of over 39,000 landed at Walcheren in the Netherlands, the largest British expedition of the Napoleonic Wars.

The Treaty of Schönbrunn, signed on 14 October 1809, took Carinthia, Carniola and the Adriatic ports from Austria, ending its access to the Mediterranean. West Galicia went to the Duchy of Warsaw, Salzburg to Bavaria and the district of Tarnopol to Russia. Austria lost over three million subjects, about 20 per cent of its population, and agreed to pay an indemnity of almost 85 million francs. After the war Napoleon married Marie Louise, the daughter of Emperor Francis.

Aspern-Essling showed that Napoleon could be beaten on the battlefield. The war also saw risings against French rule, among them Andreas Hofer's rebellion in Tyrol, the Gottscheer rebellion and revolts in Italy, which were suppressed but foreshadowed later nationalist risings.
war-of-the-first-coalition: Other European monarchies watched developments in France with alarm from 1791. Leopold II, Holy Roman Emperor and brother of Queen Marie Antoinette, at first looked on calmly but grew concerned as the Revolution radicalised. On 27 August 1791 he and King Frederick William II of Prussia issued the Declaration of Pillnitz, threatening vague but severe consequences if harm came to Louis XVI. Paris saw this as a serious threat. France declared war on Austria on 20 April 1792, after the Assembly voted for it. The coalition was only loosely allied and fought with little coordination, since each power wanted to annex a different part of France.

The French army was disorganised and its first invasion of the Austrian Netherlands failed. In July 1792 an army under the Duke of Brunswick, mostly Prussians, invaded France and took Longwy and Verdun. At Valmy on 20 September a tactical draw boosted French morale and the Prussians chose to retreat. Two days later the National Convention proclaimed the French Republic. Dumouriez won at Jemappes on 6 November and occupied the Austrian Netherlands. After the execution of Louis XVI in January 1793 France declared war on Britain and the Netherlands, and the First Coalition took shape.

France met reverses at Neerwinden and in the Vendée. It formed the Committee of Public Safety and introduced the levée en masse. In 1794 victory at Fleurus won the Austrian Netherlands and the Rhineland. France seized the Low Countries and set up the Batavian Republic. Prussia withdrew and signed the Peace of Basel, and Spain made peace later in 1795.

In 1796 Napoleon Bonaparte separated the armies of Sardinia and Austria in Italy, forced peace on Sardinia, captured Milan and besieged Mantua. Archduke Charles defeated Jourdan on the Rhine. Mantua fell on 2 February 1797 with 18,000 Austrians surrendering.

Austria sued for peace in April 1797 and the Peace of Leoben led to the Treaty of Campo Formio in October. Austria ceded the Austrian Netherlands to France, and northern Italy became several French sister republics. The coalition collapsed, leaving only Britain at war with France.
war-of-the-fourth-coalition: The Fourth Coalition formed within months of the collapse of the Third. After the victory at Austerlitz, Napoleon sought a general peace with Britain and Russia while trying to isolate Prussia. Several quarrels pushed Prussia towards war. Hanover, a German state in personal union with the British monarchy, had been secretly promised to Britain by Napoleon in the course of peace overtures, although it had earlier been offered to Prussia. In July 1806 Napoleon created the Confederation of the Rhine under his protection, which ended the Holy Roman Empire. Prussia took offence at this interference in German affairs, and on 9 October 1806 it declared war.

Napoleon marched the Grande Armée in three parallel columns through the Franconian Forest in his bataillon-carré formation. After skirmishes at Schleiz and Saalfeld, he defeated the Prussians at the double Battle of Jena–Auerstedt on 14 October 1806. At Auerstedt a single corps under Marshal Davout defeated the bulk of the Prussian army. The Prussians sustained 65,000 casualties and lost a further 150,000 prisoners, while the French suffered about 15,000 casualties. Napoleon entered Berlin on 27 October and issued the Berlin Decree on 21 November, beginning the Continental System.

The French then entered Poland, where Napoleon created the Duchy of Warsaw. The inconclusive and bloody Battle of Eylau on 7–8 February 1807 forced the Russians to withdraw north, and on 14 June Napoleon routed them at Friedland. Alexander I sued for peace at Tilsit. In Swedish Pomerania the French took Stralsund on 24 August 1807 after a siege.

In the Treaties of Tilsit of July 1807 Russia agreed to join the Continental System. Napoleon demanded much Prussian territory, from the lower Rhine west of the Elbe, which went to the new Kingdom of Westphalia under his brother Jérôme Bonaparte, and from the former Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which went to the Duchy of Warsaw, ruled by the king of Saxony. Napoleon was then master of almost all western and central Europe except Spain, Portugal and Austria. Britain remained at war, and Napoleon's invasion of Portugal began the Peninsular War.
war-of-the-pacific: After independence, the frontiers of the Atacama coast were uncertain. The Boundary Treaty of 1866 set the border at 24° S and shared the tax on mineral exports between 23° and 25° S, and the arrangement caused discontent. In February 1873 Peru and Bolivia signed a secret treaty of alliance against Chile, revealed only in 1879. In 1874 a new boundary treaty kept the border at 24° S, gave Bolivia the tax revenue between 23° and 24° S and guaranteed Chilean enterprises against tax increases for 25 years.

In February 1878 Bolivia nevertheless raised taxes on the Chilean company Compañía de Salitres y Ferrocarril de Antofagasta, a ten-centavo tax that gave the conflict the name Ten Cents War. Chile asked for arbitration, but the Bolivian president Hilarión Daza treated it as a domestic matter, cancelled the company's licence and seized its property.

On the day of the planned auction in February 1879, about 200 Chilean soldiers landed at Antofagasta and seized it without resistance, supported by a local population that was 93 to 95 per cent Chilean. Peru tried to mediate while preparing for war. None of the three states had a general staff or medical corps, and Chile's army had shrunk to 2,400 men. Control of the sea was decisive, because supply by sea was faster than moving it through the Atacama Desert. For the first five months the war was naval, and Peruvian raiding delayed the Chilean invasion by six months until the capture of the ironclad Huáscar at the Battle of Angamos gave Chile naval supremacy. Chile then occupied the Peruvian province of Tarapacá.

Bolivia withdrew after the Battle of Tacna on 26 May 1880, leaving Peru to fight alone. Chilean forces occupied Lima in January 1881. Remnants of the Peruvian army and irregulars under Cáceres waged a guerrilla war, and in Peru's highlands there were also uprisings of indigenous peasants and Chinese labourers.

Chile and Peru signed the Treaty of Ancón on 20 October 1883. Peru ceded Tarapacá, and Chile was to occupy Tacna and Arica for ten years before a plebiscite, which the two countries failed to agree on for decades. In 1929 a settlement mediated under President Herbert Hoover gave Arica to Chile and Tacna to Peru. Bolivia signed a truce in 1884, and the Treaty of Peace and Friendship of 1904 ceded the whole Antofagasta region to Chile, in return for a railway from Arica to La Paz and freedom of transit for Bolivian trade. Authors have called the war a national trauma for Peru and Bolivia, and Bolivians commemorate the lost coast each year on 23 March.
war-of-the-polish-succession: Since 1572 the king of Poland and grand duke of Lithuania had been elected by the nobility, and the Sejm, the legislature, was often paralysed by the liberum veto. By the early 18th century neighbours, especially Russia, interfered increasingly. Augustus II died on 1 February 1733. In the secret Treaty of the Three Black Eagles of 1732, Russia, Austria and Prussia had agreed to oppose both Stanisław Leszczyński and Augustus II's son, and to support Manuel of Portugal. France's chief minister Cardinal Fleury backed Stanisław, whose daughter Marie Leszczyńska was married to Louis XV, hoping to weaken Austria and secure Lorraine. Philip V of Spain wanted to regain Italian territories, and the two Bourbon courts signed a Pacte de Famille in 1733.

On 12 September 1733 a sejm of 12,000 delegates elected Leszczyński, but about 3,000 nobles under Russian protection elected Frederick August II of Saxony as Augustus III on 5 October. Russian troops under Peter Lacy took Warsaw, and Stanisław fled to Danzig, which capitulated in June 1734; he escaped to France. France declared war on Austria and Saxony on 10 October 1733 and soon took Lorraine and the fortress of Kehl. Prince Eugene of Savoy could not relieve Philippsburg, which fell in July 1734, and the Duke of Berwick was killed there.

In northern Italy, Charles Emmanuel III of Sardinia and the French took Milan, but the allies quarrelled and made little progress against Mantua. In the south Don Carlos led a largely Spanish army into Naples, defeated the Austrians at Bitonto in May 1734 and subdued Sicily. Austria was left isolated: Britain and the Dutch Republic stayed neutral, and Robert Walpole argued that the Anglo-Austrian alliance was purely defensive.

A preliminary peace was made in October 1735 and ratified in the Treaty of Vienna in November 1738. Augustus III was confirmed as king of Poland. Stanisław received Lorraine, which passed to France on his death in 1766, and Francis Stephen of Lorraine became heir to Tuscany. Don Carlos gave up Parma, which went to Austria, and was confirmed as king of Naples and Sicily, while Charles Emmanuel gained territory west of the Ticino including Novara and Tortona. France recognised the Pragmatic Sanction. The war reaffirmed that Poland-Lithuania's affairs, including the election of its ruler, were controlled by the great powers.
war-of-the-quadruple-alliance: Under the Peace of Utrecht of 1713, which ended the War of the Spanish Succession, Spain ceded Sardinia to Austria and Sicily to Savoy. Recovering them was a priority for Philip V of Spain, a priority reinforced by his chief minister Cardinal Giulio Alberoni and by his second wife Elisabeth Farnese, both natives of Parma.

Utrecht barred Spain from ever uniting with France or Austria, and Philip gave up any claim to the French throne. After deaths in the French royal family in 1711 and 1712 made him heir presumptive to the young Louis XV, he cast doubt on that renunciation. Britain and France agreed an alliance in 1716 and formed the Triple Alliance with the Dutch in January 1717 to enforce the terms.

Spanish forces landed on Sardinia in August 1717 and held it by November, meeting little opposition. In July 1718 the Spanish landed 30,000 men on Sicily. By then Austria had signed a treaty with the Ottoman Empire and joined the Quadruple Alliance. On 11 August a British squadron under Sir George Byng destroyed the Spanish fleet at the Battle of Cape Passaro. An Austrian force was defeated at the First Battle of Milazzo on 15 October. After the discovery of the Cellamare conspiracy, Alberoni's plot to replace the regent of France with Philip V, France declared war, and by 17 December 1718 France, Britain and Austria were all at war with Spain; the Dutch joined in August 1719.

In April 1719 a French army under the Duke of Berwick invaded the Basque districts and besieged San Sebastián. An expedition under the Duke of Ormonde to put James Stuart on the British throne was scattered by a storm in March 1719, and a small force of Spanish marines was defeated with its Highland allies at Glen Shiel in June. A British raid took Vigo in October. In Sicily the Austrians under Count de Mercy lost at Francavilla on 20 June 1719 but won the second Battle of Milazzo, took Messina in October and besieged Palermo.

Philip dismissed Alberoni in December 1719 and made peace by the Treaty of The Hague on 17 February 1720. He relinquished all territory captured in the war, but his third surviving son's right to the Duchy of Parma and Piacenza was recognised. France returned Pensacola and its conquests in northern Spain in exchange for commercial benefits, and Victor Amadeus II of Savoy exchanged Sicily for Sardinia. The war was unusual in the 18th century in having Britain and France on the same side.
war-of-the-second-coalition: The war followed the War of the First Coalition (1792–97), which ended with the Treaty of Leoben on 18 April 1797 and the Treaty of Campo Formio in October 1797, leaving Britain to fight on alone. Peace between France and Austria was uneasy: the French demanded territory the treaty did not name, the Habsburgs were reluctant to hand over what it did, and in 1798 Napoleon Bonaparte's seizure of Malta angered Emperor Paul I of Russia, the honorary head of the order of knights that ruled the island.

The coalition took months to form. Naples allied with Austria on 19 May 1798 and with Russia on 29 November, and Russia allied with the Ottoman Empire on 23 December and with Britain on 26 December. Prussia declined to join.

Britain and Russia aimed to stop the French Republic's expansion and restore the monarchy, while Austria, weakened and deep in debt, sought chiefly to recover its position. In 1799 the Russian general Alexander Suvorov won a series of victories in Italy and drove the French back to the Alps. The Anglo-Russian invasion of Holland failed, and in Switzerland an Austro-Russian army was routed at the Second Battle of Zurich. These reverses, and British searches of shipping in the Baltic, led Russia to leave the coalition. Napoleon returned from Egypt in October 1799 and a coup made him First Consul.

In 1800 Napoleon led an army across the Great St. Bernard Pass and narrowly defeated the Austrians at the Battle of Marengo, after which Austria agreed to evacuate Piedmont, Liguria and Lombardy. Moreau invaded Bavaria and won the Battle of Hohenlinden, and the Armistice of Steyr followed on 25 December. In 1801 the British navy attacked the Danish fleet at the Battle of Copenhagen, after the Second League of Armed Neutrality had formed against searches of neutral ships, and the Ottomans and British forced the French in Egypt to surrender.

Austria signed the Armistice of Treviso on 16 January 1801 and, on 9 February, the Treaty of Lunéville for the whole Holy Roman Empire, in effect accepting the terms of Campo Formio. France kept all its earlier gains and obtained new lands in Tuscany, while Austria was granted Venetia and the former Venetian Dalmatia. Most other allies signed separate peaces in 1801. Britain and France signed the Treaty of Amiens in March 1802, followed by the Ottomans in June 1802. The peace lasted several months, until Britain declared war on France in May 1803 and began the Napoleonic Wars. The coalition had failed to overthrow the revolutionary government, largely because of differences of strategy among its three major powers.
war-of-the-sixth-coalition: Napoleon invaded Russia in June 1812 to compel Emperor Alexander I to remain in the Continental System. The Grande Armée numbered as many as 650,000 men, about half of them French. After the inconclusive Battle of Borodino and the French occupation of Moscow, which Alexander refused to bargain over, Napoleon was forced to withdraw. The Prussian corps that had been compelled to serve with him was neutralised by the Convention of Tauroggen, signed on 30 December 1812 without the consent of the Prussian king, and the Treaty of Kalisch on 28 February 1813 ranged Prussia on the Allied side.

Napoleon raised new forces and inflicted 40,000 casualties on the Allies at Lützen on 2 May and at Bautzen on 20 and 21 May 1813, though he lost about as many men. An armistice ran from 4 June to 13 August, during which Austria joined the Allies. Napoleon won at Dresden on 26 and 27 August, but at the Battle of Leipzig, the Battle of Nations, from 16 to 19 October, a French army reinforced to 191,000 faced more than 430,000 Allied troops. He retreated in fairly good order, though the bridge over the White Elster was blown early and 30,000 men were left to be captured.

Meanwhile Wellington routed Joseph Bonaparte's army at Vitoria on 21 June 1813. In France, Napoleon won several battles in the Six Days' Campaign in early 1814 with fewer than 80,000 men against a Coalition force of 370,000 to 405,000. At the Treaty of Chaumont on 9 March the Allies agreed to keep the Coalition until Napoleon's total defeat. Their armies entered Paris on 31 March.

On 2 April the French Senate declared Napoleon deposed. He wished to fight on, but on 4 April his marshals, led by Ney, refused to march. Napoleon abdicated on 11 April 1814, and the Treaty of Paris followed on 30 May. He was exiled to Elba and the Bourbon monarchy was restored under Louis XVIII. The Congress of Vienna, from September 1814 to June 1815, was held to redraw the map of Europe. Norway declared independence on 17 May 1814, and Bernadotte invaded it in July.
war-of-the-spanish-succession: Charles II of Spain became king in 1665 at the age of four, and his poor health and lack of children made the succession a long-standing European diplomatic issue. Louis XIV of France and the Holy Roman Emperor Leopold I were both grandsons of Philip III of Spain, through his daughters, and the Spanish throne could pass through women. Spain remained a global power supported by silver from the Americas, yet most of that income was already committed to creditors, and the Bourbons later found the empire bankrupt and almost defenceless, with fewer than 15,000 troops in Spain itself and a navy of 20 ships.

Charles II died in November 1700 and named Philip of Anjou his universal heir, with the support of Louis XIV. Philip was proclaimed king on 16 November 1700, which triggered the war. Britain and the Dutch Republic were driven largely by access to Spanish markets in the Americas, and they feared that France or Austria would acquire an undivided Spanish monarchy.

The Second Grand Alliance backed Charles of Austria. In Italy, Prince Eugene of Savoy led an Imperial army against the French from May 1701, and by February 1702 victories at Carpi, Chiari and Cremona forced them behind the Adda. In the Low Countries the Allies took Kaiserswerth, Venlo, Roermond, Liège and, in 1703, Bonn, but failed to take Antwerp. Britain's interest lay in protecting its Mediterranean trade routes, and by 1708 it held permanent bases at Gibraltar and Menorca. The fighting spread to North America, where it is known as Queen Anne's War, and to the West Indies.

By 1709 the Allies had put France on the defensive, but Philip had secured his position in Spain, and the Great Frost of that year caused famine in France and Spain. Talks at Geertruidenberg in 1710 broke down. The pro-peace Tories won the British election of October 1710, and when Charles of Austria became Holy Roman emperor in 1711 the British government began negotiating its withdrawal.

The Peace of Utrecht of 1713 was followed by the treaties of Rastatt and Baden in 1714. Philip was confirmed as king of Spain but renounced his rights in the French line, and Spain ceded the Spanish Netherlands, most of its Italian possessions, Gibraltar and Menorca. Austria gained the bulk of the Spanish Netherlands, together with Milan, Mantua, Naples and Sardinia, and Britain became the leading naval and commercial power while the Dutch were left bankrupt. Catalonia fought on until the fall of Barcelona in September 1714. Philip's Bourbon successors have held the Spanish throne ever since. Louis XIV died on 1 September 1715.
war-of-the-third-coalition: The Peace of Amiens broke down in 1803, and Britain declared war on France on 18 May 1803. Tensions had grown as Napoleon made himself president of the Italian Republic, annexed Piedmont and kept French troops in the Netherlands. After he crowned himself Emperor on 2 December 1804, the annexation of Genoa, Parma and Piacenza and his coronation as King of Italy left little doubt about his intentions. On 21 January 1805 William Pitt the Younger proposed an alliance with Russia and Austria. Sweden joined Britain in December 1804, Russia on 11 April 1805 and Austria on 9 August; Naples and Sicily completed the coalition on 11 September. Prussia stayed neutral.

Napoleon turned the army he had gathered at Boulogne for an invasion of England towards the Rhine. In the Ulm campaign, 210,000 French troops marched east to envelop the Austrian army of General Mack, who had made Ulm the centre of his defence while waiting for the Russians under Mikhail Kutuzov. When Mack heard that Bernadotte's corps had crossed Prussian Ansbach, he chose to stay at Ulm instead of retreating south. Murat forced General Werneck to surrender with 8,000 men at Trochtelfingten on 19 October. Two days later the Royal Navy under Horatio Nelson defeated the combined Franco-Spanish fleet at Trafalgar.

At Austerlitz, Napoleon gave the Allies the impression that his army was weak and deliberately thinned his right flank, expecting them to weaken their own centre in attacking it. He ordered Davout's corps to march 110 km in 48 hours to support that flank, then sent Soult's IV Corps against the centre, saying, "One sharp blow and the war is over." In Italy, the French defeated the Austrians at Caldiero between 29 and 31 October. In February 1806 Masséna invaded Naples, and King Ferdinand IV fled to Sicily under British naval protection.

On 26 December 1805 Austria and France signed the Treaty of Pressburg, which confirmed Austrian cessions in Italy and Germany and imposed an indemnity of 40 million francs. After Austerlitz Napoleon created the Confederation of the Rhine, whose German states pledged to raise an army of 63,000 men. In 1806 Francis II abdicated the imperial throne and the Holy Roman Empire ceased to exist. The French lost 12,000 killed, 22,200 wounded and 5,000 captured in 1805. Peace was not lasting: neither Russia nor Britain stopped fighting, and Prussian worries about French influence led to the War of the Fourth Coalition in 1806.
warangal: Warangal lies at an average elevation of 266 metres on the eastern Deccan Plateau, a landscape of granite rocks and hills. No major river flows near it, so the city relies on the Kakatiya Canal for water. During the 160 years of Kakatiya rule between 1163 and 1323 it was known by names such as Orugallu, Ekashila Nagaram and Omatikonda, all meaning a single stone, in reference to a huge granite boulder in the Warangal fort. Three lakes, Bhadrakali, Dharmasagar and Waddepally, lie around it, with several hills carrying temples.

Beta Raja I founded the Kakatiya dynasty, and his son Prola Raja I shifted the capital to Hanamkonda. Under Ganapathideva it moved from Hanamkonda to Warangal. Later rulers included Rudradeva, Mahadeva, Prataparudra and Rani Rudrama Devi, the only woman to rule the Telugu region. Kakatiya inscriptions praised Warangal as the best city in the Telugu region, up to the shores of the ocean, and Marco Polo mentioned the dynasty's cultural and administrative distinction. The Kakatiyas left a fortress, four massive stone gateways, the Swayambhu temple of Shiva and the Ramappa temple near Ramappa Lake.

In 1323 the Delhi Sultanate defeated the Kakatiya dynasty, and Juna Khan, crown prince of Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq, conquered the city and renamed it Sultanpur. In 1336 the Musunuri Nayaks, who united 72 Nayak chieftains, recaptured it, restored the name Orugallu and ruled for fifty years. Warangal then belonged to the Bahmani Sultanate and the Sultanate of Golconda. Aurangzeb conquered Golconda in 1687, and in 1724 the southern provinces split away as the state of Hyderabad, which was annexed to India in 1948. Telangana state, including Warangal, was formed on 2 June 2014.

Together with Kazipet and Hanamkonda, Warangal forms the Warangal Tri-City. The Warangal Fort, the Thousand Pillar Temple and the Ramappa Temple are listed among the World Heritage Sites recognised by UNESCO. The Kakatiya Kala Thoranam, the gateway of the fort, appears in the emblem of Telangana. The Greater Warangal Municipal Corporation, established in 1899, is one of the oldest urban local bodies in India. The women of the city celebrate the floral festival of Bathukamma, honouring the goddess with flowers for nine days.
waren-muritz: Waren lies at the northern end of Lake Müritz, which has an area of 117 square kilometres and is the largest inland lake lying entirely within Germany, about 40 kilometres west of Neubrandenburg. It also lies on several smaller lakes, and the Herrensee is in the middle of the town. Waren was the capital of the former district of Müritz until the district reform of 2011. Its name may come from a Slavic word for a place of crows or ravens, or from the Germanic Warini; the lake's name derives from a Wend word for sea.

Claudius Ptolemy mentioned a place called Virunum around 150 CE that is identified with Waren. The medieval town was founded around 1260 by settlers from Westphalia, on the trade route from Stargard Land to Wismar, near a castle and a Slavic village. It grew up around St George's Church, first mentioned in 1273, with a New Town around St Mary's Church, which was merged with it in 1325. Waren is called a civitas in 1292 and an oppidum from 1331, and received fishing rights on the Müritz in 1306. From 1347 to 1425 it was the residence of a branch of the House of Werle.

Fires in 1568, 1637, 1671, 1673 and 1699, and the Thirty Years' War, repeatedly devastated the town. The present town hall dates from 1791 to 1797. The canalisation of the Elde and the Bolter Canal brought an economic boom in the 19th century, and railways opened in 1879, 1885 and 1886 made Waren a transport hub. During the Kapp Putsch in March 1920 a Freikorps group under Stephan von le Fort fired on the town from Gallows Hill, killing five people; a bullet hole at the town hall recalls it.

Under the Nazis the Jewish community, some 150 in the mid-19th century, dwindled to nine by April 1938, and none remained in 1942. From 1936 a metal works supplying military aircraft used thousands of prisoners of war and forced labourers. The Red Army occupied the town without a fight on 1 May 1945. Large parts of the old town were demolished in the 1970s, which prompted a citizens' movement to save it, and the centre was renovated from 1991.

Waren has been a state-approved health resort since 1 May 1999. Its two brick churches, St George's from the early 14th century and St Mary's, a town hall on the New Market and a harbour with old warehouses stand in the historic centre. The Müritzeum is a freshwater aquarium and an information centre for the Müritz National Park, and the town lies beside the park and the Nossentiner/Schwinzer Heath Nature Park.
warli: Until the 1870s the Warli were the primary owners of all land in the Umbergaon, Dhanu and Palghar talukas of the Thane district. In that decade the British colonial administration brought their territories under direct control, and outsiders, among them Mahajans and petty officers, used the Warlis' illiteracy to take their lands. The Warli became labourers on land they had owned. Under the begar system they cultivated the landlords' holdings without pay; as sharecroppers on small plots of inferior land they surrendered at least half the produce. Records of the period document public whippings, torture and the sexual oppression of Warli women.

In 1939 an inquiry by the British magistrate David Symington found that their living conditions had reached an abysmal depth. Organised resistance followed, led by Shamrao and Godavari Parulekar. In May 1945 about 5,000 Warlis gathered at Zari and pledged to end the begar system. In October 1945 police fired on a rally of 7,000 people at Talwada, killing five activists, among them the leader Jethya Gangad. The begar system was abolished and minimum wages were established, and by the early 1950s most of the feudal exactions had ended.

The Warli speak Varli, an unwritten language of the southern zone of the Indo-Aryan languages. They have animistic beliefs of their own and have also adopted many Hindu beliefs. Traditionally semi-nomadic, living in small groups led by a headman, they are today mainly agriculturists who grow rice and wheat among other crops. Married women wear toe rings and necklaces, and some Warli practise polygyny.

Their ritual paintings are made inside the huts, for occasions such as weddings and harvests, in white rice paste on walls of branches, earth and cow dung, with a bamboo stick chewed at the end as a brush. At the centre stands a square, the chauk, which in one type encloses the mother goddess Palaghata, symbol of fertility; around it are scenes of hunting, fishing, farming and dancing. Human and animal bodies are drawn as two triangles joined at the tip.

Painting was the preserve of Warli women until the late 1970s. In that decade Jivya Soma Mashe and his son Balu Mashe began to paint outside any ritual, as an artistic pursuit of their own. The writer Yashodhara Dalmia, in The Painted World of the Warlis, claimed that the tradition reaches back to 2500 or 3000 BCE.
warren-hastings: Warren Hastings was born at Churchill, Oxfordshire, on 6 December 1732; his mother died soon after, and he was raised by his grandfather and then by an uncle, who sent him to Westminster School. He left at sixteen when his uncle died, and joined the East India Company as a writer in 1750. He learned Urdu and Persian, and in 1752 was sent to the trading post at Kasimbazar. In 1756 he was imprisoned by Siraj ud-Daulah, escaped, and served as a volunteer in Robert Clive's force that retook Calcutta in January 1757.

In 1758 he became the British resident at Murshidabad. Back on the Calcutta council from 1761, he protested against abuses of private trade, was overruled, and resigned in December 1764. He returned to India in 1769 as deputy ruler at Madras, and in 1772 became governor at Calcutta.

The Regulating Act 1773 put Madras and Bombay under Bengal and made Hastings the first Governor-General, as one member of a five-man Supreme Council. According to William Dalrymple, he moved government from Murshidabad to Calcutta, unified currency systems, ordered the codification of Hindu and Muslim law, reformed the tax and customs system, backed James Rennell's survey of India and built granaries to guard against a repeat of the famine of 1770-71. In 1774 he sent troops to help the wazir of Oudh against the Rohillas, the first of several wars that harmed his reputation.

From 1779 to 1784 he faced a coalition of Hyder Ali of Mysore, the Nizam of Hyderabad and the Marathas, with a French fleet under Admiral Suffren also in the field. He made peace with the Marathas in 1782 and broke up the coalition. He raised funds from local treasuries, which later became the main line of attack against him. In 1781 he founded the Madrasa 'Aliya at Calcutta.

Hastings resigned in 1785 and was replaced by Lord Cornwallis. Impeached by the House of Commons in 1787 over embezzlement, extortion and coercion, he was tried before the House of Lords from 13 February 1788, with Edmund Burke among the prosecutors. The trial took 148 days over seven years, and he was acquitted on 24 April 1795, though he complained of being bankrupted by its cost. He was made a privy councillor in 1814 and died on 22 August 1818.

His introduction to Charles Wilkins's translation of the Bhagavad Gita, dated 4 October 1784, argued that knowledge of a conquered people was useful to the state. Historians note that his reliance on Brahmin advisers to interpret Hindu law helped solidify caste privileges.
warring-states-period: The Warring States period covers the final centuries of the Zhou dynasty, after the Spring and Autumn period. Several dates have been proposed for its beginning, but Sima Qian's choice of 475 BCE is the most often cited. The king of Zhou still formally ruled as sovereign but had lost political power and functioned in practice as a figurehead. The name comes from the Record of the Warring States, a history compiled in the early Han dynasty, and also reflects how the scale of warfare grew. In 403 BCE the Zhou court recognised the rulers of Zhao, Wei and Han as marquises after they conquered Jin, and in 376 BCE the three divided the last Jin territory between them.

As Qin grew disproportionately powerful, the policies of many states became oriented towards dealing with it. The Vertical Alliances, led by Su Qin, tried to stop Qin's advance, while Qin pressed neighbours into the Horizontal Alliances led by Zhang Yi; the Zhan Guo Ce records their dealings. A cycle of abortive alliances followed, and Qin invaded Zhou and ended its line of monarchs in 256 BCE.

The last stage began under Zheng, who succeeded King Zhuangxiang of Qin at the age of 13. In 230 BCE Qin ordered Neishi Teng to conquer Han, and over about ten years Zheng's armies annexed each of the other contender states. By 221 BCE Qin had founded the Qin dynasty, the first imperial dynastic state in East Asian history.

Warfare changed in scale. Near the start of the period chariots gave way to massed infantry with swords and crossbows, battles could last months or even years, and iron weapons began to replace bronze. The first native Chinese cavalry unit was formed in 307 BCE under King Wuling of Zhao. Reported casualties, such as 240,000 killed at the Battle of Yique, are thought exaggerated by scholars including Michael Loewe and Edward L. Shaughnessy, but warfare clearly became excessive.

Wandering scholars offered advice to competing rulers, and the Hundred Schools of Thought arose, among them Mohism, Confucianism, Legalism and Taoism. Four of the Seven Military Classics, including the Art of War, belong to the period. Linzi, the capital of Qi, was a centre of trade in salt, silk and iron.
wars-of-alexander-the-great: Alexander became king of Macedon in 336 BCE, after his father Philip II was assassinated by Pausanias of Orestis, the captain of his bodyguards. He also succeeded Philip as head of the League of Corinth, the confederation of Greek states under Macedonian hegemony that had been formed to oppose the Achaemenid Empire. The news of Philip's death roused Thebes, Athens, Thessaly and the Thracian tribes to revolt, and Alexander acted quickly, riding south with 3,000 Macedonian cavalry and going round the Thessalians by crossing Mount Ossa.

In the spring of 335 BCE Alexander marched into Thrace and defeated the Triballi and the Illyrian kings Cleitus and Glaukias. While he was in the north, Thebes rebelled again; the city was razed and its territory divided among the other Boeotian cities, which cowed Athens into submission. In 334 BCE he crossed the Hellespont into Asia. He won at the Granicus River in May 334 BCE, at Issus in November 333 BCE, where Darius III fled the field, and at Gaugamela in 331 BCE. In 332 BCE he took Tyre, the last Persian port to hold out, which held about 40,000 people.

From 329 BCE he fought in Bactria and Sogdiana, against Spitamenes and the Sakas, and in 327 BCE his men took the Sogdian Rock by night. There he met Roxana, whom he later married. In 327 and 326 BCE he fought the hill clans of Gandhara, and Curtius reports that the whole population of Massaga was killed. He defeated the king Porus at the Hydaspes in 326 BCE, the most costly battle the Macedonians fought. At the Hyphasis River his exhausted army refused to go further east, and the river marks the limit of his conquests.

Alexander sent part of his army to Carmania under Craterus and a fleet under Nearchus along the Persian Gulf, and led the rest back to Persia through the Gedrosian Desert. According to Plutarch, he lost three quarters of his army on the sixty-day march. He had also planned an expedition into Arabia and then a campaign westward against Carthage, but after his death his generals, the Diadochi, abandoned these plans. His empire proved unstable. It broke up in the Wars of the Diadochi, which lasted about forty years and belong to the Hellenistic period.
wars-of-the-roses: The wars were known at the time and for long afterwards as the Civil Wars. The name Wars of the Roses refers to the white rose of York and the red rose of Lancaster, which was the Lancastrian emblem by 1485. Historians disagree over the main causes. They point to the economic and social troubles that followed the Hundred Years' War with France, and to the powerful duchies Edward III created for his sons, which fed a bastard feudalism in which great lords kept private forces. The succession after Edward III's death in 1377 is held by the historian Ian Mortimer to be the root cause.

Henry IV took the throne in 1399 from Richard II, basing his right on descent in the male line from John of Gaunt, though Edmund Mortimer, descended through Lionel, Duke of Clarence, could be argued to be the heir presumptive. The mental instability of Henry VI revived the interest of his cousin Richard of York, 3rd Duke of York, in a claim of his own.

Fighting began on 22 May 1455 at the First Battle of St Albans, where York captured the king and several of his rivals were killed, among them Edmund Beaufort, 2nd Duke of Somerset. After Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick, took Henry again at Northampton, York was killed at Wakefield, and his 18-year-old son Edward inherited the claim. Edward defeated the Lancastrians at Towton and was crowned on 28 June 1461.

Edward IV's secret marriage to Elizabeth Woodville, discovered by Warwick in October 1464, and his refusal to follow Warwick's policy of closeness to France led to Warwick's rebellion. With Margaret of Anjou, Warwick invaded in September 1470 and Henry VI was restored, while Edward fled to Flanders. Edward returned with Burgundian aid, killed Warwick at Barnet, and on 4 May 1471 defeated Margaret's army at Tewkesbury, where Henry's only son Edward of Westminster was killed.

Edward IV ruled for twelve more years. After his death in 1483 his twelve-year-old son Edward V reigned for 78 days before his uncle Richard of Gloucester took the throne as Richard III, amid controversy over the disappearance of Edward IV's two sons. Henry Tudor, in exile in Brittany and then France, returned and killed Richard at Bosworth Field in 1485.

Henry was crowned Henry VII on 30 October 1485 and married Elizabeth of York, Edward IV's eldest daughter, on 18 January 1486, uniting the two claims. Challengers remained, and the wars ended in 1487 with his defeat of the Yorkist opposition at Stoke Field. The Tudors ruled until 1603. Some historians, such as K. B. McFarlane, hold that the effects of the conflict on English society were exaggerated: many parts of England, East Anglia above all, were largely unaffected.
wars-of-the-three-kingdoms: England, Ireland and Scotland were separate kingdoms joined in a personal union when James VI of Scotland succeeded Elizabeth I in 1603. His son Charles I faced disputes with the English Parliament over taxation, military expenditure and the limits of its role, and he held to the divine right of kings. Religion deepened the quarrel. English Puritans and Scottish Covenanters opposed his changes to the state churches, while in Ireland, the one kingdom with a Catholic majority, Catholics wanted an end to discrimination, more self-government and a reversal of land grants to Protestant settlers. The name itself appears first in a 1662 chronicle by James Heath, and historians use other labels as well.

The Bishops' Wars of 1639 and 1640 began when Scottish Covenanters, who had signed the National Covenant of 1638 against religious innovations, took control of Scotland and briefly occupied northern England. An Irish Catholic rebellion followed in 1641, with widespread assaults on Protestant communities, and the Irish Catholic Confederation came to hold most of Ireland. Because Parliament and the king each distrusted the other with an army, the English Civil War began in 1642. The Covenanters joined Parliament in late 1643, and Charles surrendered to the Scottish army on 5 May 1646.

Fighting resumed in 1648 in the Second English Civil War, in which the New Model Army defeated the Royalists and the Scottish Engagers. After the army purged Parliament, the Rump Parliament approved the trial of Charles, who was executed on 30 January 1649, and declared England a republic. Oliver Cromwell landed in Ireland in August 1649 and defeated the Covenanters at Dunbar on 3 September 1650. The last Royalist army, under Charles II, was beaten at Worcester on 3 September 1651.

Ireland and Scotland were ruled by military governors, their parliaments were abolished, and in Ireland almost all land held by Catholics was confiscated, with Penal Laws restricting them further. After Cromwell died in 1658, George Monck marched from Scotland to London in early 1660, and the Convention Parliament invited Charles II to return on 1 May 1660. The Restoration brought back the prewar constitutional position and the parliaments of Scotland and Ireland, and those held responsible for the regicide were executed or imprisoned. The issues of religion, the powers of Parliament and the relations between the kingdoms remained unresolved and re-emerged in the Glorious Revolution of 1688.
warsaw: Warsaw lies in east-central Poland on both banks of the Vistula, in the heartland of the Masovian Plain, about 260 km from the Baltic Sea and 523 km east of Berlin. The name in Polish is Warszawa, and its origin is uncertain. One hypothesis reads it as belonging to Warsz, a short form of the Old Polish name Warcisław, and the original Warszawa was a small fishing settlement on the river bank. Folk etymology tells of the fisherman Wars and the mermaid Sawa, who lived in the Vistula.

The first fortified settlements on the site were at Bródno in the 9th or 10th century and at Jazdów in the 12th or 13th century. Bolesław II of Masovia, Prince of Płock, established the town in about 1300, and in 1413 it was officially made capital of the Masovian Duchy, when it had about 4,500 inhabitants. The city rose to prominence after 1596, when Sigismund III moved the Polish capital and royal court from Kraków. By the 18th century Warsaw had passed Gdańsk as the most populous city of Poland. It was the capital of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth until 1795 and afterwards the seat of Napoleon's Duchy of Warsaw.

The 19th century and the Industrial Revolution made it one of the largest and most densely populated cities in Europe. Before the Second World War it held the world's second-largest Jewish population after New York, about 30 percent of its people in the late 1930s. The city was bombed and besieged in 1939. Much of the historic city was destroyed and its diverse population decimated by the Ghetto Uprising of 1943, the Warsaw Uprising of 1944 and systematic razing.

Warsaw is the capital and most populous city of Poland, with about 1.87 million residents, and the seat of both houses of the Polish Parliament. The reconstructed Old Town was listed as a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 1980. Other landmarks are the Royal Castle, Sigismund's Column and Wilanów Palace.
warsaw-pact: The formal name of the pact was the Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation and Mutual Assistance. Before it, the Czechoslovak leadership, fearful of a re-militarised West Germany, sought a security pact with East Germany and Poland. In 1954 the Soviet Union proposed German reunification under neutrality and a General European Treaty on Collective Security, and then asked to join NATO, but the United States, the United Kingdom and France rejected all of these.

On 23 October 1954 the admission of the Federal Republic of Germany to NATO was decided, and it joined on 9 May 1955. On 14 May 1955 the Soviet Union and seven other Eastern European states established the pact in response. NATO officials, noting that the Soviet Union already had troops and political dominance in these states, called it a cardboard castle.

The founding members were the Soviet Union, Albania, Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, East Germany, Hungary, Poland and Romania. In November 1956, after the government of Imre Nagy declared Hungary's withdrawal, Soviet troops entered and crushed the revolt, which killed an estimated 2,500 Hungarian citizens. The Soviet Union then made twenty-year bilateral treaties with Poland, East Germany, Romania and Hungary to keep its troops there. The pact's one joint action was the invasion of Czechoslovakia in August 1968, in which every member took part except Romania and Albania, and East Germany gave only minimal support. Albania, which had withheld support since 1961, withdrew formally on 13 September 1968.

In 1989 popular discontent toppled the communist governments of Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, East Germany, Romania and Bulgaria. East Germany left the pact on 24 September 1990, before German reunification. On 25 February 1991 the defence and foreign ministers of the remaining members declared the pact disbanded at a meeting in Hungary, and on 1 July 1991 in Prague the Czechoslovak president Václav Havel formally ended the treaty. The Soviet Union dissolved itself in December of that year.

The organisation had two parts: the Political Consultative Committee, for political matters, and the Combined Command of Pact Armed Forces, with its headquarters in Warsaw. On paper, members pledged mutual defence and non-intervention in each other's internal affairs. In practice the commanders were always senior Soviet officers, and the Supreme Commander was also a First Deputy Minister of Defence of the Soviet Union. The Soviet Ground Forces shaped the Eastern European armies in their own image for a possible confrontation with NATO. The pact was the military counterpart of Comecon, the economic organisation of the Eastern Bloc.
warsaw-pact-invasion-of-czechoslovakia: De-Stalinization in Czechoslovakia began under Antonín Novotný in the late 1950s and early 1960s but progressed more slowly than in most Eastern Bloc states. An economic downturn in the early 1960s, and the New Economic Model of 1965, increased demand for political reform. On 5 January 1968 Alexander Dubček was elected First Secretary of the Communist Party of Czechoslovakia (KSČ), beginning the Prague Spring. His reforms partly decentralised the economy and loosened restrictions on the media, speech and travel, and censorship was abolished on 4 March 1968.

Leonid Brezhnev and the leaders of other Warsaw Pact countries feared that the liberalisation would harm their interests. They worried that Czechoslovakia might defect from the Eastern Bloc, leaving the Soviet Union without strategic depth or Czechoslovakia's industrial base in a war with NATO, although Czechoslovak leaders had no intention of leaving the Warsaw Pact. Negotiations in July 1968 at Čierna nad Tisou ended in a compromise.

At about 11 pm on 20 August 1968 the armies of the Soviet Union, Bulgaria, Poland and Hungary invaded. That night 250,000 troops and 2,000 tanks entered the country, and the total eventually reached about 500,000. Romania and Albania refused to take part, and Moscow ordered East German forces not to cross the border, because of the public memory of the German occupation three decades earlier. Brezhnev wanted the operation to appear multilateral, but Soviet troops outnumbered the others five to one, and the Soviet High Command was in charge throughout.

The Dubček government had taken no steps to forestall an invasion. By the morning of 21 August Dubček and other prominent reformists had been arrested and flown to Moscow. Popular opposition took the form of spontaneous nonviolent resistance, as Czechs and Slovaks met the soldiers with arguments and reproaches. During the occupation 137 Czechoslovaks were killed and 500 seriously wounded.

Reactions were divided. Most Warsaw Pact states supported the invasion, while Western nations, Romania, China and Albania condemned it, and many communist parties outside the bloc split or lost influence. Albania formally withdrew from the Warsaw Pact in September 1968. When Gustáv Husák replaced Dubček as leader of the KSČ in April 1969, his regime began normalisation, restoring firm party rule and removing the reformers. In 1989 Hungary, Poland, East Germany and Bulgaria each condemned or apologised for their part in the invasion.
