wartburg: The Wartburg stands on a precipice 410 metres high, overlooking the town of Eisenach, on an extension of the Thuringian Forest above the valley of the Hörsel, through which ran the historical Via Regia. Its name probably comes from Warte, a watchtower, in spite of a tradition that its founder exclaimed, Wait, mountain, you shall bear my castle. The foundation was laid about 1067 by a Thuringian count, who with the larger sister castle Neuenburg secured the borders of his territories. The castle is first mentioned in writing in 1080, as Wartberg, by Bruno, Bishop of Merseburg, in his account of the Saxon War.

In 1131 the founder's son Louis I was raised to landgrave of Thuringia by King Lothair of Supplinburg. From 1172 to 1211 the Wartburg was one of the most important princely courts in the German Reich. Hermann I supported poets such as Walther von der Vogelweide and Wolfram von Eschenbach, who wrote part of Parzival there in 1203. The Sängerkrieg, or Minstrels' Contest, is set at the castle in 1206 or 1207 and was later used by Richard Wagner in Tannhäuser. Elisabeth of Hungary was sent there at the age of four to be raised as consort of Landgrave Ludwig IV, and lived there from 1211 to 1228 known for her charitable work.

The Wartburg remained the seat of the Thuringian landgraves until 1440. Martin Luther stayed there from May 1521 to March 1522 as Junker Jörg, taken there for his safety at the request of Frederick the Wise after the Diet of Worms, and translated the New Testament from Greek into German in ten weeks. On 18 October 1817 about 500 students of the new Burschenschaften met there, celebrating the victory over Napoleon and the 300th anniversary of the Reformation and calling for German unity under the motto Honour, Freedom, Fatherland.

Grand Duke Karl Alexander ordered a reconstruction in 1838, in Neo-Romanesque style under the architect Hugo von Ritgen, as a national cultural monument. The Wartburg Foundation was established in 1922, and the castle was restored again in 1952–54. It contains substantial original structures from the 12th to the 15th centuries, though much of the interior dates only from the 19th century. It inspired Ludwig II when he decided to build Neuschwanstein, and in 1999 it was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List for its medieval architecture and its historical and religious significance.
warwick: Warwick is a market town adjacent to the River Avon, 14 kilometres south of Coventry and 31 kilometres south-east of Birmingham. Human activity on the hilltop goes back to the Neolithic, when a sizeable settlement stood there, and the footings of a large Roman barn of the 2nd century have been found. The town has been continuously inhabited from the 5th century. Its Old English name, Wæringwīc, may mean a settlement of a clan called the Wæring, or a fortification, or a place by a weir on the Avon.

Æthelflæd, Lady of the Mercians, built a burh on the hilltop in 914, one of ten to defend Mercia from the Vikings, on a sandstone outcrop beside the river crossing. In the early 10th century a shire was founded with Warwick as its county town, and a royal mint was established under Æthelstan (924–939) that continued to the mid-12th century. The Danes burned much of the town in 1016. William the Conqueror founded the castle in 1068, and a town wall was built close to the burh ramparts. The Earls of Warwick, mostly of the Beauchamp family, controlled the medieval town, whose prosperity rested on its role as an administrative and military centre rather than on trade. It was incorporated as a borough in 1545.

In 1642, during the Civil War, Royalists besieged the castle, which was held for Parliament, for two weeks without cannon strong enough to damage it. The Great Fire of Warwick on 5 September 1694 destroyed 460 buildings in five hours and left 250 families homeless. Most of the centre was rebuilt in the Georgian style by architects including Francis Smith and later William and David Hiorne.

Warwick was largely bypassed by the Industrial Revolution, partly because it did not lie on important roads and the Avon was not navigable as far as the town. Its Collegiate Church of St Mary, rebuilt after the fire, keeps the Beauchamp Chapel of 1443–1464, with a copper-gilt effigy of Richard Beauchamp, Earl of Warwick, cast in 1459. The Lord Leycester Hospital on the High Street has parts dating from 1383, and the east and west gatehouses are the only remains of the town wall. Warwick adjoins Leamington Spa and Whitnash, and it is the county town of Warwickshire.
warwick-rhode-island: Warwick lies in Kent County, Rhode Island, about 12 miles south of downtown Providence and 63 miles south-west of Boston. Its entire eastern edge is waterfront. The Providence River marks its northern border with Cranston, and the shore turns into Narragansett Bay at Conimicut Point. Two southern peninsulas, Warwick Neck and Potowomut, enclose Greenwich Bay. The city has a total area of 49.6 square miles, of which 35.5 are land, and includes many villages, among them Apponaug, Conimicut, Pawtuxet Village and Shawomet.

Samuel Gorton settled the area in 1642. The Narragansett sachem Miantonomi sold him the Shawhomett Purchase for 144 fathoms of wampum, but the sachems Sacononoco and Pumham claimed he had sold the land without their approval and took their case to Boston, placing their lands under Massachusetts rule. In 1643 the Massachusetts Bay Colony sent a militia force to arrest Gorton and his followers, and all but three of them surrendered.

Gorton sailed to England and sought a charter from the king, helped by Robert Rich, 2nd Earl of Warwick, after whom the settlers renamed their colony Warwick. Continuing harassment from Massachusetts led the other three Narragansett Bay colonies, Providence Plantations, Portsmouth and Newport, to unite with Warwick under a royal charter as the Colony of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations.

Warwick was badly damaged in King Philip's War of 1675 to 1676. In 1772 local patriots boarded the Gaspee, a revenue cutter enforcing the Stamp Act 1765 and the Townshend Acts in Narragansett Bay. Its commanding officer was shot and seriously wounded, and the ship was stripped of its guns and burned. This is described as the first violent act against the British Crown before the American Revolution. Warwick was also the home of General Nathanael Greene, George Washington's second-in-command, and of the Civil War general George S. Greene.

Warwick had 82,823 inhabitants at the 2020 census and is part of the Providence metropolitan area. It is home to Rhode Island's main airport, T. F. Green Airport, which also serves as a reliever for Boston's Logan International Airport. Rocky Point, which closed in 1995, is now a state park.
warwickshire: Warwickshire is a flat, lowland county, about 1,975 km2 (760 sq mi) in area, running some 56 miles (90 km) from north to south. Its far south contains a small part of the Cotswolds, and its highest point, at 261 m (856 ft), is Ebrington Hill on the border with Gloucestershire. The River Avon, a major tributary of the Severn, flows through the south.

Much of the west was covered by the ancient Forest of Arden, most of which was cut down to provide fuel for industrialisation, and many places there end in the phrase in-Arden, such as Henley-in-Arden. The remaining area, the Felden, is an undulating agricultural landscape crossed by the Avon and the Leam. The plain between the outlying Cotswolds and the Edgehill escarpment is known as the Vale of Red Horse.

The region was part of Roman Britain, and the Roman road called Watling Street later became the boundary between the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Mercia and the Danelaw. Warwickshire came into being as a division of Mercia in the early eleventh century, and its first mention, in 1001, calls it Wæringscīr, after Warwick. In the Middle Ages the county was dominated by Coventry, one of the most important cities of England because of its textile trade.

The county played a part in the English Civil War, with the Battle of Edgehill and other skirmishes fought there. The playwright William Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1564, and the Gunpowder Plot of 1605 was planned near Snitterfield. During the Industrial Revolution the Warwickshire coalfield was exploited, Coventry and the west became manufacturing centres, and Leamington Spa developed as a resort. The novelist Mary Ann Evans, known as George Eliot, was born just outside Nuneaton in 1819.

Coventry was administered separately from the rest of the county as a county corporate from 1451 to 1842. Under the Local Government Act 1972, Birmingham, Coventry, Solihull and Sutton Coldfield were transferred in 1974 to the new West Midlands county, so that the county has no cities today.

Warwickshire is a largely rural ceremonial county with its county town at Warwick. Its largest town is Nuneaton, and it also contains Rugby, the birthplace of rugby football, Leamington Spa and Stratford-upon-Avon. Warwick Castle and Kenilworth Castle stand in the county, and the Forest of Arden gives its name to many villages. Some bodies, such as Warwickshire County Cricket Club in Birmingham, still follow the historic county boundaries.
washington-dc: Washington, D.C., lies in the Mid-Atlantic region of the East Coast, on the northeast bank of the Potomac River, across from Virginia and surrounded by Maryland to the north, east and south. The south bank of the Potomac forms the border with Virginia, and the Anacostia River and Rock Creek are its two major tributaries. The Chesapeake and Ohio Canal starts in Georgetown and was used in the 19th century to bypass the Little Falls of the Potomac. The district was named for Columbia, the female personification of the American nation, and the name Washington was added later, from George Washington, the first president.

The Algonquian-speaking Piscataway people inhabited the area when Europeans arrived in the early 17th century, and the Nacotchtank maintained settlements around the Anacostia River. Conflicts with colonists and neighbouring tribes displaced the Piscataway, some of whom founded a new settlement near Point of Rocks, Maryland, in 1699. The Constitution of 1789 called for a federal district under the exclusive jurisdiction of Congress. The Residence Act, adopted on 16 July 1790, approved a capital district along the Potomac and is considered the city's founding date. In 1800 the capital moved from Philadelphia, Congress began meeting in the unfinished Capitol, and President John Adams moved into the White House.

In 1791 President George Washington commissioned the French-born military engineer Pierre Charles L'Enfant to design the capital. His plan featured broad avenues radiating out from rectangles, with a grand garden-lined avenue on the site of the National Mall, inspired by Versailles and the Tuileries. Washington dismissed L'Enfant in March 1792 after conflicts with the commissioners overseeing construction, and Andrew Ellicott completed the design. In 1846 Congress returned to Virginia the land it had ceded, including Alexandria, and in 1871 it made the entire district a single municipality.

Washington, D.C., is the capital of the United States and its only federal district, not part of any state. It houses the White House, the Capitol and the Supreme Court Building, and its National Mall holds the Jefferson Memorial, the Lincoln Memorial and the Washington Monument. Since the 1973 Home Rule Act it has had an elected mayor and a 13-member council, though Congress retains the power to overturn local laws. Its residents elect one non-voting delegate to the House of Representatives. Ford's Theatre, where Abraham Lincoln was shot on 14 April 1865, is both a theatre and a museum.
washington-luis: Washington Luís was born in Macaé, in Rio de Janeiro, on 26 October 1869. He moved to São Paulo and graduated from the University of São Paulo Law School in 1891. After a short spell as prosecutor in Barra Mansa he practised law in Batatais, where he began his political career as an alderman and served as mayor from 1898 to 1899. He was elected a congressman in 1900 and was a state representative for the Republican Party of São Paulo between 1904 and 1906, then Secretary of State of Justice and Public Safety from 1906 to 1912.

He was mayor of São Paulo from 1914 to 1919, during which he faced the general strike of 1917, and governor of the state from 1920 to 1924. In 1924 he led the 3rd Battalion organized in Batatais against the rebels of São Paulo, and from 1925 to 1926 he served as a senator.

Washington Luís took office as president through direct election on 15 November 1926. The Old Republic had been worn down in the 1920s by opposition from the urban middle class, the lieutenants' and workers' movements and dissident oligarchies. Early in his term the Prestes Column ended after entering Bolivian territory with 620 men. In 1927 he created the Celerada Act, which imposed press censorship and restricted the right of assembly, and which drove the Brazilian Communist Party underground.

The crash of 24 October 1929 hit Brazilian coffee, which accounted for 70 per cent of exports, and overturned the valuation policy begun in 1906 with the Taubaté Agreement. Washington Luís refused the new currency devaluation that farmers asked for. Under the system of coffee with milk politics, a man from Minas Gerais should have succeeded him, but he backed another paulista, his friend Júlio Prestes, whose victory in the election of 1 March 1930 was questioned on suspicion of fraud.

The assassination of João Pessoa on 26 July 1930 worsened opposition, and Getúlio Vargas and Osvaldo Aranha began the conspiracy that led to the Revolution of 1930. Washington Luís was deposed on 24 October by the heads of the armed forces, and a junta of generals Tasso Fragoso and Mena Barreto and admiral Isaías de Noronha took power.

Washington Luís went into exile in Europe and the United States and returned to Brazil after seventeen years, in 1947. He settled in São Paulo and devoted himself to historical studies, and he was a member of the Academia Paulista de Letras and of historical and geographic institutes. He died in São Paulo on 4 August 1957. The Rodovia Washington Luís in the state of São Paulo is named in his honour.
washington-naval-conference: At the end of the First World War the British still had the largest navy afloat, but its big ships were becoming obsolete, while the Americans and the Japanese were rapidly building expensive new warships. Britain and Japan were allies in a treaty due to expire in 1922. Observers increasingly pointed to American-Japanese rivalry for control of the Pacific as a long-term threat to peace, and the British decided that, given their colonial interests in Asia, it was better to side with Washington than with Tokyo.

Popular demand for disarmament was strong. Women's organisations and the major Protestant denominations in the United States campaigned for peace, arguing that an end to the arms race would save money and avoid future wars. The conference was called by the United States and held outside the League of Nations.

The conference met in Washington, D.C., from 12 November 1921 to 6 February 1922 at Memorial Continental Hall. Nine nations attended: the United States, Japan, China, France, the United Kingdom, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Portugal. Germany and Soviet Russia were not invited. The American delegation was led by Secretary of State Charles Evans Hughes and included Elihu Root, Henry Cabot Lodge and Oscar Underwood. Its main aim was to restrain Japanese naval expansion in the western Pacific.

Japan sought a naval treaty with Britain and the United States and recognition of its special interests in Manchuria and Mongolia. The British brought general aims: stability in the western Pacific, no naval race with the United States, and the security of Singapore, Hong Kong and dominion countries. The American side had intercepted and decrypted secret Japanese instructions that revealed the lowest naval ratio Tokyo would accept, and used the knowledge to press the Japanese delegation, which was headed by Prince Iyesato Tokugawa.

The conference produced three major treaties: the Four-Power Treaty, the Five-Power Treaty, known as the Washington Naval Treaty, and the Nine-Power Treaty, along with smaller agreements. A ten-year agreement fixed the ratio of battleships at 5:5:3, with 525,000 tons each for the United States and Britain and 315,000 tons for Japan, and smaller limits for France and Italy. No battleship could exceed 35,000 tons, and the three main powers were allowed 135,000, 135,000 and 81,000 tons of aircraft carriers. Japan agreed on 4 February 1922 to return Shandong to Chinese control.

The treaty largely ended the building of new battleship fleets, and some ships under construction became aircraft carriers. The powers raced to build heavy cruisers from 1927 to 1930, until the London Naval Treaty of 1930 set a 10:10:7 ratio for cruisers and destroyers. Japan ended its participation in 1936.
washington-naval-treaty: After the First World War Britain still had the world's largest navy, followed by the United States and, more distantly, Japan, France and Italy. With the German threat seemingly over, a naval arms race among the allies seemed likely. American plans of 1916 to 1919 called for 50 modern battleships, and in 1920 the Japanese Diet authorised an eight-eight programme of eight battleships and eight battlecruisers. The American public and Congress disliked the new race, and Britain could ill afford the cost of capital ships. In November 1921 the administration of Warren Harding called the Washington Naval Conference, partly to forestall a British plan for a conference on the Pacific and Far East.

At the opening session on 21 November 1921 Secretary of State Charles Evans Hughes declared that the way to disarm is to disarm, and proposed a ten-year pause in capital ship construction and the scrapping of existing or planned ships to a ratio of 5:5:3 for Britain, the United States and Japan. The treaty, finalised on 6 February 1922, set tonnage ratios of approximately 5:5:3:1.75:1.75 for the United Kingdom, the United States, Japan, Italy and France. Capital ships were limited to 35,000 tons and 16-inch guns, aircraft carriers to 27,000 tons, and all other warships to 10,000 tons and 8-inch guns. The United States had to scrap 30 existing or planned capital ships, Britain 23 and Japan 17.

Article XIX barred Britain, Japan and the United States from building new fortifications or naval bases in the Pacific, though existing ones at Singapore, the Philippines and Hawaii could stay. That provision helped win Japanese acceptance of the limits. Attempts to cap cruisers and submarines failed.

The treaty ended a long period of rising battleship construction, and many ships under construction were scrapped or converted into aircraft carriers. The London Naval Treaty of 1930 extended its limits, but the Second London Naval Treaty of 1936 was largely ineffective without Japan or Italy. The American delegates had also made it clear that they would not agree unless Britain ended its alliance with Japan, which the Imperial Conference of 1921 had already decided not to renew.

In Japan the treaty split the navy between the Treaty Faction and the Fleet Faction. The delegation's director, Katō Tomosaburō, accepted the lower ratio rather than an arms race the country would lose, while Katō Kanji opposed it. Isoroku Yamamoto argued for remaining in the treaty. On 29 December 1934 Japan gave formal notice of termination, and the provisions stayed in force until the end of 1936. American cryptographers had read Japanese delegation communications during the conference.
wassily-kandinsky: Kandinsky was born in Moscow, the son of Lidia Tikheeva and Vassily Silvestrovich Kandinsky, a tea merchant. He studied law and economics, and later recalled being fascinated as a child by colour. In 1889 he joined an ethnographic research group that travelled to the Vologda region north of Moscow, where houses and churches were decorated in such shimmering colours that he felt he was entering a painting. His study of the region's folk art, with its bright colours on a dark background, shaped much of his early work.

In 1896 he gave up a promising career teaching law and economics, at the age of 30, and enrolled at the Munich Academy, where his teachers eventually included Franz von Stuck. Before leaving Moscow he had seen an exhibition of paintings by Monet. He found he could not recognise the subject of Haystacks, yet the picture stayed in his memory, and this convinced him that colour could work almost independently of objects.

From 1896 Kandinsky lived in Munich, where he was first the teacher and then the partner of Gabriele Münter. He helped found the Neue Künstlervereinigung München and became its president in 1909, but the group could not reconcile his radical approach with conventional ideas and dissolved in late 1911. He then formed The Blue Rider with artists including August Macke, Franz Marc, Albert Bloch and Münter. The group issued an almanac and held two exhibitions, and the outbreak of the First World War in 1914 ended its plans and sent him back to Russia.

From 1918 to 1921 he took part in Russia's cultural politics, collaborated in art education and museum reform, and was the first director of the Institute of Artistic Culture in Moscow, whose radical members rejected his spiritual view of art as too individualistic. In 1921 Walter Gropius invited him to the Bauhaus. He taught basic design and advanced theory there from 1922 until the Nazis closed the school in 1933, then moved to France and became a French citizen in 1939.

Kandinsky likened painting to music, writing that colour is the keyboard and the artist the hand that plays. He called his most spontaneous paintings improvisations and his more elaborate ones compositions. His text Concerning the Spiritual in Art, published in Munich in 1911, defines three types of painting: impressions, improvisations and compositions. Point and Line to Plane followed in 1926. His influence on Western art stems perhaps more from his theory than from his paintings. Works of his were confiscated in the Nazi campaign against "degenerate art", and the first three Compositions were destroyed during the Second World War. He died in Neuilly-sur-Seine on 13 December 1944.
wat-arun: A Buddhist temple stood on the site in the Ayutthaya period, before the reign of King Narai, and was known as Wat Bang Makok, later shortened to Wat Makok after the village in which it was built. According to the historian Prince Damrong Rajanubhab, French maps drawn during Narai's reign (1656-88) show it. After the fall of Ayutthaya, Taksin (1767-82) founded his new capital at Thonburi beside the temple and renamed it Wat Chaeng. He is believed to have vowed to restore it after passing it at dawn.

The temple stood within the grounds of Taksin's royal palace and enshrined the Emerald Buddha until the image was moved to Wat Phra Kaew on the eastern bank of the river in 1785. Rama I (1782-1809) moved the palace across the river, and the temple was abandoned until Rama II (1809-24) had it restored and began plans to raise the main pagoda to 70 metres. Work began under Rama III (1824-51), and the main prang was finished in 1851 after nine years of construction.

The name comes from the Hindu god Aruna, the charioteer of the sun god Surya. The central prang is encrusted with coloured porcelain and with shells of Mauritia mauritiana. The porcelain had earlier served as ballast in boats coming to Bangkok from China. Four smaller satellite prang stand at the corners, and the satellite prang is devoted to the wind god Phra Phai. The central prang is topped with a seven-pronged trident, and statues of the Hindu god Indra riding on Erawan stand over its second terrace.

The central prang stands for Mount Meru in Hindu cosmology, and in Buddhist iconography it has three symbolic levels, the base for the Traiphum, the middle for Tavatimsa and the top for Devaphum. Beside it is the ordination hall, whose Buddha image was supposedly designed by Rama II, whose murals were made under Rama V and whose entrance is guarded by two demons from the Ramakien, the white Sahassa Deja and the green Thotsakan, who is Ravana. The prang was restored in 1980 and again from 2013 to 2017, when lime plaster replaced the cement of earlier work.
wat-phra-kaew: When King Rama I made Bangkok the capital of the Rattanakosin Kingdom on 6 April 1782, the new Chakri dynasty needed a royal palace and temple to legitimise it. He wished to distance himself from the regime of King Taksin, whom he had replaced, and the old palace at Thonburi was small and hemmed in between Wat Arun and Wat Tai Talat. The temple stands within the Grand Palace precincts. Each later king has added to, restored or embellished it as a way of making religious merit and glorifying the dynasty, and has donated sacred objects to its treasury.

The Emerald Buddha, the temple's namesake, is a meditating Buddha in the lotus position, about 66 centimetres tall, of a green semi-precious stone usually described as jade and clothed in gold. It sits on a pedestal at the western end of the ordination hall, the Ubosot, which is ringed by forty-eight columns covered in glass mosaic and by eight pavilions with gilded boundary stones. Its murals depict the life of the Buddha, the Buddha's victory over Mara and Buddhist cosmology.

A raised terrace carries the Phra Mondop, a library for the Tripitaka that Rama I had revised in 1788 after the sack of Ayutthaya in 1767; the Phra Si Rattana Chedi, a gilded stupa holding relics from Sri Lanka; and the Royal Pantheon, rebuilt under Rama VI after a fire in 1903 and opened each year on 6 April, Chakri Memorial Day. Rama IV had a scale model of Angkor Wat made after that temple was rediscovered.

Important state and royal ceremonies are held in the temple each year, presided over by the king in person and attended by government officials, which makes it a national shrine for the monarchy and the state. A covered gallery around the complex carries murals of the Ramakien, the Thai version of the Ramayana, in 178 scenes; Rama I had the epic recomposed in Thai verse around 1797. The murals were repainted under Rama III and have been restored often. Twelve guardian giants, each about 5 metres tall and drawn from the Ramakien, stand at the gates.
wat-phu: Vat Phou is a ruined Khmer-Hindu temple complex in southern Laos. A sanctuary stood there from prehistoric times, centred on a spring and an offering place for a tutelary spirit. The first megalithic stone structures were probably built as early as the second century BCE, with two stone cells, a carving of a crocodile, serpent stairs and offering platforms. One of the pre-Angkor brick buildings was erected in the 7th century and became the focus of later building.

The site was first associated with the city of Shrestapura, on the Mekong directly east of Lingaparvata Mountain, later called Phou Khao. By the later part of the fifth century the city was the capital of a kingdom that texts and inscriptions connect with Chenla and Champa, and the first structure on the mountain was built about then. A lingam-shaped protuberance on the summit made the mountain the home of Shiva, with the river representing the ocean or the Ganges.

The earliest inscription found there, K.365, names Devanika, who established a sacred tīrtha in the area; it records that he had won countless victories, came from afar to found a kingdom and gave thousands of cattle to a temple foundation. The site museum holds standing Buddhas in Gupta and post-Gupta style, which Pierre-Yves Manguin groups with statues from Thailand and from Cham sites in central Vietnam as evidence of an artistic vocabulary shared across the region between the 5th and the late 7th or early 8th century.

After its first scientific description in the 19th and 20th centuries there was little scientific work until the 1990s. Lao-UNESCO projects began in 1987, and the site became a World Heritage Site in 2001. Conservation has included Italian work on the hall of Nandin from 2006, an Indian survey of the northern quadrangle in 2009 and French work on the southern palace. The site is open for religious activities and visits, and a festival is held there each February.
water-clock: The word clepsydra comes from the Greek for water thief. Two types of water clock exist. In an outflow clock a container is filled with water and drains slowly and evenly, and markings on the container show how much time has passed as the level falls. An inflow clock works the same way, except that a marked container fills.

The flow follows Torricelli's law if viscosity is neglected. Because water becomes less viscous as it warms, a clock with a long, thin nozzle would gain or lose about half an hour a day for each degree Celsius of change. Ancient clocks were probably reset daily from a sundial, so the cumulative error would not have been great.

Egyptian outflow clocks were stone vessels with sloping sides and a small hole near the bottom. Twelve columns of markings, one for each month, allowed for the changing length of seasonal hours, and priests used the clocks to find the time at night so that temple rites could be performed at the correct hour.

In Babylon the clocks were cylindrical and measured time by the weight of water flowing out, and clay tablets record their use to pay the night and day watches. In Greek and Roman courts a small earthenware clepsydra allocated time to speakers; in important cases it was filled completely, and its hole was stopped with wax if proceedings were interrupted. In Persia, water clocks timed the share of water that each farmer could take from a qanat.

Between 270 BCE and 500 CE Hellenistic and Roman engineers, among them Ctesibius, Hero of Alexandria and Archimedes, built more elaborate clocks that rang bells, opened doors to show figurines or moved pointers and dials. Ctesibius added gears and a dial indicator to show the changing length of the days automatically, and Philo of Byzantium mentioned clocks fitted with an escapement.

In China, Zhang Heng used a clepsydra in 117 to drive a model of the heavens, and in 1088 Su Song powered an astronomical clock tower, over 30 feet tall, in the same way. Al-Jazari described his elephant clock and castle clock in 1206. Water clocks stayed the common timekeeper for millennia, until verge escapement mechanical clocks replaced them in Europe around 1300.
water-wheel: A water wheel is a machine that turns the kinetic energy of flowing or falling water into useful power, often in a watermill. It is a large wheel, usually of wood or metal, with blades or buckets on its rim, fed from a mill pond formed by damming a stream. The water reaches it along a headrace and leaves by a tailrace.

There are two basic designs: a horizontal wheel on a vertical axle, often called a tub wheel, Norse mill or Greek mill, and a vertical wheel on a horizontal axle. The vertical type is divided into stream, undershot, breastshot, overshot and backshot wheels according to where the water strikes. An overshot wheel can reach 90 per cent efficiency, while a flat-board undershot wheel used about 20 per cent of the energy, as John Smeaton measured in the 18th century.

Water wheels served two main purposes: lifting water for irrigation and milling, particularly of grain. The wheel first appeared in the ancient Near East, specifically Egypt, in the 4th century BCE. By the 3rd century BCE it was used there to move millstones, and the sāqiya spread rapidly across the Near East in the Hellenistic period.

The Roman architect Vitruvius, in the late 1st century BCE, gave the first clear description of a geared watermill, a combination of the Greek toothed gear and the water wheel. A poem by Antipater of Thessalonica praised the wheel for freeing women from the labour of grinding. In China the Xin Lun, written by Huan Tan about 20 CE, suggests that water wheels were used for pounding machinery in grain mills, and by the 1st century CE the wheel was in widespread use there.

After the spread of Islam, engineers continued the technology of the ancient Near East. Hama in Syria preserves large wheels on the Orontes, one with a diameter of about 20 metres and 120 compartments, and some medieval compartmented wheels lifted water as high as 30 metres. In Ireland the oldest known horizontal wheels, at Ballykilleen, date to about 636. Smeaton's investigation in the mid to late 18th century raised efficiency and supplied power for the Industrial Revolution.

Water wheels were in commercial use well into the 20th century. Their main limitation is their dependence on flowing water, which restricts where they can stand. The turbine, developed by Benoît Fourneyron beginning with his first model in 1827, was smaller, cheaper and more efficient, and it handles high heads that wheels of practical size cannot. Modern hydroelectric dams can be viewed as the descendants of the water wheel.
waterford: Waterford lies in the province of Munster at the head of Waterford Harbour, on the River Suir. Downriver the Nore and the Barrow join the Suir at a place the Irish call Cumar na dTrí Uisce, the confluence of the three waters. Its name comes from the Old Norse Veðrafjǫrðr, meaning ram or wether fjord, while the Irish name, Port Láirge, means Lárag's port.

Waterford Port has been one of Ireland's major ports for over a millennium, and in the 19th century shipbuilding was a major industry. The Malcomson family of the Neptune Shipyard operated the largest fleet of iron steamers in the world between the mid-1850s and the late 1860s.

Viking raiders first established a settlement near Waterford in 853. It and the other longphorts were vacated about 902, when the native Irish drove the Vikings out. The Vikings re-established themselves at Waterford in 914, led first by Jarl Ottar until 917, then by Ragnall ua Ímair and the Uí Ímair dynasty, and built what would be Ireland's first city.

Among its most prominent rulers was Ivar of Waterford. The medieval city was attacked several times and earned the motto Urbs Intacta Manet, the Untaken City, after repelling a siege in the 15th century. The office of Mayor of Waterford was established in 1377. In the 15th century the city was enlarged with an outer wall on the west side.

The population grew from 1,555 in 1653 to about 28,000 in the early 19th century, then declined to just over 20,000 at the end of the century before rising to more than 40,000 in the 20th. Waterford Crystal, the city's best-known export, was made there from 1783 to 1851, from 1947 to 2009 and again from 2010.

Waterford is the county town of County Waterford, with 60,079 people at the 2022 census, and the main city of Ireland's South-East Region. The Viking Triangle, the oldest quarter, lies within the original tenth-century fortifications and is triangular, with its apex at Reginald's Tower. The tower is the oldest urban civic building in Ireland and the oldest monument to keep its Viking name. Waterford keeps more of its city walls than any other Irish city except Derry. The Theatre Royal dates from 1785, and the Waterford Greenway, opened in 2017, links the city with Dungarvan. Ryanair's first flight ran between Waterford and Gatwick.
watergate-scandal: Richard Nixon, elected the 37th president of the United States in 1968, secretly expanded the bombing of the Vietnam War to Cambodia. When The New York Times exposed the bombing in May 1969, he ordered the wiretapping of reporters and suspected leakers, and his domestic policy chief John Ehrlichman directly arranged some of it after the Federal Bureau of Investigation could not bug certain targets. Of the leaks Nixon said that the government could not function if anyone could run out and leak.

In December 1971 G. Gordon Liddy became general counsel of the Committee for the Re-Election of the President, which also recruited a retired CIA officer, James McCord, as its security chief. Nixon had also had the Secret Service install microphones in the Oval Office. From 16 February 1971 to 12 July 1973 the system recorded 3,432 hours of conversation, and it was kept secret even from his secretary, Rose Mary Woods.

Two attempts in May 1972 to break into the Democratic National Committee headquarters in the Watergate complex failed. On the night of 17 June 1972 the burglars, mostly Cuban exiles led by the former intelligence agents E. Howard Hunt and Liddy, were caught planting listening devices. The break-in was an implementation of Operation Gemstone. The next morning Liddy destroyed Gemstone files, and investigators found that McCord worked for the committee and that the White House had run a background check on Hunt.

Nixon denied involvement, but his administration destroyed evidence, obstructed investigators and bribed the burglars. The Washington Post reporters Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein, guided by the source called Deep Throat, exposed an illegally funded political espionage programme. The cover-up helped Nixon to a landslide re-election, until revelations at the burglars' 1973 trial led to a Senate investigation.

Special prosecutor Archibald Cox subpoenaed the Oval Office tapes, and Nixon invoked executive privilege, then fired Cox in the Saturday Night Massacre, which forced the resignations of the attorney general and his deputy. In July 1974 the Supreme Court ordered the tapes released, and the House Judiciary Committee recommended impeachment for obstruction of justice, abuse of power and contempt of Congress. The Smoking Gun tape showed that Nixon had ordered the CIA to stop the FBI's investigation. On 9 August 1974 he became the first United States president to resign, and 69 people were charged in all.

The motive for the break-in, and who ordered it, has never been established, and no one was charged for ordering it. The scandal brought heavy Republican losses in the 1974 midterm elections and Gerald Ford's failed re-election bid in 1976, and the suffix -gate entered the language to denote scandals.
wehrmacht: The word Wehrmacht, from wehren, to defend, and Macht, power, had long been used for any nation's armed forces. After the First World War the Treaty of Versailles limited the army to one hundred thousand men and the navy to fifteen thousand, with at most six battleships, six cruisers and twelve destroyers, and it forbade submarines, tanks, heavy artillery and an air force. A new force, the Reichswehr, was established on 23 March 1921.

After Paul von Hindenburg died on 2 August 1934, Adolf Hitler became commander in chief. In that month the entire military took the Hitler oath, a pledge of personal obedience, on the initiative of Defence Minister Werner von Blomberg and General Walther von Reichenau. Hitler was surprised at the offer, and the view that he imposed the oath is false. In 1935 the Reichswehr was replaced by the Wehrmacht, made up of the Heer, the Kriegsmarine and the Luftwaffe, and conscription returned.

Hitler made himself Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces. After the Blomberg-Fritsch Affair he abolished the Ministry of War and put the Wehrmacht High Command, the Oberkommando der Wehrmacht, under Field Marshal Wilhelm Keitel in its place. Early campaigns in Poland, France and elsewhere relied on combined arms tactics of aircraft, tanks and infantry, which foreign journalists called Blitzkrieg. The advance into the Soviet Union brought its first major defeat at the Battle of Moscow in 1941, and by late 1942 Germany was losing the initiative in all theatres.

Resistance within the forces began with the Oster conspiracy of 1938. After the defeat at Stalingrad trust in Hitler's leadership waned, and on 20 July 1944 a group of officers led by Claus von Stauffenberg attempted to assassinate him. The attempt failed, 4,980 people were executed, and the military salute was replaced by the Hitler salute. The Wehrmacht's unconditional surrender took effect on 8 May 1945.

German forces, including the Waffen-SS and collaborator units, lost about 5,318,000 men killed, dead in custody or missing. The Wehrmacht cooperated closely with the SS and its Einsatzgruppen and committed war crimes, chiefly in the Soviet Union, Poland, Yugoslavia, Greece and Italy. Of 3.2 million Soviet prisoners taken between the start of Operation Barbarossa and the following spring, 2.8 million died in German hands.

After the war former officers and veterans' groups promoted the myth of a clean Wehrmacht, an apolitical force innocent of the regime's crimes. German historians began to challenge this view in the late 1970s and the 1980s. Historians have also reassessed the Wehrmacht's fighting power, noting that it often inflicted heavier losses than it took while outnumbered.
wei-river: The Wei River is 818 km long and drains an area of 135,000 square kilometres. It is the largest tributary of the Yellow River. It rises in the mountains of southern Weiyuan County in Gansu, less than 110 km from the Yellow River at Lanzhou. Because the Yellow River turns sharply north there to form the Ordos Loop, the two rivers do not meet for more than 2,000 km further along the Yellow River's course.

The Wei runs east past Tianshui, enters Mount Long and emerges as the principal river of the Guanzhong Basin. It passes Baoji, Xianyang, Xi'an and Weinan and joins the Yellow River at Tongguan County, near where Shaanxi, Shanxi and Henan meet. Its tributaries include the Luo, Jing, Niutou, Feng and Chishui. The valley has a continental climate, with hot summers and cool, dry winters. Its natural steppe-forest vegetation has been transformed by human activity, and it is mostly agricultural.

In Chinese myth the giant Kua Fu drained the Yellow and Wei rivers to quench his thirst as he pursued the Sun. The valley was one of the early cradles of Chinese civilisation. The capitals of the Zhou, Qin, Han and Tang dynasties were situated along it, and the area of Dingxi near its headwaters has numerous Stone Age sites. The valley is likely the earliest centre of Chinese civilisation and the site of China's first major irrigation works. Some Chinese historians believe the Wei is the ancient Jiang River that gave its name to the families of Shennong and the Yan emperor, credited with early agriculture there.

The headwaters served as China's natural gateway to the west. The Northern Silk Road ran from Chang'an through Baoji and Tianshui, then to Lanzhou and Dunhuang, and looped north of the Taklamakan on its way to Kashgar. The 1556 Shaanxi earthquake had its epicentre in the valley.

The Sanmenxia Dam, built in 1960, caused extensive sedimentation in the lower reaches. The Baojixia diversion works of 1972 created an irrigation district of 128,000 hectares, which reduced flows. Heavy rain in September 2003 caused flooding that killed over 30 people and displaced over 300,000. A train bridge over the Wei appeared on the 5000-yuan note of the first series of the renminbi, dated 1953.
weikersheim: Weikersheim is a town in the Main-Tauber district of Baden-Württemberg, Germany. The township covers 80.92 square kilometres of the Tauberland, a landscape of muschelkalk crossed by many river valleys, above all those of the Tauber and the Vorbach. The lowest point of the municipal area, 213 metres above sea level, lies on the Tauber near Elpersheim, and the highest, 444 metres, to the south-east near the border with Oberndorf. Part of the federally protected Steinriegel landscape between Weikersheim and Elpersheim nature reserve lies within its bounds.

Town rights were granted to Weikersheim in 1313. As one of the seats of the House of Hohenlohe, the town centre was dominated until 1756 by Weikersheim Castle, the residence of the Hohenlohe-Weikersheim line. During the German mediatization of 1806 to 1809 Weikersheim was awarded to the Kingdom of Württemberg, whose government assigned it to Oberamt Mergentheim. In 1938 the Oberamt was reorganized as Landkreis Mergentheim. Between 1 January 1972 and 1 January 1975 Weikersheim incorporated eight municipalities, and in the administrative reorganization of Baden-Württemberg it was assigned to the newly created Main-Tauber district.

In 2000 the old town and palace were placed under protection as cultural monuments. The coat of arms shows a large silver W below a golden crown on a red field. The first seal associated with the town, dated 1435, contained the W; from 1593 it was supported by two lions and set above images of the Sun, Moon and the planet Mercury. Baden-Württemberg awarded the present arms, based on the original pattern, on 7 November 1949. Notable people connected with the town include Raphael Levi Hannover (1685–1779), a German Jewish mathematician and astronomer, and Joseph von Maier (1797–1873), a rabbi and Landesrabbiner.
weil-der-stadt: Weil der Stadt lies in the valley of the River Würm, about 30 km west of the centre of Stuttgart, in the Stuttgart Region of Baden-Württemberg, and is often called the Gate to the Black Forest. It has about 19,000 inhabitants.

The name Weil derives from the Latin word villa, an estate or manor, and the suffix der Stadt, the town, was added to distinguish it from nearby villages of the same name, such as Weil im Dorf and Weil im Schönbuch. The modern name is unusual because it contains the dative article der rather than the nominative die. The town's coat of arms bears the motto SPQR, recalling its supposed Roman origins.

The village of Wile was first mentioned in 1075, when it was described as the property of the abbey of Hirsau. It had existed for centuries before as an important trading place, and in 1272 it became a free imperial city. In 1294 Augustinian monks became established in the town. It was completely destroyed during the Thirty Years' War in 1648 and subsequently rebuilt, and it is still dominated by buildings from that period. Its fortifications, with city walls, gates and several towers, have survived largely intact.

Weil der Stadt is best known as the birthplace of the astronomer Johannes Kepler (1571 to 1630), and it bears the unofficial title Keplerstadt. Another native was the Protestant reformer Johannes Brenz (1499 to 1570). The cityscape is dominated by the church steeple of St. Peter and Paul. The town keeps a traditional carnival, called Fasnet, which is based on Alemannic traditions shared by towns in south-western Germany and Switzerland. According to the account kept there, the town escaped destruction in World War II when a French artillery barrage was called off in honour of its being Kepler's birthplace.
weilburg: Weilburg lies in the Lahn valley between the Westerwald and the Taunus, just upstream from where the Weil flows into the Lahn, 80 km southeast of Koblenz. The Old Town stands on and around a rocky hill that the Lahn almost encircles. The earliest traces of settlement nearby are thought to be La Tène finds from the Scheuernberger Kopf near Kirschhofen. The site gave control of the Lahn and of two long-distance routes, the Hohe Straße from Frankfurt to Cologne and the Via Publica from Flanders to Bohemia.

Weilburg was first mentioned in 906 in a chronicle by Abbot Regino of Prüm as a fortification called Wilineburch. King Conrad I founded a church and abbey there, and the St. Walpurgis monastery was founded in 912. In 918, on his deathbed at the castle, Conrad recommended that his brother Eberhard deliver the imperial insignia to his bitterest rival, the Saxon duke Heinrich, an episode known as the Weilburger Testament. From 993 to 1062 the town was gradually given to the Bishopric of Worms, which about 1225 pledged overlordship to the House of Nassau.

Count Johann I of Nassau made his residence there in 1355, turning the castle into a palace and building the town fortifications, and in 1359 a stone bridge over the Lahn. Count Johann Ernst, who lived from 1664 to 1719, expanded the Renaissance high palace and laid out a park, so that Weilburg became one of the best preserved small German residence towns of the age of absolutism. From 1806 it was the seat of government of the new Duchy of Nassau, until Duke William moved his residence to Biebrich in 1816. Prussia annexed the duchy in 1866, and in 1871 it became part of the German Empire.

Weilburg has just under 13,000 inhabitants and is the third largest town of the Limburg-Weilburg district in Hesse. Schloss Weilburg, dating to the 14th century with Renaissance and Baroque parts, takes in almost half the Old Town and has been a museum since 1935, when Charlotte of Nassau-Weilburg, Grand Duchess of Luxembourg, sold it to Prussia. The Luxembourg ruling house kept the burial chapel of its ancestors. The town is also known for loam buildings in the Pisee style and for its Gymnasium Philippinum, which grew out of a school founded in 1540.
weimar: The oldest records of Weimar date to 899, and its name derives from Old High German words for holy and for standing water. It was the seat of the County of Weimar, first mentioned in 949, one of the most powerful jurisdictions in early medieval Thuringia, and fell to the Wettins after 1346. The Reformation was introduced in 1525, and Martin Luther stayed in the city several times. After the Ernestines lost the Schmalkaldic War in 1547 and Wittenberg passed to the Albertines, the ruler made Weimar his residence in 1552, and it remained one until the end of the monarchy in 1918.

The period from the regency of Anna Amalia, which began in 1758, through her son Carl August to Goethe's death in 1832 is called the golden or classical age. Goethe, Schiller, Herder, Wieland and Bertuch lived there. Goethe moved to Weimar in 1775 and served the Grand Duke of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach as Privy Councilor. A liberal Saxe-Weimar constitution came into effect in 1816. In 1842 Franz Liszt became the Grand Ducal court conductor and organised the premiere of Richard Wagner's Lohengrin in 1850. Friedrich Nietzsche moved to the city in 1897 and died there three years later.

The Weimar Republic's constitution was drafted in the city rather than in Berlin because the capital was considered too dangerous for the National Assembly after street rioting during the Spartacist uprising. Reich President Friedrich Ebert hoped the choice would remind the Allies of Weimar Classicism while they deliberated the Treaty of Versailles. Artists and architects including Walter Gropius, Wassily Kandinsky and Paul Klee founded the Bauhaus there. The Nazis held a party convention in Weimar in 1926, and the first concentration camps were set up near the city in 1933.

Weimar is a city in Thuringia, in central Germany between Erfurt and Jena, with a population of about 65,000. It was the capital of Thuringia until 1948. Two World Heritage Sites include buildings in the city: Classical Weimar, with 11 sites linked to the 18th and early 19th centuries, and the Bauhaus sites. The Bauhaus University, the Liszt School of Music and the Duchess Anna Amalia Library are among its institutions.
weimar-constitution: After the First World War the imperial government collapsed in the German revolution of 1918–1919. The moderate left, led by Friedrich Ebert of the Social Democrats, defeated the far left parties that wanted a soviet republic and called an election on 19 January 1919, in which women had equal voting rights with men for the first time, for a National Assembly to draft a constitution. Because Berlin was unsettled, it met at Weimar, a name Ebert wished to recall to the Allies as the city of Goethe and Schiller while they deliberated the terms of the Versailles Treaty.

The first draft was written by the liberal lawyer Hugo Preuss, who headed the Ministry of the Interior, largely on the Frankfurt Constitution of 1849. In July 1919 the Assembly moved quickly through it, mostly without public discussion, and adopted it on 31 July by 262 votes to 75 with one abstention. Ebert, the first president, signed it on 11 August, and it took effect on the 14th.

The constitution had 181 articles in two parts, one on the organisation of the Reich and one on the fundamental rights and duties of Germans. It made the Reich a republic whose power derived from the people, with a Reichstag elected by equal, secret ballot of all Germans over 20, and a Reichsrat representing the states. The president commanded the armed forces, appointed and dismissed the chancellor and, under Article 48, could suspend civil liberties in an emergency. Individual rights included equality before the law, the abolition of privileges of birth and rank, protection of the home and of correspondence, a guarantee of arrest being notified within a day, freedom of expression, and freedom of religion with no state church.

William L. Shirer called it on paper the most liberal and democratic document of its kind the twentieth century had seen, yet its legitimacy was weak in German eyes. Preuss intended a strong president as a replacement monarch above the parties. Article 48 was meant for rare use but was invoked 205 times before Adolf Hitler became chancellor, and the Reichstag Fire Decree of 1933 used it to suspend civil rights. The Enabling Act of 23 March 1933, passed by 441 votes to 94 after the 81 Communist members were forcibly excluded, made the other provisions a dead letter, though the constitution was never formally repealed.

Hitler still used it to give his dictatorship the look of legality. The Allied Control Council repealed the Enabling Act on 20 September 1945, and the constitution was replaced in 1949 by the Basic Law of West Germany and the constitution of East Germany, which copied many passages from the 1919 text.
weimar-republic: The Weimar Republic is dated from 9 November 1918 to 23 March 1933. Its official name remained the German Reich, but it was more commonly called the German Republic, and the name Weimar comes from the city where its National Assembly met from 6 February to 11 August 1919 and adopted the constitution. A rebellion among sailors at Wilhelmshaven on 29 October 1918 spread into the Kiel mutiny on 3 November, and sailors, soldiers and workers began electing councils modelled on the soviets of the Russian Revolution. The power takeovers were achieved with little or no violence.

Early years were marked by hyperinflation, political murders and two attempted coups by contending paramilitaries. From 1924 to 1929 the republic was relatively stable, a period known in Germany as the Goldene Zwanziger, with a growing economy and a cultural flourishing. Under the Locarno Treaties of 1925 Germany recognised most territorial changes made by the Treaty of Versailles, and in 1926 it joined the League of Nations. The stability rested partly on American loans, and when American banks withdrew credit after the Great Depression began in 1929, unemployment rose to 4 million in 1930.

In the Reichstag election of September 1930 the Nazi Party won 19% of the vote. From March 1930 President Paul von Hindenburg backed chancellors who governed by presidential decree: Heinrich Brüning, Franz von Papen and Kurt von Schleicher. On 30 January 1933 Hindenburg appointed Adolf Hitler chancellor. The Reichstag Fire Decree and the Enabling Act of 1933 gave him broad power to act outside parliamentary control, and he used it to suspend civil liberties and set up a one-party dictatorship.

The constitution of 1919 created a federal semi-presidential republic. The Reichstag was elected by universal suffrage using proportional representation, and the Reichsrat represented the states. The president commanded the military, held extensive emergency powers and appointed and removed the chancellor, who answered to the Reichstag. Under the Treaty of Versailles the army, the Reichswehr, was limited to 100,000 men. Historians still debate why the republic failed and group the causes as economic, institutional and the roles of individuals. Nazi propaganda called the period the time of the System.
weingarten-wurttemberg: Weingarten lies in the valley of the Schussen River in the District of Ravensburg, with Ravensburg to the south and Friedrichshafen on Lake Constance. Before 1865 the town was called Altdorf, from the Frankish alach for church, so that the name means a village with the parish church; Weingarten was then the name of the abbey alone, which stood on the Martinsberg above the town.

An Alemannic burial place of the 5th century was excavated near the old town in 1954 to 1957. In the 8th century the region became part of the Frankish empire, and around the 9th century the Elder Welfs became counts of the Schussengau and made Altdorf their seat. In 1056 Welf IV moved the ancestral seat to the new castle of Ravensburg and founded a Benedictine abbey on the Martinsberg, which was named Weingarten Abbey. In 1191 Frederick Barbarossa acquired the Schussengau from Welf VI by a contract of inheritance. After the Hohenstaufen line ended with Conradin's death in Naples in 1268, the abbey won the status of an Imperial Abbey, while Altdorf was ruled by the imperial bailiff of Swabia.

The abbey became one of the wealthiest monasteries in southern Germany, with about 306 km2 of estates, until it was confiscated in the secularisation of 1803. Weingarten went first to the House of Nassau and in 1806 was incorporated into Württemberg, while Altdorf had passed to the dukedom of Württemberg. Barracks made it a military site in the 19th century, and an engineering industry developed in the second half of the century. In 1922 monks from Beuron founded a new Benedictine abbey. Since 1949 most of the abbey buildings have housed a teachers' college.

The Abbey Church of St. Martin and Oswald is the largest Baroque church north of the Alps, about half as long as St. Peter's Basilica in Rome. Its organ by Joseph Gabler has four manuals and nearly 7,000 pipes. The relic of the holy blood of Jesus Christ is carried in the Blutritt, a large equestrian procession of about 3,000 riders held on the Friday after Ascension. The Alemans Museum displays finds from the burial place, and the Schlössle, built around 1550 for the imperial bailiff, houses the municipal museum.
weissenburg-in-bayern: The history of the town is generally traced back to the Roman fort built in the area towards the end of the first century. The settlement, which included baths, lay on the border of the Roman Empire and appears on the Tabula Peutingeriana from the 4th century under the name Biriciana. Germanic tribes destroyed the fort and settled in what is still the town centre. The name Weißenburg is first mentioned in a deed of 867. The town became the seat of a royal residence under the Franks, and according to legend Charlemagne stayed there to supervise the construction of the Fossa Carolina.

Weißenburg became a free imperial city in 1296 and continued to grow until the Reformation. Following the example of Nuremberg it joined the Protestant side, but it suffered heavily in the wars that followed. Its rights as a free imperial city and imperial estate were restored in the final peace treaty.

Despite its small size and economic weight it was, like the other fifty or so free imperial cities, virtually independent. It lost its independence in 1802 and became part of the Bavarian kingdom in 1806. A railway between Nuremberg and Augsburg through the town supported industrialisation, and after World War II over 6,000 refugees and expelled people settled there.

Weißenburg in Bayern is the capital of the district of Weißenburg-Gunzenhausen in Middle Franconia, with 18,345 inhabitants. Many Roman ruins survive, among them a Roman bath excavated in 1977 and made into a museum. The medieval town wall stands almost intact with its towers, and the Gothic Town Hall has hosted the town's elected members since 1476.

The Wülzburg, a fortress about 2 kilometres east of the centre on a hill 200 metres above the town, began as a Benedictine monastery of the 11th century and was converted into a fortress from 1588 to 1605. It is one of the best-preserved Renaissance fortresses in Germany. Charles de Gaulle was imprisoned there in the First World War, and the Czech composer Erwin Schulhoff was held there by the Nazis before he died of tuberculosis.
weissenfels: Weißenfels is the largest city of the Burgenlandkreis district in southern Saxony-Anhalt, central Germany, on the river Saale about 30 kilometres south of Halle. The area is perhaps first mentioned in 806, when Charles the Younger, King of the Franks, fought and killed two West Slavic princes nearby, Miliduch of the Sorbs and Nessyta. The settlement arose around a castle at a ford over the Saale and received municipal rights in 1185. It belonged to the Electorate of Saxony from 1485.

The Thirty Years' War badly damaged the town, and its population fell from 2,200 to 960. On 7 November 1632 the body of King Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden was first laid out there, the day after he was killed at the Battle of Lützen. Duke Augustus, of the Saxon House of Wettin, established the Duchy of Saxe-Weissenfels in 1656 and made the town its capital and residence. From 1660 he built the Baroque Neu-Augustusburg Castle on a hill, completed in 1680, which was the duchy's administrative and cultural centre until the duchy ended in 1746.

Composers such as Johann Philipp Krieger and Georg Philipp Telemann worked there, and in 1713 Johann Sebastian Bach dedicated his hunting cantata BWV 208 to Duke Christian. According to John Mainwaring, Duke Johann Adolf I discovered the musical talent of the young George Frideric Handel. With the extinction of the Wettin line in 1746 the town fell back to Saxony, and after 1815 it went to the Prussian Province of Saxony.

By 1900 Weißenfels was one of the largest shoe-making centres in Germany, with 64 factories employing about 3,200 people. In 1950 it was designated the centre of shoe manufacture in East Germany, with a workforce that eventually reached 5,000, and the last factory closed in 1991. Food processing has since grown. The castle's chapel keeps a pipe organ completed in 1673, for which Bach wrote the Toccata and Fugue in F major.
wellington: Wellington stands at the south-western tip of the North Island, between Cook Strait and the Remutaka Range. Steep hills shape and constrain much of the city. The Kāpiti Coast lies to the north, and the Remutaka Range divides the city from the plains of the Wairarapa. It lies at 41° 17' South and has a temperate maritime climate, generally windy all year with high rainfall.

In Māori oral history the explorer Kupe stayed in the harbour from about 925, and a later explorer, Whatonga, named it Te Whanganui-a-Tara after his son Tara. Iwi such as Rangitāne and Muaūpoko settled the area first; the disruptions of the Musket Wars in the early 19th century left them overwhelmed by northern iwi such as Te Āti Awa, who centred themselves at Pipitea.

European settlement began in 1839, when Colonel William Wakefield arrived to buy land for the New Zealand Company to sell to British settlers. In 1840 Captain William Mein Smith, the company's first Surveyor General, designed the town as interconnected grids that in practice spread along valleys and lower hill slopes. The settlers named it in November 1840, on the directors' suggestion, after Arthur Wellesley, the first Duke of Wellington, in recognition of his support for the company's principles of colonisation.

Earthquakes in 1848 destroyed most brick buildings, which led to the widespread use of timber. The Wairarapa earthquake of 1855, of an estimated magnitude of at least 8.2, raised land out of the harbour; much of it was later reclaimed and is now part of the central business district. The capital moved to Wellington in 1865, a status established by convention rather than in legislation.

Wellington is the capital of New Zealand and its third-largest city, with 210,800 people in the city and a metropolitan area including Lower Hutt, Porirua and Upper Hutt. The government, Parliament and Supreme Court are based there. Its architecture includes the Old Government Buildings, one of the largest wooden buildings in the world, and the Beehive, the executive wing of Parliament Buildings. It is the home of the National Archives, the National Library and the national museum, Te Papa, and is one of the country's chief seaports.
welsh-people: The English words Wales and Welsh descend from the Anglo-Saxon wealh, itself from a Proto-Germanic word derived from the name of the Gaulish people the Romans called Volcae. It first meant inhabitants of the Roman Empire in general, then the Britons in particular, and as their territories shrank it came to name the area that best kept continuity with pre-Anglo-Saxon Britain. The Romans met tribes in what is now Wales that they called the Ordovices, the Demetae, the Silures and the Deceangli. All the peoples of southern Britain were Britons who spoke Common Brittonic, a Celtic language that seems to have arrived in the Iron Age, though some archaeologists see no evidence of large-scale migration and favour cultural diffusion.

When the Roman legions left Britain around 400, a Romano-British culture remained where the Romans had settled. The people of what is now Wales kept speaking Common Brittonic with much Latin influence, and it evolved into Old Welsh. Offa's Dyke, raised in the mid-8th century, formed a barrier between Wales and Mercia. How the native population came to think of itself as Welsh is not clear. The Welsh word Cymry, from a Brythonic word meaning fellow-countrymen, drew on the relationship with the Brittonic peoples of the Old North in England and Scotland. Probably in use before the 7th century, it is attested in a praise poem to Cadwallon ap Cadfan around 633, and after about 1100 it prevailed over the older Brythoniaid.

Immigration followed the Norman Conquest, and the Landsker Line dividing the Pembrokeshire Englishry from the Welshry can still be traced. The population of Wales more than doubled from 587,000 in 1801 to 1,163,000 in 1851 and reached 2,421,000 by 1911, mostly in the coal-mining districts. English, Irish and Italian migrants came during the Industrial Revolution.

Before the 20th century many Welsh people spoke only Welsh. Parts of the culture are closely tied to the language, notably the Eisteddfod tradition, poetry and aspects of folk music and dance. Forms of Christianity have dominated religious life for more than 1,400 years, and Wales has a long tradition of nonconformism and Methodism. The Sunday Closing (Wales) Act of 1881 was the first legislation issued specifically for Wales since the Middle Ages. The flag shows the red dragon, which Henry VII carried at Bosworth in 1485 and which is recorded as a Welsh symbol in the Historia Brittonum around 820. Welsh emigrants settled in England, Pennsylvania, Canada, Brazil and Patagonia, where the settlement is called Y Wladfa.
welshpool: Welshpool, in Welsh Y Trallwng, is a market town and community in Powys, Wales, historically in Montgomeryshire. It lies low on the River Severn, four miles from the border with England, and the Welsh name means the marshy or sinking land. In English it was at first called Pool, and the name was changed to Welshpool in 1835 to distinguish it from Poole in Dorset. The Long Mountain forms a backdrop to the town and once served as the last ground of defence for fortresses, when the site was a swampy marsh. Powis Castle stands to the south-west.

St Cynfelin is reputed to have founded two churches in the town, St Mary's and St Cynfelin's, in the 5th and 6th centuries. The parish roughly coincides with the medieval commote of Ystrad Marchell in the cantref of Ystlyg, in the Kingdom of Powys. After its prince was forced to flee Mathrafal in 1212 by the prince of Gwynedd, Welshpool served briefly as capital of Powys Wenwynwyn, or South Powys; help from the English crown restored the dynasty. In 1284 the family converted the principality into a marcher lordship, the Lordship of Powys, and the heir Owain called himself Owen de la Pole, after the town.

Forces of Owain Glyndŵr devastated the town in 1400 at the start of his rebellion against Henry IV. Adam of Usk was priest of St Mary's in 1411. The waymarked National Trail called Glyndŵr's Way, 135 miles long, ends in Pont Howell Park beside the Montgomery Canal.

The 2011 census counted 5,948 people in the town and 6,664 in the community, which also includes Cloddiau and Pool Quay. St Mary's Church is a Grade I listed building. Its tower keeps lower courses of a church of about 1250, the nave was rebuilt in the 16th century, and Bishop William Morgan, translator of the Bible into Welsh, was vicar there from 1575 to 1579. The town also has an octagonal brick cockpit built in the early 18th century and a town hall completed in 1874. It is the starting point of the Welshpool and Llanfair Light Railway, and its livestock market is the largest one-day sheep market in Europe.
wenceslaus-i-duke-of-bohemia: Wenceslaus was the son of Vratislaus I, Duke of Bohemia of the Přemyslid dynasty, and Drahomíra, the daughter of a chief of the Havelli, who was baptized at her marriage. His grandmother Ludmila, converted to Christianity with his grandfather Bořivoj I by Cyril and Methodius, saw that he was educated in Old Church Slavonic, and he was sent to the college at Budeč. In 921, when he was about 13, his father died and Ludmila became regent. Jealous of her influence, Drahomíra arranged for her to be killed, and assassins murdered Ludmila at Tetín Castle on 15 September 921. Drahomíra then became regent and began measures against Christians. When Wenceslaus was 18, the Christian nobles who remained rebelled, and she was exiled to Budeč.

With the nobles' support Wenceslaus took control of the government. He reined in the dependent dukes who had become restive under the regency and used Christianity to strengthen his state. After the fall of Great Moravia, Bohemia faced raids by the Magyars and the eastern campaigns of the Saxon and East Frankish king Henry the Fowler. Early in 929 the joint forces of Duke Arnulf of Bavaria and Henry reached Prague in a sudden attack that forced Wenceslaus to resume payment of a tribute first imposed by Arnulf of Carinthia in 895.

Wenceslaus introduced German priests and favoured the Latin rite over the old Slavic rite, which had gone out of use in many places for want of priests. He also founded a rotunda consecrated to St Vitus at Prague Castle, the basis of the present St Vitus Cathedral.

In September 935 nobles allied with his younger brother Boleslav plotted to kill him. After Boleslav invited him to a feast of Saints Cosmas and Damian at Stará Boleslav, three of Boleslav's companions stabbed him to death, and Boleslav ran him through with a lance. The killing has been seen as a turning point, since Boleslav I renounced the Franks, centralised power and expanded the territory of Bohemia.

A cult of Wenceslaus arose at once, and within a few decades four biographies were in circulation, influencing the medieval idea of the rex justus, the righteous king. Otto I posthumously conferred the royal title on him, which is why legend and song call him king. His feast day, 28 September, has been a public holiday in the Czech Republic since 2000, and John Mason Neale published the carol Good King Wenceslas in 1853.
wenceslaus-ii-of-bohemia: Wenceslaus was the only surviving son of Ottokar II of Bohemia and Kunigunda, daughter of Rostislav Mikhailovich, lord of Slavonia, and Anna of Hungary. In November 1276 Rudolf I, King of the Romans, compelled Ottokar to give up his claims to Austria and keep only Bohemia and Moravia, and Wenceslaus was betrothed to Rudolf's daughter Judith. Ottokar died on 26 August 1278 in the Battle on the Marchfeld, shortly before his son's seventh birthday.

Otto V, Margrave of Brandenburg, governed until Wenceslaus returned to Bohemia in 1283, aged twelve. He then ruled without a regent but under the influence of his mother and her partner Záviš of Falkenstein. He married Judith on 24 January 1285, and in 1290 he had Záviš beheaded for alleged treason and began ruling independently.

In 1291 High Duke Przemysł II of Poland ceded the Duchy of Kraków to Wenceslaus. After Przemysł's death in 1296 Wenceslaus became overlord of Poland, and in 1300 he had himself crowned its king. In 1298 silver was discovered at Kutná Hora. He made its production a royal monopoly and issued the Prague groschen, which became the most popular of the early Groschen-type coins. Between 1300 and 1340 the mine may have produced as much as 20 tons of silver a year. In 1300 he issued the mining code Ius regale montanorum, and he founded cities such as Plzeň in 1295.

In 1301 Andrew III of Hungary died and the Árpád dynasty became extinct in the male line. Wenceslaus accepted the crown from a party of Hungarians on behalf of his young son, who was betrothed to Andrew's only child, Elizabeth, and was crowned at Székesfehérvár on 27 August 1301. In 1303 some of the son's supporters switched to Charles Robert of Anjou. Wenceslaus invaded Buda with a large army in 1304 but, having considered the situation, took his son and the Hungarian crown back to Bohemia.

Wenceslaus died on 21 June 1305, aged 33, probably of tuberculosis, and was succeeded by his son Wenceslaus III, the last of the Přemyslid kings. His realm stretched from the Baltic Sea to the Danube, and he is considered one of the most important Czech kings. His son could not maintain it, and soon after the early death of Wenceslaus II it began to crumble.
wenceslaus-iii-of-bohemia: Wenceslaus was born in Prague on 6 October 1289, the son of Wenceslaus II of Bohemia and Judith of Habsburg, and was the only one of their sons to survive infancy. His mother died on 18 June 1297, and on 12 February 1298 he was betrothed to Elizabeth, the only child of Andrew III of Hungary. Andrew was the last male of the House of Árpád, though the legitimacy of his rule had not been universally accepted. In 1300 his father, who had occupied parts of Poland, was crowned King of Poland at Gniezno.

When Andrew III died on 14 January 1301, Charles I of the House of Anjou was crowned king by an archbishop-elect, backed by Pope Boniface VIII. Bribed by Wenceslaus II's agents, most Hungarian lords and prelates offered the crown to the boy. He was crowned with the Holy Crown at Székesfehérvár on 27 August 1301 and signed his charters as Ladislaus, but the Croatian lords stayed loyal to Charles, and Hungary had split into provinces held by about a dozen powerful lords, so his rule was nominal. The pope declared Charles the lawful king on 31 May 1303.

In August 1304 his father took him back to Bohemia with the Holy Crown. He succeeded in Bohemia and Poland on 21 June 1305, and on 9 October handed his Hungarian claim and the crown to Otto III of Bavaria at Brno. He broke his engagement and married Viola of Teschen. In Bohemia he gave large land grants to young friends, and in Poland Władysław I Łokietek took Kraków in early 1306.

Wenceslaus planned to invade Poland, dismissed his favourites and made his brother-in-law Henry governor, but on 4 August 1306 he was stabbed at Olomouc, aged sixteen. His assassin was never identified. He was the last male Přemyslid ruler of Bohemia.
wenceslaus-iv-of-bohemia: Wenceslaus was born in Nuremberg on 26 February 1361, the eldest son of Charles IV by his third wife, Anna of Svídnická, a descendant of the Silesian Piasts. He was raised by the Prague archbishops Arnošt of Pardubice and Jan Očko of Vlašim. His father had him crowned King of Bohemia at the age of two, in 1363, and obtained the Electoral Margraviate of Brandenburg for him in 1373. When the electors chose him King of the Romans on 10 June 1376, two of the seven votes, those of Brandenburg and Bohemia, were held by Charles and his son themselves. He was crowned at Aachen on 6 July.

To secure his son's election Charles had revoked the privileges of many imperial cities and mortgaged them to nobles. In response fourteen Swabian cities formed the Swabian League of Cities. The league was defeated at Döffingen on 24 August 1388, and in 1389 Wenceslaus proclaimed an arrangement at Cheb that prohibited leagues between cities while confirming their autonomy.

In Bohemia he held a tenuous grip on power and clashed repeatedly with the nobility led by the House of Rosenberg; twice he was imprisoned for long spells by rebellious nobles. After officials of the king tortured and murdered the archbishop's vicar-general, Saint John of Nepomuk, in 1393, a noble rebellion followed, and in 1394 he was arrested while his cousin Jobst of Moravia became regent. His family weakened him further, because Charles had divided his holdings among his sons and relatives. In religious matters he sought to protect Jan Hus and his followers, and under the Decree of Kutná Hora in 1409 Hus's party drove German academics from the University of Prague.

The four Rhenish electors accused him of failing to keep the public peace or end the Schism. At Lahneck Castle on 20 August 1400 they declared him deposed for futility, idleness, negligence and ignobility and chose Rupert, Count Palatine, as King of the Romans. Wenceslaus never acknowledged this. In 1402 his half-brother Sigismund of Hungary captured him and held him in Vienna; he escaped on 11 November 1403 and returned to Prague.

After 1411 Wenceslaus agreed to give up his claim to the crown of the Romans provided he kept Bohemia, and Sigismund reigned as king. Wenceslaus was twice married and had no children. He was a patron of the arts, and the Wenceslas Bible, an illuminated manuscript, was drawn up between 1390 and 1400. He died in 1419 of a heart attack during a hunt near his castle Nový Hrad at Kunratice, leaving Bohemia in political crisis; fifteen years of Hussite Wars followed.
wends: The name Wends refers not to one people but to various peoples, tribes or groups, depending on where and when it was used. According to one theory, Germanic peoples first applied it to the ancient Veneti, who are mentioned by Pliny the Elder and Ptolemy as inhabiting the Baltic coast. For medieval Scandinavians, Wends meant the Slavs living near the southern shore of the Baltic, such as the Obotrites, the Rugian Slavs, the Veleti or Lutici and the Pomeranian tribes. In the south, Germans used the form Winde for the Slavs of Bavaria Slavica or the Slovenes, a usage preserved in names such as Windischgraz.

In the first millennium CE some West Slavs moved into the lands between the Elbe and the Oder and assimilated the remaining Germanic population. They split into many small tribes, separated by woodland and sheltered in round wooden and clay strongholds. Some joined into larger units. The Obotrites were led by dukes, while the Lutici remained independent and met in the temple of Rethra. In 983 many Wend tribes took part in a great uprising against the Holy Roman Empire, which delayed Germanisation by about two centuries.

After 983 the Wends came under pressure from Germans, Danes and Poles. A German expedition destroyed Rethra in 1068/69, and the Wend crusade took place in 1147. In 1168 a Danish crusade under Bishop Absalon and King Valdemar the Great captured and destroyed Arkona and tore down the statue of the god Svantevit. With the surrender of the Rugian Wends the last independent pagan Wends were defeated.
