From the 12th to the 14th centuries German settlers moved into their lands in large numbers in the Ostsiedlung, and new towns were founded under German law.

The Wends were gradually assimilated into German-speaking culture, and the Polabian language was spoken in parts of Lower Saxony and Brandenburg until the 17th or 18th century. Many place names in central and northern Germany are of Slavic origin, among them Delitzsch and Rochlitz, and the names of Leipzig and Berlin are most likely Wendish. The Dukes of Mecklenburg, Rügen and Pomerania had Wendish ancestors. The Danish kings used the title King of the Wends from 1362, and the Swedish kings were styled kings of the Swedes, the Goths and the Wends from 1540. Both usages were dropped in 1972 and 1973. In 1854 Wends from Lusatia emigrated to Texas.
wenzhou: Wenzhou, formerly called Yongjia, lies at the lower reaches and estuary of the Ou River on the south-eastern coast of China, between the Zhejiang-Fujian Hills to the west and the East China Sea. The Ou, Feiyun and Ao rivers drain the area, and the terrain falls from mountains in the west to plains, tidal flats and offshore islands in the east. The Caowan Mountain site, excavated in 2002, shows human activity here some 5,000 years ago, in the Neolithic period. A Neolithic cultural complex represented by the Haochuan culture gave rise to the Ou people, also called the Ouyue, part of the wider Yue people, whose capital was at Dong'ou.

The Ou had established the polity of Dong'ou by at least the fourth century BCE, and it surrendered to the Han dynasty in 138 BCE. That year Yongning County was created, the first county-level administration in Wenzhou. Later names were Yongjia Commandery from 323 and Wenzhou Prefecture from 675. The walled city first established in the 4th century remained the seat of the prefecture and county until 1958. After the Tang takeover in the early 7th century Yongjia became a major trading port, with marine trade with Japan beginning in 659. It was authorised as a foreign trade port in the Song and Yuan periods and is regarded as one of the places of origin of Chinese celadon.

In 1367 the Ming dynasty took Wenzhou from an anti-Yuan revolt. Pirates called wokou were active off its coast, and the Ming court set up a tightly organised garrison system for coastal defence. Wenzhou became a treaty port under the Chefoo Convention of 1876, and a customs office opened the next year. Steamship travel allowed local scholars to return with hospitals, schools and libraries. Britain set up a consulate on Jiangxin Islet in 1894, and in 1984 Wenzhou was named among China's first 14 open coastal cities.

After 1978 Wenzhou was among the first places in China to try market-oriented reforms, the Wenzhou Model, building on households with savings of over 10,000 yuan that had appeared in the 1970s. Since the 1990s large numbers of its people have migrated within China and abroad, forming communities such as Belleville in Paris and Prato in Italy. The city has the highest proportion of religious believers among Chinese cities, with Buddhism the predominant religion, and has more Christians than any other Chinese city, which has earned it the name China's Jerusalem.
wernigerode: Wernigerode lies at about 250 metres above sea level on the Holtemme river, on the north-eastern flank of the Harz Mountains and at the foot of their highest peak, the Brocken. The Northern Harz Boundary Fault crosses its borough, and along it runs the watershed between the Weser and the Elbe. The town lies in the rain shadow of the Harz, so less rain falls there than in comparable places without the mountains. It stands on the German Timber-Frame Road.

No written source gives the date of the town's founding. The name suggests a protected clearance settlement, the suffix rode meaning clearing, and the first area settled was the Klint, where a lowland castle called the Schnakenburg stood. The town is first mentioned in 1121, in connection with Count Adalbert of Haimar, who moved there from the region near Hildesheim and was henceforth titled Count of Wernigerode. On 17 April 1229 it received town rights on the model of Goslar's. A new settlement, later called the Neustadt, grew up outside the old town's walls as people arrived from the surrounding villages.

The counts were vassals of the margraves of Brandenburg from 1268 and of the archbishops of Magdeburg from 1381. When the family died out in 1429 the county fell to the counts of Stolberg, who founded the Stolberg-Wernigerode branch in 1645. It surrendered its military and fiscal independence to Prussia in 1714 but kept some sovereign rights until 1876, and its counts were raised to princely rank in 1890. After the Napoleonic Wars the town became part of the Prussian Province of Saxony in 1815. After 1945 it lay close to the inner German border and was part of East Germany.

Wernigerode has a Gothic town hall with a timber facade from 1498. Some of the old houses that escaped the town's many fires are adorned with wood-carving. The castle of the princes of Stolberg-Wernigerode rises above the town. The original dates from the 12th century, and the present castle was built between 1862 and 1893 by Karl Frühling and includes parts of the medieval building. The Harzer Schmalspurbahn, a narrow-gauge railway, leads from the town to the Brocken. The Hasseröder brewery was founded there in 1872, and the town is a site of the Harz University of Applied Studies.
wesel: Wesel stands at the confluence of the Lippe and the Rhine in North Rhine-Westphalia, and it is the capital of the Wesel district. The city grew from a Franconian manor first recorded in the 8th century. In the 12th century the Duke of Clèves took possession of it, and in the 15th century it became a member of the Hanseatic League. It was second only to Cologne in the lower Rhine region as an entrepôt, a clearing station for the transshipment and trading of goods.

A Walloon community with French-language church services was noted in Wesel in 1545, and a French Huguenot commune was founded there in 1688. In 1590 the Spanish captured the city after a four-year siege, and it changed hands between the Dutch and the Spanish several times during the Eighty Years War. A French force under Louis II de Bourbon, Prince de Condé, captured it in 1672. The Hohenzollerns of the Margraviate of Brandenburg inherited Wesel in 1609 but could not take control of it until the Treaty of Nijmegen in 1678.

In 1805 the city was ceded to the French Empire under the Treaty of Schönbrunn. It became part of the Grand Duchy of Berg under Joachim Murat in 1806 and was annexed to France itself in January 1808. The French fortified it heavily, building the Citadelle Napoleon at Büderich, which was renamed Fort Blücher after the Napoleonic Wars, when the city passed to Prussia in 1815.

As a strategic depot Wesel was bombed by the Allies, and air raids on 16 to 19 February 1945 destroyed 97 per cent of the town. The Wehrmacht blew up the bridges over the Rhine and Lippe, and on 23 March a bombardment by over 3,000 guns and a raid by RAF bombers prepared Operation Plunder, the Allied crossing of the Rhine. Operation Varsity dropped 18,000 troops behind the town. The population fell from almost 25,000 in 1939 to 1,900 in May 1945. In 1946 Wesel became part of North Rhine-Westphalia. A restored 15th-century city hall, the Willibrordi-Dom and the citadel remain among its sights.
weser: The Weser is the longest river wholly in Germany. Together with the Werra, which rises in Thuringia, it is 744 km long, while the Weser itself measures 452 km. Weser and Werra are the same word in different dialects, the difference reflecting the old linguistic border between Central and Low German that passes through Hannoversch Münden. The name probably derives from an Old Germanic word meaning flow or ooze, and is cognate with the Wear in England and the Vistula in Poland. After Hannoversch Münden the river runs between the Wiehengebirge and the Weserbergland to the Porta Westfalica, then on to Bremen. Its largest tributary, the Aller, joins south of Bremen.

Between Minden and the North Sea the river has been largely canalised for ships of up to 1,200 tons, and eight hydroelectric dams stand at the ends of adjacent weir streams. A large reservoir, the Edersee on the Eder, the main tributary of the Fulda, keeps enough water in the river for shipping all year. Its dam, built in 1914, was bombed and severely damaged by British aircraft in May 1943, causing great destruction and about 70 deaths downstream, and was rebuilt within four months.

The Weser enters the North Sea in the southernmost part of the German Bight, where it splits into two arms, the Alte Weser and the Neue Weser, which are the waterways for ships bound for Bremerhaven, Nordenham and Bremen. The Alte Weser Lighthouse replaced the Roter Sand Lighthouse in 1964. Since the 19th century the river has been deepened twelve times, which altered the tides and caused severe ecological damage and a greater risk of flooding along its banks.
wessex: The Anglo-Saxons believed that Wessex was founded by Cerdic and Cynric of the Gewisse, though some consider this a legend. The two main sources for its early history are the West Saxon Genealogical Regnal List and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, which sometimes conflict. The first event that can be dated with reasonable certainty is the baptism of King Cynegils by Birinus at the end of the 630s, perhaps in 640. Birinus became bishop of the West Saxons with his seat at Dorchester-on-Thames. Cynegils's successor Cenwealh was a pagan at his accession but was baptised a few years later, after an exile in East Anglia, and Wessex became firmly Christian. He established a second bishopric at Winchester.

Wessex's fortunes were transformed in 802 by the accession of Egbert. In 825 or 826 he defeated King Beornwulf of Mercia at Ellendun and seized Surrey, Sussex, Kent and Essex. In 829 he conquered Mercia and secured the overlordship of the king of Northumbria, though Mercian independence was restored in 830. In 851 his son Æthelwulf crushed a Danish army at the Battle of Aclea.

The Great Heathen Army, which landed in 865, overwhelmed Northumbria and East Anglia, and in 871 invaded Wessex. At the beginning of 878 the Danes overran much of the kingdom and Alfred took refuge in the Somerset Levels, but he gathered an army and defeated them at the Battle of Edington. He issued a law code, built ships and organised an army and a system of burhs. His son Edward the Elder annexed London and Oxford, and by 918 took direct control of Mercia after the death of his sister Æthelflæd. In 927 Æthelstan conquered Northumbria, bringing all England under one ruler for the first time.

The Kingdom of Wessex was thus transformed into the Kingdom of England. After Cnut the Great conquered England in 1016 he created the earldom of Wessex, and in 1066 Harold Godwinson reunited the earldom with the crown, after which Wessex ceased to exist. The wyvern or dragon often used to symbolise it was popularised only in the 19th century, largely through the writings of E. A. Freeman. Thomas Hardy took the name for a fictionalised setting of his novels in Dorset and neighbouring counties, and Wessex remains a common term for the area.
west-africa: West Africa is the westernmost region of Africa. Its climate is shaped by the dry Sahara to the north and east, which produces the Harmattan winds, and by the Atlantic Ocean to the south and west, which brings seasonal monsoons, so that biomes range from tropical forest to dry land. The Sahel, a transition zone between the Sudanian savannas and the Sahara, crosses several of its countries. The United Nations defines the region as 16 countries, from Mauritania and Senegal to Nigeria, with an area of about 6.1 million square kilometres.

West African hunter-gatherers occupied the coast by 12,000 years ago and moved north as far as Mali, Burkina Faso and Mauritania between 12,000 and 8000 years ago. Centralised states followed, beginning with Dhar Tichitt from 1600 BCE and Djenné-Djenno from 300 BCE. The Ghana Empire flourished roughly between the 2nd and 12th centuries CE and gave way to the Mali Empire. Positioned at a crossroads of trade between North Africa and the Sahel, the region supplied gold, ivory and advanced ironworking.

Portuguese traders began establishing settlements along the coast in 1445, followed by the French, English, Spanish, Danish and Dutch, and the African slave trade began not long after. It encouraged the formation of states such as the Bono state, the Bambara Empire and Dahomey, which exchanged slaves for European firearms. In the early 19th century Fulani reformist jihads swept across the region, among them Usman dan Fodio's Fulani Empire, which replaced the Hausa city-states. Britain and France then controlled nearly the whole region. Ghana under Kwame Nkrumah became the first West African colony to gain independence, in 1957, and by 1974 the region's nations were entirely autonomous.

The region is culturally and demographically diverse, home to the Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo, Fulani, Akan, Mandé, Wolof, Songhai, Kanuri, Zarma, Tuareg and many other peoples. Islam, Christianity and traditional African religions are the most common religions. Its traditional building styles include the Sudano-Sahelian style in the inland areas and coastal forest styles, and typical formal dress includes the boubou robe and the Akan kente cloth.
west-african-vodun: Vodún, also called vodúnsínsen, meaning spirit worship, has no central authority and shows much diversity among its practitioners, known as vodúnsɛntó or vodúnisants. Its followers believe in a single divine creator, below whom an uncountable number of spirits, the vodún, govern different aspects of nature and society. Some are tied to particular cities and others to families.

The word comes from the Gbé languages and means spirit, God, divinity or presence. Belief is centred on efficacy rather than on faith. Followers hold that the vodún physically manifest in shrines, which are not mere images but their incarnations, and that an object's power comes from its acɛ, divine power. New spirits are readily admitted, and some practitioners call Jesus Christ the vodún of the Christians.

Initiation gives a person the power of a vodún and brings long-term obligations to honour, feed and pay the spirit, which in turn promises protection, abundance, long life and a large family. It may last from a few months to a few years, though Fá initiation in Benin usually takes less than a week. Spirits are given offerings, and animal sacrifice, called vɔ in Fon, nourishes the spirit's acɛ and the meat is eaten by the attendees.

Many cults include possession, when a person receives the spirit and speaks as it, giving advice. Divination, above all Fá, is performed by diviners called bokónó. The all-male secret societies Oró and Egúngún command respect, and Egúngún is held to have spread west from the Yoruba of Oyo. Charms called bǒ are used for healing and protection.

Before European colonialism, Vodún was not a single religion but, in the words of the anthropologist Timothy R. Landry, a social system of countless spirit and ancestor cults, some of them bound up with political structures. In the 18th century the Fon-dominated kingdom of Dahomey became a vassal of the Oyo Empire, and many Yoruba traditions passed to the Fon and Ewe, so that Vodún overlaps with Yoruba religion.

Enslaved vodúnsɛntó were carried to the Americas during the Atlantic slave trade, and their religions influenced Haitian Vodou, Louisiana Voodoo and Brazilian Candomblé Jejé. Christian missions worked in the region from the 18th century. After Mathieu Kérékou seized power in Dahomey in 1972, he made it a Marxist-Leninist state, banned Vodún ceremonies during the rainy season in 1973 and pressed further measures against the religion, so that initiations were done in secret and shortened.

About 17 per cent of the people of Benin, some 1.6 million, follow Vodún, and many Christians also practise it alongside their faith. Some foreign observers have considered it a form of Satanism, a view that its followers do not share.
west-bank: The West Bank is a landlocked territory on the western bank of the Jordan River, in the Levant. It is bordered by Jordan and the Dead Sea to the east and by Israel along the Green Line to the south, west and north. It has a land area of about 5,640 square kilometres and mostly rugged upland. Its elevation runs from the shore of the Dead Sea, 408 metres below sea level, to Mount Nabi Yunis at 1,030 metres. The name West Bank emerged for the territory occupied in 1948 and annexed in 1950 by Jordan, to distinguish it from Jordanian land east of the river.

From 1517 to 1917 the area was under Ottoman rule, as part of Ottoman Syria. In the early Ottoman period much of the northern West Bank formed part of the Turabay Emirate, a semi-autonomous Bedouin polity centred at Lajjun. Turkey renounced its claims in 1923, and the area became part of the British Mandate for Palestine. In 1947 the UN General Assembly recommended that it become part of a future Arab state, a proposal the Arab states opposed.

In the 1948 war the 1949 Armistice Agreements fixed the interim boundary between Israel and Jordan. After the Jericho Conference of December 1948, Transjordan annexed the area west of the river in 1950. Palestinian Arabs there were granted Jordanian citizenship and half the seats in the Jordanian parliament, and only the United Kingdom and Iraq recognised the annexation formally.

In June 1967 Israel captured the West Bank and East Jerusalem in the Six-Day War. Apart from East Jerusalem, the territory was not annexed, and it remained under military control until 1982. The Arab League summit at Rabat in 1974 named the Palestine Liberation Organization the sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people. Jordan did not formally relinquish its claim until 1988. The Oslo Accords of 1993 left the final status of the territory to later negotiation.
west-bengal: West Bengal is on the eastern bottleneck of India, stretching from the Himalayas in the north to the Bay of Bengal in the south. The Darjeeling Himalayan hill region in the far north is part of the eastern Himalayas. The narrow Terai separates the hills from the plains of North Bengal, which give way southward to the Ganges delta, and the Sundarbans mangrove forests, part of the world's largest mangrove forest, mark the delta's southern edge.

Stone Age tools some 20,000 years old have been found in the state. According to the Mahabharata the region was part of the Vanga kingdom. Greek writers around 100 BCE mention a land called Gangaridai at the mouths of the Ganges. The region belonged to several pan-Indian empires, including those of the Mauryans and the Guptas, and the citadel of Gauḍa was the capital of the Gauda kingdom, the Pala Empire and the Sena Empire. After the Ghurid conquests led by Bakhtiyar Khalji, Islam spread across Bengal. Under the Bengal Sultanate the region was a major trading land, and it was absorbed into the Mughal Empire in 1576.

The British East India Company defeated the last independent Nawab, Siraj ud-Daulah, at the Battle of Plassey in 1757, and after the Battle of Buxar in 1764 it won the right to collect revenue in Bengal. The Bengal famine of 1770 claimed millions of lives. Calcutta, the company's headquarters, became the capital of British-held India, and from 1912 to 1947 it was the capital of the Bengal Province. The region was a centre of the Indian independence movement and of the Bengali Renaissance.

In 1947 the Bengal Legislative Council and Assembly voted to partition Bengal along religious lines. The western part, with a Hindu majority, became the Indian state of West Bengal; the eastern part went to Pakistan as East Bengal, later East Pakistan, and became Bangladesh in 1971. Refugees from the east arrived in large numbers for decades.

West Bengal is a state of India with Kolkata as its capital and largest city. Its population was 91,347,736 at the 2011 census. Bengali and English are the official languages, and the main ethnic group is the Bengalis. Its cultural heritage includes the Charyapada, Baul music, the songs of Rabindranath Tagore and the Bengal School of Art, and the state has three World Heritage sites.
west-berlin: The London Protocol of 1944 and the Potsdam Agreement set the framework for the occupation of Germany after the war. Germany was to be administered by four Allies, the United States, the United Kingdom, the Soviet Union and France, and divided into four zones. Berlin, surrounded by the Soviet zone, was divided likewise, with the Western Allies occupying an enclave of its western parts. The occupation of Berlin could end only by a quadripartite agreement, and the Western Allies were guaranteed three air corridors to their sectors. West Berlin consisted of the American, British and French sectors established in 1945.

When the Federal Republic of Germany was established on 23 May 1949, Berlin remained occupied territory under the formal sovereignty of the Allies, so the Basic Law was not fully applicable to it. West Berlin nonetheless aligned itself politically with the Federal Republic, and most of its residents were West German citizens. It was heavily subsidised by West Germany as a showcase of the West. West Berliners could travel freely except during the Berlin Blockade by the Soviet Union, from 24 June 1948 to 12 May 1949, when the airlift limited flights. Road and rail travel to West Germany passed through East German border checks along transit routes, and air traffic under Allied control was the only link not directly under East German control.

On 27 May 1952 East Germany closed its border with West Berlin, and West Berliners then needed a permit to enter the East. Movement between the two halves of the city remained free for more than a decade until the Berlin Wall was built in 1961. After its construction Konrad Adenauer suggested that the United States propose to swap West Berlin for Thuringia and parts of Saxony and Mecklenburg; the Kennedy administration considered the idea but did not make the offer. Three underground and S-Bahn lines ran through tunnels beneath East Berlin, with their eastern stations shut and empty.

West Berlin had about two million inhabitants, the largest population of any city in Germany during the Cold War, and was noted for its cosmopolitan character and as a centre of education, research and culture. It had its own postal administration, issuing its own stamps, though in practice its post and telephones were integrated with West Germany's. The Wall fell in 1989. On 3 October 1990, the day Germany was officially reunified, East and West Berlin united and joined the Federal Republic as a city-state.
west-francia: West Francia, or the Kingdom of the West Franks, was created from the division of the Carolingian Empire after the death of Louis the Pious. In August 843, after three years of civil war, his three sons signed the Treaty of Verdun. The youngest, Charles the Bald, received the western part, while Lothair took Middle Francia and Louis the German East Francia. The West Frankish Annales Bertiniani say the rest, as far as Spain, was ceded to Charles. It did not include Lorraine, Alsace, Provence or Brittany. Aquitaine was assigned to Charles by the treaty, but he had to fight Pippin II of Aquitaine, and by 849 had secured most of it.

West Frankish kings were elected by the secular and ecclesiastical magnates. Charles the Bald was crowned Emperor of Rome in 875. After the death of Carloman II in 884 the nobles elected Charles the Fat, already king in East Francia and Italy, and for a time all of Francia was reunited under one ruler. His handling of the Viking siege of Paris in 885–86 reduced his prestige, and he was deposed in 887. The nobles then elected Odo, Count of Paris, as king. Between 888 and 936 candidates from the Carolingian and Robertian houses were chosen alternately, and the kings grew weaker as regional dukes and nobles became semi-independent. Duchies such as Burgundy, Aquitaine, Normandy and Champagne emerged.

Vikings settled in Normandy and Magyars invaded from 919. The nobles deposed Charles the Simple in 922, and he died in captivity in 929. By the time of Lothair, who inherited his father Louis IV's lands in 954 under his mother Gerberga's regency, the royal lands were so small that the Carolingian practice of dividing them among the sons was dropped.

After Lothair and his son Louis V died prematurely, the nobles elected Hugh Capet king in 987. This traditionally marks the end of the Carolingian line in France and the end of West Francia as a kingdom. Hugh was the first ruler of the House of Capet, which ruled France through the High Middle Ages, though at first they controlled little beyond the Île-de-France. Historians generally see the period as the gradual transition toward the Kingdom of France. By the 13th century the term Regnum francorum had evolved into Regnum Francia.
west-germany: At the Yalta Conference of 4 to 11 February 1945, leaders of the United States, the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union agreed that post-war Germany would be divided into four occupation zones: French in the far west, British in the north-west, American in the south and Soviet in the east. Berlin was divided into four zones as well. The divisions were not meant to dismember Germany. The Federal Republic was founded on 23 May 1949 from twelve states formed in the three western zones, and at first it claimed an exclusive mandate for all of Germany. Three south-western states merged to form Baden-Württemberg in 1952, and the Saarland joined in 1957.

The Federal Republic obtained the full authority of a sovereign state on 5 May 1955 under the Bonn–Paris conventions, although full sovereignty came only with the Two Plus Four Agreement in 1990. It joined NATO on 9 May 1955. Konrad Adenauer was chancellor from 1949 to 1963, and he worked for full alignment with NATO and for agreements that grew into the European Union. Ludwig Erhard and Kurt Georg Kiesinger followed, and Willy Brandt became chancellor in October 1969. His Ostpolitik aimed to improve relations with Eastern Europe, and in 1970 he knelt at the memorial to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising. Helmut Schmidt served from 1974 to 1982 and Helmut Kohl from 1982.

Denazification, an Allied programme to remove Nazi personnel and ideology from public life, was unpopular and opposed by Adenauer's government. Laws of 1951 granted amnesties and ended it, and many people with a Nazi past returned to the state apparatus. In 1967 the student Benno Ohnesorg was shot by a policeman during protests against emergency laws.

West Germany was a federal parliamentary republic with its capital at Bonn. The president was a largely ceremonial head of state, and the chancellor, elected by the Bundestag, headed the government. The upper house, the Bundesrat, represented the Länder. West Berlin was treated as an unofficial eleventh state, though it was under Allied control. After the opening of the Berlin Wall, East Germany voted to accede to the Federal Republic, and the five reconstituted eastern Länder and a reunited Berlin joined on 3 October 1990, raising the number of states from ten to sixteen. The reunited Germany is the direct continuation of West Germany and kept its memberships in NATO and the European Economic Community.
west-indies: The West Indies form an island subregion of the Americas, surrounded by the North Atlantic Ocean and the Caribbean Sea. They comprise 13 independent island countries and 18 dependencies in three archipelagos: the Greater Antilles, the Lesser Antilles and the Lucayan Archipelago, which includes the Bahamas and the Turks and Caicos Islands. The term is often used interchangeably with Caribbean. The islands are a geologically complex system of some 7,000 islands and islets stretching over 3,000 km from the Florida peninsula to the northern coast of Venezuela.

The Greater Antilles are the oldest group and hold the largest islands, Cuba, Hispaniola, Jamaica and Puerto Rico. The Lesser Antilles are a volcanic island arc with 19 active volcanoes, and the Lucayan islands are low islands on the Bahama Platform.

Many cultures were indigenous to these islands, with evidence dating some of them to the mid-sixth millennium BCE. Christopher Columbus, who left Spain in 1492 seeking a western sea route to the spice trade of the Indies, believed he had reached the easternmost part of them. The Spanish therefore called the new lands Indias Occidentales, the West Indies, to tell them from the East Indies, and the term first applied to all the Americas. Later the Spanish, Dutch, French, British and Danish West Indies were distinguished by the European power to which they belonged.

In the late sixteenth century French, English and Dutch merchants and privateers began to attack Spanish and Portuguese shipping in the Caribbean. They gained a foothold in the Lesser Antilles with the colonisation of Saint Kitts in 1624 and Barbados in 1626. When the Sugar Revolution took off in the mid-seventeenth century they brought in thousands of enslaved Africans to work the fields and mills, who replaced or joined the indigenous Kalinago and the European indentured servants. In 1916 Denmark sold the Danish West Indies to the United States for US$25 million in gold, creating the United States Virgin Islands.

Between 1958 and 1962 the United Kingdom reorganised its island territories, except the British Virgin Islands and the Bahamas, into the West Indies Federation, in the hope that it would become a single independent nation. It had limited powers, practical problems and little popular support. Nine provinces later became independent states and four became British Overseas Territories.
west-java: The oldest archaeological finds come from Anyer on the western coast, with evidence of bronze and iron metallurgy from the first millennium CE. The prehistoric Buni culture, near present-day Bekasi, made clay pottery, and artefacts dated between 400 BCE and 100 CE, mostly containers laid as burial gifts, have been found. The Batujaya Archaeological Site holds evidence from the 2nd century, and the Jiwa Temple at Batujaya is thought to date from about then.

One of the earliest recorded histories in Indonesia is that of the kingdom of Tarumanagara, whose kings are described on seven fourth-century stones inscribed in Wengi letters, used in the Pallava period, and in Sanskrit. Its records last to the sixth century, which coincides with the attack of Srivijaya mentioned in the Kota Kapur inscription of 686. The Sunda Kingdom then became the ruling power, as recorded on the Kebon Kopi II inscription of 932. It reached its peak under King Sri Baduga Maharaja, whose reign from 1482 to 1521 is traditionally remembered as an age of peace and prosperity.

In the 16th century Dutch and British trading companies set up in western Java after the fall of the Sultanate of Banten, and for the next three hundred years the region was under Dutch East Indies administration. The Dutch introduced tea, coffee and quinine as cash crops, and the Preanger became a productive plantation area. West Java was one of the first eight provinces of independent Indonesia and was re-established on 14 July 1950. Jakarta was split off in 1961, and Banten became a separate province on 17 October 2000.

The provincial capital is Bandung, in the mountainous centre of the province, and the largest city is Bekasi. West Java borders Banten and Jakarta to the west, Central Java to the east, the Java Sea to the north and the Indian Ocean to the south. With Banten it is the homeland of the Sundanese people, the second-largest ethnic group of Indonesia. Rice cultivation has long underpinned its economy, and the rice goddess Nyai Pohaci Sanghyang Asri is revered in Sundanese culture.
west-nusa-tenggara: West Nusa Tenggara comprises the western portion of the Lesser Sunda Islands, with the exception of Bali, which is its own province. Its area of 19,675.89 km2 consists of two main islands, Lombok in the west and the much larger but less densely populated Sumbawa in the east, with several small islands such as the Gili Islands. Mount Rinjani, an active volcano on Lombok, is the highest mountain in the province at 3,726 metres and has a crater lake called Segara Anak. The climate is tropical, with a rainy season from November to March, and the east of Sumbawa is dry and often short of rain.

Prehistoric objects such as sarcophagi, decorated stoneware and axes suggest the region was first inhabited by people from Southeast Asia. The Sasak are the most numerous indigenous people, mostly on Lombok, while Sumbawa has the Sumbawa (Samawa) and Bima. In 1365 the Negarakertagama of Mpu Prapanca listed places on both islands among the lands of the Majapahit Empire. As Majapahit collapsed, Hindu influence declined and Islam spread along the coasts, brought generally by Malays; in Bima it came with King Abdul Kahir, the first Bima king to embrace Islam.

The Dutch East India Company's influence grew in the 17th century. In 1669 Sultan Ambela Abdul Khair Sirajuddin of Bima made an agreement recognising Dutch power, which barred foreign traders except by Company permit. The eruption of Mount Tambora in 1815 destroyed the two kingdoms of Tambora and Papekat and killed more than 10,000 people. After independence the area belonged to the State of East Indonesia and then to the province of the Lesser Sunda Islands. Law No. 64 of 14 August 1958 created West Nusa Tenggara, with Ruslan Djakraningrat as first governor.

Mataram, on Lombok, is the capital and largest city of the province. Rice, corn, soybeans, peanuts and tobacco are the main crops, and fishing and seaweed cultivation are important on the coasts. The Batu Hijau mine on Sumbawa is among the world's larger copper and gold mines. The Sasak villages of Lombok, Mount Rinjani and the Gili Islands draw many visitors.
west-pakistan: At independence in 1947 Pakistan comprised two regions separated by about 1,600 km of India. The western wing was made up of three governor's provinces, the North-West Frontier, West Punjab and Sind, together with Baluchistan, the Baluchistan States Union, several princely states including Bahawalpur, Chitral, Dir, Hunza, Khairpur and Swat, the Karachi Federal Capital Territory and the tribal areas. The eastern wing was the single province of East Bengal. The partition divided resources unequally: Pakistan received 22 percent of the land, 9 percent of the population and 36 percent of the military forces, and its facilities were mostly obsolete, with a week's ammunition reserve.

The western wing dominated politics, although East Pakistan held more than half of the population and a disproportionately small number of seats in the Constituent Assembly. This inequality and the distance between the wings were believed to be delaying a constitution. The government therefore announced the One Unit policy on 22 November 1954, merging the western provinces, states and tribal areas into one province to mirror the single province in the east.

The province was composed of twelve divisions. Its capital was first Karachi, later Lahore, and in 1965 Islamabad. The constitution of 1956 confirmed a parliamentary form of government, with Islam as the state religion and Urdu, English and Bengali as state languages. Violence in Lahore from 1953 led to martial law there. From 1947 to 1959 the government was only partly stable, with seven prime ministers removed. A military coup in 1958 brought General Ayub Khan to power, and the capital moved to Rawalpindi in 1959.

The One Unit programme met harsh opposition and civil unrest, and the four provinces struggled for its abolition. A committee for its dissolution worked with the government of Yahya Khan. West Pakistan was abolished on 1 July 1970 under the Legal Framework Order, and the provinces of Balochistan, the North-West Frontier, Punjab and Sindh were restored.

In the general elections of December 1970 the Bengali Awami League under Mujibur Rahman won all but two of the 162 seats allocated to East Pakistan. The military government did not allow him to form a government. A war followed between Pakistan and Bengali nationalists, the Mukti Bahini, and India intervened in support of them. East Pakistan became the independent state of Bangladesh on 16 December 1971, and the term West Pakistan became redundant. The 1961 census counted 42.8 million people in West Pakistan, about 45 percent of the 93 million in the whole country.
west-prussia: The province lay on the lower Vistula near its mouth at the Baltic Sea and on the lands to the west and east. In the west it bordered the easternmost part of Brandenburg and lay between the provinces of Posen and Pomerania, a region of the Baltic Uplands with the Tuchola Forest and the Kashubian Lake District, where the Turmberg reached 329 metres. In the southeast the river crossed a flat plain and the fertile Culmerland, with the cities of Culm, Thorn and Graudenz. Danzig was the largest city of the province.

The Teutonic Order took Danzig and Pomerelia in 1308, and German-speaking settlers were encouraged to move in. Under the Second Peace of Thorn, which ended the Thirteen Years' War, Poland gained most of the region, which became Royal Prussia and kept its own legislature, the Prussian Estates, until the Union of Lublin in 1569.

After the First Partition of Poland, King Frederick II of Prussia incorporated the annexed lands into the new Province of West Prussia in 1773, giving Prussia a land link between Pomerania and East Prussia. German-speaking Protestants made up 54% of the annexed area. Danzig and Thorn were added in the Second Partition of 1793. After the Treaties of Tilsit of 1807 the region around Thorn went to the Duchy of Warsaw and Danzig became a free city; the Congress of Vienna returned them. West Prussia was joined with East Prussia as the Province of Prussia in 1829, and the two were separated again in 1878 within the German Empire.

Under the German Empire the authorities pursued Germanisation and settlement policies and the Kulturkampf against Catholics. The census of 1910 counted 1,703,474 inhabitants, of whom 64.5% were German and 35.5% Polish; a Polish author argued in 1918 that the Polish share was nearer 42.5%.

The Treaty of Versailles divided the province into four areas: the Free City of Danzig under the League of Nations, the eastern districts as the administrative district of West Prussia in East Prussia, the westernmost districts as part of Posen-West Prussia from 1922, and a central region given to Poland as the Pomeranian Voivodeship, known as the Polish Corridor. In a plebiscite in 1920 the Marienwerder area voted by 92.4% to stay with Germany. After the invasion of Poland in 1939 the region became part of the Reichsgau Danzig-West Prussia, where Poles and Jews were expelled, enslaved or killed. In 1945 it was restored to Poland, and most of the remaining Germans were expelled.
west-sumatra: West Sumatra lies in the middle of Sumatra's western coast, facing the Indian Ocean along a coastline of 375 km, and includes the Mentawai Islands offshore. Plains and the volcanic highlands of the Barisan mountains make up the land, with lakes such as Maninjau and Singkarak, and peaks such as Kerinci at 3,805 m and Marapi at 2,891 m.

Dense tropical forest shelters Sumatran tigers and Rafflesia arnoldii, the largest flower in the world, and the province holds Siberut National Park and part of Kerinci Seblat National Park. It is known as Bumi Minangkabau, the Land of the Minangkabau, though the traditional Minangkabau region is wider than the province and reaches Negeri Sembilan in Malaysia.

According to the Minangkabau chronicle, the Tambo, many small kingdoms stood in the area between the 1st and 16th centuries, usually under the influence of larger ones such as Malayu and Pagaruyung. The Pagaruyung Kingdom was founded by Adityawarman in 1347. The name Minangkabau is explained by a legend in which locals faced a foreign kingdom, usually taken to be Majapahit, in a contest of cattle: a suckling calf tore open the large bull, giving the phrase manang kabau, winning cattle. The first European to reach the region was the French explorer Jean Parmentier, around 1523.

In the early 17th century Pagaruyung had to recognise the sovereignty of the Aceh Sultanate. Around 1665 the Minangkabau of the west coast rebelled against Aceh's governor, and the Dutch East India Company, which wished to end Aceh's monopoly on gold and pepper, expelled Aceh from the coast in 1666. Under the Dutch the region became the residency Sumatra's West Coast. During the Japanese occupation it was renamed Sumatora Nishi Kaigan Shu. Before becoming a province in 1957, West Sumatra was part of the province of Central Sumatra, which existed from 1948 to 1957.

The capital and largest city is Padang, and the province is divided into twelve regencies and seven cities. About 5.5 million people lived there at the 2020 census, most of them Minangkabau, who speak Minangkabau and are predominantly Muslim, with followers of Christianity mainly in the Mentawai Islands. Minangkabau society is matrilineal, and the traditional house is the Rumah Gadang, with its horned roof called gonjong, built with wooden pegs rather than iron nails. Andalas University is the oldest university in Indonesia outside Java. Padang cuisine, built on gulai curry, chili and rice, is the food of the Minangkabau.
west-sussex: West Sussex has a land area of 1,991 square kilometres (769 sq mi) and is bordered by Surrey to the north, East Sussex to the east, Hampshire to the west and the English Channel to the south. The South Downs, a chalk escarpment, cross it from east to west and divide the north from the south, falling sharply into the Weald to the north and more gently towards the south, where a narrow strip of flat land lies between the hills and the coast. The strip widens to the west, where it is broken by Chichester Harbour, a ria. The Rivers Arun and Adur drain most of the county, and its highest point is at Blackdown, on the Lower Greensand ridges along the Surrey border.

Human settlement goes back to the Lower Paleolithic: the oldest hominin remains known in Britain were found at Eartham Pit, Boxgrove. Prehistoric monuments include the Bronze Age burial mounds called the Devil's Jumps and the Iron Age hill forts of Cissbury Ring and Chanctonbury Ring. The Romans conquered the Atrebates, the indigenous Britons, and built Fishbourne Roman Palace, rural villas such as Bignor and roads such as Stane Street. They also used the Weald for iron production on an industrial scale.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records the foundation of the Kingdom of Sussex in 477, when Ælle arrived at Cymenshore in three ships with his three sons and killed or put to flight the local inhabitants. Most historians regard the story as somewhat of a myth, although archaeology suggests that Saxons began to settle in the late fifth century. The name Sussex comes from the Old English Sūþseaxe, the South Saxons. The kingdom was absorbed into Wessex and became the county of Sussex, which was traditionally divided into six units called rapes.

By the sixteenth century the three western rapes were grouped informally and had their own Quarter Sessions. They were governed by a separate county council, and Sussex was divided into the administrative counties of East and West Sussex. In 1974 West Sussex became a single ceremonial county under the Local Government Act 1972, and a large part of the rape of Lewes, the Mid Sussex district, was transferred to it.

West Sussex is a ceremonial county of South East England with Chichester, a cathedral city, as its county town. Its largest settlement is Crawley, and the largest towns on the coast are Bognor Regis, Littlehampton and Worthing. It contains Gatwick Airport and stately homes such as Goodwood, Petworth House and Uppark, and castles such as Arundel Castle and Bramber Castle.
west-timor: West Timor covers the western part of the island of Timor, apart from the district of Oecussi-Ambeno, an exclave of East Timor. It has an area of 14,513 square kilometres. More than 60 per cent of the surface is rugged low mountain ranges cut by deep, V-shaped river valleys, and the highest point is Mount Mutis at 2,427 metres. The monsoon climate brings heavy rain from October to May and a dry season for the rest of the year, which has produced wide savannas. In the past these isolated plateaus and mountain landscapes favoured politically autonomous territories.

Anthropologists assume that the island was settled in three waves, beginning with Australo-Papuans between about 40,000 and 20,000 BCE. The Atoin Meto, who dominate West Timor, are regarded as descendants of the first wave. When the Portuguese reached Timor in the 16th century they found many small, relatively independent kingdoms. The kingdom of Wehale, with its capital at Laran, formed the spiritual centre of the island, and the Sonba'i kingdom arose on its model. Dominicans founded Lifau in 1556 to secure the sandalwood trade.

The Dutch East India Company made treaties with five small rulers around Kupang, the so-called five loyal allies, between 1665 and 1688. In 1749 a Portuguese and Topasse attack on Kupang ended in disaster at the Battle of Penfui, and their rule in West Timor collapsed. In 1904 the Dutch could hold an audience with the ruler of Wehale only by force. When they demanded an oath from the rulers in 1905, rebellions broke out from 1906 and continued until 1916, when the rulers had to accept Dutch authority. West Timor was a centre of Dutch loyalists during the Indonesian National Revolution of 1945 to 1949.

West Timor is part of the Indonesian province of East Nusa Tenggara, and its main port and largest city is Kupang. The Atoin Meto form the dominant population, speaking Uab Meto, alongside Tetum, Kemak, Bunak, Helong and other languages. About 95 per cent of the people are Christian, 54 per cent Protestant and 41 per cent Catholic, and ancestor worship and belief in spirits remain widespread. The economy is mainly agricultural, producing corn, rice, coffee, copra and fruit.
west-yorkshire: West Yorkshire covers 2,029 km2 and borders North Yorkshire, South Yorkshire, Derbyshire, Greater Manchester and Lancashire. Its western part lies in the South Pennines, with steep valleys and a small part of the Peak District National Park, and the land flattens eastward towards the Vale of York. The rivers Aire and Calder drain the county from west to east. Geologically it rests almost entirely on rocks of carboniferous age, including the Yorkshire coalfield, with younger Magnesian Limestone in the extreme east.

The county was formed in 1974 under the Local Government Act 1972 from the central part of the West Riding of Yorkshire, and it corresponds roughly to the historic core of the Riding and the county boroughs of Bradford, Dewsbury, Halifax, Huddersfield, Leeds and Wakefield. Its five metropolitan boroughs are Bradford, Calderdale, Kirklees, Leeds and Wakefield. The Local Government Act 1985 abolished the county council in 1986 and passed its powers to the boroughs and to joint bodies, but West Yorkshire remains a metropolitan and ceremonial county with a Lord Lieutenant and a High Sheriff.

Wakefield's parish church became a cathedral in 1888 and the town was granted city status that July. The Industrial Revolution then made Leeds and Bradford the area's two largest cities; Leeds received city status in 1893 and Bradford in 1897. Coal was mined around Wakefield, Castleford, Pontefract and South and East Leeds. Bradford, Halifax and Huddersfield grew through woollen mills, Leeds was a centre of cloth manufacture, and the Heavy Woollen District included Dewsbury, Batley, Morley, Ossett, Cleckheaton and Heckmondwike. The woollen and cloth industries declined through the twentieth century, and the last colliery in the county, Hay Royds at Denby Dale, closed in 2012 after a flood.

Leeds is the largest settlement, and the five boroughs work together through the West Yorkshire Combined Authority, established in 2014. The Rhubarb Triangle, wholly in the county, still produces forced rhubarb, which received protected designation of origin status in 2010. Saltaire is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and other landmarks include Kirkstall Abbey, Pontefract Castle, Sandal Castle, Harewood House and the Brontë Parsonage Museum at Haworth. The Middleton Railway is described as the world's oldest steam railway.
western-african-ebola-epidemic: The epidemic was caused by the Ebola virus, one of four disease-causing viruses in the genus Ebolavirus. Since its discovery in 1976, Ebola virus disease had been confined to Middle Africa, where it is native. Studies have shown that the outbreak was likely caused by a lineage that spread from Middle Africa through an animal host within the preceding decade, with the first transfer to humans in Guinea. Bats are strongly implicated as reservoir hosts, and the index case is suspected to have followed a child's contact with an insectivorous bat from a colony near the village of Meliandou.

The first cases were recorded in Guinea in December 2013. On 25 March 2014 the World Health Organization reported an outbreak in four southeastern districts of Guinea, with 86 suspected cases including 59 deaths. Thinking the spread contained, Médecins Sans Frontières closed its treatment centres in May, but large numbers of new cases reappeared in late August. The disease spread to Liberia and Sierra Leone, with minor outbreaks in Nigeria and Mali, and isolated cases in Senegal, the United Kingdom and Italy. Secondary infections of medical workers occurred in the United States and Spain.

Extreme poverty, dysfunctional health systems, distrust of government after years of armed conflict, a delay of several months in responding, burial customs of washing the body and spread into densely populated cities all contributed to the failure to control it. A public health emergency of international concern was declared on 8 August 2014, and a cordon sanitaire was set up that day around the area where Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone meet and where 70 per cent of known cases had been found. Cases peaked in October 2014 and then declined after substantial international resources were committed.

By the end, 28,616 people had been infected and 11,310 had died, a case fatality rate of 40 per cent, although the WHO believes the figures understate the outbreak. It ended its emergency status on 29 March 2016, and the epidemic was declared over on 9 June 2016, 42 days after the last case tested negative.

About 17,000 people survived, many with post-Ebola syndrome, symptoms severe enough to need care for months or years. Later the WHO announced that a two-year trial of the rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine appeared to protect against the strain responsible. The WHO called the aftermath an emergency within an emergency for families, health systems, economies and social structures.
western-bug: The Bug rises in the Lviv Oblast in western Ukraine and flows north into the Volyn Oblast. It then follows the border between Ukraine and Poland and then that between Poland and Belarus, where it runs along part of the boundary between the Masovian and Podlaskie Voivodeships, and joins the Narew at Serock. Its total length is 774 kilometres. It forms part of the boundary between Belarus and Poland for 178 kilometres and part of that between Ukraine and Poland for 185 kilometres. Its drainage basin covers 38,712 square kilometres, half in Poland, just over a quarter in Belarus and slightly under a quarter in Ukraine.

The Slavic river name Bug is explained by Zbigniew Gołąb as deriving from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning to bend or turn, so that it originally referred to a river bend. The river has often served as a frontier. Its line has traditionally been treated as the ethnographic border between East and West and between Orthodox Ukrainians and Belarusians and Catholic Poles, with Podlachia a borderland where these peoples mixed.

After the Third Partition of Poland in 1795 the Bug was part of the frontier between the territories held by Austria, Russia and Prussia. It was later part of the eastern border of the Duchy of Warsaw and of Congress Poland, and then of the Vistula Land. A clause of the German-Soviet Frontier Treaty of 28 September 1939, signed after the invasion of Poland, made it part of the dividing line between the German Wehrmacht and the Soviet Red Army.

The Bug is linked to the Dnieper by the Dnieper-Bug Canal, which joins it through the Mukhavets. A few kilometres from Vysokaye in Belarus's Brest Region, on the Bug, lies the westernmost point of Belarus. Zegrze Lake, an artificial lake with a hydroelectric complex, was built a little downstream of the confluence with the Narew in 1963. The river floods each spring as the snow melts, and ice jams in winter can raise its level by up to 2 metres.
western-dvina: The Daugava, also known as the Western Dvina or the Väina River, rises in the Valdai Hills of Russia close to the source of the Volga. It flows through Belarus and Latvia into the Gulf of Riga of the Baltic Sea. It is 1,020 kilometres long, of which 352 are in Latvia and 325 in Russia, and it traces a great south-bending curve through northern Belarus. Its catchment area is 87,900 square kilometres. Riga, the capital of Latvia, bridges the estuary four times, and its centre lies 15 kilometres from the river's mouth.

According to Max Vasmer's etymological dictionary, the name Dvina cannot come from a Uralic language and possibly derives from an Indo-European word for "river" or "stream", resembling Danuvius, which comes from the Proto-Indo-European dānu, "large river". The Finno-Ugric names, such as Livonian Vēna and Estonian Väina, stem from Proto-Finnic väin, roughly "a large, peacefully rolling river".

People have settled at the river's mouth and along the Gulf of Riga for millennia, at first as hunter-gatherers who fished the estuary. From about the sixth century CE Viking explorers crossed the Baltic and sailed upriver into the interior. In medieval times the Daugava formed part of the trade route from the Varangians to the Greeks, carrying furs from the north and Byzantine silver from the south. The Riga area, inhabited by the Finnic-speaking Livs, was a key place of settlement and defence at the river's mouth at least as early as the Middle Ages, as the now destroyed fort at Torņakalns on the west bank shows.

From the end of the Livonian War much of the river formed the north-eastern border of the Duchy of Courland and Semigallia, dividing it from Livonia, later Swedish Livonia. Under the Russian Empire it separated the governorate of Courland on the west bank from Livonia and Vitebsk on the east. The Ķegums Hydroelectric Power Station was built in Latvia from 1936 to 1939, and the Pļaviņas station began work in 1968 and the Riga station in 1974.

Towns on the river include Vitebsk, Polotsk and Daugavpils, and Riga stands at its mouth. Polotsk is home to the Boris stones. The river's tributaries include the Mezha, the Dysna, the Aiviekste and the Ogre.
western-front-world-war-i: The Western Front was where the German and French armies, the most powerful in Europe, met. At the outbreak of war in August 1914 Germany executed a modified Schlieffen Plan, bypassing the French border defences by moving through neutral Belgium and then turning south to encircle the French army. Britain had guaranteed Belgian neutrality under the Treaty of London of 1839 and joined the war when its ultimatum expired at midnight on 4 August.

Luxembourg was occupied on 2 August, Liège fell after a siege from 5 to 16 August, and Brussels was taken on 20 August. The Germans came within 70 km of Paris, but at the First Battle of the Marne from 6 to 12 September French and British troops forced them to retreat.

After the Marne both sides extended their trenches in the Race to the Sea, from the Swiss frontier to the North Sea. Between 1915 and 1917 massive bombardments and infantry advances met entrenchments, machine guns and barbed wire, and no significant advances were made.

Verdun in 1916 cost a combined 700,000 casualties, the Somme in the same year over a million, and Passchendaele in 1917 487,000. On the first day of the Somme, 1 July, the British Army suffered about 57,000 casualties. Poison gas, aircraft and tanks were tried; at Cambrai on 20 November 1917 the British launched the first massed tank attack, with 324 tanks.

The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk of March 1918 released divisions from the east, and Germany's spring offensives advanced nearly 100 kilometres, the deepest advance by either side since 1914. Operation Michael led the entente to place General Ferdinand Foch in command of all its forces in France. American troops, the first of whom had arrived in June 1917, came to number 2.1 million on this front. On 8 August 1918, at Amiens, Hindenburg named the Black Day of the German army, and the Hundred Days Offensive followed.

German troops began to surrender in large numbers, Ludendorff was forced out, and the German Revolution put a new government in power. The Armistice of Compiègne stopped hostilities on the Western Front on 11 November 1918. The Treaty of Versailles, signed in June 1919, returned Alsace-Lorraine to France and limited the German army to 100,000 men. The war left tens of thousands of maimed soldiers and war widows, and Belgium lost 30,000 and France 40,000 civilians dead.
western-ghats: The Western Ghats, also known as the Sahyadri, stretch 1,600 km (990 mi) along the west coast of India and cover about 160,000 km2 (62,000 sq mi). They run through Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu, from the Tapti River to Swamithoppe in Kanyakumari district at the southern tip of the peninsula. They meet the Eastern Ghats in the Nilgiris. Geologists hold that they formed during the break-up of the supercontinent of Gondwana, rising along the coast in the Late Jurassic and Early Cretaceous when India separated from Africa. They are the faulted and eroded edge of the Deccan Plateau, and their average elevation is about 1,200 m (3,900 ft), with Anamudi, at 2,695 m (8,842 ft), the highest peak.

The name joins ghat, a word that can mean a range of stepped hills or the steps leading down to water, to the direction west. The linguist Thomas Burrow traced ghat to Dravidian words such as kattu, meaning mountain side, ridge or dam, in Tamil. Sahyadri, from Sanskrit, means benevolent or tolerant mountain. Three gaps break the range: the Goa Gap, the oldest and widest, the Palghat Gap, and the narrow Sengottai Gap in the south.

Historically the Western Ghats were covered in dense forest, the natural habitat of wildlife and of native tribal people. Their inaccessibility made it difficult for people from the plains to cultivate the land and build settlements. After the establishment of British colonial rule in the region, large areas were cleared for agricultural plantations and timber, and the forests were severely fragmented by clear-felling. Introduced species threatened the rare endemic species, and the complex tropical rainforests suffered more than other habitats. Other threats included overexploitation, illicit grazing, mining and poaching.

The range forms one of India's major watersheds, whose rivers drain almost 40 per cent of the country's land area, among them the Godavari, Kaveri and Krishna. Most flow east to the Bay of Bengal, and many are dammed for irrigation and hydroelectric power. The mountains block the monsoon winds from the Arabian Sea, bringing heavy rain to the west coast and leaving a rain shadow over the interior of the Deccan.

The Western Ghats are a biodiversity hotspot that holds nearly 30 per cent of the species of flora and fauna found in India, most of them endemic, and at least 325 globally threatened species. The Government of India has established protected areas, including two biosphere reserves and 13 national parks, and the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve is the largest contiguous protected area. In 2012 UNESCO declared 39 sites in seven clusters across the range World Heritage Sites.
western-new-guinea: The region covers 412,214.61 square kilometres, 1,200 kilometres from east to west and 736 kilometres from north to south, and includes the Biak and Raja Ampat archipelagoes. It is largely rainforest, home to traditional peoples such as the Dani of the Baliem Valley, and its largest city is Jayapura. Names carry political meaning: Papua is the official name in the ISO standard, while independence activists say West Papua. Over the centuries it has also been called West New Guinea, West Irian and Irian Jaya.

Papuan habitation is estimated to have begun more than 50,000 years ago. Research indicates that the highlands were an early and independent centre of agriculture, and the banana has been cultivated there for at least 7,000 years. Austronesian peoples settled the area at least 3,000 years ago, especially around Cenderawasih Bay. Trade with neighbouring Indonesian islands is documented as early as the seventh century, and from the Moluccas Muslim merchants built trading ties with the coast by the 17th century. Knowledge of ironworking reached the region around the 16th century.

In 1606 Luís Vaz de Torres reached the western part of the island and claimed it for the King of Spain. The Dutch later claimed the region and made it part of the Dutch East Indies, and began missionary work in the nineteenth century. Japan occupied the northern coast in 1942, and Dutch guerrillas under Mauritz Christiaan Kokkelink resisted behind its lines. In 1944 Jan van Eechoud set up a school for administrators at Hollandia, now Jayapura, whose graduates went on to found nationalist movements both for Indonesia and for Papuan independence.

Sukarno made the takeover of the territory a focus of his struggle against Dutch imperialism. In December 1961 he created a Supreme Operations Command, and in January 1962 Suharto was appointed to lead Operation Mandala. Infiltrations by sea and parachute drops met difficult terrain and Papuan fighters; of 1,429 paratroopers, 216 were killed or missing and 296 captured. The Dutch transferred the region in 1962 to a United Nations Temporary Executive Authority, which passed it to Indonesia, and the Act of Free Choice followed in 1969.

Indonesia granted the region Special Autonomy status in 2001 and divided it in 2003 into Papua and West Papua provinces, to which Central Papua, Highland Papua, South Papua and Southwest Papua were added in 2022. The 2020 census counted 5,437,775 people, most of them indigenous. The official language is Indonesian, with Papuan Malay the most used lingua franca, and estimates of the local languages range from 200 to over 700. Christianity is the predominant religion, followed by Islam. The main industries are agriculture, fishing, oil production and mining.
western-sahara: Western Sahara lies on the north-west coast of Africa, on the cusp of North Africa and West Africa, bordering the North Atlantic Ocean, Morocco, Algeria and Mauritania. It covers 272,000 square kilometres, mostly desert flatland. The coast is low and flat, and in the north the land rises to small mountains of up to 600 metres on the eastern side. There are no permanent streams, though spring flash floods occur, and a cool offshore current can bring fog and heavy dew. Summer highs in the interior reach 43 to 45 degrees.

The earliest known inhabitants were the Gaetuli. Roman-era sources describe the area as inhabited, depending on the century, by the Gaetulian Autololes or the Gaetulian Daradae. Other early inhabitants may have been the Bafour and the Serer; the Bafour were later replaced or absorbed by Berber-speaking populations, and religious and ethnic persecution of the Serer led to their southward migration in the 11th century. Islam arrived in the 8th century, and the territory may have been on caravan routes between Marrakesh and Tombouctou.

In the 11th century the Maqil Arabs settled in Morocco. Towards the end of the Almohad Caliphate the Beni Hassan, a sub-tribe of the Maqil, were called to put down a rebellion in the Sous. Under the Marinid dynasty they rebelled, were defeated by the Sultan and escaped beyond the dry river Saguia el-Hamra, where they were in constant war with the Lamtuna Berbers of the Sahara. Over roughly five centuries some Berber tribes mixed with the Maqil Arab tribes, forming a culture unique to Morocco and Mauritania.

Spanish colonisation lasted roughly from 1884 to 1976, and Spanish became one of the territory's main languages. Spain tried to transfer its administration to Morocco and Mauritania, though an advisory opinion of the International Court of Justice held that those countries had no sovereignty over Western Sahara. A war followed in which the Polisario Front proclaimed the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic. Mauritania withdrew its claims in 1979 and Morocco secured control of most of the territory. A UN-sponsored ceasefire was reached in 1991.

The United Nations designates Western Sahara a non-self-governing territory, and sovereignty remains contested between Morocco and the Polisario Front, whose government in exile is based at Tindouf, Algeria. A wall about 2,700 kilometres long, the Berm, divides the territory. The main ethnic group is the Sahrawis, a mainly nomadic people of mixed Arab-Berber descent who speak the Hassānīya dialect of Arabic; they are Sunni Muslims of the Maliki school. Many were settled in refugee camps at Tindouf after 1975.
western-schism: Under pressure from King Philip IV of France, the popes had resided in Avignon since 1309, in an enclave surrounded by France. The Avignon Papacy developed a reputation for corruption, attributed to strong French influence and to efforts to extend patronage and raise revenue. Gregory XI decided to return to Rome on 17 January 1377, and died there on 27 March 1378. The Romans used intimidation and violence to ensure the election of a Roman pope, and on 8 April 1378 the cardinals elected Bartolomeo Prignano, archbishop of Bari, as Urban VI.

Most of the cardinals soon regretted their choice and withdrew to Anagni. Meeting at Fondi, thirteen cardinals elected Clement VII on 20 September 1378, arguing that Urban's election was invalid because it had been made in fear of rioting crowds. Clement settled at Avignon, and France under Charles V became his highest protector. He also won Castile, Aragon, Navarre, Poland, Lithuania, Hungary, Scotland and most of Italy outside Naples. The schism bred fierce partisanship: in 1382 the French oriflamme was raised against the Flemings because they were Urbanists.

It outlived both original claimants. Boniface IX was crowned in Rome in 1389 and Benedict XIII reigned at Avignon from 1394. Benedict and Gregory XII agreed in December 1406 to abdicate but balked at the last moment, and both groups of cardinals abandoned them. The Council of Pisa in 1409 tried to depose both. It elected Alexander V, followed by John XXIII, and so created a third line of claimants.

John XXIII convened the Council of Constance in 1414, and Gregory XII endorsed it. On 6 April 1415 it issued Haec sancta, declaring the council the Church's highest governing body. The council secured Gregory's resignation and the removal of John, excommunicated Benedict XIII on 27 July 1417 and elected Martin V in 1417. Benedict died on 23 May 1423, and his successor Clement VIII resigned in 1429 and recognised Martin V.

The schism gave impetus to conciliarism, the view that a general council is superior to the pope, argued by Jean Gerson. Pope Pius II forbade appeals to councils in the bull Execrabilis on 18 January 1460. Scholars note that it eroded the Church's authority, and the loss of unity is seen as leading towards the Reformation. The Church has never officially ruled on the rival lines for this period, though it now recognises the Roman line.
western-thrace: Western Thrace, also called Greek Thrace, is the western part of the wider region of Thrace; the European part of Turkey is Eastern Thrace, and most of southern Bulgaria is Northern Thrace. It is divided into the regional units of Xanthi, Rhodope and Evros, which with Drama, Kavala and Thasos form the region of Eastern Macedonia and Thrace. It is bounded by the Aegean Sea to the south and by the Nestos and Evros rivers to the west and east. Its largest city is Alexandroupolis. The name comes from the Thracians, an ancient people of Southeast Europe.

Greeks colonised the coast and built cities such as Maroneia and Abdera, the home of the philosophers Democritus and Protagoras. The Achaemenid Empire took the region in the late 6th century BCE as the Satrapy of Skudra, and in the 4th century BCE Philip II of Macedon and Alexander the Great conquered most of it. Claudius annexed the Sapaean kingdom, and the Roman province of Thracia was founded in 46 CE. The region lay near Constantinople in the heart of the Byzantine Empire. The Ottoman Empire conquered most of it in the late 14th century and ruled it until the Balkan Wars of 1912 to 1913, with a mixed population of Greeks, Turks and Bulgarians, and smaller numbers of Pomaks, Jews, Armenians and Romani.

In the First Balkan War, Bulgarian troops occupied Western Thrace, and Bulgaria kept it by the Treaty of Bucharest in August 1913. It had to surrender the region under the Treaty of Neuilly in 1919, and in April 1920 the San Remo conference gave it to Greece. Greek refugees from Eastern Thrace and Anatolia were settled there, and the Greek-Turkish population exchanges of 1923 reversed the earlier population balance. The Treaty of Lausanne granted the Muslims of Western Thrace the status of a minority. In 1941 Bulgarian troops occupied the area, and some 4,500 Jews of the region were arrested and deported, none of whom survived.

About two thirds of the population are Orthodox Christian Greeks and about a third are Muslims, an officially recognised minority of Greece made up of Turks, Pomaks and Muslim Romani. The Democritus University of Thrace is based in Komotini. Archaeological sites include the ancient theatre at Maroneia and the sanctuary on Samothrace.
westminster-abbey: Formally the Collegiate Church of Saint Peter at Westminster, the abbey has obscure beginnings. Historians agree that a monastery dedicated to Saint Peter stood on the site before the 11th century, and an abbey housing Benedictine monks was there by the mid-10th century. Legend credits Sæberht of Essex or a fictional 2nd-century king, Lucius, with founding it, and a tradition tells of a fisherman on the Thames who had a vision of Saint Peter; the Fishmongers' Company still gives the abbey a salmon each year in memory of it.

Between 1042 and 1052 Edward the Confessor began rebuilding it as a royal burial church. It was Romanesque and the first church in England on a cruciform plan, with Leofsi Duddason as master stonemason. The community grew from a dozen monks to as many as 80. Edward died about a week after the consecration, and was buried in the church.

Henry III began the present church on 6 July 1245 under his master mason Henry of Reynes, intending a shrine for Edward and a burial place for his own family, to match great French churches such as Reims Cathedral. It was designed with long transepts to hold many guests at coronations. Abbot Nicholas Litlyngton and Richard II paid for the completion of the nave from 1376, and the mason Henry Yevele followed the original design even though it was more than a century out of date.

Henry VIII seized the monastery in the 1530s and his agents removed relics and treasures, melting down the golden feretory of Edward the Confessor. Elizabeth I dissolved the monastery in 1559 and in 1560 chartered the church as a royal peculiar, answerable directly to the sovereign. Early in the 17th century the Jerusalem Chamber hosted meetings of translators of the King James Version of the Bible, and the abbey's western towers, by Nicholas Hawksmoor and John James, were built in the 1740s. In June 1914 a suffragette bomb damaged the Coronation Chair.

The church is chiefly Geometric Gothic, with an eleven-bay nave and a vault 102 feet (31 m) high. The Henry VII Chapel, in late Perpendicular Gothic, was called orbis miraculum, the wonder of the world, by John Leland. Coronations take place on the Cosmati pavement before the shrine of Edward the Confessor. Over 3,300 people are buried or commemorated there, among them Geoffrey Chaucer, whose burial began Poets' Corner, and Isaac Newton, whose lavish funeral in 1727 boosted the honour of burial there. The Unknown Warrior was buried in the nave on 11 November 1920. The abbey, the Palace of Westminster and St Margaret's Church form a UNESCO World Heritage Site, listed in 1987.
westminster-system: The term derives from the Palace of Westminster, the seat of the British parliament. In the system, the head of state, usually a monarch or president, formally holds executive power but in practice acts on the advice of elected ministers. The head of government, called the prime minister, premier or chief minister, is the person who commands a majority in the lower house, and the head of state appoints that person to form a government. Executive authority is exercised by the cabinet, which is bound by collective responsibility, and the prime minister dominates it because cabinet members can be replaced or moved at any time.

A government that loses a vote of no confidence, or fails to pass an important bill such as the budget, must either resign or ask for a dissolution and new elections. Parties outside the government form the opposition and mirror the government with a shadow cabinet. Most Westminster parliaments have a lower house modelled on the House of Commons and a smaller upper house, chosen in different ways: by appointment, as in the Senate of Canada, by direct election, as in the Australian Senate, or, until the House of Lords Act 1999, by hereditary right. Chambers are usually long rooms with government and opposition benches facing each other and a Speaker's Chair at one end.

The system was used in the legislatures of most former colonies of the British Empire on gaining self-government, beginning with the Province of Canada in 1848, and the British Parliament has been called the mother of parliaments. Many countries later changed course. South Africa abolished the model in its 1983 constitution, Nigeria's ended with the military coup of 1966, and Zimbabwe's constitution of 1987 abolished it. Australia combines it with a powerful elected Senate, a blend nicknamed the Washminster mutation. The 1975 Australian constitutional crisis and the Canadian King–Byng affair of 1926 showed the reserve powers of the head of state in use.
westphalia: Westphalia covers about 20,210 square kilometres and has some 7.9 million inhabitants. Its north belongs to the North German Plain and is mostly flat, while the German Central Uplands rise in the south. The region lies roughly between the Rhine and the Weser, both north and south of the Ruhr, and the Ems and the Lippe are other important rivers. Its highest summits are the Langenberg, at 843 metres, and the Kahler Asten, at 842 metres, both in the Sauerland part of the Rothaar Mountains. Its counterpart to the east is Eastphalia.

Around 1 CE there were numerous incursions through the region and perhaps some Roman or Romanized settlements. The Battle of the Teutoburg Forest took place near Osnabrück, then a settlement of the Westphalians, who were part of the Germanic tribe of the Saxons. Charlemagne is thought to have spent considerable time in Paderborn, and his Saxon Wars were partly fought here. Westphalia was originally a district of the Duchy of Saxony, with Eastphalia, Angria and Nordalbingia. After the deposition of the Saxon duke Henry the Lion in 1180, Emperor Barbarossa made it a duchy in its own right, though the Duchy of Westphalia covered only a small area south of the Lippe.

The Reformation left no dominant religion: Lutheranism was strong in the east and north, while Münster and especially Paderborn were Catholic and Osnabrück was divided almost equally. The Peace of Westphalia, signed in Münster and Osnabrück in 1648, ended the Thirty Years' War, and the idea of state sovereignty that came from it became known as Westphalian sovereignty. After the Treaty of Tilsit in 1807 the easternmost part of the region belonged to the French client Kingdom of Westphalia until 1813, a state that took in mostly Hessian and Eastphalian lands. After the Congress of Vienna, Prussia created the Province of Westphalia in 1815. The former Duchy of Westphalia and the county of Wittgenstein joined it in 1816 and the condominium of Lippstadt in 1851.

In 1946 the British military government joined the Prussian Province of Westphalia with the northern half of the Rhine Province to form North Rhine-Westphalia, and the former Free State of Lippe joined in 1947. No administrative division bears the name Westphalia now, but its inhabitants call themselves Westphalians. The seventeen districts and nine independent cities of the region, with the district of Lippe, belong to the Westphalia-Lippe Regional Association. The region's emblem is the Westphalian Steed, a white horse on a red field derived from the Saxon Steed of the medieval Duchy of Saxony. The Westphalian variant of Low German is spoken in the region and beyond its borders.
wethersfield-connecticut: Wethersfield is a town in Hartford County, Connecticut, immediately south of Hartford along the Connecticut River. Colonial records spell the name Weathersfield and Wythersfield, and Native Americans called the place Pyquag. The colonists named it after Wethersfield, a village in the English county of Essex. The 2020 census counted 27,298 people.

Its neighbourhood Old Wethersfield, added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1970, is the largest historic district in Connecticut, covering two square miles and holding 1,100 buildings, many dating to the 17th, 18th and 19th centuries.

A Puritan settlement party of ten men, among them John Oldham, Robert Seeley, Thomas Topping and Nathaniel Foote, founded the town in 1634, and it is arguably the oldest in Connecticut. It was called Watertown until 21 February 1637, when it was incorporated with Windsor and Hartford. The three are the towns represented by the grapevines on the Flag of Connecticut. On 23 April 1637, during the Pequot War, the Wangunk chief Sequin attacked with Pequot help and killed six men and three women. Four witch trials and three executions took place in the 17th century, among them Mary Johnson in 1648.

From 1716 to 1718 the Collegiate School was briefly located there before moving to New Haven and becoming Yale University. In May 1781, at the Webb House, George Washington and the French general Rochambeau planned the Siege of Yorktown. Silas Deane, envoy to France during the American Revolutionary War, also lived in the town.

For a century at least, Wethersfield was the centre of the onion trade in New England, in the late 1700s and the early to middle 1800s, and outsiders called it Oniontown. In 1820 William G. Comstock founded what became Comstock, Ferre & Company, described as America's oldest continuously operating seed company, which pioneered sealed packets of seeds.
