The Wethersfield Volunteer Fire Department, chartered on 12 May 1803, was the first formally chartered fire department in the state. The town was the setting of the novel The Witch of Blackbird Pond by Elizabeth George Speare.
wewoka-oklahoma: Wewoka's history begins with the Black Seminole John Horse, also known as Gopher John. In the spring of 1849 he and a group of Black Seminoles founded a settlement near the modern town, seeking safety and autonomy from the Creek Nation. It stood at the falls of a small stream between the North and South Canadian Rivers, and the name is said to come from the rush of water, We-Wo-Ka, meaning Barking Water in the Mvskoke language. Other historians say it was named after Osceola's second wife. In the autumn of 1849 Horse and the chief Wild Cat led families into Mexico to escape slavers.

The Seminole Nation had sided with the Confederacy in the American Civil War, and many of its members fled to Kansas. After the war the United States required a new treaty in 1866, which obliged the nation to emancipate its slaves and give freedmen who stayed full citizenship. Elijah J. Brown led the refugees back from Kansas, built a house and a trading post, and a post office opened in 1867. Seminole Governor John Brown had a log house built as the Seminole capitol in 1877, and the Wewoka Trading Company, run by the brothers John F. and A. J. Brown, was formed in 1891.

The town was platted in 1897. Lots were at first to be sold only to American Indians, but the decision was overturned in 1902 and sales opened to white settlers. Wewoka became part of the state of Oklahoma in 1907 and in 1908 won an election against Seminole to become the seat of Seminole County.

Oil was discovered two miles southeast of Wewoka in 1923, within the Greater Seminole Oil Field. The population grew from 1,520 in 1925 to over 20,000 by 1927, making it briefly the third-largest city in Oklahoma. As the oil declined, jobs and people left, and the population was 6,753 in 1950 and 6,300 in 1960.

Wewoka is the county seat of Seminole County and the capital of the Seminole Nation of Oklahoma. Its population was 3,133 at the 2020 census. The house built by Andrew Jackson Brown and his wife Mannie Lou, the last remaining structure of the Nineteenth Seminole Republic, is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. The Seminole National Museum, opened in 1974, is housed in a building put up by the Works Progress Administration in 1934.
wexford: Wexford is the county town of County Wexford, on the south side of Wexford Harbour, the estuary of the River Slaney near the south-eastern corner of Ireland. The Vikings named it Veisafjǫrðr, meaning inlet of the mudflats, which became Weiseforthe in the Yola dialect of Middle English and then Wexford. Its Irish name, Loch Garman, comes according to a story in the dindsenchas from Garman mac Bomma Licce, who stole the queen's crown from Temair during the feast of Samhain, was chased to the river mouth and drowned.

From the 9th to the early 12th century Wexford was a Viking town, largely independent and owing only token dues to the Irish kings of Leinster. In May 1169 Dermot MacMurrough and his Norman ally Robert Fitz-Stephen besieged it; the Norse inhabitants resisted fiercely until the Bishop of Ferns persuaded them to accept a settlement. Afterwards it was an Old English settlement, where the Anglo-Frisian dialect Yola was commonly spoken in the south of the county until it declined in the mid-19th century. The town received its first charter in 1318, and the Knights Templar had a presence there.

In the 1640s the county strongly supported Confederate Ireland, and a fleet of Confederate privateers, with sailors from Flanders and Spain as well as local men, was based at Wexford and raided English Parliamentarian shipping. For this the town was sacked in 1649 during the Cromwellian conquest; many inhabitants were killed and much of the town was burned. In 1798 Wexford was held by the United Irishmen throughout the Wexford Rebellion, which brought a massacre of loyalists at nearby Scullabogue and executions and reprisals at Wexford Bridge.

Wexford's port declined in the first half of the 20th century because the sands of the harbour kept shifting, and it closed to commercial shipping in 1968; a deepwater port at Rosslare Harbour, about 20 kilometres to the south, took the traffic. The town keeps Dutch Billy houses from the 18th century and twin churches with distinctive spires. It hosts the Wexford Opera Festival every October, begun by Dr Tom Walsh in 1951. The Wexford Wildfowl Reserve, a Ramsar site, shelters wintering Greenland white-fronted geese.
wheelbarrow: The wheelbarrow is designed to share the weight of its load between the wheel and the person pushing it, so that heavier and bulkier loads can be carried than a person could carry alone. A stone relief in the tomb of Shen Fujun in Sichuan, dated to about 150 CE, shows a man pushing one, and a mural in the Wu Liang tomb-shrine in Shandong, dated to 147 CE, depicts the story of the dutiful Dong Yuan pushing his father in a single-wheeled barrow. The commentator Pei Songzhi described the wooden ox of Zhuge Liang as a large single central wheel and axle with a wooden frame built around it.

Chinese barrows came in two kinds. Earlier ones were front-wheeled, while the more common type after the third century had a large central wheel and could carry up to six passengers. In 1797 Andreas Everardus van Braam Houckgeest of the Dutch East India Company described them accurately, and also reported near the southern border of Shandong a fleet of larger barrows fitted with matting or cloth sails.

The question of ancient Europe is open. M. J. T. Lewis argued that a temple inventory from Eleusis of 408/407 and 407/406 BCE, which lists a body for a one-wheeler, points to a wheelbarrow on Greek building sites, but he admitted that this was speculation, and there is no secure evidence for the wheelbarrow in ancient Greece and Rome.

Research on the early European barrow is hard because there was no common word for it. Lewis found four mentions in English and French sources between 1172 and 1222, three of them under different terms. The first archival reference, according to Andrea Matthies, dates from 1222 and records the purchase of several for the English king's works at Dover, and the first picture is in Matthew Paris's Vitae duorum Offarum, completed in 1250. By the 13th century the barrow served in building, mining and farming, but it stayed rare until the 15th century and seems to have been confined to England, France and the Low Countries.
whig-party-united-states: The Whigs emerged in the 1830s in opposition to President Andrew Jackson, pulling together former members of the National Republican Party, the Anti-Masonic Party and disaffected Democrats. The Nullification Crisis of 1832 to 1833 briefly scrambled the existing partisan divisions. The name Whig was first suggested by James Watson Webb, editor of the Courier and Enquirer of New York City, and implicitly compared King Andrew to King George III. The party's economic programme was Henry Clay's American System, which called for a protective tariff, federal subsidies for infrastructure and a national bank. Its base included entrepreneurs, professionals, Protestant Christians, particularly Evangelicals, the urban middle class and nativists.

In the 1836 election four Whig candidates received electoral votes, but Martin Van Buren won. William Henry Harrison defeated him in 1840 but died one month into his term, and Vice President John Tyler vetoed Clay's national bank bills in 1841; the Whig congressional caucus expelled him from the party on 13 September 1841. Clay won the nomination in 1844 and lost to James K. Polk, under whom the Mexican–American War was fought; the Whigs were hostile to territorial expansion into Texas and the Southwest. Zachary Taylor won the presidency in 1848 and died in 1850, and Millard Fillmore succeeded him. Fillmore, Clay, Daniel Webster and the Democrat Stephen A. Douglas led the passage of the Compromise of 1850.

The Whigs suffered a decisive defeat in 1852 partly through sectional divisions. They collapsed after the Kansas–Nebraska Act of 1854, which allowed slavery in territories north of the 36°30′ parallel. Most Northern Whigs eventually joined the anti-slavery Republican Party, and most Southern Whigs joined the nativist American Party and later the Constitutional Union Party.

The last vestiges of the party faded after the start of the American Civil War, but Whig ideas stayed influential. Under Abraham Lincoln, former Whigs dominated the Republican Party and enacted much of the American System. Lincoln, Rutherford B. Hayes, Chester A. Arthur and Benjamin Harrison were Whigs before they became Republicans. Historians such as Allen C. Guelzo note that the Whigs long suffered dismissal from political historians, and their reputation began to recover with Daniel Walker Howe's The Political Culture of the American Whigs in 1979, which portrayed them as modernisers who valued property, social order and the rule of law. The True Whig Party of Liberia, founded in 1869, was named in emulation.
whigs-british-political-party: The word Whig began as a shortening of Whiggamore, a nickname for a Scottish Presbyterian, particularly a Covenanter. It first appeared in connection with the Whiggamore Raid of 1648, when thousands of Covenanters marched on Edinburgh to overthrow the Engagers, who wanted to reinstate Charles I. The precursor of the party was the parliamentarian faction of Denzil Holles, marked by opposition to absolute monarchy.

Under Anthony Ashley Cooper, 1st Earl of Shaftesbury, the Whigs, also called the Country Party, tried in the Exclusion Crisis to bar the Duke of York, the later James II, from the throne because of his Roman Catholicism, his favouring of absolutism and his connections to France. A bill passed the Commons in October 1680 but was rejected in the Lords. Charles II dissolved Parliament in 1681 and resolved to rule without it. After the Rye House Plot, repression broke the Whigs, and Algernon Sidney and William Russell, Lord Russell, were executed for treason.

After the Glorious Revolution of 1688, William III and Mary II governed with both Whigs and Tories, and gradually the Junto Whigs, a tightly organised group of younger politicians, came to dominate the government. The Whig Supremacy of 1714 to 1760 was made possible by the Hanoverian succession of George I in 1714 and the failure of the Jacobite rising of 1715. In 1715 the Whigs took full control and purged Tories from major positions in government, the army, the Church of England and the law.

Robert Walpole held control of the government from 1721 to 1742, and his protégé Henry Pelham led it from 1743 to 1754. Great Britain approximated a one-party state until George III came to the throne in 1760 and allowed the Tories back. By 1784 both were formal parties, with Charles James Fox leading a reorganised Whig party against William Pitt the Younger. After the fall of the Ministry of All the Talents in 1807 the Foxite Whigs stayed out of power for most of 25 years.

By the first half of the 19th century the Whig manifesto included the supremacy of parliament, the abolition of slavery, the expansion of the franchise and equal rights for Catholics, a reversal of the party's anti-Catholic position of the late 17th century. In the 1850s the Whigs merged with the Peelites and Radicals to form the Liberal Party. Many Whigs left it in 1886 over Irish Home Rule to form the Liberal Unionist Party, which merged into the Conservative Party in 1912.
white-movement: The movement took its colour from the French Revolution, where the opponents of the Revolution who supported the Bourbon monarchy used white, and from the white uniforms of the Imperial Russian Army worn by some soldiers. It was led mainly by conservative officers of the Russian Empire, who were able to organise an armed movement and shared a military culture. It included republican-minded liberals, monarchists and members of the ultra-nationalist Black Hundreds, and it lacked a universally accepted programme. Its main slogan was a united and indivisible Russia, which meant restoring the imperial borders and denying the right of peoples to self-determination, with possible exceptions for Poland and Finland. In November 1918 the movement united around Alexander Kolchak, who became Supreme Ruler of Russia.

The Volunteer Army in South Russia was organised from November 1917 under General Mikhail Alekseyev, then Lavr Kornilov, and after Kornilov's death in April 1918 Anton Denikin. It grew from 64,000 to 150,000 soldiers between May and October 1919, and on 3 July 1919 Denikin's forces began an attack towards Moscow, which failed.

In the east Kolchak led an army with the Czechoslovak Legions and with Japanese support; defeated, the Whites fought on in the Far East until October 1922. In the north and northwest, Nikolai Yudenich, Evgeni Miller and Anatoly Lieven acted with less co-ordination, and Operation White Sword in autumn 1919 failed to take Petrograd. Remnants of the Volunteer Army evacuated from Novorossiysk to Crimea on 26 and 27 March 1920 and merged with the army of Pyotr Wrangel.

The Whites are associated with pogroms and antisemitism, and White commanders sifted prisoners and executed those they judged undesirable in a practice they called filtering. Denikin's troops committed 17.2% of the pogroms recorded, though White officers praised soldiers who committed such crimes, and Denikin did little to stop them. Territories under White control had unstable currencies, and the generals often relied on officials of the old regime to administer them.

The defeated Whites went into exile in Belgrade, Berlin, Paris, Harbin, Istanbul and Shanghai and built military and cultural networks that lasted through the Second World War. Organisations such as the Russian All-Military Union and the National Alliance of Russian Solidarists, founded in 1930, sought to overthrow the Soviet government by guerrilla warfare. During the Second World War some White émigrés, among them Pyotr Krasnov, collaborated with Nazi Germany. Historians such as Vladimir Brovkin argue that the Whites fought for a mythical Holy Russia and saw the struggle in religious terms.
white-nile: The White Nile is the less voluminous but longer, wider and shallower of the two main tributaries of the Nile, the larger being the Blue Nile. Its name comes from the pale clay sediment in its water. In the strict sense the name belongs to the river formed at Lake No by the meeting of the Bahr al Jabal and the Bahr el Ghazal. In a wider sense it covers all the stretches from Lake Victoria to the merger with the Blue Nile, the most remote headwaters lying 3,700 km from that point.

The Kagera River is the longest feeder of Lake Victoria, and the source of the Nile is variously placed at the Ruvyironza in Burundi or the Nyabarongo, which flows from the Nyungwe Forest in Rwanda. The two meet near Rusumo Falls. The river leaves Lake Victoria at Jinja in Uganda as the Victoria Nile, passes Lake Kyoga, and is squeezed to a passage seven metres wide at Murchison Falls before it enters Lake Albert.

From Lake Albert to the border of South Sudan the river is the Albert Nile. At Nimule it becomes the Mountain Nile, Baḥr al-Jabal, which runs through rapids to the Sudan plain and the vast Sudd swamp. From Lake No the White Nile flows east, very gently sloping through swamps and lagoons, to the mouth of the Sobat, whose sediment in flood adds to its pale colour. It then runs past Malakal and Kodok to Khartoum, where it joins the Blue Nile to form the River Nile.

Kodok was the site of the Fashoda Incident of 1898, which marked the end of the Scramble for Africa. Karuma Bridge, built in 1963 to help the cotton industry, later served as a convoy assembly point during the insurgency of the Lord's Resistance Army. On 28–29 April 1994 about 250,000 Rwandans crossed the bridge at Rusumo Falls into Tanzania in 24 hours, which the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees called the largest and fastest refugee exodus in modern times.

The river is a navigable waterway from Lake Albert to Khartoum by way of the Jebel Aulia Dam, although the section between Juba and Uganda would need upgrading. At some seasons boats can reach Gambela in Ethiopia and Wau in South Sudan. The Nalubaale and Kiira power stations stand at the outlet of Lake Victoria, and the Bujagali Power Station at Bujagali Falls. A Sudanese state takes its name from the river.
white-revolution: The White Revolution, also called the Shah and People Revolution, was a series of reforms to modernise Iran, announced by the Shah in January 1963 and extended over some sixteen years to nineteen elements. The first six were introduced on 9 January 1963 and put to a national referendum on 26 January. They were land reform, the nationalisation of forests and pastures, the sale of state-owned factories, profit-sharing for industrial workers, the vote for women and a Literacy Corps, in which high school graduates could serve their military service as village teachers.

Under the land reform, landlords were compensated with shares in privatised state factories, and the land was sold to peasants at 30 percent below market value on a loan payable over 25 years. Later elements added a Health Corps, a Reconstruction and Development Corps, village Houses of Equity with five elected elders, the nationalisation of water resources, free and compulsory education, social security and measures against corruption. The Shah hoped through land reform to ally himself with the peasantry and sever its ties with the aristocracy.

In the referendum 5,598,711 people voted for the reforms and 4,115 against, although the Shah's opponents boycotted it. The landlords objected to selling land at a lower price, and the Shi'a clergy objected to the loss of their traditional powers in education and family law, to the vote for women and to the break-up of lands held under charitable trusts, a considerable part of their income.

Ruhollah Khomeini became the most open critic. In a speech at the Feyziyeh School in June 1963 he attacked the Shah as a person, and on Ashura he called him a wretched miserable man. Two days later, on 5 June (15 Khordad), he was arrested, and three days of rioting left several hundred dead, though Khomeini claimed the army had slaughtered no less than 15,000.

Supporters point to new roads, factories, dams and schools. Enrolment in elementary schools rose from 1,640,000 to 4,080,000, the literacy rate from 26 to 42 percent, and women gained the right to stand for office and to serve as lawyers and later judges. Critics note that only about half of the rural population received land, often too little to live on, and that a new group of commercial farmers emerged while many villagers migrated to cities. The reforms made Khomeini a figure around whom opponents could rally, and the failures of land reform, the lack of democratic change and the hostility of the clergy and landed elites contributed to the Shah's downfall and the Revolution of 1979.
white-sea: The White Sea is a southern inlet of the Barents Sea on the north-west coast of Russia. Karelia lies to the west, the Kola Peninsula to the north and the Kanin Peninsula to the north-east. A narrow strait called the Gorlo, Russian for throat, joins it to the Barents Sea. It has four main bays: Kandalaksha Gulf in the west, the deepest part at 340 metres, Onega Bay in the south, Dvina Bay in the south-east, which receives the Northern Dvina at Arkhangelsk, and Mezen Bay east of the Gorlo. The main island group is the Solovetsky Islands, near the middle of the sea, and the sea freezes in winter from October or November until April or May.

Residents of Novgorod knew of the White Sea from at least the 11th century and soon explored its value for navigation and its coastal forests rich in fur animals. One of the earliest settlements on its shores grew up in the late 14th century at Kholmogory, on the Northern Dvina. In 1492 a merchant fleet carrying ambassadors of Ivan III sailed from there to Denmark, marking the establishment of the first international seaport in Russia. Trade was conducted by the Pomors, the seaside settlers.

The first foreign ship to reach Kholmogory was the English Edward Bonaventure under Richard Chancellor in 1553. He and Hugh Willoughby had been seeking a northern route to the Indies. Willoughby's ships were lost, but Chancellor passed the White Sea and was escorted from Kholmogory to Moscow to meet Ivan IV. He returned in 1554 with a description of Moscow and a letter from the tsar expressing a wish for trade with England. In 1555 Queen Mary issued a charter authorising the Muscovy Company to trade with Russia by the White Sea route.

Dutch ships soon followed, and Kholmogory became busy with shipments of fur and fish. The port was overloaded, so in 1584 Ivan IV established a new one down the river, New Kholmogory, which from 1596 became known as Arkhangelsk. Between the 15th and the early 18th centuries the White Sea was the major trade route in and out of Russia. That role declined after the foundation of Saint Petersburg in 1703 opened a more direct ice-free route to Western Europe over the Baltic.

The White Sea is under Russian sovereignty and is considered part of the internal waters of Russia. The White Sea–Baltic Canal links it to the Baltic Sea. From the 1920s most northern Russian sea shipments turned from it to the port of Murmansk, where the water did not freeze in winter.
white-sea-baltic-canal: Until 1961 the canal bore the name Stalin White Sea–Baltic Canal. It was built from 1931 to 1933 under the Belbaltlag camp directorate of the OGPU Gulag, which supplied a workforce estimated at 100,000 convicts. Prisoners worked in brigades of 25 to 30 with primitive hand tools, under labour norms such as 2.5 cubic metres of hand-dug stone per day per brigade. Those who exceeded the norm received larger bread rations, bonus dishes and cash, and prisoners were also promised shortened sentences. The canal was originally proposed with a depth of 5.4 metres, but the cost and time limits of the first five-year plan forced a much shallower channel.

Of the canal's 227 km, 48 km are man-made; the rest runs along canalised rivers and lakes, among them Lake Vygozero. It starts near Povenets on Lake Onega, climbs through seven locks, the Stairs of Povenets, to a summit level at 103 metres, and descends through twelve more locks to the White Sea at Belomorsk. Ships leaving Lake Onega can reach Saint Petersburg by the Svir, Lake Ladoga and the Neva, or join the Volga–Baltic Waterway. The channel is 36 metres wide and 3.5 metres deep, suited to river craft carrying up to about 600 tonnes.

The Soviet authorities showed the canal as proof of the efficiency of the Gulag and of the reforging of class enemies through labour. Officially 12,300 workers died, 8,870 of them in 1933, in a year of famine; the journalist Anne Applebaum estimates 25,000. On completion 12,484 prisoners were freed and 59,516 sentences shortened. In August 1933 a group of 120 writers and artists, among them Maxim Gorky, toured the canal and compiled a 600-page volume in its praise, published at the end of 1934; some contributors probably knew of the camp's brutality.

In December 1941 the canal route became the front line between Finnish and Soviet troops. Soviet sappers blew up the locks at Povenets, and the line held until June 1944. Navigation was restored on 28 July 1946. Cargo peaked at 7.3 million tonnes in 1985. A monument at Povenets commemorates the prisoners who died, and the building of the canal gave Russian the slang word zek for a prisoner.
widukind: Very little is known about Widukind, whose name literally translates as child of the forest. All sources about him come from his enemies, the Franks, who painted him as an insurgent and a traitor, and his exact role in the campaigns is unknown. In the chronicles he is accompanied by Abbi, who may have been a close relative. The Royal Frankish Annals mention him first in 777, when he was the only Saxon noble not to appear at Charlemagne's court in Paderborn. He stayed instead with the Danish king Sigfred, possibly Sigurd Hring, whose sister Geva he had recently married.

By 782 Widukind had returned from Denmark and goaded the Saxon nobles into rebellion. From 782 to 784 Saxons and Franks fought annually, and Charlemagne had 4,500 Saxons executed at the Massacre of Verden. Widukind allied himself with the Frisians, but Charlemagne's winter attacks of 784 and 785 pushed him and his allies back to their homelands. In the Bardengau in 785 Widukind agreed to surrender in return for a guarantee that no bodily harm would be done to him. He and his allies were baptised, possibly at Attigny, with Charlemagne as his godfather, and the peace brought acknowledgement of Saxon noble rank by the Frankish overlords.

No contemporary source tells of his life or death after baptism. The historian Gerd Althoff assumed he was held in a monastery, perhaps Reichenau Abbey, but this is widely rejected. The Vita Liudgeri has him accompany Charlemagne against the Veleti, and the 12th-century Kaiserchronik says Gerold of Baar killed him.

Legends made him a saintly builder of churches, and a Catholic Blessed with a feast day on 7 January. Since the 9th century he was treated as a mythical hero. The Ottonian kings claimed descent from him through Matilda, wife of King Henry I, as did the House of Billung. A tomb made around 1100 at Enger held the remains of a young woman, and three early 9th-century graves found in 1971 in front of the altar include a man assumed to be Widukind. German nationalists later made him a symbol, and after 1933 many plays were written about him.
wieliczka: Wieliczka lies 13 kilometres south-east of Kraków, in the Lesser Poland Voivodeship, in a valley between two ridges that run from west to east. The Wieliczka Salt Mine, one of the world's oldest operating salt mines, was established on significant salt deposits that are also present at nearby Bochnia. The town's Latin name was Magnum Sal.

The first settlers were probably from Celtic tribes and were later driven out by West Slavic, or Lechitic, clans. The importance of the mineral deposits grew after Casimir I the Restorer moved the Polish capital from Gniezno to Kraków in the 11th century, but the Mongol invasion of the 13th century halted mining. Migrating Germans then settled the area and called it Gross Salz, from which the Polish name Wielka Sól came, later becoming Wieliczka. After the discovery in 1252 of large salt and potassium deposits across southern Poland, salt was extracted on a much wider scale. In 1290 Duke Premislaus II, later king, granted the town privileges.

A plague decimated the population in 1651, and during the Swedish Deluge of 1655 to 1660 the Swedes plundered and burned the mine and raised taxes. After the First Partition of Poland in 1772 the town passed to the Habsburg monarchy and became part of Galicia, and many German, Hungarian, Croatian and Transylvanian miners settled there. Fryderyk Chopin visited in 1828, and in 1846, after the Kraków uprising began, rebellious miners seized the salt mines.

German forces entered Wieliczka on 7 September 1939. A ghetto held as many as 11,000 Jews by the time of deportation in 1942. In August 1942 all the Jewish population was rounded up: about 700 were shot in a nearby forest, some 700 young men were taken to forced labour camps, and the rest were sent to the killing camp at Belzec. Very few survived. The Red Army liberated the town on 21 January 1945. The Wieliczka Salt Mine was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1978, and the old town core was entered in the Register of Historic Monuments of Poland in 1994.
wiener-neustadt: The area once belonged to the County of Pitten, inherited by Margrave Ottokar III of Styria in 1158. When the Otakars died out, the Duchy of Styria passed to the Austrian House of Babenberg under the Georgenberg Pact. Duke Leopold V of Austria established the town called Neustadt in 1194 and paid for a fortress close to the Hungarian border with the ransom for the English king Richard the Lionheart, whom he had captured and held at Dürnstein Castle.

In 1241 a small Mongol squadron raided the town and was repulsed by Duke Frederick and his knights, and in 1246 it was the scene of a Hungarian victory over the Austrians. Its privileges let it prosper, and after the Battle on the Marchfeld in 1278 Styria fell to the House of Habsburg.

In the fifteenth century the town grew when Emperor Frederick III of Habsburg took up residence there, and he founded the Diocese of Wiener Neustadt in 1469. His wife, Eleanor of Portugal, died there in 1467. His son Maximilian I held his court in the town and is buried at St George's Cathedral.

King Matthias Corvinus of Hungary conquered the city in August 1487 after a two-year siege, and Maximilian reconquered his native city in 1490. In the sixteenth century it lost its status as an imperial residence. In 1609 Emperor Rudolf II granted the Bohemian Protestants the Majestätsbrief, a patent of equal rights, at Neustadt, and its revocation helped to precipitate the Thirty Years' War.

Wiener Neustadt lies some 50 kilometres (31 mi) south of Vienna in Lower Austria. Empress Maria Theresa established the Theresian Military Academy in the imperial castle to train officers for the Austrian army. An earthquake destroyed the city in 1768 and a fire in 1834 destroyed it again, after which it was almost entirely rebuilt and became an industrial town, especially after the Austrian Southern Railway opened in 1841.

In 1909 the first official Austrian airfield was inaugurated north of the city. In January 1918 a strike began there among workers of the Austro-Daimler factory, who opposed the war and the halving of the flour ration. During World War II, repeated bombing left only 18 of 4,000 buildings undamaged. The castle, rebuilt to its original appearance, still houses the academy, and the late Romanesque cathedral was consecrated in 1279.
wiesbaden: Wiesbaden lies on the right bank of the Rhine above its confluence with the Main, at the southern foot of the Taunus mountains and opposite Mainz. The city centre is in the wide valley of the small Salzbach stream, and the city lies in the Rheingau wine-growing region. Frankfurt am Main is about 38 kilometres to the east. The site is a mountain basin protected by hills to the north and west, which gives it a mild climate. Three boroughs, Amöneburg, Kastel and Kostheim, were part of Mainz until 1945 and still carry Mainz in their names.

The first Roman fort, erected in 6 CE, housed an auxiliary cavalry unit, and the thermal springs are first mentioned by Pliny the Elder, who records them as noted for their pools for the horses of the Roman army. After the Franks defeated the Alamanni, they displaced them in this area during the sixth century, and in the eighth century Wiesbaden became the site of a royal palace of the Frankish kingdom. Einhard, the biographer of Charlemagne, first uses the name, as Wisabada, between 828 and 830.

From 1170 to 1629 the town lay in the County of Nassau, then in Nassau-Idstein until 1721, and in 1728 in the principality of Nassau-Usingen, whose house made Biebrich Palace its main residence in 1744. For its part in the German Peasants' War of 1525 Wiesbaden lost all its privileges for over forty years, and it became Protestant with the appointment of its first Lutheran pastor on 1 January 1543. The privileges were restored in 1566. In 1806 it became the capital of the Duchy of Nassau, and the ducal palace on the Schloßplatz was completed in November 1841.

After the First World War the city was occupied by the French army in 1918, and in 1921 the Wiesbaden Agreement on German reparations to France was signed there. After the Second World War, Wiesbaden suffered much less from bombing than Frankfurt and became the capital of the new state of Hesse.

Wiesbaden is the capital of Hesse and the state's second-largest city after Frankfurt. It is one of the oldest spa towns in Europe: its name means meadow baths, and fifteen mineral springs rise in the city centre, fourteen of them hot. By 1370 sixteen bath houses were in operation. The Neo-Classical Kurhaus, built between 1904 and 1907 at the request of Kaiser Wilhelm II, houses a casino. Other sights include the Russian Orthodox Church of Saint Elizabeth on the Neroberg, built from 1847 to 1855, and the Waterloo Obelisk on the Luisenplatz.
wilfrid-laurier: Henri Charles Wilfrid Laurier was born on 20 November 1841 in Saint-Lin, Canada East, the second child of Carolus Laurier and Marcelle Martineau. He was a sixth-generation French Canadian with partial Acadian ancestry through his mother. His father, a farmer and surveyor who held posts such as mayor and justice of the peace, had liberal ideas. At eleven Wilfrid left home for two years in New Glasgow, a village largely settled by immigrants from Scotland, where he learned English. He began studying law at McGill University in 1861, joined the Parti rouge and graduated in 1864. He was elected to the Legislative Assembly of Quebec in 1871 and to the House of Commons in 1874. He became Liberal leader in 1887.

Laurier became prime minister after the Liberal victory of 1896, which followed Conservative controversy over the Manitoba Schools Question. He reached a compromise with the Manitoba premier, Thomas Greenway, that allowed religious instruction for 30 minutes at the end of the day where parents of enough children asked for it, though it did not restore separate Catholic schools. It earned him the nickname the Great Conciliator. His government sharply increased immigration, oversaw the creation of Alberta and Saskatchewan in 1905 and started the Grand Trunk Pacific and National Transcontinental railways. He was knighted at Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee on 22 June 1897.

In 1899 Britain asked for Canadian troops in the Second Boer War. Caught between English Canada, which wanted support, and French Canada, which opposed it, Laurier sent a volunteer force of roughly 7,000. His government also created the Department of External Affairs and passed the Naval Service Act to establish a Canadian navy. The Liberals won again in 1900, 1904 and 1908. In 1911 a reciprocity agreement with the United States, negotiated by William Stevens Fielding, lowered tariffs on natural products; it pleased western farmers but alienated businessmen, and the Conservatives under Robert Borden won the election.

Laurier stayed on as Liberal leader. In 1912 he led a filibuster against the Conservatives' Naval Aid Bill, which the Senate blocked. In the Conscription Crisis of 1917 pro-conscription Liberals joined Borden's Unionist government, and Laurier's anti-conscription Liberals were heavily defeated in the election of that year. He died of a stroke on 17 February 1919, still Leader of the Opposition, and between 50,000 and 100,000 people filled the streets of Ottawa for his funeral procession. His nearly 45 years in the House of Commons are a record, and his fifteen years in office remain the longest uninterrupted term of any Canadian prime minister.
wilhelm-frick: Frick was born in Alsenz in the Palatinate, then part of the Kingdom of Bavaria, the youngest of four children of a Protestant teacher. He studied philology in Munich and then law at Heidelberg and Berlin, receiving his doctorate in 1901, and joined the Bavarian civil service in 1903. Rejected as unfit, he did not serve in the First World War. As head of the political department of the Munich police from 1923 he took part in Hitler's Beer Hall Putsch on 9 November, and in April 1924 the People's Court gave him a suspended sentence of 15 months for aiding and abetting high treason.

Elected to the Reichstag in May 1924, he joined the re-established Nazi Party on 1 September 1925 and became its parliamentary group leader in 1928. On 23 January 1930 he was appointed to the Thuringian ministries of the Interior and Education, the first Nazi to hold a ministerial post at any level in Germany. He dismissed Communist and Social Democratic officials, banned newspapers and anti-war films, and was removed by a motion of no confidence on 1 April 1931.

He became Reich Minister of the Interior in Hitler's cabinet on 30 January 1933. His ministry at first had no authority over the police, but his power grew with the Reichstag Fire Decree and the Enabling Act. He drafted many of the Gleichschaltung laws, including the Law Against the Formation of Parties of 14 July 1933, and laws of racial policy, among them the Nuremberg Laws of September 1935. His power was greatly reduced in June 1936 when Heinrich Himmler became Chief of German Police.

Himmler replaced him as Interior Minister in August 1943. Frick then became Protector of Bohemia and Moravia, where he used ruthless methods to counter dissent. At the Nuremberg trials he refused to testify on his own behalf. He was convicted of planning and waging wars of aggression, war crimes and crimes against humanity, including for his role in formulating the Enabling Act and the Nuremberg Laws, and was sentenced to death on 1 October 1946. He was hanged at Nuremberg Prison on 16 October, and his body was cremated in Munich and the ashes scattered in the river Isar.
wilhelm-i: Wilhelm was born on 22 March 1797 in Berlin, the second son of Prince Frederick William and Louise of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, and was not expected to become king. His father became King Frederick William III the year he was born. Appointed an officer at twelve, he served in the Wars of Liberation against Napoleon I from 1814, won the Iron Cross, and fought at Ligny and Waterloo under Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher. He rose to commanding general of the III Army Corps by 1825 and argued for a strong, well-equipped army. In 1829 he married Princess Augusta of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach.

His brother became King Frederick William IV in 1840, and Wilhelm, as heir, took the title Prince of Prussia. In the Revolutions of 1848 he put down a revolt in Berlin with cannon, which earned him the nickname Kartätschenprinz, the Prince of Grapeshot, and he briefly fled to England. After the king's stroke in 1857 he became regent in 1858 and swore an oath on the Prussian constitution.

Wilhelm became king on 2 January 1861 and crowned himself at Königsberg on 18 October. In 1862 the liberal Landtag refused the budget for an army reform that raised the peacetime army from 150,000 to 200,000 men. Wilhelm first thought of abdicating, then on the advice of his war minister Albrecht von Roon appointed Otto von Bismarck Minister President. Bismarck effectively directed affairs and on several occasions won Wilhelm's assent by threatening to resign.

Wilhelm commanded in the Second Schleswig War of 1864 and the Austro-Prussian War of 1866, in which his army defeated the Austrians at Königgratz. He wanted to march on Vienna but was dissuaded by Bismarck and his son, Crown Prince Frederick. In 1867 he became head of the North German Confederation. In the Franco-Prussian War he commanded at Sedan and Gravelotte. He accepted the title of German Emperor reluctantly, fearing it would overshadow that of King of Prussia, and was proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles on 18 January 1871. He left most of the governing to Bismarck.

In May and June 1878 the anarchists Max Hödel and Karl Nobiling made attempts on his life; Nobiling's shots wounded him severely. They gave Bismarck's government the pretext for the Anti-Socialist Laws of 19 October 1878, which lapsed in 1890. He later agreed to the Dual Alliance with Austria-Hungary, directed against Russia, again after Bismarck threatened to resign.

Wilhelm died in Berlin on 9 March 1888, aged 90, and was succeeded by Frederick III, who reigned 99 days. Many memorials were raised in his honour, among them the Kyffhäuser monument and the mounted statue at the Deutsches Eck in Koblenz. In his later years he and Augusta were popular as figures of the old Prussia.
wilhelm-ii: Wilhelm was born on 27 January 1859 at the Crown Prince's Palace in Berlin, the son of Prince Frederick William of Prussia and Victoria, Princess Royal, the eldest child of Queen Victoria. He was the eldest of Victoria's 42 grandchildren. After 1871 he was second in line to the imperial throne, which under the constitution was held by the Prussian king.

His birth was traumatic, since the infant was in the breech position. His father succeeded as Frederick III after the death of Wilhelm I on 9 March 1888, but was already suffering from incurable throat cancer and died after 99 days, and on 15 June 1888 the 29-year-old Wilhelm became German Emperor and King of Prussia.

Bismarck's successor as chancellor, Leo von Caprivi, was followed by Chlodwig von Hohenlohe-Schillingsfürst in 1894 and by Bernhard von Bülow in 1900, whom Wilhelm regarded as his own Bismarck. Wilhelm promoted the arts and sciences and sponsored the Kaiser Wilhelm Society for scientific research. His impatient, impulsive handling of foreign policy brought a series of incidents: the Kruger telegram of 1896, his speech of 1900 telling German soldiers leaving for China to be merciless in the spirit of the Huns, and a visit to Tangier on 31 March 1905 that set off the Moroccan Crisis.
The Daily Telegraph Affair of 1908 damaged him badly, and he had less influence for the rest of his reign. A naval programme under Alfred von Tirpitz, from 1897, set Germany against Britain.

In the war he was a shadow Kaiser, confined to ceremonial duties; by 1916 the empire was effectively a military dictatorship under Hindenburg and Ludendorff. He could not decide whether to abdicate in the revolution of 1918, hoping to keep the Prussian crown, but the imperial crown was tied to it.

Wilhelm went into exile in the Netherlands and lived at Doorn. In 1922 he published the first volume of his memoirs, insisting that he was not guilty of starting the war. His first wife, Augusta Victoria, died on 11 April 1921, and on 5 November 1922 he married Hermine Reuss of Greiz. He died of a pulmonary embolism at Doorn on 4 June 1941, aged 82.

Hitler wanted a state funeral in Berlin, but Wilhelm had ordered that his body not return to Germany unless the monarchy was restored. Writing about him has followed three trends: court writers who saw a martyr, those who judged him unable to bear his responsibilities, and, after 1950, scholars seeking an objective portrait.
wilhelm-karl-duke-of-urach: Wilhelm Karl Florestan Gero Crescentius, Count of Württemberg, was born on 3 March 1864, the elder son of Wilhelm, 1st Duke of Urach, head of a morganatic branch of the royal house of Württemberg, and his second wife Princess Florestine of Monaco. At the age of four he succeeded his father as Duke of Urach. He grew up largely in Monaco, where his mother often managed the government. Through his mother he was a legitimate heir to the throne of Monaco, but under French pressure Monaco recognised Louis, the only son of Albert I, and later Louis's illegitimate daughter Charlotte as heirs ahead of him, so that he stood third in line. He renounced his rights in 1924.

Wilhelm entered the army in 1883 as a professional officer. At the outbreak of the First World War he was a Generalleutnant commanding the 26th Infantry Division. The division was largely destroyed at the Somme in 1916 while holding the Schwaben Redoubt. From 1917 he commanded the 64th Corps on the Western Front until it was deactivated on 10 December 1918. Erwin Rommel was among his aides.

He was also considered for other thrones. In 1913 he was among the princes thought of for Albania, supported by Catholic groups in the north, but Prince William of Wied was chosen in 1914. In 1917 he sounded out the possibility of becoming Grand Duke of Alsace-Lorraine after the war.

On 4 June 1918 the Council of Lithuania voted to invite him to become king of an independent Lithuania, and he was elected on 11 July 1918 as Mindaugas II. He was a Roman Catholic and not a Hohenzollern, whereas Emperor William II wanted Lithuania in personal union with Prussia. Four socialist members of the council left in protest, and the German government did not recognise the choice. He never visited Lithuania, staying at Lichtenstein Castle, and on 2 November 1918, as Germany's defeat became clear, the council reversed its decision. Wilhelm died on 24 March 1928.
wilhelm-maybach: Wilhelm Maybach was born on 9 February 1846 in Heilbronn, in the Kingdom of Württemberg, the son of a carpenter. His mother died in 1854 and his father in 1856, and a philanthropic institution at Reutlingen took him in. Its founder, Gustav Werner, noticed his technical inclination and sent him to its engineering workshop. By the age of 19 he was a qualified designer working on stationary engines. His workshop manager, Gottlieb Daimler, then 29, took him on as his main assistant, a post he held until Daimler's death in 1900.

Maybach followed Daimler to Karlsruhe in 1869 and to the Deutz gas engine works in Cologne in 1872, where he became chief designer. When Daimler left Deutz after disagreements with Nicolaus Otto in 1880, Maybach followed him to Cannstatt. In their workshop in a garden summer house they developed small engines that ran fast. In 1883 they patented one, running at 750 rpm, and a smaller version of their engine of 1885, nicknamed the grandfather clock, was installed on a wooden bicycle, creating the first motorcycle. Maybach also helped to fit engines to a boat in 1887 and to an airship in 1888, and in 1889 they built their first automobile designed from scratch.

Daimler and Maybach founded the Daimler Motoren Gesellschaft in 1890, but new financiers doubted that automobiles would pay, and Maybach left the board in 1891. His engine for the Phoenix, designed in 1894, used four cylinders and a spray-nozzle carburettor and won him the title King of Designers in France. In 1900 he designed a low, powerful car for the dealer Emil Jellinek, whose daughter Mercedes gave the engine its name. He left the company in 1907 after being moved to an inventors' office.

In 1909 Maybach and his son Karl founded an engine company for Count Zeppelin's airships, later called Maybach-Motorenbau, at Friedrichshafen. The Treaty of Versailles banned airship production in Germany, so after 1919 the firm made diesel engines and then, from 1921, complete luxury cars, beginning with the Maybach W3. Its V12 car was the first German 12-cylinder automobile, but only a few dozen were sold in the postwar economic crisis. Maybach died in Stuttgart on 29 December 1929 and was succeeded by Karl. From about 1935 the firm built almost all the engines for German tanks and half-tracks in the Second World War. Maybach himself never owned a car and walked or took the tram.
wilhelm-von-humboldt: Humboldt was born in Potsdam and died in Tegel. His father, Alexander Georg von Humboldt, belonged to a prominent noble family from Pomerania and was a major in the Prussian Army; he was rewarded for his service in the Seven Years' War with the post of royal chamberlain. Wilhelm and his younger brother Alexander were the two sons of his marriage to Maria Elisabeth Colomb. Wilhelm was educated at home and never finished his comparatively short university studies at Frankfurt (Oder) and Göttingen. In June 1791 he married Caroline von Dacheröden; they had eight children, of whom five survived to adulthood.

Between 1802 and 1819 Humboldt was a diplomat: Prussian minister at Rome from 1802, then ambassador at Vienna from 1812. At the congress of Prague in 1813 he was instrumental in drawing Austria into an alliance with Prussia and Russia against Napoleon. He signed the peace treaty at Paris and the treaty between Prussia and defeated Saxony in 1815, and attended the congress at Aachen in 1818. The increasingly reactionary policy of the Prussian government made him give up political life in 1819.

In 1809 the Prussian king asked him to leave Rome and lead the directorate of education. He had hoped to become minister of education but never did, and he would have preferred to stay in Rome. He installed a standardised system of public instruction from basic schools to secondary education, standardised state examinations and inspections, created a department to oversee curricula and textbooks, and founded Berlin University. His model went beyond vocational training: he wrote to the king that people cannot be good craftworkers, merchants or soldiers unless they are good and well-informed human beings and citizens.

In 1791 and 1792 he wrote The Limits of State Action, one of the boldest defences of the liberties of the Enlightenment, though it was not published until 1850. It influenced John Stuart Mill's On Liberty of 1859, and Humboldt outlined an early version of what Mill called the harm principle. A section on education appeared in the Berlinische Monatsschrift in December 1792 as "On public state education".

As a linguist he studied Basque and translated Pindar and Aeschylus into German. His two visits to the Basque country produced Researches into the Early Inhabitants of Spain by the help of the Basque language (1821), which has since been superseded in its details. He died while preparing a major study of the ancient Kawi language of Java, whose introduction appeared in 1836 as The Heterogeneity of Language and its Influence on the Intellectual Development of Mankind. It introduced the idea of the inner form of language, holding that a language's structure expresses the inner life and knowledge of its speakers.
wilhelmina-of-the-netherlands: Wilhelmina Helena Pauline Maria of Orange-Nassau was born on 31 August 1880 at Noordeinde Palace in The Hague, the only child of King William III and his second wife, Emma of Waldeck and Pyrmont. Her father was 63 at her birth. His three sons by his first marriage had died or were dying, and in 1887 the king settled the throne on his only surviving child. He died on 23 November 1890, and the ten-year-old Wilhelmina became queen. She turned 18 on 31 August 1898 and was sworn in at the Nieuwe Kerk in Amsterdam on 6 September.

She married Duke Henry of Mecklenburg-Schwerin on 7 February 1901. The marriage was unhappy, and she suffered several miscarriages and a stillbirth before Princess Juliana was born on 30 April 1909. The birth was met with relief, since a childless queen would have been succeeded by a German prince.

The Netherlands stayed neutral in the First World War, partly through her political influence, though the Allies included it in their blockade of Germany. After the war she gave asylum to the fleeing Kaiser Wilhelm II. When the socialist leader Pieter Jelles Troelstra sought to abolish the monarchy in the unrest after the war, her popularity helped restore confidence, notably when she rode through crowds in an open carriage with her daughter. Her investments in the United States made her the world's richest woman.

On the voyage to Britain in 1940 she arrived on 13 May. There she took charge of the government in exile, and relations with her ministers were tense. With the help of the minister Pieter Gerbrandy she removed the prime minister Dirk Jan de Geer, who believed the Allies would not win and wished to negotiate a separate peace. Her broadcasts on Radio Oranje were awaited by listeners who had to hide to hear them. On 5 August 1942 she became the first queen to address the United States Congress, and in 1944 she was admitted to the Order of the Garter.

She was disappointed that the old political factions returned to power in 1945. Ill health forced her to hand her duties to Juliana temporarily in 1947 and again on 12 May 1948, and she abdicated on 4 September 1948 after a reign of 57 years and 286 days. She retired to Het Loo Palace, where she wrote the memoir Lonely but Not Alone, and died there on 28 November 1962. At her request her funeral, in the Nieuwe Kerk in Delft, was entirely in white.
wilhelmine-of-bayreuth: Wilhelmine was born in Berlin on 3 July 1709, the eldest daughter of Frederick William I of Prussia and Sophia Dorothea of Hanover, and a granddaughter of George I of Great Britain. She shared the unhappy childhood of her brother Frederick the Great, whose friend and confidante she remained all her life except for one short interval. Her governess beat and abused her until the governess was replaced. As the eldest daughter she was the subject of marriage plans. Her mother wished her to marry her nephew Frederick, Prince of Wales, but the British would offer marriage only in exchange for concessions her father would not accept, while her father preferred a Habsburg match.

In 1731 Wilhelmine married her kinsman Frederick, Margrave of Brandenburg-Bayreuth, who had been engaged to her younger sister Sophie until her father changed the plan. She accepted only under threats from her father and to lighten her brother's disgrace. The marriage was at first happy but was clouded by limited funds and by the margrave's affair with Dorothea von Marwitz, which her brother resented and which estranged them for about three years. Her only child, Elisabeth Fredericka Sophie, was born on 30 August 1732.

When her husband inherited in 1735 the pair set about making Bayreuth a miniature Versailles. They rebuilt the summer residence, now part of the Hermitage, rebuilt the great Bayreuth opera house, built a second opera house and a theatre, and reconstructed the palace. They developed what is called the Bayreuth Rococo style. They also founded the University of Erlangen. These projects brought the court to the verge of bankruptcy. She surrounded herself with wits and artists and the court was visited by Voltaire and Frederick the Great. She also acted as her brother's eyes and ears in southern Germany.

Wilhelmine was a lutenist, a student of Sylvius Leopold Weiss, and employed Bernhard Joachim Hagen. Her compositions include a concerto in G minor for harpsichord, strings and continuo, an opera, Argenore, performed in 1740 for her husband's birthday, short songs called Cavatinen, and a flute sonata of about 1730. Her memoirs, Memoires de ma vie, were written or revised in French between 1748 and her death and were first printed in 1810. They are regarded as entertaining but not very trustworthy.

She died at Bayreuth on 14 October 1758, the day of Frederick's defeat at the Battle of Hochkirch. He suffered a week of severe illness and a depression from which he never fully recovered. On the tenth anniversary of her death he had the Temple of Friendship built at Sanssouci in her memory.
wilhelmshaven: The Siebethsburg castle, built before 1383, was a pirate stronghold until the Hanseatic League destroyed it in 1433. Four centuries later the Kingdom of Prussia planned a fleet and a harbour on the North Sea. In 1853 Prince Adalbert of Prussia arranged the Jade Treaty with the Grand Duchy of Oldenburg, by which Oldenburg ceded 3.13 km2 (1.21 sq mi) of its territory at the Jade Bight to Prussia. In 1869 King William I of Prussia founded the town as an exclave of the Province of Hanover and as a naval base for Prussia's developing fleet, while all its hinterland remained part of Oldenburg. A shipyard, the Kaiserliche Werft Wilhelmshaven, developed there, and trams ran from 1913.

The pocket battleship Admiral Graf Spee was launched at Wilhelmshaven on 30 June 1934, and the battleship Tirpitz, the largest European warship of the Second World War, was built at the same yard between 1936 and 1941. In 1937 Wilhelmshaven merged with the adjacent town of Rüstringen, and the united city became part of the Free State of Oldenburg. In World War II it was the main base of the Kriegsmarine. Allied bombing destroyed two thirds of the town's buildings, although the shipyard, the main target, remained operational. On 28 April 1945 the Polish First Armored Division captured the city and took the surrender of the whole garrison, including over 200 ships.

After 1945 the shipyard was totally disarmed under the British commander in chief and military businesses were prohibited. The city used the opportunity to provide a site for the Olympia Werke, a typewriter factory, which employed 7,000 workers in 1953. In 1947 the council chose the figure of a Frisian warrior as the city's emblem. A British boarding school for the children of service personnel stayed in the city from 1947 to 1972.

Wilhelmshaven is on the western side of the Jade Bight, has 76,089 inhabitants and is Germany's only deep-water port and its largest naval base. The deep channel led to the building of the first oil tanker jetty at the end of the 1950s, and the city has since been the most important German import terminal for crude oil, with pipelines supplying refineries in the Rhine-Ruhr region and Hamburg. The container terminal JadeWeserPort has been operational since 2012. The nearby Lower Saxony Wadden Sea National Park, part of a UNESCO World Natural Heritage Site, supports a large tourism industry.
wilhelmus: The melody of the Wilhelmus is a contrafactum of a Catholic French song, Autre chanson de la ville de Chartres assiégée par le prince de Condé, which mocked the failed siege of Chartres in 1568 by the Huguenot prince the Prince of Condé. The Dutch text replaced the ridicule of one Protestant prince with a tribute to another, William of Orange. The earliest known notation of the tune dates from 1574, when it was still sung at a rapid, military pace.

The authorship of the words is uncertain. Soon after the song appeared it was ascribed either to Philips of Marnix, Lord of Saint-Aldegonde, or to the politician Dirck Coornhert, but neither ever claimed it, and some odd rhymes are taken as a sign that an experienced poet did not write it. The oldest surviving complete Dutch text is in a Geuzenliedboek printed in 1577–1578.

The Wilhelmus is a monologue in the first person, spoken by William of Nassau, who describes how he tries to stay faithful to Philip II of Spain while serving God and his conscience. Its first stanza presents his quarrel as one with the king's emissaries in the Low Countries, such as the Duke of Alba, rather than with the king himself. The text has 15 stanzas, and their first letters form the acrostic Willem van Nassov, a contemporary spelling of Nassau.

The stanzas are arranged symmetrically, so that the first and fifteenth resemble one another in meaning, as do the second and fourteenth, and so on towards the eighth. That stanza compares William to David fleeing the tyranny of King Saul, and the Spanish crown to Saul.

During the Dutch Revolt the song served as a political and military signal. It was sung by a soldier during the siege of Haarlem in 1573 and played mockingly by Spanish musicians at the siege of Alkmaar the same year. In the 17th century the Dutch East India Company used it at sea and in colonial wars, and in 1626 Adriaen Valerius published a slower, solemn version for singing at home to the lute. In the 18th century it became a quick Orangist march, the Prinsenmars, and the young Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart wrote seven variations on it at The Hague in 1766.

Wilhelmina asked for the Wilhelmus at her inauguration in 1898, and on 10 May 1932 it replaced the older song. During the German occupation of the Second World War it was taken up by all factions of the Dutch resistance.
willem-drees: Willem Drees was born in Amsterdam on 5 July 1886 into an orthodox reformed middle-class family. His father, a banker, died when Drees was five, and he could continue his studies thanks to the support of his uncle Frits. He rejected the Christian creed at the age of eighteen. After hearing a speech by Pieter Jelles Troelstra in December 1902 he became a democratic socialist, and he joined the Social Democratic Workers' Party (SDAP) on his eighteenth birthday.

Drees chaired the party's branch in The Hague until 1931 and sat on the municipal council from 1913 to 1941. As alderman from 1919 he was responsible for social affairs, and after 1931 for finance and public works. He favoured a pragmatic, reformist course. Elected to the House of Representatives in 1933, he opposed the National Socialist Movement in the Netherlands, saying in 1935 that fascists are not opponents but enemies.

Drees succeeded Willem Albarda as party leader on 14 May 1940. During the German occupation he was taken hostage to Buchenwald concentration camp on 7 October 1940, was moved to Sint-Michielsgestel in 1941 and was released on 11 May 1942 because of poor health. He then took a prominent part in the illegal executive committee of the SDAP. After the war he became Minister of Social Affairs and Deputy Prime Minister on 25 June 1945, and in February 1946 he was a co-founder of the Labour Party (PvdA) and its first leader.

After the 1948 general election Drees formed a cabinet with the Catholic People's Party and became Prime Minister on 7 August 1948. He held the office until 22 December 1958 in four successive cabinets. His years in office saw decolonisation, economic reconstruction, the establishment of the Dutch welfare state, and international integration, including Benelux, NATO and the European Economic Community. His cabinets also faced the North Sea flood of 1953. He advocated austerity and was known for thrift and simplicity: he went to work on foot or by bicycle.
Drees received the honorary title of Minister of State on 22 December 1958. He remained active as a historian and author. He died in The Hague on 14 May 1988, at the age of 101.
willemstad: Punda was established in 1634, when the Dutch West India Company captured the island from Spain. It was originally called de punt, "the point", and was built as a walled city. It soon became one of the major centres of the Atlantic slave trade, which triggered rapid population growth. In 1674 Sephardic Portuguese Jews from Amsterdam and Recife, Brazil, who had settled as traders, built the Curaçao synagogue. In the late 17th century there were over 200 houses inside the walls.

In 1675 it was decided to build Pietermaai outside the walls, separated from the city by about 500 metres in which no building was allowed, so as not to obstruct the cannons of Fort Amsterdam. The name Willemstad, "William Town", honours William II or William III, Prince of Orange, and is first recorded in 1680. Otrobanda, its name from the Papiamentu otro banda, "the opposite side", was founded in 1707, and Scharloo followed. By 1818 the population was 9,536. On 13 May 1861 it was decided to demolish the walls and build houses in the gap.

Around 1925 the oil and phosphate industries stimulated growth. Royal Dutch Shell, which had built the refinery in 1915, created Julianadorp and Emmastad between 1945 and 1955 for its workers. On 30 May 1969 a strike at a subcontractor of the refinery turned into the Curaçao uprising, a riot in which two people died, 300 were arrested and part of the historic centre was burnt down. In 1985 Shell closed the refinery, which then employed 12,000 people, and the government bought it for one guilder.

Willemstad is the capital and largest city of Curaçao, a constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, and was capital of the Netherlands Antilles until its dissolution in 2010. Its historic centre has four quarters: Punda and Otrobanda, either side of the Sint Anna Bay, an inlet leading into the natural harbour of the Schottegat, and Scharloo and Pietermaai Smal on the smaller Waaigat harbour. The Curaçao synagogue is the oldest surviving synagogue in the Americas. The centre and the harbour entrance were designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997. Punda and Otrobanda are linked by the Queen Emma Bridge, a long pontoon bridge.
william-adelin: William Ætheling, commonly called Adelin, was born in Winchester on 5 August 1103. His father, King Henry I of England, had married his mother, Matilda of Scotland, to conciliate his English subjects. Matilda was descended from Edmund Ironside and was a great-niece of Edward the Confessor, so the marriage joined the new Norman rulers of England with the old Anglo-Saxon dynasty. Henry's hopes for the succession rested on William, whom the chronicler Henry of Huntingdon described as a prince so pampered that he seemed destined to be food for the fire.

William was invested as Duke of Normandy during his father's lifetime, a title he held more in name than in practice. Henry made the investiture when pressed by Louis VI of France to do homage for Normandy; as a king, he was loath to comply, and in 1115 offered to have William do it instead. The offer was accepted in 1120, after a period of war, and William did homage to Louis in the middle of that year. He received the homage of the Norman barons in 1115 and of the English barons in March 1116.

In February 1113 Henry betrothed William to Matilda of Anjou, eldest daughter of Count Fulk V of Anjou, to secure Anjou's loyalty. They married in June 1119 at Lisieux. After his mother's death in 1118, William served as regent in England in her place, advised by royal administrators such as Roger of Salisbury, and was sometimes called rex designatus, king designate.

William died in the White Ship disaster of 25 November 1120. He and his companions were crossing the Channel from Barfleur in the Blanche-Nef, the swiftest and most modern ship in the royal fleet. They had stayed drinking on shore until after dark, and in the middle of the night the drunken helmsman drove the ship onto a rock. William got into a dinghy but went back to rescue his illegitimate half-sister Matilda FitzRoy, Countess of Perche; the dinghy was overloaded and capsized. His wife was on another ship.
His death left the succession uncertain. After Henry died in 1135, William's sister Empress Matilda and her cousin Stephen of Blois fought a long war for the English throne, known as the Anarchy.
william-blake: William Blake was born on 28 November 1757 in Soho, London, the third of seven children of James Blake, a hosier, and Catherine Blake. He attended school only long enough to learn to read and write and was otherwise educated at home by his mother. The family were Moravians and English Dissenters. The Bible was a profound influence on him throughout his life,.

On 4 August 1772 he was apprenticed to the engraver James Basire for seven years and then became a professional engraver. In 1779 he entered the Royal Academy, where he came to detest the ideas of its first president, Joshua Reynolds, who prized general truth and general beauty. Blake wrote in the margin of Reynolds's Discourses that to generalise is to be an idiot. In 1782 he married Catherine Boucher, who became his partner in work as printer and colourist.

About 1783 patronage allowed him to publish his first poems, Poetical Sketches. In 1784 he opened a print shop with James Parker and began to work with the radical publisher Joseph Johnson, whose circle included Joseph Priestley, Mary Wollstonecraft and Thomas Paine. Blake had great hopes for the French and American revolutions but despaired at the Reign of Terror.

In 1788 he invented relief etching, or illuminated printing, with which he produced most of his later books. He drew words and images backwards in acid-resistant varnish on copper plates and let acid bite away the rest, so that the design stood in relief. His commercial work consisted largely of intaglio engraving. In 1800 he moved to Felpham in Sussex to illustrate the works of William Hayley, and began Milton there. He returned to London in 1804 and began Jerusalem.

Blake lived in London all his life except for three years at Felpham, and was considered mad by contemporaries for his idiosyncratic views. He was hostile to the Church of England and to almost all organised religion, and was influenced by Emanuel Swedenborg. His early work, such as The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, is rebellious and protests against dogmatic religion. In the later Milton and Jerusalem he presents a humanity redeemed by self-sacrifice and forgiveness. The preface to Milton includes the poem beginning And did those feet in ancient time, which became the words of the anthem Jerusalem.
Blake died on 12 August 1827 at Fountain Court, off the Strand, having worked on his Dante series that day. Largely unrecognised during his life, he became a seminal figure of the Romantic age,.
william-bligh: Bligh was born on 9 September 1754, though it is not clear where. He was baptised on 4 October 1754 at St Andrew's Church in Plymouth, where his father, Francis, served as a customs officer, and his ancestral home of Tinten Manor in Cornwall is also a possibility. His mother, Jane Pearce, née Balsam, was a widow. He was signed for the Royal Navy at the age of seven, a common way of recording sea experience for a commission, and in September 1771 he was transferred to HMS Crescent, where he stayed three years.

Bligh first came to notice as Master of Resolution under Captain James Cook, who praised him on the voyage that proved Cook's last. In 1787 he took command of HMAV Bounty to carry breadfruit trees from Tahiti to the Caribbean, where the plant was wanted as food for enslaved Africans on British plantations. On 28 April 1789 Fletcher Christian, a master's mate who had been Bligh's friend, led a mutiny. Bligh and eighteen loyalists were set adrift in the open launch, and after a voyage of more than 3,500 nautical miles they reached Kupang in Timor.

The causes are debated: some sources describe Bligh as a tyrant, others argue he was no worse than the average captain and that the crew were drawn back to life in Tahiti. He was honourably acquitted at the court-martial in October 1790 and published a narrative of the mutiny. From 1791 to 1793 he commanded HMS Providence on a second breadfruit voyage, which succeeded as a transport but not as a food, since most of the enslaved people refused it.

The ackee, Blighia sapida, is named for him. At the Battle of Camperdown on 11 October 1797 his ship Director captured the Batavian flagship Vrijheid, and he received the Naval Gold Medal. He was a captain whose crews took part in the mutinies at Spithead and the Nore.

Bligh became governor of New South Wales in 1806 and moved against the rum trade of the New South Wales Corps. His confrontational style angered settlers and officials, among them John Macarthur, and on 26 January 1808 the Corps arrested him in the Rum Rebellion, an act the Foreign Office later declared illegal. Major Johnston was cashiered after a court martial, and Bligh was promoted to rear admiral and in 1814 to vice-admiral, though he never again held an important command. He surveyed Dublin Bay and died in London on 7 December 1817.

His logbooks of the mutiny were inscribed on the UNESCO Australian Memory of the World register in 2021, and the films of 1935 and 1962 largely perpetuate the image of him as a tyrant, while that of 1984 attempts a more neutral portrayal.
william-caxton: Caxton's parentage and date of birth are not certain. Records place his birth between 1415 and 1424, based on the payment of his apprenticeship fees in 1438. In the preface to his first printed work, the Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye, he says he was born and educated in the Weald of Kent, and Tenterden, Tonbridge and Hadlow have each been proposed as his birthplace. By 1438 he was in London, where the registers of the Mercers' Company record his apprenticeship to Robert Large, a wealthy dealer in luxury goods who served as Lord Mayor of London in 1439. Large died in 1441 and left Caxton £20, less than some other apprentices received.

Caxton was making trips to Bruges by 1450 and had settled there by 1453. He prospered in trade and became governor of the Company of Merchant Adventurers of London. His business brought him into the household of Margaret, Duchess of Burgundy, sister of Edward IV, and his travels, including to Cologne, let him observe the new printing industry. With a Fleming, Colard Mansion, he set up a press in Bruges. The first book printed in English, in 1473, was his own translation, the Recuyell. In its epilogue he writes that his pen was worn and his eye dimmed with copying it by hand, so he practised and learnt to print it.

In 1476 he set up the first press in England, in the Almonry at Westminster. The first book known to have been produced there was an edition of Chaucer's The Canterbury Tales. He printed chivalric romances, classical works and English and Roman histories, among them Sir Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur in 1485 and the first English translation of Aesop's Fables in 1484. He is credited with as many as 108 books, 87 of them different titles, and translated 26 of the titles himself.

Caxton worked under pressure to publish quickly, and his limited skill as a translator often led him to carry French words straight into English. Because his books sold widely, he is credited with helping to establish the London dialect, later called Chancery Standard, as the standard form across England, although Richard Pynson, who began printing in London in 1491 or 1492, pushed standardisation further. After Caxton's death, Wynkyn de Worde, a Fleming, became owner of the printing house and carried it on for forty-three years.
william-ewart-gladstone: Gladstone was born on 29 December 1809 at 62 Rodney Street in Liverpool, the fourth son of Sir John Gladstone, a wealthy Scottish merchant, slave owner, planter and Tory politician. He was named after his father's friend William Ewart, another Liverpool merchant. The family name was changed from Gladstones to Gladstone by royal licence in 1835. He studied at Eton and Oxford and entered the House of Commons in 1832 as a High Tory, winning a seat at Newark with 887 votes; the Duke of Newcastle controlled about a quarter of its small electorate.

Gladstone served in both of Sir Robert Peel's governments and was President of the Board of Trade from 1843 to 1845. When Peel's government fell in 1846 he followed Peel into the Peelite faction, which merged into the new Liberal Party in 1859. He was Chancellor of the Exchequer under Lord Aberdeen from 1852 to 1855, and again from 1859 to 1866 under Lord Palmerston and Lord Russell. In October 1862 he said in a speech at Newcastle that Jefferson Davis and the Confederate leaders had "made a nation", which caused consternation on both sides of the Atlantic. He became leader of the Liberal Party in 1867. He had earlier been a fierce critic of the Opium Wars, calling the trade "infamous and atrocious".

Gladstone's first ministry, from 1868 to 1874, passed the disestablishment of the Church of Ireland and the introduction of secret voting. Told that he was about to become prime minister while he was felling a tree at Hawarden, he declared: "My mission is to pacify Ireland." After electoral defeat in 1874 he resigned the party leadership. From 1876 he made a comeback on moral opposition to the Ottoman massacres of Bulgarians, publishing Bulgarian Horrors and the Question of the East on 6 September 1876. His Midlothian campaign of 1879 to 1880 is considered the first modern political campaign in Britain.

His second ministry, from 1880 to 1885, saw the Third Reform Act, an Irish Coercion Act in 1881 and a Second Land Act that gave Irish tenants fair rent, fixity of tenure and free sale. Public outrage at the death of General Gordon at Khartoum forced him to resign. His brief 1886 ministry was dominated by a home rule proposal for Ireland that was defeated in the Commons and split the Liberals. In 1893 a second Government of Ireland Bill passed the Commons but was defeated in the House of Lords. He resigned in March 1894, aged 84, the oldest prime minister, and left Parliament in 1895.
william-harvey: Harvey was born on 1 April 1578, the eldest of nine children of Thomas Harvey, a jurat of Folkestone who served as its mayor in 1600, and Joan Halke. He was educated at Folkestone and the King's School in Canterbury, and entered Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, in 1593, taking his Bachelor of Arts in 1597. He then travelled through France and Germany to Italy and entered the University of Padua in 1599, where he came to know Fabricius and read his work on the valves of the veins. He graduated Doctor of Medicine at Padua on 25 April 1602.

Returning to England, Harvey took a Cambridge doctorate in the same year and became a fellow of his college. He joined the Royal College of Physicians on 5 October 1604, married Elizabeth Browne a few weeks later, and was elected a Fellow of the College in 1607. As Lumleian lecturer from 4 August 1615 he began lectures on anatomy in April 1616, intending to cut up as much as possible before the audience and to illustrate man by the structure of animals. In 1618 he became Physician Extraordinary to James I.

After the De Motu Cordis appeared in 1628 he is said to have fallen mightily in his practice because of the criticism of other physicians, but he was re-elected Censor of the College in 1629 and later became its treasurer. From 1632 he served Charles I as Physician in Ordinary, and the king's hunts gave him many deer to examine. He was also a sceptic about witchcraft. Sent to examine a woman accused in 1632, he dissected her toad and found it ordinary, and his report on four Lancashire women in 1634 led to their acquittal.

The De Motu Cordis, a quarto of 72 pages in 17 chapters, was printed at Frankfurt, where an annual book fair would spread it quickly. Harvey wrote that the heart's movement was so rapid that he was almost tempted to think it could be understood only by God. With only a small lens he had to rely on reasoning in places. Before him Galen held that blood passed between the ventricles through invisible pores, and Ibn al-Nafis had described blood moving from the heart to the lungs and back. Some doctors said they would rather err with Galen than proclaim the truth with Harvey.

His On Animal Generation (1651) began with the development of the hen's egg. It stated that all life comes from the egg, which was the first definite statement against spontaneous generation. Harvey retired from public life after the surrender of Oxford in 1646 and died at Roehampton on 3 June 1657, probably of a cerebral haemorrhage.
william-henry-harrison: William Henry Harrison was born on 9 February 1773 at Berkeley Plantation on the James River in Virginia, the youngest of seven children of Benjamin Harrison V, who signed the Declaration of Independence and served as governor of Virginia. He was the last United States president born a British subject. On 16 August 1791, aged 18, he was commissioned an ensign in the United States Army and assigned to Fort Washington at Cincinnati during the Northwest Indian War. He married Anna Tuthill Symmes on 25 November 1795, after eloping when her father refused permission.

Harrison was appointed secretary of the Northwest Territory in 1798 and elected its delegate to Congress in 1799, where he championed settlers who wanted lower land prices. As governor of Indiana Territory from 10 January 1801 he made his home at Vincennes, built Grouseland there in 1805 and founded a university that was incorporated as Vincennes University in 1806. His treaties with American Indian leaders ceded large tracts of land to the nation. Resistance to expansion grew under Tecumseh and Tenskwatawa. After the War of 1812 he sat in the House of Representatives from 1816 to 1819 and was elected to the Senate in 1824.
