He lost the presidential race of 1836 as one of four Whig candidates and won in 1840.

Harrison took the oath of office on 4 March 1841, a cold, wet day, without a hat or overcoat, and delivered the longest inaugural address in American history, at 8,445 words. His brief term was marked by a struggle with Henry Clay over patronage. After a walk in the rain on 24 March he fell ill, and his doctors diagnosed pneumonia. John Tyler was sworn in on 6 April. His death exposed an ambiguity in Article II of the Constitution about whether the vice president became president or only assumed the duties of the office. Congress voted his widow Anna a pension of $25,000.
william-howard-taft: William Howard Taft was born on 15 September 1857 in Cincinnati, Ohio, to Alphonso Taft and Louise Torrey. His father served as a judge and an ambassador, and was United States Secretary of War and Attorney General under President Ulysses S. Grant. Taft attended Yale University and the Cincinnati Law School. After admission to the Ohio bar he was appointed assistant prosecutor for Hamilton County in October 1880 and Collector of Internal Revenue for Ohio's First District by President Chester A. Arthur in 1882. His professional goal was always a seat on the Supreme Court.

In 1890 Harrison appointed Taft Solicitor General, and from 1892 to 1900 he served as a federal judge of the Sixth Circuit. In 1900 President William McKinley asked him to join the commission to organise a civilian government in the Philippines, with the assurance of the next Supreme Court vacancy. Taft accepted on condition that he head the commission, and sailed in April 1900. In 1902 he refused a Supreme Court seat from Theodore Roosevelt because his work in the islands was not done. He became Secretary of War in 1904, and Roosevelt made him his chosen successor.

Taft defeated William Jennings Bryan in 1908 and was sworn in on 4 March 1909. As president he focused on East Asia more than Europe and repeatedly intervened to prop up or remove Latin American governments. He restructured the State Department, which was for the first time organised into geographical divisions. He brought 70 antitrust suits in four years, against Roosevelt's 40 in seven, and made six appointments to the Supreme Court. Disputes over the tariff, conservation and antitrust cases separated him from Roosevelt, who challenged him for the Republican nomination in 1912. Taft kept a bare majority of delegates and Roosevelt left the party. In the three-way election Taft carried only Utah and Vermont, and Woodrow Wilson won.

He returned to Yale as a professor and worked against war through the League to Enforce Peace. In 1921 President Warren G. Harding appointed him chief justice. On the court he was conservative on business issues, individual rights advanced under him, and his work on administrative reform culminated in the Judiciary Act of 1925.

In poor health, Taft resigned in February 1930 and died on 8 March 1930. He was the first president and the first Supreme Court justice buried at Arlington National Cemetery. He is the only person to have been both president and chief justice.
william-i-of-sicily: William was the fourth son of King Roger II of Sicily and Elvira of Castile, grandson of Count Roger I of Sicily and great-grandson of Tancred of Hauteville. He grew up with little expectation of ruling. The deaths of his three older brothers, Roger, Tancred and Alfonso, between 1138 and 1148 changed matters, though he was still poorly prepared when his father died. His epithet, the Bad, seems little merited and expresses the bias of the historian Hugo Falcandus and of the baronial class against the king and the official class who guided him.

William kept his father's administration and promoted the chancellor Maio of Bari, a man of low birth with the title ammiratus ammiratorum, who held real power at first. Maio continued Roger's policy of excluding much of the nobility from central administration.

On the mainland, however, royal authority still depended on the cooperation of counts and barons in Apulia and the Terra di Lavoro. They were encouraged to revolt by Pope Adrian IV, the Byzantine Emperor Manuel I Comnenus and the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick I. At the end of 1155 Byzantine troops took Bari and other towns. William landed and destroyed the Byzantine fleet and army at Brindisi on 28 May 1156, and by the Treaty of Benevento of 18 June 1156 Adrian abandoned the rebels and confirmed him as king.

The African dominions were lost to the Almohads. A revolt began in Sfax in 1156 and nothing was done to put it down, and Mahdia surrendered on 11 January 1160, ending the African empire. In November 1160 Maio was murdered in Palermo by Matthew Bonello. The royal palace was then stormed, and the king and his family were captured, but the people and the army rallied round him. He recovered power, had Bonello blinded and reduced the rest of the kingdom. His son Roger was killed by a wayward arrow, though Falcandus has the king kicking him dead.

Afterwards William entrusted the government to a triumvirate of Matthew of Ajello, Count Sylvester of Marsico and Bishop Palmer of Syracuse. His last years were peaceful, and he supported the true pope against the Holy Roman Emperor, so that Alexander III was installed in the Lateran Palace in November 1165 by a guard of Normans. He died on 7 May 1166 and was buried in Palermo Cathedral, later moved to Monreale Cathedral by his son and heir, William II of Sicily. By his wife Margaret of Navarre he had four sons.
william-i-of-the-netherlands: William was born on 24 August 1772, the son of the last stadtholder, William V, Prince of Orange, and Wilhelmina of Prussia. In 1791 he married his cousin Wilhelmina of Prussia, daughter of King Frederick William II. As commander of the Dutch field army he fought in the Flanders campaign of 1793–95 against the French, but the Batavian Revolution forced the family into exile in 1795. In 1803 he received the Principality of Nassau-Orange-Fulda as compensation, and he lost it in 1806 after fighting on the Prussian side at Jena–Auerstedt. In 1809 he served with the Austrian army and was wounded at Wagram.

After Napoleon's defeat at Leipzig, a provisional government invited William back. He landed at Scheveningen on 30 November 1813, refused the title of king and proclaimed himself Sovereign Prince of the Netherlands. The Allies also gave him the former Austrian Netherlands, and on 16 March 1815 he proclaimed the kingdom, urged by the powers at the Congress of Vienna. He later gained Luxembourg in exchange for ceding his German lands to Prussia. The constitution gave him near-absolute powers, with ministers responsible only to him. He was nicknamed the King-Merchant for his trade policies. In 1817 he founded the universities of Leuven, Ghent and Liège, and in 1822 the Algemeene Nederlandsche Maatschappij.

The constitution divided the 110 seats of the Second Chamber equally between north and south, though the south had 3.5 million people against 2 million in the north. William, a strong supporter of the Reformed Church, imposed Dutch as the official language in Flanders and required schools to teach the Reformed faith and the Dutch language. Many in the Catholic south resented this, and also felt economically disadvantaged. After riots in Brussels in August 1830 the Belgian Revolution followed. He sent his sons to invade in the Ten Days' Campaign the next year, but French intervention was threatened, and he fought on until 1839, when the Treaty of London dissolved the united kingdom.

William disapproved of the constitutional changes of 1840, which introduced ministerial responsibility, and he grieved the loss of Belgium. He also intended to marry Henrietta d'Oultremont, a Roman Catholic. He abdicated on 7 October 1840 in favour of his eldest son, William II. He spent his last years in Berlin, where he died on 12 December 1843 at the age of 71. A new national anthem, Wien Neêrlands Bloed, replaced the Wilhelmus during his reign and remained in place until 1932.
william-i-of-wurttemberg: Born Frederick William Karl at Lüben on 27 September 1781, he was the son of Duke Frederick William Charles of Württemberg and Augusta of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel. His parents' marriage was one of strife, and his mother, who sought sanctuary from it, died in 1788. In 1790 his father and his two sons moved to Ludwigsburg Palace, where the boys received a strict education. In 1805 he returned to Stuttgart as Württemberg was forced to ally with Napoleon. When Talleyrand suggested a coup in which the son would replace his father, Frederick William opposed it, an act regarded as the main reason for his later aversion to Napoleon.

King Frederick died on 30 October 1816, in the Year Without a Summer, when Württemberg suffered crop failures and famine. His son chose his second name as regnal name, simplified the royal title and the coat of arms, reduced the state flag to black and red, announced an amnesty and replaced most of the ministers. His reforms led the Estates to approve a constitution on 25 September 1819. In his reign of 47 years Württemberg moved from a kingdom of different denominational principalities and a heterogeneous agricultural country to a constitutional state with a common identity. On 28 September 1818 an agricultural festival with horse races and prizes for cattle-breeding was held on the Cannstatter Wasen, the origin of the Cannstatter Volksfest.

In foreign policy he imagined a third major German power beside Prussia and Austria, formed of Bavaria, Saxony, Hanover and Württemberg. The plan never succeeded. After poor harvests in 1846 and 1847 liberal demands grew, and in March 1848 he reinstated the liberal press law of 1817 and agreed to a liberal government under Friedrich Römer. He was the only German monarch forced to recognise the Frankfurt Constitution of 1848. After the revolution failed he followed reactionary policies. In the Crimean War he pushed for the neutrality of the German Confederation, and on 27 September 1857 he organised a meeting in Stuttgart between Napoléon III and Tsar Alexander II.

He died on 25 June 1864 at Rosenstein Castle in Bad Cannstatt and was buried in the Württemberg Mausoleum. In old age European princes often sought his advice, and his biographer Paul Sauer called him the Nestor among the princes of Europe. He married three times. By his second wife, Grand Duchess Catherine Pavlovna of Russia, he had two daughters, one of whom, Sophie, married King William III of the Netherlands. By his third wife, Pauline, he had a son, Charles, who succeeded him as king.
william-ii-of-england: William's date of birth is not known, but according to the historian Frank Barlow it fell by 1060. He was the third of four sons of William the Conqueror and Matilda of Flanders: Robert Curthose was the eldest, Richard the second and Henry the youngest. William became king of England on his father's death in 1087, when Robert inherited Normandy. Relations among the brothers were strained, and the chronicler Orderic Vitalis tells of an incident at L'Aigle in 1077 or 1078 when William and Henry emptied a chamber pot on Robert, causing a brawl that their father had to end.

The division of the Conqueror's lands left nobles with estates on both sides of the Channel unsure which brother to please, and many wanted England and Normandy united again. They revolted in favour of Robert in the Rebellion of 1088, led by Bishop Odo of Bayeux. Robert failed to appear, and William won the English with silver and promises of better government. In 1091 he invaded Normandy and forced Robert to cede part of his lands. Malcolm was killed at the Battle of Alnwick on 13 November 1093.

In the Church, William kept Canterbury vacant for years after Lanfranc died in 1089 and took its revenues. When he fell ill in 1093 he named Anselm archbishop, but they disagreed over many issues, and Anselm went into exile in October 1097. Robert pledged Normandy to William for 10,000 marks in 1096 before leaving on the First Crusade, and William raised the sum by a heavy tax on all England. In 1097 he began the original Westminster Hall.

William went hunting in the New Forest on 2 August 1100 and was killed by an arrow through the lung. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says he was shot by one of his own men, and later writers name Walter Tirel, who fled. Henry, who was in the hunting party, rode to Winchester, seized the treasury and was crowned within days. Modern historians disagree: Barlow holds that accidents were common and there is no hard evidence of murder, while others find the suspicion of a plot credible.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle said William was hated by almost all his people. Chroniclers were mostly churchmen and were hostile after his struggles with the Church. William never married and had no children, and some writers have speculated about his sexuality. His remains lie in Winchester Cathedral, and a memorial stone at Beaulieu Abbey and the Rufus Stone near Minstead recall his death.
william-ii-of-holland: William was the eldest son and heir of Count Floris IV of Holland and Matilda of Brabant. His father was killed at a tournament at Corbie when William was only seven years old. His paternal uncles William and Otto, bishop of Utrecht, were his guardians until 1239. He was Count of Holland and Zeeland from 1234 until his death.

With the help of his maternal uncle Duke Henry II of Brabant and Konrad von Hochstaden, Archbishop of Cologne, William was elected king of Germany after Pope Innocent IV excommunicated Emperor Frederick II. He succeeded Landgrave Henry Raspe of Thuringia, who had died within a year of his own election as anti-king. William extended his father's hunting residence into a palace worthy of his new status, later called the Binnenhof, which began the city of The Hague. He then besieged Aachen for six months before capturing it from Frederick's followers, and only then could Archbishop Konrad crown him king.

On 25 January 1252 he married Elizabeth, daughter of the Welf duke Otto of Brunswick-Lüneburg, which brought him a degree of theoretical support from some German princes, and on 25 March 1252 he was elected King of the Romans a second time, at Brunswick. His power, however, never extended beyond the Rhineland. In Holland he fought Countess Margaret II of Flanders for control of Zeeland, and defeated the Flemish army at Westkapelle in July 1253. He granted city rights to Haarlem, Delft, 's-Gravenzande and Alkmaar, and from 1254 fought several wars against the West Frisians, for which he built castles at Heemskerk and Haarlem.

On 28 January 1256, in a battle near Hoogwoud, William was lost and tried to cross a frozen lake alone. His horse fell through the ice, and the Frisians killed him and buried him in secret under the floor of a house. His son Floris V recovered the body 26 years later, took terrible vengeance on the West Frisians, and had his father buried in Middelburg. Contemporary sources, including the chronicle of Melis Stoke, portray William as an Arthurian hero. A golden statue of him stands on the Binnenhof in The Hague, the inner court of the parliamentary complex of the Netherlands.
william-ii-of-sicily: William was born in Palermo to King William I and Margaret of Navarre. His father died when he was twelve, and the government came under his mother's regency, run first by the chancellor Stephen du Perche until a coup in 1168, then by Walter Ophamil, archbishop of Palermo, and Matthew of Ajello. William was declared adult in 1171. The sources leave his character indistinct: he is described as secluded and pleasure-loving, seldom leaving his palace, yet his reign had an ambitious foreign policy. He championed the papacy and was in secret league with the Lombard cities against Frederick Barbarossa.

His marriage in February 1177 to Joan, daughter of King Henry II of England and Eleanor of Aquitaine, marked his high position in European politics. He had refused Barbarossa's offer of his daughter Beatrice in 1173, so as not to offend the pope, and in July 1177 he sent a delegation to sign the Treaty of Venice with the emperor.

William first attacked Ayyubid Egypt, where Saladin threatened the Latin kingdom of Jerusalem. In July 1174 a force of 30,000 men landed before Alexandria, but Saladin's arrival made the Sicilians re-embark in disorder. After the death of the Byzantine Emperor Manuel Comnenus in 1180 he turned against the Byzantine Empire. Dyrrhachium was captured on 11 June 1185, and the fleet took Corfu, Cephalonia, Ithaca and Zakynthos on its way to Thessalonica, which fell in August 1185 and was sacked.

Troops marching on the capital were defeated on the Strymon on 7 November 1185 by the army of Emperor Isaac Angelus under Alexios Branas. In 1189 William made peace with Isaac, giving up all the conquests. His admiral Margarito kept the eastern Mediterranean open for the Franks and forced Saladin to retire from Tripoli in the spring of 1188.

In 1184 William released his aunt Constance from her convent and in January 1186 married her to Henry, son of Frederick Barbarossa, causing an oath to be taken to her as heir presumptive. William died at Palermo in November 1189, leaving no surviving children. Norman officials led by Matthew of Ajello then supported his cousin Tancred of Lecce, rather than Constance, to avoid German rule. The nickname the Good arose only decades after his death, from the end of the troubles of his father's reign and the wars under his successor. Dante places him in Paradise.
william-ii-of-wurttemberg: William II, born Wilhelm Karl Paul Heinrich Friedrich on 25 February 1848, was the only child of Prince Frederick of Württemberg and Princess Catherine Frederica of Württemberg, who were first cousins. His growing years coincided with a progressive diminution of Württemberg's sovereignty during German unification. In 1870 the kingdom took Prussia's side in the Franco-German War, and in 1871 it became a state of the German Empire.

William succeeded his childless maternal uncle Charles I on 6 October 1891. This did not depart from the Salic law that governed succession in the German states: he was the nearest agnatic heir, as the senior male-line descendant of Frederick I of Württemberg through his younger son Prince Paul. William held the rank of Generalfeldmarschall in the First World War.

He was considered a popular monarch and used to walk his two dogs in the public parks of Stuttgart without bodyguards, greeted by his subjects with a simple Herr König. Although his kingdom was landlocked, he was a yachting enthusiast and was instrumental in founding the Royal Yacht Club of Württemberg on Lake Constance in 1911.

His first wife, Princess Marie of Waldeck and Pyrmont, whom he married in 1877, died in 1882 after the birth of their third child, a stillborn daughter; their son Ulrich had died in infancy in 1880. William, already depressed, is said never to have recovered. In 1886 he married Princess Charlotte of Schaumburg-Lippe, and the marriage was childless.

In 1918 William was deposed along with the other German rulers, and he abdicated on 30 November 1918, ending more than 800 years of rule by the House of Württemberg. He was the last German ruler to abdicate in the wake of the November Revolution. He died at Bebenhausen in 1921 without a male heir, and the royal branch of the house became extinct. Headship of the house passed to Albrecht, Duke of Württemberg, of the Catholic cadet branch at Altshausen.
william-iii-of-england: William was born on 4 November 1650 at The Hague, the only child of the stadtholder William II, Prince of Orange, who died before his birth, and Mary, Princess Royal, daughter of Charles I of England. His mother took little personal interest in him, and from April 1656 the Calvinist preacher Cornelis Trigland gave him daily instruction in the Reformed religion. After his father's death most provinces left the office of stadtholder vacant.

In 1672, the Rampjaar or disaster year, France and its allies England, Münster and Cologne invaded the Dutch Republic, and the French army overran Gelderland and Utrecht. William withdrew into Holland, where the dikes were flooded, and the people turned against de Witt and his allies. William became Louis XIV's chief opponent and reorganised the Dutch army. In 1677 he married his first cousin Mary, elder daughter of the Duke of York, later James II.

James's reign was unpopular with British Protestants. In June 1688 the birth of a son, James Francis Edward Stuart, displaced Mary from first place in the succession. William, invited by leading English Protestants, landed at Brixham in November 1688 with a Dutch force, and James was deposed. A Convention Parliament met on 22 January 1689. William insisted on reigning as king in his own right, and he and Mary were offered the crown jointly. Parliament passed the Toleration Act 1689 and, in December 1689, the Bill of Rights, which limited the royal prerogative. William disliked such limits but agreed to abide by the statute.

A minority, the Jacobites, refused to recognise William, and over 400 clergy, the nonjurors, would not take oaths of allegiance. He spent each campaigning season abroad in the Nine Years' War against France, while Mary governed. She died of smallpox on 28 December 1694. The Treaty of Rijswijk of 20 September 1697 ended the war, and Louis XIV recognised William as king. After the death in 1700 of Anne's last surviving child, the Act of Settlement 1701 named Sophia, Electress of Hanover, and her Protestant heirs as heirs to the throne.

William died at Kensington Palace on 8 March 1702, aged 51, of pneumonia after a fall from his horse broke his collarbone. Some Jacobites toasted the mole whose burrow had tripped the horse as the little gentleman in the black velvet waistcoat. He was buried in Westminster Abbey beside Mary, and Anne succeeded him. Contemporaries, even his enemies, praised him as a field commander. In Ulster he is called King Billy, and his victory at the Boyne in 1690 is commemorated each year in the Twelfth of July parades of the Orange Order.
william-iii-of-the-netherlands: William was born on 19 February 1817 in the Palace of the Nation in Brussels, the eldest son of the future King William II and Anna Pavlovna of Russia. He and his brothers were raised by military men and expected to join the army, and he studied for a time at Leiden University without taking a degree. On 18 June 1839 he married his cousin Sophie of Württemberg in Stuttgart. The marriage was unhappy, and she bore him three sons, William, Maurice and Alexander.

William disliked the constitutional changes of 1848 introduced by his father and Johan Rudolf Thorbecke, seeing them as useless limits on royal power, and he would have preferred to govern as an enlightened despot like his grandfather William I. His father died on 17 March 1849, when William was a guest at Raby Castle, and he was reluctant to return to take the throne.

His first act as king was to install the cabinet of Thorbecke, designer of the liberal constitution of 1848, which had stripped the crown of most of its political powers. When the Catholic hierarchy of bishops was restored in 1853, he found growing conservative support and a reason to dismiss Thorbecke. In the first two decades of his reign he dismissed several cabinets and dissolved parliament several times. In the Luxembourg Coup of 1856 he unilaterally imposed a reactionary constitution on Luxembourg. In 1867 France offered to buy Luxembourg, which almost brought war between Prussia and France until the Second Treaty of London confirmed Luxembourg as independent.

He grew unpopular with his bourgeois-liberal subjects but stayed popular with the common man. Queen Sophie died in 1877, and in 1879 William married Emma of Waldeck and Pyrmont, who was 41 years younger. Their daughter Wilhelmina was born in 1880 and became heir presumptive in 1884, after the last of William's sons from his first marriage died.

William fell seriously ill with a kidney ailment in 1887 and was increasingly demented in 1889 and 1890, when the Council of State and then Queen Emma became regents. He died at Het Loo Palace in 1890, and Emma served as regent for Wilhelmina until 1898. Having reigned for 41 years, he is the second-longest reigning Dutch monarch, surpassed only by Wilhelmina.
william-iv-grand-duke-of-luxembourg: William was born on 22 April 1852, with the French name Guillaume Alexandre, and succeeded his father, Adolphe. Although the duchy of Nassau was annexed by Prussia after the Austro-Prussian war of 1866, he and his heirs kept the title of Duke of Nassau. William was a Protestant, the religion of the House of Nassau. On 21 June 1893, at Fischhorn Castle in Zell am See, he married Infanta Marie Anne of Portugal, a daughter of the former King Miguel I of Portugal. He believed that Luxembourg, a Catholic country, should be headed by a Catholic monarch, and the marriage made his successors Catholic.

William became Grand Duke on 17 November 1905. Like his father, he did not take part in politics, although the Constitution vested considerable power in him. When his uncle, Prince Nikolaus-Wilhelm, died in 1905, the only other legitimate heir of the House of Nassau-Weilburg was a cousin, Georg Nikolaus, Count of Merenberg, the child of a morganatic marriage. In 1907 William declared the Counts of Merenberg non-dynastic and named his eldest daughter, Marie-Adélaïde, heiress presumptive to the throne.

William died on 25 February 1912, and he is the last monarch of Luxembourg to have died on the throne. He and Marie Anne had six daughters. Marie-Adélaïde became grand duchess in her own right on his death and abdicated in 1919, when her younger sister Charlotte succeeded her. Charlotte married her first cousin, Prince Felix of Bourbon-Parma, a son of Marie Anne's younger sister. Another daughter, Princess Antonia, married Rupprecht, Crown Prince of Bavaria, as his second wife, and Princess Sophie married Prince Ernst Heinrich of Saxony. William held foreign honours including the Knight of the Elephant of Denmark in 1876, the Seraphim of Sweden-Norway in 1889 and the Black Eagle of Prussia in 1890.
william-iv-of-the-united-kingdom: William was born on 21 August 1765 at Buckingham House, the third child and son of George III and Queen Charlotte. With two elder brothers, George, Prince of Wales, and Prince Frederick, he was not expected to inherit the Crown. He was educated by private tutors at Richmond and Kew Palace, and at thirteen joined the Royal Navy as a midshipman. He was present at the Battle of Cape St Vincent in 1780, and was arrested with his shipmates after a drunken brawl in Gibraltar before being hastily released. He was later nicknamed the "Sailor King".

He ceased active service in 1790 and was never given a command during the Napoleonic Wars; his rank as admiral from 1798 was purely nominal. From 1791 to 1811 he lived with the Irish actress Dorothea Bland, known as Mrs Jordan, and they had ten children. In 1818 he married Princess Adelaide of Saxe-Meiningen. As Lord High Admiral from 1827 he clashed repeatedly with his Council, and the king asked for his resignation in 1828 after he put to sea with a squadron for ten days without saying where.

George IV died on 26 June 1830 and William succeeded him at the age of 64. He discouraged pomp, and walked unaccompanied through London and Brighton. The Duke of Wellington said he did more business with William in ten minutes than with George IV in as many days. The general election of 1830 brought the Whigs under Lord Grey to power, and Grey pledged to reform an electoral system that had seen few changes since the fifteenth century, in which small boroughs such as Old Sarum, with seven voters, elected two members while Manchester and Birmingham elected none. The Reform Act 1832 refashioned it. His popularity was eroded by the Reform Crisis.

In Hanover, William signed a new constitution in 1833 that empowered the middle class and expanded the role of the parliament; his brother Ernest Augustus later revoked it. He supported Belgian independence and favoured Prince Leopold of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha for its throne. In 1834 he became the last British sovereign to choose a prime minister against the will of Parliament, when he disliked the policies of Lord Melbourne's government.

William died on 20 June 1837 with no surviving legitimate children. The British throne passed to his niece Victoria, but under Salic Law a woman could not rule Hanover, so that throne went to his brother Ernest Augustus. His death ended the personal union of Britain and Hanover that had lasted since 1714. The main beneficiaries of his will were his eight surviving children by Mrs Jordan.
william-iv-prince-of-orange: William was born in Leeuwarden on 1 September 1711, six weeks after the death of his father, John William Friso, head of the Frisian branch of the House of Orange-Nassau. His mother was Landgravine Marie Louise of Hesse-Kassel. He succeeded his father as Stadtholder of Friesland and, under his mother's regency until 1731, of Groningen. In 1722 he was elected Stadtholder of Guelders. The four other provinces, Holland, Zeeland, Utrecht and Overijssel, had decided in 1702, after the death of William III, to appoint no stadtholder, which began the Second Stadtholderless Period.

In 1733 William was made a Knight of the Order of the Garter. On 25 March 1734 he married, at St James's Palace, Anne, Princess Royal, eldest daughter of King George II of Great Britain. They had three children, of whom Carolina and William V survived infancy. In 1739 William inherited the estates of the Nassau-Dillenburg branch of his family, and in 1743 those of the Nassau-Siegen branch.

The War of the Austrian Succession broke out in 1740. The Dutch Republic sided with Austria in 1747, to keep a buffer zone between itself and France, and French troops invaded the Austrian Netherlands. In a few weeks they took most of the towns where the Dutch kept troops under the Barrier Treaty, as well as the main towns of Zeelandic Flanders. The Republic was divided internally, and the Dutch decided that they needed a single strong executive and turned to the House of Orange. William moved with his family from Leeuwarden to The Hague, and on 4 May 1747 the States General named him General Stadtholder of all seven provinces and made the office hereditary for the first time.

William was at first popular, despite little experience of state affairs. He stopped the practice of indirect taxation by which independent contractors made large sums for themselves. He was also a Director-General of the Dutch East India Company, and his alliance with the business class deepened while the gap between rich and poor grew. He appointed Duke Louis Ernest of Brunswick-Lüneburg field marshal of the Dutch States Army two years later. William died of a stroke at The Hague on 22 October 1751.
william-ix-duke-of-aquitaine: William was born on 22 October 1071, the son of William VIII of Aquitaine and his third wife, Hildegarde of Burgundy. Because of his father's earlier divorces and his parents' consanguinity, the Church at first regarded him as illegitimate, and his father made a pilgrimage to Rome to seek papal approval of the marriage and of the boy's legitimacy. William inherited the duchy at fifteen, in 1086. In 1094 he married Philippa, daughter and heiress of William IV of Toulouse. In 1098 he and Philippa captured Toulouse, for which they were threatened with excommunication. At Philippa's urging he gave land in northern Poitou to Robert of Arbrissel, which became Fontevraud Abbey.

William joined the Crusade of 1101, mortgaging Toulouse to finance it. He fought mostly skirmishes in Anatolia and was often defeated. In September 1101 his army was destroyed by the Seljuk Turks under Kilij Arslan I at Heraclea, and according to Orderic Vitalis he reached Antioch with only six companions. Orderic also reports that he later told of the miseries of his captivity in rhythmic verses.

His relations with the Church were rocky. He was excommunicated in 1114 and again for taking Dangereuse, the wife of his vassal Aimery I de Rochefoucauld, whom he installed in the Maubergeonne tower at Poitiers. Philippa retired to Fontevraud and died there on 28 November 1118. William was readmitted to the Church around 1120 after concessions that may have included taking part in the Reconquista. Between 1120 and 1123 Aquitanian troops fought beside the Castilians in an attempt to take Cordoba. He died on 10 February 1126.

Eleven of his songs survive, in Occitan, composed under his title as Count of Poitou. They treat sex, love, women, his own prowess and feudal politics. One, traditionally numbered eighth, is of doubtful attribution because of its different style and language, and another exists in two quite different versions. In several poems he honours a woman he calls midons. Pos de chantar m'es pres talenz, possibly written around his first excommunication, muses on mortality and renounces chivalry and pride.

An anonymous 13th-century vida calls him one of the most courtly men in the world and a great deceiver of women, but it may rest on a literal reading of songs written in the first person. The nickname the Troubadour was applied only in the nineteenth century. His children included William X, his successor, and Raymond, later Prince of Antioch.
william-lloyd-garrison: Garrison was the youngest son of immigrants from the British colony of New Brunswick. His father, Abijah Garrison, a merchant-sailing pilot and master, moved the family to Newburyport in 1806 but lost work after the Embargo Act of 1807 and deserted the family in 1808. His mother, Frances Maria Lloyd, began calling the boy by his middle name to keep her family name; she died in 1823. He worked as a typesetter, which helped him later run his newspaper, and he often composed his editorials directly in type.

At twenty-five he joined the anti-slavery movement, later crediting John Rankin's Letters on Slavery of 1826. For a short time he was associated with the American Colonization Society, which promoted resettling free Black Americans in West Africa. By late 1829 or 1830 he rejected colonization and publicly apologised for his error. In 1829 he became co-editor with Benjamin Lundy of the Quaker newspaper Genius of Universal Emancipation in Baltimore. There he moved from Lundy's gradualism to a demand for immediate and complete emancipation, and he ran a column, The Black List, reporting the cruelties of slavery.

In 1831 he returned to New England and co-founded the weekly The Liberator with Isaac Knapp. In January 1832 he organised the New-England Anti-Slavery Society, and in December 1833 abolitionists from ten states founded the American Anti-Slavery Society. His appeals for women to take part sparked controversy over women's right to a political voice. In December 1837 he announced that The Liberator would support the rights of woman to their utmost extent. In 1834 he married Helen Eliza Benson; they had two daughters and five sons, of whom two died as children.

He promoted what he called no-governmentism, rejecting the validity of a government engaged in war, imperialism and slavery. He began as an advocate of Christian pacifism, but at the outbreak of the American Civil War he accepted armed struggle as a means of abolition and supported President Abraham Lincoln. In May 1865 he proposed dissolving the American Anti-Slavery Society, but Wendell Phillips argued that its task was not complete until Black Southerners had full political and civil equality, and the resolution was defeated 118 to 48. Garrison resigned and ended The Liberator at the end of 1865. He died on 24 May 1879. Leo Tolstoy was influenced by his writings and published a short biography of him in 1904.
william-longsword: William was born overseas to Rollo, while he was still a pagan, and his wife more danico, Poppa of Bayeux, whose parentage is uncertain. Poppa was a Christian and seems to have passed her beliefs to her son, who according to his planctus was baptised probably at the same time as his father. He is sometimes called duke of Normandy, but the title dux did not come into common use until the eleventh century. At the time he was known as count of Rouen, and the chronicler Flodoard called both Rollo and William principes of the Normans. The byname Longsword first appears in later eleventh-century sources.

William succeeded Rollo in 927. Early in his reign, in 933 or 934, Normans who thought him too Gallicised rebelled under Riulf, who besieged him in Rouen, according to Dudo of Saint-Quentin; William sallied out and won a decisive battle. In 933 he recognised King Rudolph of Western Francia, who gave him lordship over much of the Breton lands, including Avranches, the Cotentin Peninsula and the Channel Islands, though these lay outside Carolingian power. The Bretons resisted under Alan II, Duke of Brittany, but they were defeated with great slaughter. In 935 he married Luitgarde, daughter of Count Herbert II of Vermandois, and arranged his sister Adela's marriage to William, Count of Poitou.

After Rudolph died in January 936, William's promise of loyalty helped persuade the exiled Louis IV to return as king. In 939 he went to help his brother-in-law Herluin II of Montreuil against Arnulf I of Flanders, who retaliated by attacking Normandy. William was excommunicated for destroying several of Arnulf's estates, but he pledged loyalty to Louis IV in 940 and was confirmed in the lands given to his father. He also began the Norman monastic revival, rebuilding Jumièges Abbey on a grander scale.

A peace treaty brokered by Louis IV in 941 limited Norman expansion into Breton lands. On 17 December 942 William was ambushed and killed by followers of Arnulf on an island on the Somme at Picquigny, while attending a peace conference. He had no children with Luitgarde but fathered a son, Richard, with Sprota, his wife more danico. Richard, then aged ten, succeeded him as ruler of Normandy.
william-mckinley: William McKinley Jr. was born in 1843 in Niles, Ohio, the seventh of nine children of William McKinley Sr. and Nancy Allison McKinley. When the Civil War began in 1861 he and his cousin William McKinley Osbourne enlisted as privates in the Poland Guards, which became part of the 23rd Ohio Infantry. He received a commission as second lieutenant in recognition of his service at Antietam and ended the war as a brevet major, the only president to begin as an enlisted man and finish at that rank.
After the war he studied law and was admitted to the bar in Warren, Ohio, in March 1867. That year he moved to Canton, Ohio, where he practised law and later married Ida Saxton.

McKinley was elected to Congress in 1876 and became the Republican expert on the protective tariff. Democrats repeatedly redistricted his seat to remove him; he won anyway in 1878 and 1884. His McKinley Tariff of 1890 was highly controversial and, with another Democratic redistricting, contributed to his defeat that year. He was elected governor of Ohio in 1891 and 1893.

In 1896, amid a deep depression, he won the Republican nomination with the help of Mark Hanna and defeated the Democrat William Jennings Bryan in a front-porch campaign. He backed the gold standard unless altered by international agreement and promised that high tariffs would restore prosperity. In office he signed the Dingley Tariff of 1897 and the Gold Standard Act of 1900.

The United States annexed Hawaii in 1898. McKinley hoped to persuade Spain to grant Cuba independence without conflict, but when talks failed he requested and signed Congress's declaration of war in the Spanish–American War of 1898. Spain turned over Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines, and Cuba was promised independence but stayed under American control until 1902. A pro-independence rebellion began in the Philippines and was eventually suppressed.

McKinley defeated Bryan again in 1900. On 6 September 1901 the anarchist Leon Czolgosz shot him, and he died eight days later. Vice President Theodore Roosevelt succeeded him, and Roosevelt's popularity overshadowed McKinley's legacy. Historians regard the election of 1896 as a realignment that began the Republican-dominated Fourth Party System.
william-morris: William Morris was born at Elm House in Walthamstow, Essex, on 24 March 1834, into a wealthy middle-class family that followed the evangelical Protestant form of Christianity. His father, a financier, was a partner in the City of London bill brokers Sanderson & Co. Morris entered Exeter College at Oxford in 1852 but disliked the teaching of classics. He turned instead to medieval history and architecture, within the Romantic medievalist movement that rejected the values of Victorian industrial capitalism. Reading Thomas Carlyle's Past and Present and the Christian socialists Charles Kingsley and Frederick Denison Maurice deepened his dislike of contemporary capitalism.

In January 1856 he became an apprentice to the Neo-Gothic architect George Edmund Street, where he befriended Philip Webb, and he soon shared a flat in Bloomsbury with Edward Burne-Jones. Webb designed the Red House at Upton in Kent for Morris, who lived there from 1859 to 1865.

The firm of Morris, Marshall, Faulkner & Co. produced interiors that were in great demand. After taking total control in 1875, Morris studied dyeing with the silk dyer Thomas Wardle at Leek, rejecting chemical aniline dyes in favour of indigo, walnut, madder and other natural ones. In 1881 he leased the Merton Abbey Works, where within three years 100 craftsmen were employed.

His socialism grew in the 1880s. In December 1884 he founded the Socialist League with other defectors from the Social Democratic Federation, advocating revolutionary international socialism. In 1888 he was elected to the Art Workers' Guild, of which he became master in 1892, and in 1892 he became president of the Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society.

Morris believed that design and making should not be separated and that craftsmen should be designer-makers. His translations of the Icelandic sagas, made with Eiríkur Magnússon, and his poems such as The Earthly Paradise (1868–1870), his novella A Dream of John Ball (1888) and the novel The Well at the World's End (1896) were widely read. The Kelmscott Press, founded in 1891, printed more than fifty works before it closed in 1898, among them an edition of Geoffrey Chaucer illustrated by Burne-Jones. In his lifetime he was best known as a poet. The William Morris Society, founded in 1955, is based at Kelmscott House in Hammersmith.
william-of-ockham: William of Ockham was probably born in Ockham, Surrey, around 1287. At an early age he joined the Franciscan Order and received the first stages of his theological education in the Franciscan school in London. He then studied in the Franciscan school at the University of Oxford, probably until 1321. Although he completed all the requirements for a master's degree in theology, he never became a regent master, and was therefore later called the Venerabilis Inceptor. His disputations on Peter Lombard's Sentences were held probably in 1317 to 1319.

The Order then sent him to one of its schools, probably in London, where he wrote mostly philosophical works, including commentaries on Aristotle's logical treatises and Physics and a Summary of Logic. In 1324 a summons to the papal court at Avignon interrupted his teaching, so that he could defend his Sentences commentary. Pope John XXII had the former Oxford chancellor John Lutterell collect suspect passages, and a committee of theologians reviewed them. Its preliminary reports were critical, but the process was never concluded.

At Avignon Ockham became involved in the dispute over apostolic poverty. The Franciscans held that Jesus and the apostles owned nothing, individually or in common, and the pope rejected this doctrine in several bulls; in Cum inter nonnullos he condemned it as heresy. The Minister General, Michael of Cesena, asked Ockham to study the bulls, in which Ockham found much that was heretical and erroneous. Ockham and others left Avignon secretly on 26 May 1328 and took refuge in Munich under the protection of the Holy Roman Emperor Louis IV of Bavaria. They were excommunicated on 6 June 1328 for leaving without permission.

Most Franciscans submitted, but Ockham and the small band of Michaelists campaigned for years to have John XXII and his successors Benedict XII and Clement VI deposed. His writings of these years, the Opera Politica, deal with political philosophy. He died probably on 9 or 10 April 1347, just before the Black Death reached Munich.

Ockham took much from Duns Scotus, including his view of divine omnipotence, but disagreed with him on predestination, penance and universals. He held that theology is not a science: only faith gives access to theological truths. Fifteenth-century nominalists regarded him as a founder of their movement, though some modern scholars prefer the terms terminism or conceptualism. His name is attached to the principle of parsimony in explanation known as Occam's razor, although the familiar Latin formulation is not found in his surviving writings.
william-of-rubruck: William was born in Rubrouck, in the County of Flanders in the Kingdom of France. In 1248 he accompanied King Louis IX of France on the Seventh Crusade. His was the fourth European mission to the Mongols, after those of Giovanni da Pian del Carpine and Ascelin of Lombardia in 1245 and André de Longjumeau in 1249. Louis had been encouraged to send another mission by reports of Nestorian Christians at the Mongol court, but because of an earlier rebuff he declined to send a formal one.

On 7 May 1253, on Louis's orders, William set out to convert the Tatars to Christianity. At Constantinople he conferred with Baldwin of Hainaut, who had recently been to Karakorum, and received letters to some Tatar chiefs. With him were Bartolomeo da Cremona, an attendant called Gosset and an interpreter named Homo Dei. After reaching Sudak in Crimea he went on by ox cart, met Sartaq Khan and was sent to Sartaq's father Batu Khan at Sarai. Batu was offended by William's preaching but sent the party on to the Great Khan Möngke.

They set off on horseback on 16 September 1253 on a journey of about 9,000 km, arrived at Karakorum in late December and were given an audience on 4 January 1254. William described the city's walls, markets and temples and the separate quarters for Muslim and Chinese craftsmen. Among Europeans he met was the French silversmith Guillaume Boucher. In May 1254 the khan arranged a formal debate among Christians, Buddhists and Muslims, with a judge from each faith. The party left on 10 July 1254 and reached the County of Tripoli on 15 August 1255.

William could not meet Louis in person and wrote him a long Latin report, the Itinerarium, in 40 chapters: chapters 1 to 10 give general observations on the Mongols and their customs, and chapters 11 to 40 relate the journey. He recorded geographical and anthropological details, and by passing north of the Caspian Sea showed that it was an inland sea and did not flow into the Arctic Ocean. He also recorded German slaves at Talas in what is now southern Kazakhstan.

Roger Bacon cited him at length in his Opus Majus. After Bacon the narrative seems to have dropped out of sight until Richard Hakluyt published part of it in 1599. A critical edition of the complete Latin text appeared in 1839, and an English translation by William Woodville Rockhill in 1900. In 1958 the Russian poet Nikolay Zabolotskiy wrote a long poem, Rubruck in Mongolia.
william-penn: Penn was born on 24 October 1644 at Tower Hill, London. His mother, Margaret Jasper, was a Dutchwoman, widow of a Dutch sea captain and daughter of a rich Rotterdam merchant. His father served in the Commonwealth Navy, was rewarded by Oliver Cromwell with Irish estates and later took part in the restoration of Charles II. Penn was educated at Chigwell School, by private tutors in Ireland and at Christ Church, Oxford, where he arrived in 1660. Though his father's position made him a Cavalier, his sympathies lay with the persecuted Quakers, and he was expelled from the university in 1662 for religious nonconformity.
At Cork he began attending Quaker meetings, was arrested, and joined the Quakers at the age of 22. His furious father ordered him out of the house and withheld his inheritance.

Penn became a prolific Quaker writer. In 1668, after his tract The Sandy Foundation Shaken, he was held in the Tower of London on a charge of publication without a licence, though the real accusation was blasphemy. He wrote No Cross, No Crown in 1669 while in jail, and answered the charge of denying the Trinity in Innocency with her open face. In 1677 a group of Quakers including Penn bought West Jersey, and East Jersey followed in 1682.

Seeing conditions worsen for Quakers in England, Penn proposed mass emigration. In 1681 Charles II granted him land to offset debts owed to his father, and the next year Penn sailed up Delaware Bay and the Delaware River and founded Philadelphia. He framed a government on Quaker ideals of peace, equality and representative government. His land was also claimed by Lord Baltimore, and the dispute with the Calverts ran for eighty years. Penn returned to England in 1684 and went back to Pennsylvania in December 1699, finding it grown to nearly 18,100 inhabitants, with over 3,000 in Philadelphia.

In his later years Penn was in financial trouble. His agent Philip Ford cheated him, and after Ford died in 1702 his widow Bridget claimed title to Pennsylvania; Penn was held in debtors' prison, then under house arrest, until Quaker friends paid the claim.

He died on 10 August 1718, aged 73, at Ruscombe in Berkshire, and is buried at Jordans near Chalfont St Giles. After his death Pennsylvania drifted from a colony founded on religion towards a commercial, secular state, but many of his legal and political ideas took root, as did the Quaker school in Philadelphia for which he issued charters in 1689 and 1701. Delegates to the 1787 Constitutional Convention were inspired by the principles of his Frame of Government. A statue of Penn tops Philadelphia City Hall.
william-pitt-the-elder: Pitt was the grandson of Thomas Pitt, the governor of Madras, known as "Diamond" Pitt for having sold a diamond of extraordinary size to the Duke of Orléans for about £135,000. That sale and other trading deals in India made the family's fortune. In 1691 the governor bought the property of Boconnoc in Cornwall, which gave him control of a seat in Parliament, and he became one of the dominant political figures of the West Country.

As a younger son, William Pitt chose a career in the army and obtained a cornet's commission in the King's Own Regiment of Horse. George II never forgot the jibes of "the terrible cornet of horse". Pitt soon joined the Patriots, a faction of discontented Whigs in opposition who met at Stowe House, the estate of Lord Cobham, and he swiftly became one of its most prominent members.

In the 1730s Pitt was a leading advocate of a hard line against Spain and often attacked Robert Walpole's government for weakness. He spoke against the Convention of El Pardo on 8 March 1739. After poor election results and the disaster at Cartagena, Walpole resigned in February 1742. The king resented Pitt, and only in February 1746 did he receive a place in government, as Vice-Treasurer of Ireland.

In December 1756 Pitt became Secretary of State for the Southern Department and Leader of the House of Commons. A coalition with the Duke of Newcastle was formed in June 1757 and held power until October 1761. In 1758 Pitt put into practice a strategy of tying down French troops in Germany while Britain used its naval supremacy to attack French possessions around the world. He chose young commanders such as Keppel, and it was his judgement that selected Wolfe to lead the attack on Quebec.

In July 1766 the king asked Pitt to form a government of his own selection. His principle was "measures not men". He took the office of Lord Privy Seal, which required his elevation to the House of Lords, and on 4 August became Earl of Chatham. His ministry faced the observance of the Treaty of Paris, tension with the American colonists and the status of the East India Company. The Townshend Acts of 1767 were enacted by Charles Townshend without consulting him. In October 1768 he resigned on grounds of poor health.

He returned to the House of Lords in 1770 and spoke for a firm line with Spain in the Falklands Crisis. His last appearance there was on 7 April 1778, in support of making peace with America. He died on 11 May 1778. Pittsburgh in Pennsylvania was named after him.
william-pitt-the-younger: William Pitt, the second son of William Pitt, 1st Earl of Chatham, was born on 28 May 1759 at Hayes Place in Kent. His mother, Hester Grenville, was the sister of the former prime minister George Grenville. Often in poor health as a boy, he was educated at home by the Reverend Edward Wilson and became proficient in Latin and Greek. He was admitted to Pembroke College, Cambridge, on 26 April 1773, a month before turning fourteen, and there befriended William Wilberforce, who became a lifelong friend and ally in Parliament.

At the general election of September 1780 Pitt contested the University of Cambridge seat and came bottom of the poll, having campaigned as an independent Whig. A by-election in the pocket borough of Appleby, controlled by James Lowther, sent him to the House of Commons in January 1781, ironically as he later railed against such boroughs. In the government of the Earl of Shelburne he was Chancellor of the Exchequer.

The Fox–North Coalition fell in December 1783 after the King secured the defeat in the House of Lords of Edmund Burke's bill to reform the East India Company, and George III entrusted the premiership to Pitt, after offering it three times before. In 1785 Pitt introduced a bill to remove thirty-six rotten and pocket boroughs and slightly widen the franchise, but it was defeated, and it was his last reform proposal. In May 1798 he fought a duel with George Tierney after accusing him of obstructing national defence.

He engineered the Acts of Union 1800 and tried to secure Catholic emancipation as part of the Union, but the King strongly opposed it as contrary to his coronation oath. Pitt resigned on 16 February 1801, so that Henry Addington could form a new administration.

During the opposition years of 1801 to 1804 he often stayed at Walmer Castle, organised a local Volunteer Corps against a French invasion and encouraged the construction of Martello towers and the Royal Military Canal. He returned to the premiership on 10 May 1804, but the King's opposition to including Charles James Fox weakened his second ministry. It renewed the alliance with Austria, Prussia and Russia against Napoleonic France.

Pitt, who had long suffered from gout and ill health, died on 23 January 1806 at Bowling Green House on Putney Heath, probably of peptic ulceration, unmarried and childless. Parliament agreed to pay his debts of £40,000, and he was buried in Westminster Abbey on 22 February. He helped define the prime minister as the supervisor and coordinator of the government departments, and he rehabilitated the nation's finances after the American War of Independence. Wilberforce wrote that he had never known his equal for personal purity and love of his country.
william-prince-of-albania: Wilhelm Friedrich Heinrich, Prince of Wied, was born on 26 March 1876 at Neuwied Castle, near Koblenz, in the Prussian Rhineland. He belonged to the mediatised house of Wied-Neuwied and was the third son of William, 5th Prince of Wied, brother of Queen Elisabeth of Romania, and Princess Marie of the Netherlands, sister of Queen Louise of Sweden. He served as a Prussian cavalry officer and became a captain in the German General Staff in 1911.

Albania declared independence from the Ottoman Empire in November 1912, during the First Balkan War, and the Treaty of London recognised it in 1913. The six powers selected him, and the announcement was made in November 1913. Wilhelm II thought the choice unwise.

On 7 February 1914 William told the Great Powers he would accept the throne, and on 21 February a delegation of Albanian notables led by Essad Pasha Toptani formally asked him. He arrived at the provisional capital Durrës on 7 March and formed a cabinet dominated by aristocrats, with Essad Pasha as minister of defence and foreign affairs. He was styled sovereign prince abroad, but in Albania he was called mbret, or king.

His reign was turbulent. Revolts of Muslims broke out in central Albania against Essad Pasha and against foreign domination that was not Turkish, and Greece encouraged a separatist provisional government in North Epirus. Essad Pasha accepted money from Italy to finance a revolt and a coup. The plot was exposed, and he was arrested on 19 May 1914, tried for treason and sentenced to death, but the Italian government saved his life and he went into exile in Italy. When the First World War began, Austria-Hungary demanded Albanian soldiers; he refused, citing Albania's neutrality in the Treaty of London, and his remuneration was cut off.

William left Albania on 3 September 1914, heading for Venice, and insisted that he remained head of state. He returned to Germany and rejoined the army. His hopes of restoration rose in early 1916 and came to nothing, and after the war the Paris Peace Conference was unlikely to restore the throne to someone who had fought against its participants.

Several factions in post-war Albania billed themselves as regencies for him, but the country was declared a republic on 31 January 1925, officially ending his reign. When Ahmet Zogu was set to become king, William reaffirmed his claim for himself and his heirs. He died at Predeal, near Sinaia, in Romania, and was buried at the Lutheran Church in Bucharest, leaving his son Carol Victor as heir to his Albanian claims.
william-shakespeare: William Shakespeare was the son of John Shakespeare, an alderman and glove-maker originally from Snitterfield in Warwickshire, and Mary Arden, whose affluent landowning family was influential in the Recusant Catholic community. He was baptised in Stratford-upon-Avon on 26 April 1564. His date of birth is unknown, but it is traditionally observed on 23 April, which is also the day he died in 1616. He was the third of eight children. Most biographers agree he was probably educated at the King's New School in Stratford, although no attendance records survive.

At 18 he married 26-year-old Anne Hathaway, and a marriage licence was issued on 27 November 1582. Their daughter Susanna was baptised on 26 May 1583, and the twins Hamnet and Judith on 2 February 1585. Hamnet died at the age of 11 and was buried on 11 August 1596. Sometime between 1585 and 1592 Shakespeare began a career in London as an actor, writer and part-owner of the Lord Chamberlain's Men.

Shakespeare produced most of his known works between 1589 and 1613. His first recorded works are Richard III and the three parts of Henry VI, written in the early 1590s, and his first histories draw heavily on the 1587 edition of Raphael Holinshed's Chronicles. When the theatres were closed by plague in 1593 and 1594, he published the narrative poems Venus and Adonis and The Rape of Lucrece, dedicated to Henry Wriothesley, 3rd Earl of Southampton. The 154 Sonnets were printed in 1609, though evidence suggests he wrote sonnets throughout his career for a private readership.

His verse is mostly blank verse in iambic pentameter. His early plays follow the conventional, rhetorical style of the day, and by the mid-1590s, in Romeo and Juliet, Richard II and A Midsummer Night's Dream, he had begun to write a more natural poetry. He used soliloquies to explore characters' minds, and he wrote mainly tragedies until 1608, then tragicomedies such as The Winter's Tale and The Tempest.

At about 49, around 1613, Shakespeare appears to have retired to Stratford, where he died three years later. Few records of his private life survive. In 1623 two fellow actors, John Heminges and Henry Condell, published the First Folio, which includes 36 of his plays, with a poem by Ben Jonson calling him 'not of an age, but for all time'.

Doubts about authorship first appeared some 230 years after his death, naming candidates such as Francis Bacon, Christopher Marlowe and Edward de Vere, 17th Earl of Oxford, but all but a few scholars regard this as a fringe theory. Samuel Johnson quoted him more often than any other author in his Dictionary.
william-tecumseh-sherman: Sherman was born on 8 February 1820 in Lancaster, Ohio. His father, Charles Robert Sherman, a justice of the Ohio Supreme Court, died of typhoid fever in 1829, leaving his widow Mary Hoyt Sherman with eleven children and no inheritance. The nine-year-old was raised by a neighbour and family friend, the lawyer Thomas Ewing, later a US senator and the first Secretary of the Interior. Ewing secured him a place at the United States Military Academy at West Point, from which he graduated in 1840.

In 1853 Sherman left the army for private business, without much success. In 1859 he became the first superintendent of the Louisiana State Seminary of Learning and Military Academy, later Louisiana State University, and resigned when Louisiana seceded in January 1861. He then took a colonel's commission in the Union army and commanded a brigade at the First Battle of Bull Run on 21 July 1861.

Put in charge of Kentucky in autumn 1861, Sherman grew pessimistic, overestimated Confederate strength and asked for relief. In December Henry W. Halleck put him on leave, and the press called him insane; he later admitted to having contemplated suicide. He recovered and served under Ulysses S. Grant at Fort Donelson and at Shiloh in April 1862. There he had dismissed reports of a Confederate advance, but rallied his division and conducted an orderly retreat that helped avert a rout. He commanded a corps in the Vicksburg campaign.

When Grant went east in 1864, Sherman took command of the western theatre, and he led the capture of Atlanta. He then cut loose from his supply lines for the March to the Sea, intending to wear down the Confederacy's ability and will to fight through destruction of military and civilian infrastructure, and turned north through the Carolinas. At Bennett Place on 17 April 1865 he agreed generous terms with General Joseph Johnston; Secretary of War Edwin Stanton ordered Grant to change them. As Commanding General from 1869 he directed the army in the Indian Wars with similar hard-war methods.

Sherman published his memoirs in 1875. He settled in New York City, loved the theatre and amateur painting, and in 1884 refused any presidential nomination with the words that he would not accept if nominated and would not serve if elected. He died of pneumonia on 14 February 1891. B. H. Liddell Hart called him the first modern general, praising his mastery of manoeuvre, while historians such as Mark Grimsley use the term hard war for his campaigns. The Sherman Memorial by Augustus Saint-Gaudens stands near Central Park.
william-tell: The legend is set in the early 14th century, with a traditional date of 1307 under the rule of Albert of Habsburg. Its first written records date from the later 15th century, when the Swiss Confederacy was gaining military and political influence. The White Book of Sarnen, written in 1474 by Hans Schriber, the state secretary of Obwalden, mentions the Rütli Oath and names Tell, without a given name, as one of the conspirators whose tyrannicide triggered the rebellion.

The version that became standard is that of Aegidius Tschudi of Glarus, writing around 1570. He is known to have fleshed out his sources, so details found only in his account, including the given name Wilhelm, Tell's birthplace at Bürglen, the date 18 November 1307 and his death in 1354, may be his invention. Historians agree that there is no 14th-century evidence for Tell as a historical person, let alone for the apple shot.

In Tschudi's account the Habsburg bailiff Albrecht Gessler raised a pole in Altdorf with his hat on top and ordered the townsfolk to bow to it. Tell passed it with his young son and refused, and was arrested. Gessler, intrigued by his marksmanship, ordered him to shoot an apple from his son Walter's head with one bolt, which he did. Asked why he had taken a second bolt, Tell said it was meant for Gessler if he had killed his son, and Gessler ordered him bound.

On the way across Lake Lucerne to the dungeon at Küssnacht a storm broke, and Tell was unshackled to steer the boat. He leaped onto a rock, known as the Tellsplatte, and later shot Gessler with the second bolt in the Hohle Gasse. His act sparked the rebellion that led to the Old Swiss Confederacy.

Veneration of Tell can be traced to the early 16th century, and the first recorded Tell play, the Urner Tellspiel, was probably performed in Altdorf in the winter of 1512 or 1513. In 1653 three men dressed as the Three Tells appeared at peasant conferences during the Swiss peasant war, linking their rebellion to the original one.

Friedrich Schiller's play Wilhelm Tell, first performed on 17 March 1804 in Weimar, followed Tschudi's account, and Gioachino Rossini based his opera of 1829 on it. Parallels such as the Danish Palnatoke, found in Saxo Grammaticus, led some writers to call the legend a borrowed folk motif.
william-the-conqueror: William was born at Falaise, the only son of Duke Robert I of Normandy and Herleva, a daughter of Fulbert of Falaise, who did not marry the duke. His illegitimate birth and his youth, he was seven or eight when he succeeded, caused difficulties. After Archbishop Robert died in March 1037 Normandy descended into chaos. William put down a rebellion in 1047, and his authority was not complete until about 1060. In the 1050s he married Matilda of Flanders, which gave him a powerful ally, and he secured control of Maine by 1062.

In 1051 the childless Edward the Confessor appears to have chosen William as his successor. When Edward died in January 1066 he named Harold Godwinson, and William, arguing that Edward had promised him the throne and that Harold had sworn to support him, built a fleet. The Normans landed at Pevensey Bay on 28 September, and William defeated and killed Harold at Hastings on 14 October 1066. He was crowned at Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066.

He confirmed some English earls but took the lands of Harold's family and others who fought at Hastings. Edwin and Morcar rose in 1068, and William built castles at Warwick, York and Nottingham. In 1070 he founded Battle Abbey at the site of Hastings, partly as a penance, and councils deposed Stigand and some native abbots. His hold on England was mostly secure by 1075, and he spent most of the rest of his reign on the continent. At Christmas 1085 he ordered a survey of all landholdings, which became the Domesday Book.

William died on 9 September 1087 while leading a campaign in northern France, after seizing Mantes, and was buried in Caen. His lands were divided, Normandy going to his son Robert and England to William Rufus. He did not unite his domains but administered each separately. His reign saw castle building, a new Norman nobility settled on the land and a change in the composition of the English clergy.
william-the-lion: William was born around 1142, during the reign of his grandfather King David I of Scotland. His parents were Henry of Scotland, a younger son of David I, and Ada de Warenne, a daughter of the Anglo-Norman lord William de Warenne, 2nd Earl of Surrey. William was about ten when his father died in 1152, and from his father he inherited the Earldom of Northumbria. David I died the next year, and William became heir presumptive to his brother, the new king Malcolm IV. In 1157 he lost the earldom to Henry II of England.

Malcolm IV died on 9 December 1165, and William was inaugurated on 24 December. He quarrelled with Henry II and in 1168 arranged the first definite treaty of alliance between France and Scotland. He took part in the Revolt of 1173–1174 against Henry II, and during a raid in 1174 he was surprised at Alnwick with only 60 men against about 400 English. He charged the English himself, was unhorsed and captured, and was taken in chains to Newcastle, then Northampton, and then Normandy. As the price of his release he signed the Treaty of Falaise, acknowledging Henry as his feudal superior and agreeing to pay for the English army's occupation of Scotland.

The treaty provoked a revolt in Galloway that lasted until 1186 and led to the building of a castle at Dumfries. In 1179 William and his brother David led a force into Easter Ross and founded two castles there, to discourage the Norse earls of Orkney from expanding beyond Caithness. A rising in 1181 involved Donald Meic Uilleim, and not until Donald died in 1187 could William reclaim Inverness. In 1188 he secured a papal bull declaring that the Church of Scotland was subject only to Rome. On 5 December 1189 Richard I, needing money for the Third Crusade, ended the treaty for 10,000 silver marks, and later campaigns brought Caithness and Sutherland under the crown.

William died on 4 December 1214 and was succeeded by his son Alexander. He had followed the lines laid down by his grandfather David I: Anglo-French settlement and feudalization were extended, new burghs were founded, criminal law was clarified, the duties of justices and sheriffs were widened, and trade grew. The Bishopric of Argyll was established around 1192.

He was not called the Lion in his lifetime. The name came from his standard, a red lion rampant on a yellow background, which became the Royal Banner of Scotland. The chronicler John of Fordun called him the Lion of Justice.
william-the-silent: William was born on 24 April 1533 at Dillenburg Castle, the eldest of twelve children of Count William I of Nassau-Siegen and Countess Juliana of Stolberg. The family was devout and he was raised a Lutheran. A ward of Charles V, educated under the Emperor's sister Mary, he became a favourite of the imperial family, was made a cavalry captain in 1551 and in 1555 commanded one of the Emperor's armies at Bayonne. In November 1555 Charles leaned on his shoulder at the ceremony in which he gave the Low Countries to his son Philip II of Spain. William carried the imperial insignia to Ferdinand in 1556 and was a Spanish signatory of the Treaty of Cateau-Cambrésis in 1559.

In 1559 Philip appointed him stadtholder of Holland, Zeeland and Utrecht, and in 1561 of Franche-Comté. He soon became a leading figure of the opposition in the Council of State, with Philip de Montmorency, Count of Hoorn, and Lamoral, Count of Egmont, who sought more power for themselves and the Dutch nobility against the government of Granvelle and others, and complained of the number of Spaniards in government. He also objected to the persecution of Protestants. Brought up a Lutheran and later a Catholic, he was very religious but favoured freedom of religion for all.

In October 1568 he led a large army into Brabant, but Alba avoided a decisive battle, disorder broke out in the army, money ran short, and William turned back into France. Later invasion plans came to little for lack of money and support, but he remained popular, helped by a pamphlet campaign claiming that he fought not the king but foreign governors and troops. In March 1580 Philip declared him an outlaw and promised 25,000 crowns to anyone who killed him; William answered with his Apology, written by Villiers.

Balthasar Gérard, a Burgundian Catholic who regarded William as a traitor, learned of the reward in 1581. In May 1584 he presented himself to William as a French nobleman and gained his trust, and William was assassinated at Delft in July. He was buried in the New Church at Delft, as Breda, where the Nassau family was traditionally buried, was under royal control. Hendrik de Keyser and his son Pieter made a new monument in 1623.

William married four times. His eldest son Philip William succeeded him as Prince of Orange, though held hostage in Spain, and his son Maurice of Nassau became stadtholder. Frederick Henry, his youngest son, inherited the title in 1625. The Netherlands became formally independent by the Peace of Münster in 1648. In the Netherlands William is widely regarded as the principal founding father and is called Father of the Fatherland.
william-tolbert: William Richard Tolbert Jr. was born on 13 May 1913 in Bensonville, into an Americo-Liberian family of African American descent. His grandfather, Daniel Frank Tolbert, had been enslaved in South Carolina and emigrated to Liberia in the exodus of 1878. Tolbert took a Bachelor of Arts at the University of Liberia in 1934, entered the House of Representatives for the True Whig Party in 1943, and was elected vice president in 1951, serving under William Tubman until 1971. A Baptist minister, he became in 1965 the first African to serve as president of the Baptist World Alliance.

Tolbert became president after Tubman died in London on 23 July 1971, and the peaceful transfer was seen abroad as a sign of stability. Liberia was effectively a one-party state, and he started some liberal reforms and tried to bring more indigenous people into government, which satisfied neither the indigenous majority, who found it too slow, nor many Americo-Liberians, who found it too fast. In 1973 the Progressive Alliance of Liberia, led by Gabriel Baccus Matthews, was recognised as an opposition party. He also secured an amendment limiting a president to eight years.

In foreign policy he moved towards non-alignment, establishing relations with the Soviet Union, China and Cuba, and he severed ties with Israel in 1973. Liberia signed the treaty founding ECOWAS in 1975, and companies such as Firestone were audited and made to pay back taxes. He called his economic approach Humanistic Capitalism. Critics charged his government with nepotism and with failing to close the gap between Americo-Liberians and the indigenous population.

In April 1979 a proposed rise in the subsidised price of rice, from 22 to 26 dollars a bag, led the Progressive Alliance to call a march in Monrovia. It swelled into a riot with widespread looting, and at least 41 demonstrators were shot dead. In March 1980 Tolbert banned the Alliance and arrested its leaders for treason. In the early hours of 12 April 1980, 17 non-commissioned officers and soldiers led by Master Sergeant Samuel Doe entered the presidential palace and killed him, ending 133 years of Americo-Liberian rule. Accounts differ on how he died: one has him found sleeping in his office, another seized in his bed. Most of his cabinet was tried and many were publicly executed on 22 April 1980.
william-tubman: William Vacanarat Shadrach Tubman was born on 29 November 1895 in Harper, in south-eastern Liberia, one of five children of a poor family descended from people once enslaved in the United States. His grandfather Alexander Tubman was a stonemason, a general in the Liberian army, a Speaker of the House of Representatives and a Methodist preacher. Alexander's parents were among 69 freed people whose passage to Liberia in 1844 was paid by their former mistress, Emily Harvie Thomas Tubman of Augusta, Georgia. Tubman went to the Methodist Cape Palmas Seminary, became a lay preacher at nineteen and passed the bar in 1917 after studying law with private tutors.

He joined the True Whig Party and in 1923, aged 28, became the youngest senator in Liberian history, for Maryland County. He fought for the constitutional rights of indigenous groups, which made up the overwhelming majority of Liberians. In 1931 he resigned his seat to defend Liberia before the League of Nations against allegations that the country used slave labour. After another term in the legislature, he was appointed in 1937 an associate justice of the Supreme Court by President Edwin Barclay, where he served until 1943. An official biography speculates that Barclay did so to remove him as a rival for the presidency.

Tubman was elected president on 4 May 1943 and inaugurated on 3 January 1944. Liberia declared war on Germany and Japan on 27 January 1944, and in June he and Barclay were the first African heads of state received at the White House. His open door policy drew foreign investment, mostly American, which grew by 200 percent between 1944 and 1970, and Liberia averaged 11.5 percent annual growth from 1950 to 1960. Roads, a railway to the iron mines, hospitals and a literacy programme followed. He also worked for national unification between Americo-Liberians and the indigenous majority, and helped found the African Union of moderate states in 1961.

His rule had a harsher side. S. David Coleman and his son were hunted down and killed by soldiers for allegedly plotting against him, the constitution was changed to let him serve beyond two terms, and in 1961 he declared a state of emergency after riots and a strike. Tubman died on 23 July 1971, the longest-serving president in the country's history, and is regarded as the father of modern Liberia.
william-v-prince-of-orange: William V was born in The Hague on 8 March 1748, the only son of William IV, who had been restored as stadtholder of the United Provinces the year before. He was three years old when his father died in 1751, and a long regency began, held by his mother Anne, his grandmother Marie Louise, Duke Louis Ernest of Brunswick-Lüneburg and his sister Carolina. He took up the office of stadtholder and Captain-General of the Dutch States Army on his majority in 1766. By the secret Acte van Consulentschap he let the Duke of Brunswick keep a large influence on the government. In 1767 he married Princess Wilhelmina of Prussia, a niece of Frederick the Great.

The Dutch were neutral in the American War of Independence, and William, leading the pro-British faction, blocked attempts to bring the Republic into the war. The Dutch attempt to join the League of Armed Neutrality led to the Fourth Anglo-Dutch War in 1780. The war went badly. The Dutch lost Sint Eustatius and Nagapattinam, scandals such as the Brest Affair undermined belief in the navy, and the regime and the Duke of Brunswick were suspected of treason. The pamphlet Aan het Volk van Nederland, published in 1781 by Joan van der Capellen tot den Pol, called for political reform.

After the Treaty of Paris of 1783 the Patriots, a coalition of old regenten and democrats, challenged him more and more. In 1785 he moved his court to Het Loo, and in September 1786 sent troops to overthrow the Patriot councils of towns, whereupon the States of Holland deprived him of his command of the army. In June 1787 his wife Wilhelmina was stopped on her way to The Hague by the Gouda Free Corps. Her brother, Frederick William II of Prussia, took this as an insult and an excuse, and invaded Holland in September 1787 to suppress the Patriots.

William joined the First Coalition against France in 1793. In 1795, with the French Army supporting the revolutionaries, he went into exile in England. A few days later the Batavian Revolution replaced the Republic with the Batavian Republic.
