From Kew he wrote letters to the governors of the Dutch colonies telling them to hand the colonies to the British, which only some did; the British later returned most of them, but kept South Africa and Ceylon. He died in exile at his daughter's palace in Brunswick, the last of the Dutch stadtholders. His son William VI returned in 1813 and proclaimed himself king, the first Dutch monarch of the House of Orange.
william-wallace: Wallace was a member of the lesser nobility, but little is definitely known of his family or parentage. His seal, on a letter sent to Lübeck in 1297, names his father as Alan Wallace. Blind Harry's poem of the late 15th century gives him instead a father, Sir Malcolm of Elderslie, but no contemporary evidence links him with either place.

The surname comes from Old English wǣlisċ, meaning foreigner or Welshman, and may refer to speakers of the Cumbric language. In his youth King Alexander III ruled Scotland. After Alexander's death in 1286 and that of his granddaughter Margaret, Maid of Norway, in 1290, Edward I of England arbitrated the succession and judged in favour of John Balliol in November 1292. Edward then treated Scotland as a vassal, and he invaded in 1296 and forced Balliol to abdicate.

The first act definitely known to be Wallace's is the killing of William de Heselrig, the English sheriff of Lanark, in May 1297. When the Scottish nobles submitted at Irvine in July, Wallace and Andrew Moray carried on, and they joined their forces. On 11 September 1297 they defeated the army of the Earl of Surrey at Stirling Bridge. The bridge was so narrow that the English could cross only a few abreast, and the Scots killed them as they came over. Wallace and Moray became Guardians of Scotland, and Moray died of his wounds later that year. Wallace raided northern England and was knighted at Selkirk.

In July 1298 Edward invaded again, and at Falkirk the English longbowmen and cavalry broke the Scottish schiltrons, formations of spearmen. Wallace escaped, but his reputation suffered, and by September 1298 he had resigned as Guardian in favour of Robert the Bruce and John Comyn. A letter of 7 November 1300 from Philip IV of France to his envoys in Rome recommends him to the pope, which suggests he went to France. By 1304 he was back in Scotland.

John de Menteith, a Scottish knight loyal to Edward, handed Wallace to English soldiers at Robroyston, near Glasgow, in August 1305. He was tried at Westminster Hall for treason and for atrocities against civilians. He argued that he had never sworn allegiance to Edward.

On 23 August 1305 he was hanged, drawn and quartered at Smithfield, his head was displayed on London Bridge, and his limbs were sent to Newcastle, Berwick, Stirling and Perth. The Wallace Monument was erected near Stirling Bridge in 1869. Blind Harry's poem The Wallace, much of it at variance with contemporary sources, shaped his legend, as did Jane Porter's novel and the film Braveheart of 1995.
william-wilberforce: William Wilberforce was born in Hull on 24 August 1759, the only son of Robert Wilberforce, a wealthy merchant. His grandfather had made the family fortune in the Baltic trade and was twice elected mayor of Hull. After his father's death in 1768 he was sent to a prosperous uncle and aunt in London and Wimbledon, whose influence first drew him towards evangelical Christianity. In September 1780, at 21 and still a student, he was elected Member of Parliament for Kingston upon Hull and sat as an independent. In 1785 he underwent an evangelical conversion that changed his habits and gave him a lifelong concern for reform.

In 1787 Thomas Clarkson and a group of activists that included Granville Sharp, Hannah More and Charles Middleton persuaded Wilberforce to take up abolition of the slave trade. By 1783 the British trade in enslaved people had come to represent about 80 percent of Great Britain's foreign income, and of an estimated 11 million Africans transported into slavery, about 1.4 million died on the voyage. Illness in 1788 delayed his plans, and William Pitt introduced the first motion in his absence. A vote on 26 February 1793 was defeated by only eight votes, and war with France then pushed the issue aside, though he went on introducing abolition bills through the 1790s.

After Pitt's death in January 1806 Wilberforce worked more closely with the Whigs. A bill barring British subjects from the slave trade to the French colonies became law on 23 May 1806, and the Slave Trade Act followed in 1807. In 1816 he began to denounce slavery itself, though he preferred gradual change. He resigned his seat in 1826 because of failing health. His conservatism led him to support the suspension of habeas corpus in 1795, and critics such as William Cobbett charged him with ignoring conditions at home.

Wilberforce died on 29 July 1833, three days after hearing that the passage of the Slavery Abolition Act through Parliament was assured. Leading members of both Houses urged a burial in Westminster Abbey, and on 3 August he was laid in the north transept near Pitt while both Houses suspended their business. His sons' biography stressed his part in abolition and played down Clarkson's, and for over a century his role dominated the record. Later historians describe the two men as one of history's great partnerships. The Wilberforce Monument stands in Hull, and his birthplace there became Britain's first slavery museum.
william-wordsworth: William Wordsworth was born on 7 April 1770 at Cockermouth, Cumberland, the second of five children of John Wordsworth and Ann Cookson. His sister, the poet and diarist Dorothy Wordsworth, to whom he remained close, was born the following year. His mother died in 1778 and his father in 1783, and his father had set him to memorise long passages of Milton, Shakespeare and Spenser. He attended Hawkshead Grammar School and took his BA at St John's College, Cambridge, in 1791.

In November 1791 he visited Revolutionary France and fell in love with Annette Vallon, who in 1792 gave birth to their daughter Caroline. Financial problems and tense relations between Britain and France forced him back to England alone the following year, and the Reign of Terror left him disillusioned.

A legacy of £900 from Raisley Calvert in 1795 allowed him to pursue poetry, and that year he met Samuel Taylor Coleridge in Somerset. In 1797 he and Dorothy moved to Alfoxton House, a few miles from Coleridge's home. Together the two poets, with insights from Dorothy, produced Lyrical Ballads in 1798, which included Wordsworth's Tintern Abbey and Coleridge's The Rime of the Ancient Mariner. The second edition of 1800 named only Wordsworth and carried the preface in which some scholars see a central work of Romantic literary theory.

In the winter of 1798-99 at Goslar he began the autobiographical poem later titled The Prelude. In 1799 he and Dorothy settled at Dove Cottage in Grasmere, and Wordsworth, Coleridge and Robert Southey came to be known as the Lake Poets. On 4 October 1802 he married Mary Hutchinson, a childhood friend, after visiting Annette and Caroline in Calais with Dorothy.

He completed the first version of The Prelude in 1805 but would not publish so personal a work before finishing The Recluse. Poems, in Two Volumes appeared in 1807 and included the Ode: Intimations of Immortality, but its reception was lukewarm. In 1813 he became Distributor of Stamps for Westmorland, a post that made him financially secure, and the family moved to Rydal Mount, where he spent the rest of his life. The Excursion, published in 1814, was the second part of The Recluse, whose other parts he never completed. He was Poet Laureate from 1843 until his death from pleurisy on 23 April 1850.
williamsburg-virginia: Williamsburg stands on a ridge on the Virginia Peninsula between the James and York rivers, partly encircled by Queen's Creek and College Creek. It lies in the northern part of the Hampton Roads metropolitan area, about 45 miles south-east of Richmond. It is an independent city, legally independent of James City County to the west and south and of York County to the east, a status created by a new Virginia state constitution. It had a population of 15,425 at the 2020 census.

Before the English arrived at Jamestown in 1607, the area was part of the Powhatan Confederacy. Between 1630 and 1633, after the war that followed the Indian massacre of 1622, the colonists built a defensive palisade across the peninsula, with a settlement called Middle Plantation as its guard-station. After Jamestown burned during Bacon's Rebellion in 1676, temporary government headquarters were set up at Middle Plantation, whose high ground the House of Burgesses found safer and more pleasant than humid, mosquito-plagued Jamestown. The College of William & Mary was established there in 1693, and the city of Williamsburg was founded on the site in 1699.

Williamsburg was the capital of the Colony and Commonwealth of Virginia from 1699 to 1780 and the centre of political events leading to the American Revolution. During the Revolutionary era African Americans made up over 50 per cent of its population. In 1771 Lord Dunmore, the last royal governor, announced the first attempted canal in the United States, across the peninsula; it was never completed. In the Civil War the college was closed in 1861, and its College Building, used as a Confederate barracks and then a hospital, was burned by Union forces in 1862.

The city's economy is driven by Colonial Williamsburg, its restored Historic Area, a living history museum of the 18th-century colonial period. It includes Virginia's first capitol building, the Governor's Palace, Bruton Parish Church and the Peyton Randolph House. The Wren Building of the College of William & Mary, at the head of Duke of Gloucester Street, was among the first buildings restored by W. A. R. Goodwin and the family of John D. Rockefeller Jr. as they began creating Colonial Williamsburg. With Jamestown and Yorktown, Williamsburg forms the Historic Triangle. William & Mary is the second-oldest institution of higher education in the United States.
willibrord: Willibrord, in Latin Villibrordus, was an Anglo-Saxon monk and missionary who became the first Bishop of Utrecht. Alcuin styled his father, Wilgils or Hilgis, a Saxon of Northumbria. Wilgils, newly converted to Christianity, entrusted his son as an oblate to Ripon Abbey and withdrew from the world to build a small oratory dedicated to Saint Andrew near the mouth of the Humber. Willibrord grew up under the influence of Wilfrid, Bishop of York, and later joined the Benedictines. He spent the years between the ages of 20 and 32 at the Abbey of Rath Melsigi in County Carlow in Ireland, a centre of European learning, where he studied under Ecgberht of Ripon.

Ecgberht sent Willibrord and eleven companions to Christianise the pagan Frisians of the North Sea coast, at the request of Pepin of Herstal, the Austrasian mayor of the palace, who had nominal suzerainty over the region. Willibrord went twice to Rome. Bede notes that he did not go as a pilgrim to the graves of the apostles but to seek the licence and blessing of Pope Sergius for preaching to the Gentiles. On 21 November 695, in the Church of Santa Cecilia in Trastevere, Sergius I gave him a pallium and consecrated him. He returned to Frisia to preach and found churches, among them a monastery at Utrecht, where he built his cathedral.

In 698 he established the Abbey of Echternach on the site of a Roman villa, given to him by Irmina of Oeren, Pepin's mother-in-law, who had sought his help when a plague threatened her convent at Horren. After Pepin's death in 714 the pagan Radbod, king of the Frisians, retook Frisia in 716, burning churches and killing many missionaries, and Willibrord and his monks fled. After Radbod died in 719 Willibrord returned under the protection of Charles Martel and repaired the damage, assisted by Boniface.

Willibrord died on 7 November 739 at the age of 81 and, as he wished, was buried at Echternach. He was quickly canonised. Wells along his missionary routes were visited by people seeking cures for nervous diseases, particularly in children. A dancing procession is held at Echternach every year on Whit Tuesday, drawing thousands of participants and spectators, and he is often called the apostle of Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg. His feast day in the Catholic Church is 7 November, except in England, where it is 29 November.
willy-brandt: Willy Brandt was born Herbert Ernst Karl Frahm in the Free City of Lübeck on 18 December 1913. His mother was a single parent who worked as a department store cashier, and he never met his father. He joined the Socialist Youth in 1929 and in 1930, at sixteen, became a full member of the Social Democratic Party. He also wrote for the Volksbote, a local Social Democrat daily, under its editor Julius Leber. In exile he took the name Willy Brandt as a pseudonym to avoid detection by Nazi agents, formally adopting it in 1948.

Brandt was elected to the Bundestag in 1949 from West Berlin. From October 1957 to 1966 he was Governing Mayor of West Berlin, a period of rising tension that led to the construction of the Berlin Wall. He then served as foreign minister and vice chancellor in Kurt Georg Kiesinger's cabinet. After the 1969 elections the SPD and the Free Democratic Party formed a coalition and the Bundestag elected Brandt chancellor.

His Ostpolitik developed by stages: in 1967 he established diplomatic relations with Romania, and in 1968 he restored them with Yugoslavia. He met the East German premier Willi Stoph at Erfurt on 19 March 1970 and at Kassel on 21 May 1970. Ostpolitik cost the coalition its narrow majority, and in 1972 new elections were called, in which he led the SPD to its best-ever federal result. Günter Guillaume, one of his personal assistants, was arrested on 24 April 1974 and later sentenced to 13 years for treason. Brandt resigned on 6 May 1974, though he stayed in the Bundestag and as party chairman until 1987.

From 1976 to 1992 Brandt was president of the Socialist International, and in 1977 he became chairman of the Independent Commission for International Developmental Issues, whose report of 1980 became known as the Brandt Report. In late 1989 he was among the first left-wing leaders in West Germany to favour quick reunification. He died of colon cancer at his home in Unkel on 8 October 1992, aged 78, and was given a state funeral. The SPD's headquarters in Berlin is named the Willy Brandt Haus, and a memorial to him and the kneeling at Warsaw was unveiled in Warsaw in 2000.
wilmington-delaware: Wilmington is the county seat of New Castle County and the core city of the Wilmington metropolitan division, which is one of the major parts of the Philadelphia metropolitan area. It lies at the confluence of the Christina River and Brandywine Creek, near where the Christina flows into the Delaware River. The city covers 17.0 square miles, of which 6.2 square miles is water. Interstate 95 divides it roughly into eastern and western halves.

The city stands on the site of Fort Christina, the first Swedish settlement in North America, which was founded in 1638, and of Kristinehamn, which Peter Mårtensson Lindeström planned as the capital of the colony of New Sweden. The modern city also encompasses other Swedish settlements, among them Timmerön, or Timber Island, on the Brandywine Creek, Sidoland in what is now South Wilmington, and Strandviken on the Delaware River.

Control of the area shifted among powers. It was formally incorporated as the Village of Willingtown in 1731, and in 1739 it was granted a borough charter within the Delaware Colony as Wilmington, named after Spencer Compton, 1st Earl of Wilmington. During the 18th and 19th centuries it developed as an industrial hub, with shipbuilding, milling and later chemical manufacturing, much of it influenced by DuPont. Its modern economy centres on national banking and finance. In the 1990s the city began to revive the former shipyard area as the Wilmington Riverfront, which now has a riverwalk of 1.2 miles.

Wilmington is the most populous city in Delaware, with 70,898 residents at the 2020 census. The city designates nine historic districts, among them Quaker Hill, Delaware Avenue and the area of St. Marys and Old Swedes Church. The Holy Trinity (Old Swedes') Church, Fort Christina State Park and the Kalmar Nyckel Foundation and Tall Ship recall the Swedish settlement, and the Delaware Art Museum has a collection centred on American art and illustration and the Pre-Raphaelite movement. The Big August Quarterly, held since 1814, honours African American religious freedom. The Port of Wilmington is a deepwater port handling mostly international imports of fruit and vegetables, automobiles and steel.
wiltshire: Wiltshire is a ceremonial county of South West England covering 3,485 square kilometres, and Swindon is its largest settlement. The north-west belongs to the limestone Cotswolds, and the rest is characterised by chalk downland: the Marlborough Downs, with Savernake Forest, the Vale of Pewsey, Salisbury Plain in the centre, the West Wiltshire Downs, the Vale of Wardour and part of Cranborne Chase.

The highest point, at 295 m, is the Tan Hill and Milk Hill ridge in the Pewsey Vale. The county's two major rivers are both called the Avon. Because chalk hills hold little surface water, the main settlements grew up at wet points, and Salisbury lies between the chalk of the plain and marshy flood plains.

Wiltshire is notable for its pre-Roman archaeology. Mesolithic, Neolithic and Bronze Age people settled the hills and downland, and Stonehenge and Avebury are perhaps the best-known Neolithic sites in the United Kingdom. In the 6th and 7th centuries it lay at the western edge of Saxon Britain, since Cranborne Chase and the Somerset Levels held back the advance westward. The Battle of Bedwyn was fought in 675 between Escuin, a West Saxon nobleman who had seized the throne of Queen Saxburga, and King Wulfhere of Mercia. The county, written Wiltunscir in the 9th century, is named after the former county town of Wilton, and the Danes invaded it in 878.

After the Norman Conquest of 1066 large areas passed to the crown and the church. The Domesday Survey mentions 390 mills and vineyards at Tollard and Lacock, and in the 13th and 14th centuries the Cistercian monastery of Stanley exported wool to Florentine and Flemish markets. In the English Civil War the county was largely Parliamentarian, with a Royalist victory at the Battle of Roundway Down near Devizes. About 1800 the Kennet and Avon Canal was built through the county as a route for cargoes between Bristol and London until the Great Western Railway was developed.

Stonehenge and Avebury together form a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and Salisbury is notable for its medieval cathedral. Much of Salisbury Plain is a training area for the British Army. Large country houses open to the public include Longleat, with its safari park, and the National Trust's Stourhead. The county is mostly rural, with other major settlements at Trowbridge and Chippenham. Natives of Wiltshire are nicknamed Moonrakers, from a story of smugglers who hid contraband in a village pond and claimed to be raking for a round cheese that was in fact the moon's reflection.
wim-kok: Willem Kok was born on 29 September 1938 in Bergstoep, Bergambacht, in South Holland, the son of a carpenter. He studied business administration at Nyenrode and in 1961 began his career at the Dutch Confederation of Trade Unions. As chairman of the Federation of Dutch Trade Unions until 1986, he helped negotiate the Wassenaar Agreement.

Kok was elected to the House of Representatives on 3 June 1986, and on 21 July 1986 he succeeded Joop den Uyl as Labour leader. After the 1989 election the party formed the third Lubbers cabinet with the Christian Democratic Appeal, and Kok became Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance, serving until 22 August 1994.

In the 1994 election Labour lost twelve seats but the Christian Democrats lost twenty, making Labour the largest party. After a difficult formation with the People's Party for Freedom and Democracy (VVD) and Democrats 66 (D66), the first Kok cabinet took office on 22 August 1994, the first Dutch cabinet since 1918 without a Christian democratic party. Its main aim was to create employment after years of deep recession, and it reduced taxes, cut spending and sought to end the large state debt. The Treaty of Amsterdam was signed during this cabinet.

After the 1998 election the same coalition formed the second Kok cabinet, called the second purple cabinet because it joined the red social democrats and the blue liberals. It legalised same-sex marriage and euthanasia. Kok announced his retirement on 15 December 2001. After a government-commissioned report by the NIOD Institute criticised the Dutch role in the fall of Srebrenica in 1995, he resigned on 16 April 2002 and the cabinet followed him. It remained as a caretaker cabinet until the first Balkenende cabinet was installed on 22 July 2002.

Kok received the honorary title of Minister of State on 11 April 2003. He sat on company boards, worked as a lobbyist for the European Union and led a review of the Lisbon Strategy in 2004. He is remembered for his Third Way and polder model approach and for leading the first purple coalitions. He died of heart failure in Amsterdam on 20 October 2018, aged 80.
winchester: Winchester lies on the River Itchen at the western end of the South Downs National Park, 60 miles (97 km) south-west of London. It is the county town of Hampshire. Three Iron Age hillforts, Oram's Arbour, St. Catherine's Hill and Worthy Down, stand nearby, and in the Late Iron Age an oppidum grew up that became an important centre of the British Belgae tribe. It remains unclear how the Belgae came to control it. Caesar recorded that they crossed the Channel as raiders, though recent studies favour gradual change through trade over migration.

After the Roman conquest the town became the capital of the Belgae as Venta Belgarum. It was at first less important than Silchester and Chichester but eclipsed both by the latter half of the second century, and at the start of the third century it was given stone walls. It then covered 144 acres (58 ha), among the largest towns in Roman Britain, but declined from the later fourth century. Urban life continued into the mid fifth century, and the Christian cemeteries stayed in use.

In Old English it was Wintanceaster. King Cenwalh of Wessex built the Church of St Peter and St Paul, later the Old Minster, in 648, and it became a cathedral in the 660s when the West Saxon see moved from Dorchester on Thames. In the late 9th century Alfred the Great replaced the Roman street plan with a new grid for better defence against the Vikings, and the city's first mint seems to date from then. In the Middle Ages it was an important centre of the wool trade before slowly declining. A fire in 1141 came during the Rout of Winchester, and in the 14th century William of Wykeham, as Bishop, rebuilt much of the cathedral and founded Winchester College.

Winchester Cathedral, begun in 1079, remains the longest Gothic cathedral in Europe and holds the burials of Anglo-Saxon kings such as Egbert of Wessex, of Canute and of William Rufus. It was once a pilgrimage centre, housing the shrine of Saint Swithun. The Great Hall of the castle, rebuilt between 1222 and 1235, has displayed King Arthur's Round Table since at least 1463; the table dates from the 13th century and was painted for Henry VIII in 1522. The built-up area had 48,478 inhabitants at the 2021 census. The city is also home to the University of Winchester, and Winchester College is the oldest public school in the United Kingdom still using its original buildings.
wind-turbine: The windwheel of Hero of Alexandria, who lived from about 10 to 70 CE, marks one of the first recorded instances of wind powering a machine. The first known practical wind power plants were built in Sistan, an eastern province of Persia, now Iran, from the seventh century. These panemone windmills were vertical-axle machines with long vertical drive shafts and rectangular blades made of six to twelve sails covered in reed matting or cloth. They were used to grind grain and draw up water, and served in the gristmilling and sugarcane industries.

Wind turbines are made in a wide range of sizes, with either horizontal or vertical axes, though horizontal is the most common. Commercial horizontal-axis turbines usually have three blades, placed upwind of the tower, with the rotor shaft and generator at the top, pointed into the wind by a wind sensor and a yaw system. Most have a gearbox that turns the slow rotation of the blades into the quicker rotation suited to a generator, while direct-drive turbines couple the rotor straight to the generator. Vertical-axis designs include the Darrieus, called the eggbeater, the giromill and the Savonius, and they need not be pointed into the wind, though they produce much less energy over time.

Betz's law sets the maximum extraction of wind power at 16/27, or 59.3 per cent, of the rate at which the kinetic energy of the air arrives at the turbine. Blades are most commonly made of glass fibre composites, and carbon fibre, which is stiffer, stronger and less dense, is also used. The rotor, generator and surrounding structure of tower and yaw mechanism are the three main components, and the turbines have an average lifespan of 30 years.

Turbines in large groups, known as wind farms, feed electrical grids, and larger turbines can contribute to a domestic power supply while selling unused power back to the utility through the grid. Smaller turbines serve for battery charging and for remote devices such as traffic warning signs. The power produced varies with the wind, not with demand, so wind is an unreliable source unless energy storage is available.

A few localities have placed turbines on public display, with visitor centres around their bases or viewing areas farther away, so that they also serve for technology demonstration, public relations and education. The Bahrain World Trade Center has turbines displayed prominently for the public and was the first skyscraper to integrate wind turbines into its design.
windhoek: Windhoek lies in central Namibia on the Khomas Highland plateau, at about 1,700 m above sea level, in the geographical centre of the country. The city grew up around a hot spring known to the pastoral peoples of the area, and twelve strong springs later supplied water for gardens and grain. Rocky, mountainous ground to the south, east and west makes building costly, which leaves the area to the north as the main direction for expansion.

In 1840 Jonker Afrikaner, captain of the Orlam, settled near one of the main springs in what is now the suburb of Klein Windhoek. He built a stone church that held 500 people and also served as a school. The Rhenish missionaries Carl Hugo Hahn and Franz Heinrich Kleinschmidt began work there in late 1842 but two years later were driven out by the Methodist Wesleyans Richard Haddy and Joseph Tindall. A series of wars between the Nama and the Herero destroyed the settlement, and in June 1885 a Swiss botanist found only jackals and starving guinea fowl among the neglected fruit trees.

Germany declared a protectorate over what became German South West Africa in 1884. Major Curt von François, commanding the Schutztruppe, placed his garrison at Windhoek as a buffer between the Nama and the Herero, and on 18 October 1890 he fixed the foundation stone of the fort now called the Alte Feste. Growth accelerated after 1907 as people came from the countryside to find work. South Africa occupied the territory in 1915, and from 1920 administered it under a League of Nations mandate. In 1971 a strike of contract workers, aimed at ending the contract labour system, began in Windhoek.

Windhoek has been the national capital since independence in 1990 and is also the capital of the Khomas Region. Its population was 486,186 in 2023. The University of Namibia, the national theatre, the National Museum in the Alte Feste and the Independence Memorial Museum stand there. The Tintenpalast, built in 1912 and 1913, houses the Parliament. The Reiterdenkmal, which commemorated the German victory over the Herero and Nama in the genocide of 1904 to 1907, was moved in December 2013 from its place beside the Christuskirche to the yard of the Alte Feste.
windmill: Historical evidence does not support working windmills before the 9th century CE. Hero of Alexandria described in the first century CE what appears to be a wind-driven wheel powering a wind organ, though his text is ambiguous and the device may have been a toy or a design concept. The prayer wheel of Tibet and China is another early wind-driven wheel, but its date of first appearance is uncertain.

The first practical windmills were panemone mills, with six to twelve sails of reed matting or cloth turning in a horizontal plane around a vertical shaft. They were first built to pump water and later modified to grind grain. A medieval account places them in the reign of the caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab (r. 634–644), but because it was recorded only in the 10th century its authenticity is questioned. By the 11th century the type had reached the Iberian Peninsula through Al-Andalus.

The vertical windmill, whose sails turn on a horizontal shaft, developed in the 12th century in the triangle of northern France, eastern England and Flanders. It is unclear whether the Persian type influenced it. The earliest European type was the post mill, in which the whole body is balanced on a large upright post so that it can be turned to face the wind. Hollow-post mills, with the drive shaft passing down through the post, were used in the Netherlands from the early 15th century to drain wetlands.

By the end of the 13th century the masonry tower mill had appeared, in which only the cap rotates, so that the tower could be taller and the sails longer. The smock mill, with a wooden framework in place of masonry, was introduced by the Dutch in the 17th century and could be raised on unstable ground. In 1807 William Cubitt patented sails in which shutters replaced the cloth.

Windmills ground grain, drained land and sawed timber, and powered paper mills, threshing and the processing of oil seeds, wool, paints and stone. They were used where there was too little water, where rivers froze in winter, and on flat land where rivers flowed too slowly. The Zaan district of the Netherlands has been called the first industrialised region of the world, with around 600 wind-powered industries by the end of the 18th century.

Steam and internal combustion engines replaced wind and water as the main industrial power, though windmills were still built in large numbers late in the 19th century. About 1,000 of the 10,000 windmills working in the Netherlands around 1850 still stand.
windward-islands: The Windward Islands are a group of islands in the Lesser Antilles of the West Indies, where the south-eastern Caribbean Sea meets the western North Atlantic Ocean. They lie approximately between latitudes 10 and 16 degrees north and longitudes 60 and 62 degrees west, and extend from Dominica in the north to Trinidad and Tobago in the south. They lie south of the Leeward Islands and east of the Leeward Antilles.

The prevailing trade winds in the West Indies blow from east to west. Sailing ships heading to the New World followed the fastest route across the ocean, which brought them to a rough dividing line between two groups of islands: those that fell to windward became the Windward Islands, and those to leeward the Leeward Islands. Ships leaving Africa first met the south-easternmost of the Windward Islands.

The name was also used for a British colony that existed from 1833 to 1960 and originally consisted of Grenada, Saint Lucia and Saint Vincent. Barbados was part of it until 1885 and Tobago until 1889, but neither is now regarded as part of the Windward Islands. Dominica was traditionally considered part of the Leeward Islands until 1940, when it was transferred from the British Leeward Islands colony to the British Windward Islands. Martinique, which has been an overseas département of France since 1946, is the only windward island that is a French territory.

Four sovereign countries and one territory make up the group: Dominica, Grenada, Saint Lucia, and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, together with Martinique. Grenada includes Carriacou and Petite Martinique, and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines includes the Grenadines. In languages other than English, notably Dutch, French and Spanish, all of the Lesser Antilles from the Virgin Islands to Trinidad and Tobago are known as the Windward Islands.
winston-churchill: Winston Leonard Spencer Churchill was born on 30 November 1874 at Blenheim Palace in Oxfordshire. On his father's side he was a descendant of John Churchill, 1st Duke of Marlborough. His father, Lord Randolph Churchill, was a Conservative MP, and his mother, Jennie, was the daughter of the American businessman Leonard Jerome. He joined the British Army in 1895 and saw action in British India, the Mahdist War and the Second Boer War, gaining fame as a war correspondent.

Elected a Conservative MP in 1900, Churchill defected to the Liberals in 1904. In 1908 H. H. Asquith made him President of the Board of Trade, and at 33 he was the youngest Cabinet member since 1866. After the failed naval attack on the Dardanelles he resigned from the government on 25 November 1915 and served on the Western Front, commanding the 6th Royal Scots Fusiliers from January 1916. Under David Lloyd George he returned as Minister of Munitions in 1917. As Chancellor of the Exchequer from 1924 he restored the gold standard in April 1925, against the advice of economists including John Maynard Keynes; the return is held to have caused deflation and unemployment.

During the 1930s he was out of government, in his "wilderness years". He was reappointed First Lord of the Admiralty on 3 September 1939 and became prime minister in May 1940, succeeding Neville Chamberlain. He formed a war cabinet that included the Labour leader Clement Attlee. In 1946, as Leader of the Opposition, he gave his "Iron Curtain" speech in America.

Churchill wrote prolifically, including the six-volume The Second World War and A History of the English-Speaking Peoples, and received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1953. He also painted hundreds of works. He resigned on 5 April 1955 and remained an MP until 1964. Elizabeth II offered to make him Duke of London, but he declined. He died on 24 January 1965 and was given a state funeral. He is generally viewed as a victorious wartime leader, though as a staunch imperialist he has sometimes been criticised for comments on race and for wartime decisions such as area bombing.
winston-county-mississippi: Winston County covers 610 square miles, of which 607 are land. It lies in the east of the state and is bordered by Oktibbeha County to the north, Noxubee County to the east, Kemper County to the southeast, Neshoba County to the south, Attala County to the west and Choctaw County to the northwest. Part of the Tombigbee National Forest lies within it. The county seat is Louisville, and the other incorporated place is the town of Noxapater.

The county is one of sixteen formed from the lands that Chief Greenwood LeFlore ceded in the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek. The treaty resulted in the removal of the Choctaw Nation from its ancestral lands to Oklahoma. The county takes its name from Louis Winston, who lived from 1784 to 1824 and was a colonel in the militia, a prominent lawyer and a judge of the Mississippi Supreme Court.

Its most notable site is Nanih Waiya, an ancient mound built in the Woodland period, about 1 CE to 300 CE. The Choctaw people, who later occupied the area, have venerated it since the 17th century. In 1863, during the American Civil War, a Union force of 900 troops under Colonel Benjamin H. Grierson marched through Louisville on a raid through Mississippi. There was no fighting in Winston County and no significant destruction of property.

Winston County is entirely rural, and the 2020 census counted 17,714 residents. The Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians, a federally recognised tribe, owns the Nanih Waiya mound. The community college of the county is East Central Community College, whose service area the county joined in 1935.
winter-war: Until the early 19th century Finland was the eastern part of the Kingdom of Sweden. Russia conquered it in the Finnish War of 1808 to 1809 and made it the autonomous Grand Duchy of Finland. Late in the 19th century Russia tried to assimilate the duchy, attempts that ruined relations and strengthened support for self-determination in Finland. In the late 1930s the Soviet Union under Joseph Stalin sought to regain provinces lost after 1917 and wanted more security for Leningrad, only 32 km from the Finnish border.

In April 1938 an NKVD agent, Boris Yartsev, suggested that Finland cede or lease islands in the Gulf of Finland, which Finland refused. On 26 November 1939 the Soviet side reported the shelling of a border post near the village of Mainila. Finnish and Russian historians have concluded that it was a false flag operation carried out from the Soviet side.

On 30 November 1939 Soviet forces invaded with 21 divisions, about 450,000 men, and bombed Helsinki. The League of Nations expelled the Soviet Union on 14 December 1939. Field Marshal Carl Gustaf Emil Mannerheim became commander-in-chief. Soviet leaders had expected victory within weeks, but the land was forest, lake and swamp with few roads. Finnish ski troops in white snow capes struck Soviet columns, notably at Suomussalmi and the Raate Road, and Finnish soldiers improvised the Molotov cocktail against tanks. The winter was exceptionally cold, with a record low of −43 °C on 16 January 1940.

On the Karelian Isthmus the Finns held the Mannerheim Line, a string of strong-points that was weaker than Soviet propaganda claimed. Stalin was displeased with the results of December and in late January 1940 the Soviets ended the puppet Terijoki Government and offered to negotiate with the Finnish government. After the Red Army reorganised, it renewed its offensive in February and broke the defences. By 5 March it had entered the suburbs of Viipuri. Franco-British plans to intervene did not mature, since Norway and Sweden gave no right of passage, and Finland accepted the Soviet terms.

Under the Moscow Peace Treaty Finland ceded the Karelian Isthmus and most of Ladoga Karelia, including Viipuri, about nine per cent of its territory and 13 per cent of its economic assets. The Soviet gains exceeded its pre-war demands, yet Finland kept its sovereignty. Historians differ over whether the war was a Soviet victory or a failure to absorb Finland. The Red Army's poor showing led to reforms in the spring of 1940 and encouraged Adolf Hitler to believe that an invasion of the Soviet Union would succeed. After the 15-month Interim Peace, Operation Barbarossa began in June 1941 and the Continuation War between Finland and the Soviet Union followed.
winterthur: Winterthur lies at an elevation of 439 metres in a basin south and east of the river Töss, about 20 km north-east of Zurich. The small river Eulach runs through the middle of the town to meet the Töss at its western edge, which is why the town is colloquially called Eulachstadt. It stands at the junction of seven roads, and during the French Revolutionary Wars the army that held it commanded access to most of Switzerland and the crossings of the Rhine into southern Germany.

Vitudurum was a Roman vicus in what is now Oberwinterthur from the first century BCE to the third century CE, and was fortified as a castrum at the end of the third century, apparently against the first Alamannic invasion. There was an Alamannic settlement on the site in the seventh century. The counts of Winterthur, a cadet branch of the counts of Bregenz, built Kyburg castle in the tenth century. After they became extinct in 1053, the castle passed to the counts of Dillingen, and Hartmann III of Dillingen founded the city in 1180, shortly before his death. It was ruled by a cadet line of the House of Kyburg until 1263.

When the counts of Kyburg died out in the male line in 1263, Winterthur passed to the House of Habsburg, who granted it city rights in 1264. It was reichsfrei, subject only to the Holy Roman Emperor, from 1415 to 1442, but lost this freedom in the Old Zürich War. The Habsburgs, needing money, sold it to the city of Zurich in 1467. Under Zurich its economic freedom was restricted and it lost many market rights, until Napoleonic troops took the town in 1798. On 27 May 1799 French and Habsburg forces under Friedrich, Baron von Hotze fought the Battle of Winterthur, in which the Austrians sustained an 11-hour assault and so consolidated three Austrian forces.

In the 19th century companies such as Sulzer, Rieter and SLM built large industrial plants. The town suffered from guaranteeing loans to the National Railway of Switzerland: it sold its shares in 1878 and was in great difficulties from 1881 to 1885, helped by loans from the cantonal and federal governments. The Great Depression hit it hard, since sixty per cent of employees worked in the machine industry.

The church of St. Laurenz in the city centre dates from 1264 and the town hall from 1781. The Orchester Musikkollegium Winterthur is the oldest orchestra in Switzerland, and between 1922 and 1950 the patron Werner Reinhart and the conductor Hermann Scherchen shaped the city's musical life. Its museums include the Oskar Reinhart collections, and in 1989 the city received the Wakker Prize for the preservation of its architectural heritage.
wirtschaftswunder: The Wirtschaftswunder, meaning economic miracle, was the rapid reconstruction of the economies of West Germany and Austria after World War II. The Times first used the word for it in 1950. West Germany had a skilled workforce and a high level of technological experience in 1946, but most of its capital stock had been destroyed during and after the war, and converting the economy to civilian goods was difficult. Output was unusually low in the first post-war years. Allied dismantling of the coal and steel industries, decided at the Potsdam Conference, was virtually complete by 1950, with equipment removed from 706 plants.

The Currency Reform of 1948 replaced the Reichsmark with the Deutsche Mark and halted rampant inflation. The government, following the advice of the Minister of Economics Ludwig Erhard, cut taxes sharply on moderate incomes, and Erhard abolished price controls against the advice of the Allied occupying powers. He was opposed by the Social Democratic Party and, according to Erhard, by some of his own advisers. Before the change food had been hard to find at the controlled prices and was often bought by barter or on the black market, and once controls were removed the shortages disappeared.

The Marshall Plan, extended to West Germany in 1948 to 1952, was not the main force behind the recovery, though its aid probably contributed. The Korean War created a global shortage of goods that helped West German exports, and a large pool of skilled labour and long working hours sustained the upturn. From the mid-1950s foreign Gastarbeiter, guest workers, added labour. The purchasing power of wages rose by 73 per cent between 1950 and 1960, and unemployment reached a low of 0.7 to 0.8 per cent in 1961 to 1966 and in 1970 to 1971.

Under the chancellors Konrad Adenauer and later Erhard, West Germany became by the late 1950s one of the world's most powerful economies, and in 1957, at the founding of the European Common Market, its growth contrasted with the struggling British economy. Between 1962 and 1973 the share of households with a television rose from 34 to 87 per cent and with a car from 27 to 55 per cent. In Austria, which also received Marshall aid, nationalised industries, long hours and the Schilling's reintroduction produced a similar period of growth, under the policy known as the Raab-Kamitz-Kurs, named after Chancellor Julius Raab and Finance Minister Reinhard Kamitz.
wisconsin: Wisconsin lies between the Great Lakes and the Mississippi River and is divided into five regions. The Lake Superior Lowland runs along the north shore, and the Northern Highland has mixed forests, thousands of glacial lakes and the state's highest point, Timms Hill. The Central Plain has the sandstone formations of the Dells of the Wisconsin River and rich farmland. The Eastern Ridges and Lowlands in the southeast hold many of the largest cities, and the Western Upland, part of the Driftless Area, is a rugged landscape of bluffs along the Mississippi. Forest covers 46 per cent of the land.

The first people arrived around 10,000 BCE, during the Wisconsin Glaciation. These Paleo-Indians hunted ice age animals such as the Boaz mastodon, whose skeleton was found with spear points in the south-west. After the ice age ended around 8000 BCE, the Archaic peoples lived by hunting, fishing and gathering. Agricultural societies emerged over the Woodland period, from 1000 BCE to 1000 CE, and towards its end Wisconsin was the heartland of the Effigy Mound culture, which built thousands of animal-shaped mounds. Between 1000 and 1500 CE the Mississippian and Oneota cultures built substantial settlements, including the fortified village at Aztalan.

At European contact the Menominee, Ho-Chunk and Iowa shared the region. The Ojibwe, Sauk, Meskwaki, Kickapoo and Potawatomi had migrated there from the east between 1500 and 1700. The French explorer Jacques Marquette was the first European to reach the Wisconsin River, in 1673, which he called Meskousing. The French later wrote Ouisconsin, and English speakers anglicised it as they arrived in large numbers in the early 19th century. The legislature of Wisconsin Territory made the present spelling official in 1845. The meaning is obscure, though a leading theory takes it from the Miami word Meskonsing, meaning it lies red, after the reddish sandstone of the Dells.

Wisconsin was originally part of the Northwest Territory and was admitted as a state in 1848. Miners, many of them Cornish, settled the south-west, and the nickname Badger State comes from miners who burrowed into hillsides. They were followed by migrants from New England and upstate New York, who dominated heavy industry, finance, politics and education in the early years of statehood. Between 1850 and 1900 most immigrants were Germans, Scandinavians, Irish and Poles. The Republican Party was founded in Wisconsin in 1854.

Madison is the capital and Milwaukee the most populous city. The state is divided into 72 counties and is home to eleven federally recognised tribes. It remains a centre of German American and Scandinavian American culture, and it is known as America's Dairyland, particularly for its cheese. Taliesin and the Jacobs I House, designed by the Wisconsin-born architect Frank Lloyd Wright, form a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
wismar: Wismar lies on the Bay of Wismar of the Baltic Sea, opposite the island of Poel, midway between the port cities of Lübeck to the west and Rostock to the east. The state capital Schwerin lies to the south on Lake Schwerin. The city has a natural harbour protected by a promontory. It is the fourth-largest city of Mecklenburg and now the capital of the district of Nordwestmecklenburg. Its name was first recorded in the 12th century and is probably of Slavic origin, though this is disputed, and the area belonged to the territory of the western Slavic Obotrites.

The date of the city's foundation is not clear. It is estimated at 1226 under Henry Borwin I, Lord of Mecklenburg, and the oldest document of 1229 already shows civic rights. In 1259 Wismar joined a defensive agreement with Lübeck and Rostock against Baltic pirates, which formed a basis for the Hanseatic League. By the 13th and 14th centuries it was a flourishing trading hub and a centre of wool processing. About 2,000 inhabitants died in the plague of 1376, but the town remained reasonably prosperous until the 16th century.

After 1648 Wismar was Swedish, which entitled the Swedish kings, as imperial princes, to a seat in the Imperial Diet. After 1653 the Fürstenhof was the seat of the supreme court for all Swedish dominions in the Holy Roman Empire, and Field Marshal Erik Dahlbergh extended the fortifications. Danish forces captured the town in 1675 during the Scanian War.

In 1803 Sweden ceded Wismar to the Grand Duchy of Mecklenburg-Schwerin for 1,258,000 Riksdalers, reserving a right of redemption, and renounced its claims in 1903. In the Second World War Wismar was heavily bombed; British paratroopers took it on 2 May 1945, and it passed to the Soviet occupation zone on 1 July 1945. It was East Germany's second-largest port.

Wismar's old town, with Brick Gothic buildings of the 13th to 15th centuries and a large market square, was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2002 together with the old town of Stralsund. The square holds the Wasserkunst, a wrought-iron fountain imported from Holland in 1602, and a house called the Alter Schwede, built about 1380.

The tower of St. Mary's is all that remains of the original church. The city's Swedish period is marked each year by a Sweden Celebration. Shipbuilding, begun at the site in 1946, remains important, and the city has a university of applied sciences, the Hochschule Wismar. The 1922 film Nosferatu was partly shot there.
witigis: Little is known of Vitiges's early life. He came from an undistinguished family and was a career soldier. He gained prominence under Theodoric the Great at the siege of Sirmium in 504–505, became a spatharios in the king's bodyguard and adviser to King Athalaric, and fought again at Sirmium in the late 520s. King Theodahad later made him armiger, commander of the royal bodyguard and of the Gothic forces in Rome. When the Byzantine general Belisarius took Naples in 536, Theodahad's failure to reinforce it angered the Gothic nobility. In late 536 nobles and officers gathered near Regata in the Pontine Marshes and proclaimed Vitiges king, and he had Theodahad overtaken and killed.

Lacking royal blood, Vitiges divorced his wife and forced a marriage to Mataswintha, granddaughter of Theodoric and daughter of Amalaswintha, in Ravenna. The senator Cassiodorus delivered a panegyric to present him as protector of Theodoric's legacy. He left a garrison of 4,000 men in Rome and took senators hostage. He also bargained with the Merovingian Franks, who agreed to the territories in Gaul and the gold Theodahad had offered, but secretly sent only warriors from their tributary peoples to keep up the fiction of their alliance with Justinian I. On 9 December 536 the citizens of Rome opened their gates to Belisarius.

In early 537 Vitiges laid siege to Rome with a large army, which Procopius gives as 150,000 men. Belisarius resisted with artillery and mounted archers, and after a year, on 12 March 538, Vitiges lifted the siege. He then failed at Ariminum, and in March 539 his nephew Uraias retook Mediolanum, whose male inhabitants the Goths killed. Auximus and Faesulae fell to famine late in 539. By 540 the Byzantines encircled Ravenna. The Goths secretly offered Belisarius the throne of the Western Roman Empire, which Vitiges supported. In May 540 Belisarius feigned acceptance, entered the city, seized the treasury and took Vitiges and Mataswintha captive.

In Constantinople Vitiges was treated honourably, and Justinian gave him the title Patrikios. He died in 542 without heirs. Scholars assess him as lacking foresight and tactical adaptability, since he failed to counter the Byzantine mounted archers. In Germanic heroic legend the figure Witege represents him, and his surrender of Ravenna is portrayed as a betrayal of King Dietrich von Bern, a reimagining of Theodoric.
wittenberg: Wittenberg lies on the River Elbe, 60 kilometres north of Leipzig and 90 kilometres south-west of Berlin. Historical documents first mention it in 1180 as a small village founded by Flemish colonists under the House of Ascania. In 1260 it became the residence of the dukes of Saxe-Wittenberg, and in 1293 it received a town charter. Its central position made it an important trade centre over the following centuries.

When the local Ascanian line died out in 1422, Saxe-Wittenberg passed to the House of Wettin. Frederick III, called the Wise, Elector of Saxony from 1486 to 1525, made it his residence, and the town became an important political and cultural centre. The Castle Church was built between 1496 and 1506. Frederick founded the University of Wittenberg in 1502. Martin Luther was professor of theology there from 1508 and Philipp Melanchthon professor of Greek from 1518. On 31 October 1517 Luther is said to have nailed his Ninety-five Theses on indulgences to the door of the Castle Church, an event taken as the start of the Reformation.

The Zwickau prophets, an early Anabaptist group, arrived in late 1521 and were suppressed by Luther when he returned from the Wartburg in spring 1522. By the Capitulation of Wittenberg in 1547, John Frederick the Magnanimous gave up the electoral dignity and most of his lands to the Albertine branch of the Wettins. The town was bombarded in 1760 during the Seven Years' War and passed to Prussia after the Congress of Vienna.

Wittenberg has the title Lutherstadt because of its ties to Luther and the Reformation. Its old town keeps the Castle Church, whose present bronze doors of 1858 bear the Latin text of the theses, and holds the tombs of Luther, Melanchthon and the electors Frederick the Wise and John the Constant. St. Mary's Church, where Luther often preached, has paintings by Lucas Cranach the Elder, who ran a print shop in the town. The Lutherhaus and Melanchthon's house are museums. The buildings associated with Luther and Melanchthon were added with other sites at Eisleben to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1996. The town had 46,008 inhabitants in 2018.
wittstock: Wittstock lies in the eastern Prignitz region on the Dosse river, near its confluence with the Glinze, in the Ostprignitz-Ruppin district. It is about 20 kilometres east of Pritzwalk and 95 kilometres north-west of Berlin, in a terminal moraine landscape south of the Mecklenburg Lake District.

The town grew from a Slavic settlement and was first mentioned in the deed founding the Bishopric of Havelberg in 946. Its name possibly comes from vysoka, meaning high-lying, in the language of the local Polabian tribes. It received the Stendal town charter on 13 September 1248 from Henry I, Prince-bishop of Havelberg, which makes it one of the oldest towns of Brandenburg, and a town seal followed in 1251. Wittstock Castle, begun in 1244 on a Slavic foundation, was the residence of the Havelberg bishops from 1271. That era ended with the Reformation and the death of the last Catholic prince-bishop, Busso von Alvensleben, at the castle in 1548.

In the Thirty Years' War the fortress was long a secure stronghold. In 1636 the Swedish troops of Field Marshals Johan Banér and Alexander Leslie defeated the allied Imperial and Saxon forces under Elector John George I of Saxony at the Battle of Wittstock. A plague epidemic two years later followed, and the town lost about half of its population. Rebuilding began in 1658 under the Great Elector, Frederick William, and about 1750 many colonists from Württemberg and the Palatinate settled the region.

The main historic monument is the Brick Gothic St Mary's Church, dating from about 1240 and enlarged as a hall church in the late 13th century. It has a carved altar by Claus Berg and was used as a cathedral by the Havelberg bishops. The Bishop's Castle was greatly restored in the 1990s and houses a Thirty Years' War museum. Much of the late medieval defences still surrounds the old centre, including a 13th-century gate tower, the Daberburg bergfried north of the town and a city wall 2,500 metres long, originally 11 metres high and now 4 to 7 metres.
witwatersrand: The Witwatersrand, locally the Rand or less commonly the Reef, is a 56-kilometre-long north-facing scarp in South Africa, made of hard quartzite over which several north-flowing rivers form waterfalls. The name means white water ridge in Afrikaans. The scarp runs east to west from Bedfordview through Johannesburg and Roodepoort to Krugersdorp, and forms the northern edge of a plateau that rises about 200 metres above the Highveld. It is a continental divide between the Indian and Atlantic oceans.

The rocks of the Witwatersrand Supergroup, a layer 5,000 to 7,000 metres thick, were laid down over about 260 million years starting about 2.97 billion years ago. Gold occurs in the conglomerate strata of the younger members, called banket, which dip south at about 30 degrees and lie buried at depths of up to 4 kilometres.

Gold had been found elsewhere in South Africa, at Barberton and Pilgrim's Rest among other places, but only as alluvial concentrates or in quartz veins. In February 1886 George Harrison, probably with George Walker, found gold in a conglomerate outcrop on the farm Langlaagte, 5 km west of the future Johannesburg. They assumed it was alluvial gold in a tilted riverbed, but the conglomerate was found to continue in depth as part of a sedimentary succession, and it was soon traced east and west for 50 km as the Central Rand Gold Field. In September 1886 President Paul Kruger proclaimed nine farms public mining diggings from 20 September, which began the Witwatersrand Gold Rush.

Harrison is believed to have sold his claim for less than £10. In 1887 Cecil John Rhodes registered The Gold Fields of South Africa in London, the country's first mining house, with a capital of £250,000.

Over 40,000 tonnes of gold have been mined from these rocks since 1886, and the basin still produces most of South Africa's gold, with silver, uranium and iridium recovered as by-products. The South African currency was named the rand in 1961 when the republic was declared. The names Witwatersrand and the Rand also survive in the University of the Witwatersrand, the East and West Rand and Randburg, and Witwatersrand was the W in PWV, the first name of Gauteng province. Mining left sinkholes and acid mine drainage that carries heavy metals into surface and ground water.
wladyslaw-i-lokietek: Władysław was the son of Duke Casimir I of Kuyavia. His father died in 1267, when he was seven, and he was sent to Kraków to the court of his relative Bolesław V the Chaste. He took responsibility for governing his lands in 1275, holding them jointly with his two younger brothers. After the death of Leszek II the Black on 30 September 1288 he ruled Brześć Kujawski and Sieradz. The Polish lands had been divided under the will of Bolesław III Wrymouth in 1138, and the arrangement began nearly two centuries of constant fighting and disorder among the Piast princes.

In 1289 Władysław occupied Kraków, without Wawel Castle, but Henry Probus took the city and he escaped with the help of the Franciscans. After Wenceslaus II of Bohemia moved against him he fled the country in July 1299. According to tradition he went to Rome for the jubilee of 1300, while his wife Jadwiga and their children stayed in Kuyavia. He returned in 1304 with an army that the chronicler Jan Długosz says held more peasants than knights. The deaths of Wenceslaus II in 1305 and of Wenceslaus III on 4 August 1306 let him master Sandomierz, Sieradz-Łęczyca and Brześć Kujawski, and Kraków. In August 1314 he entered Poznań, after the nobility of Greater Poland turned to him.

Władysław sought papal consent for a coronation. Assemblies of nobles and knights at Sulejów in June 1318 and at Pyzdry prepared the request, and Bishop Gerward of Włocławek took it to Avignon. He was crowned in 1320 at Wawel Cathedral in Kraków, the first coronation held there. Surrounded by Brandenburg, the Teutonic Order and Bohemia, he sided with Pope John XXII and allied with Charles I of Hungary, who married his daughter Elizabeth in 1320, and later with Gediminas of Lithuania, whose daughter Aldona married his son Casimir. War with the Teutonic Knights followed, and Dobrzyń was lost in 1329.

Władysław died on 2 March 1333 at Wawel Castle and was buried in the cathedral. His son Casimir III the Great inherited Lesser Poland, Sandomierz, Greater Poland, Kuyavia, Łęczyca and Sieradz, while Silesia, Gdańsk Pomerania, Western Pomerania and Mazovia stayed outside the kingdom. Historians note that the deaths of several stronger opponents helped him. His reign saw the first serious clash with the Teutonic Order and the alliance with Lithuania, and he began a national administration and treasury, which Casimir continued.
wladyslaw-ii-the-exile: Władysław II, called the Exile, was the eldest son of Duke Bolesław III Wrymouth and his first wife Zbyslava, a daughter of Sviatopolk II of Kiev. His father involved him in government, and some historians believe Bolesław gave him Silesia as a hereditary fief for the eldest line. Around 1125 he married Agnes of Babenberg, daughter of Margrave Leopold III of Austria and half-sister of Conrad III, the later King of Germany, which tied him to the Holy Roman Empire. During the wars with Bohemia of 1133 to 1135 he saved Silesia by stopping the destruction of its main areas after the Bohemian forces crossed the Oder.

Bolesław III died on 28 October 1138. His testament made the eldest son High Duke, with Silesia, the central Seniorate Province from Kraków to western Kuyavia, and authority over Pomerelia. His younger half-brothers Bolesław IV the Curly and Mieszko III received Masovia and western Greater Poland as hereditary fiefs. Władysław tried at once to restore the unity of the country, as earlier rulers had done. The quarrel with his half-brothers and their mother Salomea of Berg began in 1141, when she started to divide her province of Łęczyca without his consent. With allies in Rus', Bohemia and the Empire he won the fighting of 1142 to 1143.

The Silesian voivode Piotr Włostowic had great influence. In 1146 Władysław had him seized at Ołbin by the knight Dobek; Włostowic was blinded, mutilated and exiled. Many nobles then changed sides, and Włostowic persuaded the Rus' to break their alliance. His attack on his half-brothers took Masovia but stalled at Poznań, and rebellions broke out elsewhere. Archbishop Jakub ze Żnina of Gniezno excommunicated him. He was forced to flee in 1146, and his wife Agnes and children followed after failing to hold Kraków.

Władysław stayed in Bohemia and then at the court of Conrad III, but a German expedition in 1146 failed. He administered the imperial palace at Altenburg. After Frederick Barbarossa succeeded Conrad in 1152, an expedition into Greater Poland in 1157 forced Bolesław IV to submit to the Emperor and to promise Silesia to Władysław's sons Bolesław the Tall and Mieszko Tanglefoot, but Władysław was not restored. He died in exile at Altenburg on 30 May 1159, and it was not until 1163 that Bolesław IV granted Silesia to his sons. Their descendants, the Silesian Piasts, divided Silesia into as many as 17 duchies, and the line ended with the death of Duke George William of Legnica in 1675.
wladyslaw-iii-of-poland: Władysław was born in Kraków on 31 October 1424, the eldest son of Władysław II Jagiełło and his fourth wife, the Lithuanian noblewoman Sophia of Halshany. His father was elderly, and the birth of a male heir was widely regarded as a miracle. In 1427 Polish nobles of the anti-Jagiellonian opposition tried to have Jogaila's sons declared illegitimate to the throne, since they had no blood relation to the Piast and Anjou kings. He succeeded his father in 1434, shortly before his tenth birthday. Cardinal Zbigniew Oleśnicki acted as his guardian and a council of provisores governed in his name.

The Lesser Poland nobles, who had been excluded from the vote, favoured the Piast candidate Siemowit V of Masovia. Władysław was crowned at Wawel Cathedral on 25 July 1434 under a revised ritual that obliged him to swear an oath before his anointing, so that the throne seemed to depend on meeting the nobles' requirements rather than on hereditary right. The Sejm declared him of age at Piotrków in 1438, though he is believed to have had little voice in politics. Spytko III of Melsztyn, who sympathised with the Hussites, rose against Oleśnicki in 1439 and was killed at the Battle of Grotniki; the king returned his body to his widow and restored the family's privileges.

After Albert II of Germany died in 1439, the Hungarian Estates, wary of the Habsburgs and the Ottoman threat, rejected an infant king, and elected Władysław on 8 March 1440. Albert's widow Elizabeth of Luxembourg backed her infant son Ladislaus the Posthumous, and civil war followed. The east and Transylvania supported Władysław and John Hunyadi, while the north and west stood with the queen, who hired Hussite mercenaries under John Jiskra. Her death in 1442 strengthened his position.

Urged by the papacy and the legate Julian Cesarini, Władysław launched the Crusade of Varna. On 10 November 1444 an Ottoman army of about 60,000 met about 16,000 crusaders at Varna in Bulgaria, and he was reportedly killed in a cavalry charge against Sultan Murad II. His body was never recovered, which gave rise to legends of survival, none of them confirmed. He was succeeded in Poland by his brother Casimir IV and in Hungary by Ladislaus V the Posthumous.

His record as king of Hungary was blackened by Habsburg polemic, which portrayed him as a usurper and spread the rumour that he had poisoned Elizabeth. He remains a notable figure in Bulgaria, where a boulevard in Varna bears his name and a park-museum with a cenotaph opened in 1935.
wloclawek: Włocławek lies along the Vistula in the Kuyavian-Pomeranian Voivodeship, bordered by the Gostynin-Włocławek Landscape Park. It is the third largest city of the voivodeship, after Bydgoszcz and Toruń, and the main cultural and economic centre of eastern Kuyavia. Excavations on the site have uncovered a settlement of the Lusatian culture from the late Bronze Age and early Iron Age, evidence of early Pomeranian culture, and traces of settlement from the Roman period and the early Middle Ages.

The settlement was founded in the 9th century, and in the 10th century it became part of the emerging Polish state under the Piast dynasty. The Gesta principum Polonorum, a chronicle of the 1110s, gives the oldest known mention of the city and calls it one of Poland's most important administrative centres under Bolesław I the Brave. The diocese of Włocławek is recorded in a bull of Pope Eugene III in 1148, with Warner as its first bishop. The city received its rights in 1255. In the 14th and 15th centuries the Teutonic Knights destroyed and captured it several times.

Its later prosperity came from the river transport of grain, tolls on grain floated down the Vistula towards Gdańsk, the shipment of timber for export to Western Europe, and brewing. Bishop Stanisław Karnkowski founded a theological seminary in 1569. The Swedes ravaged the city in 1657 and the Russians in 1707. After the Second Partition of Poland in 1793 it passed to Prussia, then to the Duchy of Warsaw in 1807 and to the Congress Kingdom of Poland in 1815. The first faience factory opened in 1873. In 1920 Polish forces defended the city against the Soviets.

Włocławek is the seat of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Włocławek, one of the oldest in Poland, and its Gothic cathedral is listed as a Historic Monument of Poland. The city is known for its production of faience and ketchup. Poland's largest hydroelectric power plant is located there.
woden: The Old English Wōden is a cognate of the Old Norse Óðinn, Old Saxon Wōdan and Old High German Wuotan. All derive from the reconstructed Proto-Germanic Wōðanaz, translated as "lord of frenzy" or "leader of the possessed", from an adjective meaning "possessed, inspired, delirious, raging". The root points to divine possession or inspiration and ecstatic divination. In the 11th century Adam of Bremen explicitly linked Wodan with the Latin furor, writing Wodan id est furor.

The Roman historian Tacitus, in his late 1st-century work Germania, recorded that among the gods the Suebi chiefly worshipped Mercury, to whom they offered human as well as other sacrificial victims. Through the interpretatio romana this is generally taken to refer to Odin, with Thor as "Hercules" and Týr as "Mars".

Old English royal genealogies record Woden as an ancestor of the kings of Lindsey, Mercia, Deira and Bernicia, and of Wessex and East Anglia, in seven of the eight genealogies. Only Essex traced its ancestry instead to Saxnot. Some genealogies give his father as Frealaf from the 8th century onward. The Welsh Historia Brittonum of the 9th century also places Woden in the pedigree of Hengist, with the ancestry "filii Frealaf, filii Fredulf, filii Finn, filii Fodepald, filii Geta", Geta being said to be the son of a god other than Yahweh. Other pedigrees reach further back through Geat, Beaw and Sceldi to Sceaf, who is the son of Noah from the Bible.

In such Old English texts the god is treated as a human ancestor of royalty, an approach scholars call euhemerism. Elsewhere in the Germanic world Odin was held to rule war and the dead, and he is depicted wielding a spear.

The modern English weekday Wednesday derives from Old English Wōdnesdæg, "day of Wōden". Cognates occur in Middle Low German and Middle Dutch Wōdensdach, modern Dutch woensdag, Old Frisian Wērnisdei and Old Norse Óðinsdagr, from which come Danish, Norwegian and Swedish onsdag. All derive from Late Proto-Germanic Wodanesdag, a calque of the Latin Mercurii dies, "day of Mercury", seen in Italian mercoledì and French mercredi.

Richard Wagner, in his opera cycle Der Ring des Nibelungen, called the god Wotan, a spelling of his own invention that combines the Old High German Wuotan with the Low German Wodan. Most forms of the modern religious movement Heathenry venerate him.
wolfenbuttel: Wolfenbüttel stands on the Oker river near its confluence with the Altenau, about 13 kilometres south of Brunswick and 60 kilometres south-east of Hannover. It lies roughly half-way between the Harz mountains in the south and the Lüneburg Heath in the north. It is the southernmost of 172 towns in northern Germany whose names end in büttel, meaning residence or settlement.

A first settlement, probably on a small islet in the Oker, was founded in the tenth century. It was mentioned in 1118 as Wulferisbuttle, when the Saxon count Widekind of Wolfenbüttel built a water castle on the trade route from Brunswick to Halberstadt and Leipzig. Henry the Lion destroyed it in 1191 and Duke Albert I of Brunswick-Lüneburg in 1255, and Albert took it from the House of Asseburg in 1258. The Welf duke Henry I of Brunswick rebuilt the castle from 1283. By 1432 the town was the permanent residence of the princes of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel.

The Schmalkaldic War devastated it in 1542, and Duke Julius rebuilt it in Renaissance style, with waterways laid out by Hans Vredeman de Vries. He granted the citizens market rights in 1570 and founded the Ducal Library two years later. Danish troops occupied the town in 1626 in the Thirty Years' War, and in June 1641 Swedish forces defeated the Austrians in the Battle of Wolfenbüttel but failed to occupy it. The composer Michael Praetorius was Kapellmeister there in 1604, and Leibniz and Lessing directed the library. The ducal court returned to Brunswick in 1753, and Wolfenbüttel declined in importance.

Wolfenbüttel has about 52,000 inhabitants and is the administrative capital of Wolfenbüttel District. It has the largest concentration of timber-framed buildings in Germany, around 1,000, largely undamaged by the war. The Herzog August Library, founded in 1572, holds about 10,000 manuscripts and is rich in Bibles, incunabula and books of the Reformation. It houses the Codex Carolinus and the Bible of Henry the Lion from 1170. The baroque Schloss Wolfenbüttel is now partly a museum, and the Jägermeister distillery has its headquarters in the town.
wolfgang-amadeus-mozart: Mozart was born on 27 January 1756 at Getreidegasse 9 in Salzburg, the capital of the Archbishopric of Salzburg, an ecclesiastical principality within the Holy Roman Empire. He was the youngest of seven children, five of whom died in infancy. His father, Leopold Mozart, a native of Augsburg, was a minor composer and an experienced teacher who became deputy Kapellmeister of the Salzburg orchestra in 1763. Mozart was trained on the harpsichord and also became skilled at violin, singing and dancing.

At five he was competent on keyboard and violin, had begun to compose and had performed before European royalty. His father took him on a grand tour of Europe and then three trips to Italy. A fruitless search for employment in 1777 to 1779 led through Paris, Mannheim and Munich and back to Salzburg. While visiting Vienna in 1781 his quarrels with his Salzburg employers came to a head and he was dismissed.

Mozart stayed in Vienna for the rest of his life, achieving fame and some financial success but no long-term security. His early Vienna years produced the opera Die Entführung aus dem Serail, the Great Mass in C minor and the Haydn Quartets. He composed more than a dozen piano concertos there. In 1783 he bought a fortepiano by Anton Walter, which he played often in the city's concerts, and which survives in Salzburg. He lived at the centre of the Viennese musical world and knew Joseph Haydn and some of the court of Emperor Joseph II.

In his final years he wrote the last three symphonies, ending with the Jupiter, the serenade Eine kleine Nachtmusik, the Clarinet Concerto, and the operas Le nozze di Figaro, Don Giovanni, Così fan tutte and Die Zauberflöte. Biographers rely on about 1500 pages of family letters, early biographies and surviving manuscripts, and they judge the publisher Friedrich Rochlitz untrustworthy, since he published false stories to increase sales.

Mozart died on 5 December 1791 at the age of 35, leaving the Requiem largely unfinished. Publishers soon sought a complete edition of his works. Breitkopf & Härtel and Johann Anton André negotiated with his widow Constanze, and the publication helped rescue her and her two children from poverty. Ludwig Ritter von Köchel completed the first catalogue in 1862, and his numbers, marked K or KV, remain the standard way to identify a work.

His music with Haydn's stands as an archetype of the Classical style, with clarity, balance and transparency as its hallmarks. He almost single-handedly developed the Classical piano concerto. Ludwig van Beethoven, fifteen years his junior, was deeply influenced by his work. Salzburg, which he left in frustration in 1781, has two museums in his former homes, the Salzburg Festival and the International Mozarteum Foundation.
wolfram-von-eschenbach: Little is known of Wolfram's life. No historical documents mention him, and his works are the sole evidence. In Parzival he speaks of wir Beier, meaning we Bavarians, and the dialect of his works is East Franconian. On this and on geographical references the present-day Wolframs-Eschenbach near Ansbach has been officially designated his birthplace, but the evidence is circumstantial, and at least four other places in Bavaria are named Eschenbach. His works point to several possible patrons, most reliably Hermann I of Thuringia, which suggests he served at a number of courts. He often alludes to his own poverty, and in Parzival he states that he is illiterate, a claim that some scholars treat with scepticism and many have credited.

He is best known for Parzival, sometimes regarded as the best of the German Arthurian romances. It is based on Chrétien de Troyes' unfinished Perceval, le Conte du Graal, and is the first surviving German work to treat the Holy Grail, which Wolfram presents as a gemstone. His narrator expresses disdain for Chrétien's version and names as his source a poet from Provence called Kyot.

He also wrote the fragmentary Titurel and the unfinished Willehalm, both after Parzival. Titurel mentions the death of Hermann I, which dates it after 1217, and tells of the lovers Schionatulander and Sigune. Willehalm, based on the Old French chanson de geste Aliscans, is set against wars between Christians and Saracens and survives in 78 manuscripts. His nine surviving songs, five of them dawn-songs, are regarded as masterpieces of Minnesang; no melodies survive.

The 84 surviving manuscripts of Parzival show its popularity over the next two centuries. Many manuscripts of Willehalm include a continuation written in the 1240s by Ulrich von Türheim, and around 1272 a poet named Albrecht, generally presumed to be Albrecht von Scharfenberg, expanded Titurel as the Jüngere Titurel. The modern rediscovery of Wolfram begins with Johann Jakob Bodmer's translation of Parzival in 1753. Richard Wagner drew on it for the libretto of Parsifal, and Wolfram appears as a character in Wagner's Tannhäuser.
wolgast: Wolgast lies in the district of Vorpommern-Greifswald, on the Peenestrom, facing the island of Usedom. A movable bascule bridge known as the Blaues Wunder gives access to the Baltic Sea by road and railway. The town was founded by the Wends on an island in the sound. On the mainland opposite the island with the castle a new planned town was built in the course of the Ostsiedlung, the German settlement eastwards.

The occupation of the region by Wartislaw I, Duke of Pomerania, led to the conversion of Pomerania by Otto of Bamberg in 1128, and thousands of Low German settlers came from Groningen and Drenthe. Wolgast became the seat of a Pomeranian castellany and played an important role in the 12th-century warfare between Pomeranians, Rani and Danes. A Danish-Rani fleet attacked it in 1162, and the Danes attacked again in 1167 and 1168. After a failed assault in 1177 and a campaign in 1179 in which the fleet accepted money instead of a surrender, it came under Danish control in 1185, when the Pomeranian duke accepted Danish suzerainty. It remained a Danish bridgehead after the Danes lost most of Pomerania in 1227.

The date of the German town law is not known, but a letter written in or before 1259 confirms the town, and Duke Bogislaw IV confirmed the Lübeck law in 1282. Wolgast was the capital of Pomerania-Wolgast, an inner partition of the duchy, and its castle was built as a Renaissance residential palace on what is called Castle Island. The ducal line of Pomerania-Wolgast became extinct when Philipp Julius died without issue.

Between the 1670s and the 1720s hundreds of men of the town enlisted in the VOC and emigrated to South Africa. Russian forces burned the town in 1713 during the Great Northern War, in retaliation for Swedish arson in Altona; only the church, four chapels and four other buildings were spared. After the Swedish withdrawal from Pomerania in 1815 the town passed to the Prussian Province of Pomerania, and the last remnants of the palace were removed in 1849. In the 19th century Wolgast prospered as a port for the grain trade.

Most houses of the Old Town date from the 18th and 19th centuries because of the fire of 1713. St Peter's Church, in brick Gothic, was inaugurated around 1415, and St Gertruden Chapel is a 15th-century Gothic building.
