The painter Philipp Otto Runge was born in the town, and his house is now a museum.
wolin: The town stands on the island of Wolin in the Baltic Sea, off the Polish coast. The Strait of Świna separates the island from Usedom, and the Strait of Dziwna from mainland Pomerania. It has an area of 265 square kilometres, its highest point is Mount Grzywacz at 116 metres, and its forests and postglacial hills surround the Wolin National Park. Its towns are Dziwnów, Międzyzdroje, Świnoujście and Wolin. The ford across the Dziwna on which Wolin lies has been used since the Stone Age.

Excavations show a settlement at the turn of the 5th and 6th centuries, which was then abandoned for about a century. At the end of the 8th or the beginning of the 9th century the ground was levelled and a new settlement built, with fortifications from the first half of the 9th century. The Bavarian Geographer, a mid-9th-century document, mentions the Slavic Wolinians with seventy strongholds, and Ibrahim ibn Jakub named the town Weltaba in 965. Around 896 a new port was built and the town received a palisade, a rampart and a retaining wall. Archaeologists believe it was a great trade emporium, stretching four kilometres along the shore and rivalling Birka and Hedeby.

In 967 the island came under Duke Mieszko I of Poland, whose influence ended around 1007. Wolin became known for pirates, and in 1043 the Norwegian king Magnus the Good attacked it. Boleslaw III Wrymouth captured it in the early 12th century, the inhabitants accepted Christianity, and in 1140 Pope Innocent II created a diocese there. In 1185 the dukes of Pomerania became vassals of Denmark, and in 1227 of the Holy Roman Empire. The island accepted Lutheranism in 1535, was captured by Sweden in 1630, passed to Prussia in 1720 and belonged to the German Empire from 1871. In 1945 it became part of Poland and its German-speaking population was expelled.

Some scholars have thought Wolin the basis for the semi-mythical Jomsborg and Vineta, while others, such as Gerard Labuda, reject the identification. Adam of Bremen called the town the largest in Europe, but excavations have found no harbour for the 360 warships he claimed. Its 20 hectares of finds make it the second largest Baltic marketplace of the Viking Age after Hedeby, and Slavs and Scandinavians lived there.

Wolin is the main tourist attraction of north-western Poland. Its sights include the Wolin National Park, the Gothic church of St Nicholas in Wolin, the Regional Museum, the Świnoujście Lighthouse, and the resort of Międzyzdroje. Each year the island hosts a large Germanic-Slavic Viking festival, and its protected traditional drink is the mead Trójniak woliński leśny.
womens-march-on-versailles: Fear of famine was ever present among the urban poor at the end of the Ancien Régime, and rumours of a Pacte de Famine to starve them were readily believed. After the storming of the Bastille, price inflation and severe shortages were common in Paris, and most workers spent nearly half their income on bread. Calls for a mass demonstration at Versailles had been made before, notably by the Marquis of Saint-Huruge in August. A banquet held on 1 October by the officers at Versailles for the newly arrived Flanders Regiment was reported in firebrand newspapers as a gluttonous orgy.

On the morning of 5 October a young woman struck a marching drum among market women in the Faubourg Saint-Antoine who were infuriated by the shortage and price of bread. More women joined from other markets, many with kitchen blades and makeshift weapons. At the Hôtel de Ville the crowd, perhaps as many as ten thousand, demanded bread and arms. Their aims widened to bringing the king, the court and the Assembly to Paris. They travelled to Versailles in about six hours, dragging cannons from the city hall.

At Versailles Maillard addressed the Assembly, and Maximilien Robespierre spoke in support of the women. A delegation of six women met Louis XVI, who promised food. At about six the next morning protesters found a small palace gate unguarded and entered. A guard was killed and beheaded, a second was struck down wounded, and at least one more was killed. Lafayette reconciled the former French Guards with the royal guards, and appeared with the king on a balcony, where the cry of Vive le Roi went up. He then brought out Marie Antoinette and kissed her hand.

At about one o'clock on 6 October the crowd, grown to over sixty thousand, escorted the royal family and a hundred deputies back to Paris, a journey of about nine hours, some marchers bearing pikes with the heads of the guards.

The royal family settled in the Tuileries Palace, where the king reportedly asked for a history of Charles I of England. The National Constituent Assembly followed within two weeks. Some fifty-six monarchien deputies stayed away, and many, like Jean Joseph Mounier, left the country. Suspicion fell on Louis Philippe II, Duke of Orléans, as an instigator, but an investigation proved nothing. Historians describe the march as a defining moment of the Revolution, which ended the king's independence and made no further open resistance by him possible.
woodrow-wilson: Thomas Woodrow Wilson was born on 28 December 1856 in Staunton, Virginia, the son of Joseph Ruggles Wilson, a Presbyterian pastor, and Jessie Janet Woodrow. Before he was two the family moved to Augusta, Georgia. After a PhD in history and political science at Johns Hopkins University he taught at Bryn Mawr College from 1885 to 1888, where his 1887 article The Study of Administration argued that public administration should be a field of study of its own. In June 1902 the trustees of Princeton University made him its president. He raised admission standards, introduced academic departments and groups of students guided by preceptors, and worked to keep African Americans out of the school. He served as governor of New Jersey from 1911 to 1913.

In the 1912 election Wilson defeated President William Howard Taft and the former president Theodore Roosevelt, and became the first Southerner elected president since Zachary Taylor. In April 1913 he addressed Congress in person to set out his New Freedom programme. Its early measures included the Revenue Act of 1913, which began the modern income tax, and the Federal Reserve Act. His administration intervened often in Latin America, sending troops to occupy the Dominican Republic and intervene in Haiti, and in his first year he authorised the widespread imposition of racial segregation in the federal bureaucracy.

The United States declared neutrality when the First World War began in 1914, and Wilson was narrowly re-elected in 1916 on the slogan He Kept Us Out of War. After Germany began unrestricted submarine warfare in January 1917 and the Zimmermann Telegram became public, he asked Congress in April 1917 for a declaration of war. He issued the Fourteen Points, which the Allies and Germany accepted as a basis for peace. He led the American delegation to the Paris Peace Conference, the first incumbent president to travel to Europe, and secured the League of Nations as part of the Treaty of Versailles. At home he rejected a Republican compromise that would have let the Senate ratify the treaty and join the League.

Wilson had a stroke in October 1919 that left him incapacitated, and his wife and his physician controlled access to him. Republicans won the 1920 election in a landslide. He died in February 1924 at the age of 67. Historians have criticised him for supporting racial segregation, while crediting his administration with the Federal Reserve, the Federal Trade Commission and the graduated income tax, and regarding him as a key figure in the making of modern American liberalism.
woody-guthrie: Woodrow Wilson Guthrie was born on 14 July 1912 in Okemah, a small town in Okfuskee County, Oklahoma. His parents, Nora Belle Sherman and Charles Edward Guthrie, named him after Woodrow Wilson, then Governor of New Jersey and the Democratic candidate who won the presidency that autumn. His father was a businessman who owned up to thirty plots of land in the county and stood as a Democratic candidate for local office. Guthrie left Okemah in 1929, after his mother, who suffered from Huntington's disease, was institutionalised, and followed his father to Pampa, Texas. He married Mary Jennings in 1933 and they had three children.

During the Dust Bowl, Guthrie left his wife and children in Texas and joined the thousands of migrants who went to California in search of work. In Los Angeles he became known on the radio station KFVD as a performer of hillbilly music and traditional folk music with his partner Maxine Crissman, known as Lefty Lou, and he began to write the protest songs of his later album. He befriended Will Geer and John Steinbeck and wrote a column for the communist newspaper People's World from May 1939 to January 1940. The station's owners were uncomfortable with his politics after he wrote a song praising the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, and he left for New York.

There the folk music community embraced him. He made several hours of recordings of conversation and song for the folklorist Alan Lomax at the Library of Congress, and recorded Dust Bowl Ballads for Victor Records. In February 1940 he wrote This Land Is Your Land in response to the overplaying of Irving Berlin's God Bless America. He took its melody from an old gospel song, and did not record it until April 1944. Throughout his life he was associated with communist groups, although there is no evidence that he was a member.

By the late 1940s Guthrie's health was declining and his behaviour was erratic. He received various diagnoses before it was determined in 1952 that he had Huntington's disease, inherited from his mother. He died of its complications at Creedmoor Psychiatric Center on 3 October 1967, and his remains were cremated and scattered at sea. In the folk revival of the late 1950s and 1960s a new generation took up his songs, among them Bob Dylan, who visited him in hospital. His son Arlo Guthrie became a musician. The Woody Guthrie Archives, the largest collection of his material, are held at the Woody Guthrie Center in Tulsa, Oklahoma.
worcestershire: Worcestershire is a largely rural ceremonial county of 1,741 km2 in the West Midlands of England. The River Severn flows through its centre from north to south across a wide plain, and the River Avon passes through Evesham. The Malvern Hills in the south-west hold Worcestershire Beacon, the county's highest point at 425 m, a small part of the Cotswolds lies in the south-east, and part of the Wyre Forest in the north-west. Besides Worcester, the main settlements are Kidderminster, Redditch, Bromsgrove, Evesham and the spa town of Malvern.

The area was first populated at least 700,000 years ago, became largely agricultural in the Bronze Age, and was dominated by hill forts in the Iron Age. In Roman times Droitwich, called Salinae, was probably the most important settlement because of its salt. The area became the heartland of the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of the Hwicce, was absorbed by Mercia during the 7th century, and was made a shire in the early tenth century to defend the estates of the See of Worcester and of abbeys such as Pershore, Westminster and Evesham. It became part of the unified Kingdom of England in 927.

The Domesday Book of 1086 recorded that in seven of the twelve hundreds the Crown had no authority, which was held by the bishop and abbots. In 1263 Worcester's Jewish residents were attacked by a baronial force and most were killed. Simon de Montfort was killed at the Battle of Evesham on 4 August 1265. In 1642 the Battle of Powick Bridge was the first major skirmish of the English Civil War, and the county, on the Royalist front line, suffered heavy taxation and the pressing of men. Clubmen bands formed to keep the war from their localities. The Battle of Worcester in 1651 was the last major engagement of the Wars of the Three Kingdoms.

In the 19th century Worcester made gloves and porcelain, Kidderminster carpets, and Redditch needles, springs and hooks, while Droitwich Spa produced salt, as it had since Roman times. Malvern became a spa town because its water was believed to be very pure. The county holds Berrow's Journal, founded in 1690 and said to be the world's oldest continually published newspaper. The composer Edward Elgar was born at Broadheath, and Tolkien wrote that any corner of the county was home to him. Its boundaries changed several times: in 1974 it was merged with Herefordshire, and it was re-created as a county on 1 April 1998.
world-health-organization: International cooperation on disease began with the International Sanitary Conferences, the first of which met in Paris on 23 June 1851 and which continued until 1938. The first was almost solely concerned with cholera. With the causes of epidemic diseases still disputed, agreement was hard to reach: seven conferences over 41 years were convened before any produced a multi-state agreement. The seventh, at Venice in 1892, finally resulted in a convention on the sanitary control of shipping through the Suez Canal, and in 1897 a convention on bubonic plague was signed by sixteen of the nineteen states attending.

The conferences led to the founding of the Pan-American Sanitary Bureau in 1902 and the Office International d'Hygiène Publique in 1907, and the League of Nations created its own Health Organization in 1920. After World War II, the United Nations assembled the health organizations to form the WHO. The World Health Organization was established on 7 April 1948 and began its work on 1 September 1948, taking over the assets and duties of the League's Health Organization and the Paris office, including the International Classification of Diseases.

The organisation is governed by the World Health Assembly, made up of its member states, which elects an executive board of 34 health specialists, selects the director-general and approves the budget. Its funds come mainly from member states, and then from private donors. The headquarters in Geneva was designed by the Swiss architect Jean Tschumi and inaugurated in 1966. Its regional divisions were created between 1949 and 1952, following the model of the Pan American Health Organization, and it has six regional offices and 150 country offices.

The organisation played a leading role in the eradication of smallpox, the near-eradication of polio and the development of an Ebola vaccine. It launched its Global Polio Eradication Initiative in 1988, working with Rotary International, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and UNICEF, and helped to reduce cases by 99%. In the 1970s it dropped its commitment to a global malaria eradication campaign as too ambitious. Since the late 20th century, new actors in global health such as the World Bank and the Gates Foundation have weakened its role as coordinator, and it also coordinated the international response to the COVID-19 pandemic.
world-trade-organization: The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade was set up by a multilateral treaty of 23 countries after World War II, alongside other new institutions for economic cooperation such as the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund. A proposed International Trade Organization never started, because the United States and other signatories did not ratify its treaty, so the GATT slowly became a de facto international organisation, operating for almost half a century as a provisional, semi-institutionalised treaty regime. Seven rounds of negotiation between 1949 and 1979 first cut tariffs. The Kennedy Round of the mid-sixties produced an anti-dumping agreement, and the Tokyo Round of the seventies made the first major attempt to tackle barriers that were not tariffs.

The eighth round, the Uruguay Round, was launched at Punta del Este in September 1986. It extended the system to services and intellectual property and reformed trade in agriculture and textiles. Its Final Act, the Marrakesh Agreement, was signed on 15 April 1994, and the WTO was established on 1 January 1995, with its headquarters in Geneva.

The WTO provides a framework for negotiating trade agreements and for settling disputes among its members. Its agreements cover goods, services and intellectual property, and rest on non-discrimination, expressed in the most-favoured-nation and national treatment provisions, with exceptions for purposes such as environmental protection and national security. Its highest body, the Ministerial Conference, usually meets every two years and decides by consensus. The General Council, made up of representatives of all members, handles day-to-day business, and a Secretariat led by a Director-General administers the organisation.

Unlike the GATT, whose rules were ambiguous and which let members block dispute settlement, the WTO has more numerous and more precise obligations, and members that do not comply may face punishment. Its consensus rule has also contributed to deadlock. Ministerial conferences have sometimes been contentious: the Seattle conference of 1999 provoked large demonstrations, and Doha in 2001 approved China's entry.

The Doha Development Round, launched in November 2001, aimed to make globalisation more inclusive and to cut barriers and subsidies in farming. Talks stalled over differences between developed nations and major low-income and lower-middle-income countries, and over agricultural subsidies in the European Union and the United States. The Hong Kong conference agreed to phase out agricultural export subsidies, and the Bali Ministerial Declaration of 2013 addressed bureaucratic barriers to commerce. Economic studies generally find that the WTO has boosted trade and reduced trade barriers. Critics argue that the benefits of free trade are not shared equally, that its agreements may disadvantage developing countries and that commercial interests have been put before environmental and labour concerns.
world-wide-web: Tim Berners-Lee was motivated by the problem of storing, updating and finding documents and data files in CERN, a large and constantly changing organisation, and of distributing them to collaborators outside it. In his design he rejected the tree structure used in the existing CERNDOC documentation system and in the Unix filesystem, as well as approaches that tagged files with keywords, as in the VAX/NOTES system. He adopted instead concepts he had put into practice in his private ENQUIRE system of 1980. Learning of Ted Nelson's hypertext model of 1965, in which documents are linked in unconstrained ways through hot spots embedded in the text, helped confirm that his concept was sound.

A competing system, Gopher, was created in 1991 around a hierarchical model of menus that held pointers to documents and to other menus, whereas a document on the Web holds both its content and its links. Gopher grew at first, with nearly seven thousand servers known by April 1994, but then declined while the Web accelerated. Its more rigid structure, bad early publicity and the decision not to follow open collaboration principles were among the reasons.

The Internet and the Web are not the same thing. The Internet is a global system of interconnected computer networks, while the Web is a collection of documents and other resources linked by hyperlinks and URLs and fetched with the Hypertext Transfer Protocol. The usual document is a web page written in Hypertext Markup Language, which supports text, images, audio, video and scripts as well as links. A browser requests a page from a web server, and in the 1990s following links from page to page came to be called browsing or web surfing.

The prefix www in many web addresses follows the old practice of naming a host after the service it provides, as ftp or news were. No standard requires it. According to Paolo Palazzi, who worked at CERN with Berners-Lee, its popular use was accidental: the project page was meant to sit at www.cern.ch, with info.cern.ch as CERN's home page, but the records were never switched, and others copied the practice. The first web server was nxoc01.cern.ch.

Links break as pages are moved or replaced, a phenomenon called link rot, and the Internet Archive, active since 1996, is the best known of many efforts to archive websites. Archie, an index of FTP files released in 1990, was the first search engine. In December 2007 Unicode passed ASCII and Western European encodings as the most used character map on the Web.
wroclaw: Wrocław lies on the banks of the Oder in the Silesian Lowlands, at an elevation of around 105 to 156 metres, and is supplied within the city limits by four tributaries: the Bystrzyca, Oława, Ślęza and Widawa. It is the capital of the Lower Silesian Voivodeship, created in 1999, and a major transport hub on routes between Western and Central Europe and the rest of Poland.

A place called Budorigum, at or near the site, appears on Claudius Ptolemy's map of 142 to 147 CE. The Ślężans, a West Slavic tribe, built a fortified gord on Ostrów Tumski. The city became part of the Piast-ruled Polish state in the late 10th century, and the Diocese of Wrocław was founded in 1000 under the Archbishopric of Gniezno. From the 13th century migration from German-speaking regions contributed to its growth, and German gradually became its predominant language. In the 14th century it passed to the Bohemian Crown.

The Reformation reached the city in 1518, but from 1526 Silesia was ruled by the Catholic House of Habsburg. During the Thirty Years' War the city lost thousands of inhabitants to plague. In 1811 the Viadrina university of Frankfurt an der Oder was moved to Breslau and united with the Jesuit university, forming what is now the University of Wrocław. It became part of the German Empire in 1871. In November 1939 the Germans imprisoned 173 Polish professors from Kraków's universities in the city before deporting them to Sachsenhausen. After 1945 it became part of Poland, and its German inhabitants who had not fled were expelled between 1945 and 1949.

Wrocław is the third-largest city of Poland and the historical capital of Silesia, with over 130,000 students. Its Market Square is one of the largest in Europe, and its Town Hall is the oldest preserved in Poland. The Centennial Hall is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the Old Town, with Brick Gothic and Baroque buildings, is on Poland's list of national monuments. The Wrocław Zoo is the oldest in Poland, and the city has been the seat of a Catholic archdiocese since the diocese of 1000.
wu-ding: Wu Ding, whose personal name was Zi Zhao, is the earliest figure in Chinese history mentioned in contemporary records. Later historians had thought the annals of the Shang dynasty little more than legend until oracle bone inscriptions from his reign were unearthed at his capital Yin, near modern Anyang, in 1899. They have been radiocarbon dated to 1254 to 1197 BCE, give or take ten years. The Shang practised succession by agnatic seniority, and before him succession had been split between two lines. His predecessors were three of his uncles, among them Pan Geng, who moved the capital to Huanbei, and then his father Xiao Yi. A tradition says he was sent away from the capital in his father's reign.

Sima Qian's Shiji lists him as the twenty-second Shang king, while the inscriptions record him as the twenty-first. Chapter XXI of the Book of Documents describes him staying silent at the start of his reign, even after three years of mourning, in order to cultivate his virtue. He first appointed his former tutor Gan Pan chief minister. After Gan Pan died, the chancellor was Fu Yue, whom he found, according to the Shiji and the Shangshu, after Heaven told him in a dream to expect such a man. His realm grew far larger than his ancestors', but control of distant lands was nominal, and he delegated power to regional lords who paid tribute, harvest portions and military support.

Oracle bones record wars with the fang peoples. According to the Bamboo Annals, in his thirty-second year he sent troops against the Guifang and after three years annexed them. A Shang force of up to thirteen thousand fought Ba under the command of Fu Hao, but Ba stayed independent. Women held greater official power than in later periods: his consort Fu Hao was a military commander, and Fu Jing seems to have overseen agriculture.

He died in the fifty-ninth year of his reign according to all sources, none of them contemporary. His year of death is unknown, with opinions ranging from 1197 to 1180 BCE and 1192 BCE commonly accepted. Tomb 1400 at Xibeigang is very likely his grave. Later tradition regarded him as one of the most esteemed Shang kings. Subsequent kings honoured him on the ding day, and he received the temple name Gaozong. His descendants addressed him as Grandfather Ding and Ancestor Ding. More than half of all Shang inscriptions date from his reign, and the earliest oracle bone script on tortoise plastrons and ox scapulae, with divination about war, human sacrifice and the economy, was unearthed at Yinxu.
wu-zetian: Wu Zetian was born in 624, and her personal name was Wu Zhao. Her birthplace is not documented, and scholars place it variously at Wenshui, at Lizhou in modern Sichuan, or at the capital Chang'an. She was first a concubine of Emperor Taizong, who gave her the art name Wu Mei, meaning glamorous. By early 650 she was a concubine of Emperor Gaozong, with the title Zhaoyi, the highest ranking of the nine concubines of the second rank. Gaozong was inexperienced and often incapacitated by dizzy spells, and he was named heir only because of the disgrace of his two older brothers.

In 655 Wu became Gaozong's empress consort, and in 656 the heir apparent Li Zhong was deposed in favour of her son Li Hong. In 657 she and her allies took reprisals against officials who had opposed her elevation: several chancellors were sent to remote prefectures, and in 659 Zhangsun Wuji was exiled and forced to commit suicide. After Gaozong suffered a debilitating stroke in 660 she effectively administered the empire for him until his death in 683, and she then became empress dowager and regent. Her third son, Li Zhe, took the throne in 684 as Zhongzong for about six weeks.

In 690 she had Emperor Ruizong yield the throne to her, proclaimed the Zhou dynasty and became emperor, and she is remembered as the only undisputed female sovereign in Chinese history. Her de facto rule lasted 45 years. She institutionalised the use of informants and enforced stringent legal measures, purged members of the Tang royal house and veteran officials of earlier administrations, and reformed the civil service to promote merit. She patronised Buddhism, literature and the arts and campaigned against Turkic and Tibetan incursions. Her rule formed part of the High Tang period, a peak in China's political power and cultural influence, though her later governance became increasingly autocratic and extravagant.

Wu was removed in the Shenlong Coup, which abolished the Zhou dynasty and restored the Tang, and she died on 16 December 705, a few months later. Traditional historians believed that she had killed her own children, but these rumours seem to have surfaced 400 years after her death and probably owed much to the belief that a woman was unfit to hold imperial power. Chinese writers call her Wu Hou as empress, and Wu Zetian, her posthumous title, is the name by which she is generally known.
wuchang-uprising: China's defeat by Japan in 1895 divided intellectuals. Reformers initiated the Hundred Days' Reform, which failed after the Wuxu Coup by Empress Dowager Cixi. Revolutionary groups emerged, and in 1905 leaders such as Sun Yat-sen and Song Jiaoren met in Tokyo and formed the Tongmenghui.

Unrest was heightened by a railway crisis. In 1910 the Qing court, short of money partly because of indemnity payments after the Boxer Protocol, adopted the policy of Sheng Xuanhuai to secure foreign loans by nationalising railway lines. Resistance, strongest in Sichuan, grew into the Sichuan Railway Protection Movement. In September 1911 the Viceroy of Sichuan arrested its leaders and ordered troops to fire on protesters, and troops were diverted to Sichuan from central China, which later helped the uprising to succeed.

In the Wuhan area two groups, the Wenxueshe led by Jiang Yiwu and the Gongjinhui led by Sun Wu, negotiated with the Tongmenghui from September 1911. The uprising planned for 6 October was postponed. On 9 October a bomb Sun Wu was preparing in the Russian concession at Hankou exploded and injured him. Hospital staff identified him and alerted the Qing authorities. The revolutionaries in the New Army at Wuchang faced arrest, and Jiang Yiwu decided to rise at once. The plot leaked to the Viceroy of Huguang, Ruicheng, who arrested and executed several members.

On the evening of 10 October Wu Zhaolin, as provisional commander, led the revolutionary soldiers in a mutiny against the Qing garrison. They captured the viceroy's residence and strategic points after intense fighting, and Ruicheng fled. On 11 October the mutineers set up a Hubei military government and persuaded the officer Li Yuanhong to head it. On 12 October they took Hankou and Hanyang. The Qing court called on Yuan Shikai and the Beiyang Army, who retook Hankou on 1 November and Hanyang on 27 November before Yuan began to negotiate secretly with the revolutionaries.

The uprising surprised many revolutionary leaders. Sun Yat-sen was in the United States seeking funds and learned of it from a newspaper. By the end of December 1911 eighteen provinces had agreed to secede from the Qing. Sun returned and was elected provisional president. On 1 January 1912 representatives declared the Republic of China, and he was sworn in. After negotiations with Yuan Shikai, Empress Dowager Longyu announced the abdication of the child emperor Puyi on 12 February 1912, which ended the Qing dynasty after almost three centuries. Taiwan commemorates 10 October as the National Day of the Republic of China.
wuhan: Wuhan lies in east-central Hubei, on the eastern Jianghan Plain, where the Han River flows into the Yangtze. The two rivers divide the urban area into three districts, Wuchang, Hankou and Hanyang, known together as the Three Towns of Wuhan. The name joins Wu, for Wuchang, and Han, for Hankou, whose name means Mouth of the Han. The city has long been called the Nine Provinces' Thoroughfare, and its position has also exposed it to flooding.

The Wuhan area has been settled for about 3,500 years. Panlongcheng, an archaeological site associated mainly with the Erligang culture, lies in Huangpi District. In the Han dynasty Hanyang became a fairly busy port, and walls were built to protect Hanyang in 206 and Wuchang in 223, the latter marking the foundation of Wuhan. In 223 Sun Quan, leader of the Eastern Wu, ordered the Yellow Crane Tower built on the Wuchang side, one of the Four Great Towers of China.

On 10 October 1911 the Wuchang Uprising, launched by followers of Sun Yat-sen, led to the collapse of the Qing state, ending 2,000 years of dynastic rule. In 1927 the Kuomintang government moved its capital from Guangzhou to Wuhan and combined Wuchang, Hankou and Hanyang into Wuhan City. Wuhan was briefly a capital again in 1937, as a provisional wartime capital, and in 1938, during the Second Sino-Japanese War, it was the site of the Battle of Wuhan. After 1949 the Communists rebuilt its war-damaged industry, and Wuhan Iron and Steel opened in 1958.

Wuhan is the capital of Hubei and the largest city in the province. It is a major transport hub and the centre of Central China, with institutions such as Wuhan University and the Huazhong University of Science and Technology.
wurzburg: Würzburg is the second-largest city in Franconia after Nuremberg and spans both banks of the Main river. A Bronze Age refuge castle, the Celtic Segodunum and later a Roman fort stood on the Leistenberg, where Fortress Marienberg now stands. Alamanni settled the area in the 4th or 5th century and Franks followed in the 6th and 7th. A Merovingian duke had his seat there from about 650, and Irish missionaries including Kilian Christianized it in 686. A donation of 1 May 704 mentions the place as Virteburch.

The bishops of Würzburg built a secular lordship that reached into Eastern Franconia in the 12th century, and the Prince-Bishopric of Würzburg is dated 1168 to 1803. The city hosted several Imperial Diets, including that of 1180, which banned Henry the Lion. Charlemagne consecrated a first church on the cathedral's site in 788, and the present Romanesque cathedral was built from 1040 to 1225. The University of Würzburg was founded in 1402 and re-founded in 1582 by Julius Echter von Mespelbrunn. In 1400 the bishop's troops defeated the citizens at the Battle of Bergtheim, and the city stayed under his control. Jews were massacred in 1147 and 1298.

In the Peasants' War, about 8,000 peasants were killed outside the city on 4 June 1525. The council member Tilman Riemenschneider refused to fight them and was imprisoned and tortured at Marienberg with the entire council. Between 1626 and 1631, under Bishop Philip Adolf, an estimated 600 to 900 alleged witches were burnt, until King Gustaf Adolf of Sweden invaded. The Residence was begun in 1720. The city passed to Bavaria in 1803, became a grand duchy in 1805 and joined the Kingdom of Bavaria in 1814. In 1817 Friedrich Koenig and Andreas Bauer founded a maker of steam-driven printing presses there.

On 16 March 1945 about 90 per cent of the city was destroyed in 17 minutes by 225 British Lancaster bombers, and a firestorm killed some 5,000 people. Over the next twenty years the historic buildings were carefully reconstructed, at first largely by the women known as Trümmerfrauen. About 130,000 people live in the city, whose dialect is East Franconian. Its rebuilt old town and the Würzburger Residenz are cultural heritage, the Residence being a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
wurzburg-residence: The Prince-Bishops of Würzburg lived in the Marienberg Fortress until the early 18th century. Johann Philipp Franz von Schönborn (1719–1724) moved the court to a palace built in 1701–1704, but thought it too small for an absolute monarch and wanted something comparable to Versailles or Schönbrunn. He financed a new building with 600,000 florins won in a court case in the year of his accession, and was supported by his uncle Lothar Franz von Schönborn, Archbishop of Mainz, and his brother Friedrich Carl von Schönborn, Imperial Vice-Chancellor in Vienna. The foundation stone was laid on 22 May 1720, and building began with the north block.

Balthasar Neumann, court architect of the Bishop, was the principal architect, working with Johann Lukas von Hildebrandt and Maximilian von Welsch and with Robert de Cotte and Germain Boffrand. Building stopped under Prince-Bishop Christoph Franz von Hutten once the north block was finished, and resumed in 1730 under Friedrich Carl von Schönborn. The whole shell was complete in December 1744. The Residence stands on a base of 92 by 167 metres, has almost 400 rooms and cost over 1.5 million guilders, at a time when a day labourer earned about one guilder a week.

Neumann built the staircase in 1737. It spans an area of 18 by 32 metres without pillars, beneath a vault 23 metres high. Giovanni Battista Tiepolo, assisted by his sons, above all Giovanni Domenico, painted the ceiling above it between 1752 and 1753, the largest continuous ceiling fresco in the world at about 580 square metres. He also decorated the Imperial Hall. Neumann died in 1753.

Napoleon reportedly called the building the largest parsonage in Europe. He slept there on three visits between 1806 and 1813, and signed the declaration of war against Prussia there on 2 October 1806. The prince-bishopric was abolished in 1802–03, and the Residence was opened to the public in 1921. A British air raid on 16 March 1945 burnt it almost completely out; only the central building survived, without its roofs, and Neumann's stone vaults withstood the fire. Much furniture and panelling had been removed in time. Reconstruction lasted from 1945 to 1987 and cost about €20m. The Residence, with its Court Gardens and Residence Square, was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1981.
wurzen: Wurzen stands beside the river Mulde, which is crossed there by two bridges, 25 km east of Leipzig on the railway line to Riesa and Dresden. The town lies on the central German route of the pilgrim way to Santiago de Compostela, which follows the Via Regia, a designated Cultural Route of the Council of Europe.

Slavs founded Wurzen after 600. It is first mentioned in a donation of Otto I in 961 as a Burgward, civitas vurcine, in the Gau Neletici. Early in the twelfth century it was a town, and Herwig, bishop of Meissen, founded a collegiate church there. The castle was occasionally the residence of the bishop from 1497 to 1581, the year the town passed to the elector of Saxony. In 1637, during the Thirty Years' War, the Swedish army sacked Wurzen and burned it almost completely down.

In 1768 Goethe travelled through the town between Leipzig and Dresden, and the long wait for the ferry later inspired a passage in his first edition of Faust. On 31 July 1838 Wurzen was connected to the Leipzig-Dresden line, the first German long-distance railway, opened on 7 April 1839, and the first German railway bridge was built across the Mulde. American air raids between October 1943 and April 1945 killed over 40 people. On 24 April 1945 the mayor, Armin Graebert, together with members of the SPD and KPD and the pastors of the Protestant and Catholic churches, secured the surrender of the town to the 273rd US Infantry Regiment and saved it from destruction.

The collegiate church of St. Marien, consecrated in 1114, is Romanesque to late Gothic, with bronze sculptures by Georg Wrba of 1932. The late Gothic castle also survives. The writer and painter Joachim Ringelnatz was born in Wurzen, and the town styles itself Ringelnatz City; the fabulist Magnus Gottfried Lichtwer was also born there. The main commercial focus is the making of pastries and candies.
